papers.title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure
papers.abstract:
How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. We present a teacher-student segmentation pipeline designed to meet exactly this constraint: label-free at inference, running on a recording device, and requiring no per-session calibration. The pipeline chains a lightweight voice activity detector, compactly pretrained speaker embeddings, agglomerative clustering, and a small logistic regression that assigns the teacher role based on session-relative structure rather than voice identity. We show that our structural cue transfers across classrooms, languages, and acoustic conditions.
  In leave-one-teacher-out cross-validation on 292 recordings from 63 teachers across English and German corpora, our pipeline achieves teacher F1 of 0.81 and 0.87, respectively, outperforming both enrollment-based baselines and a 30-second supervised enrollment ceiling. On a commodity smartphone, its performance matches pyannote, a strong neural diarization tool, while running 4.8x faster at comparable peak memory at a real-time factor of ~0.18. We also find that transcribing filtered audio only marginally increases teacher's word error rate from $0.26$ to 0.28. Residual failures concentrate where teacher and student voices are not acoustically separable. However, we show how to flag these sessions label-free at inference so that they can be routed to human review, enabling selective, privacy-preserving deployment.

papers.intro:
How much a teacher talks, and when, provides informative but costly-to-measure signals of teaching (Tao and Chen 2024). Distinguishing teacher from student speech enables analyses of talk-time balance, turn-taking, and instructional dialogue, but still requires intensive human annotation (Wang et al. 2025; Kelly et al. 2018; Donnelly et al. 2017). Automating this distinction supports scalable feedback and downstream analyses of classroom discourse and student engagement (Schlotterbeck et al. 2021; Hou et al. 2025).

Automating this distinction supports scalable feedback and downstream analyses of classroom discourse and student engagement (Schlotterbeck et al. 2021; Hou et al. 2025).

Speaker diarization identifies who spoke when (Anguera et al. 2012; Park et al. 2022), but classroom deployment adds two requirements. First, a deployed system meets a new, unknown teacher in every session, and it must identify the teacher in unseen classrooms without enrollment audio or speaker-specific fine-tuning. Second, recordings are among the most sensitive data because they involve minors and sensitive interactions. In our intended downstream workflow, teacher speech must leave the device for further processing, making it necessary to identify and filter teacher segments locally before transmission. This motivates local processing without transferring raw audio or retaining reference voiceprints (Sümer et al. 2020; Granqvist et al. 2020). Together, these constraints rule out the commonly used large, cloud-based GPU neural diarization pipelines with enrollment and demand a label-free, CPU-based inference system.

We present such a system. Our pipeline combines lightweight voice activity detection (Silero Team 2024), compact pretrained speaker embeddings (Wang et al. 2023), and agglomerative clustering with a small logistic regression that assigns teacher/student roles using session-relative features. The strongest cue we consider is centrality: the cosine similarity between speech segments in a lesson and a lesson’s mean embedding. When the teacher is a recurrent, acoustically coherent voice in a classroom, this mean provides an in-session reference for recovering the teacher across fragmented segments. The role classifier is trained on annotated recordings; inference uses only audio and the frozen models.

papers.title: Efficient Spectra and Dynamics with Tangent-Space Chebyshev Tree Tensor Networks
papers.abstract: We present a tangent-space Chebyshev method (TaChe), which combines tree tensor network states with Chebyshev recursion and maximum entropy spectral analysis in a tree tensor network tangent space, for quantum many-body spectra and dynamics. Implemented tensor network state calculations in the tangent space of the ground state, the core advantage of TaChe is that it can substantially reduce the computational complexity, memory usage, and numerical instability associated with tensor network state compression. Implemented on the GPU platform, it produces accurate spectra with speedups of up to $46.8$ over the previous Chebyshev tensor network method and $13.7$ over one-site time-dependent variational principle propagation in the reported benchmarks. Applications to acetonitrile, thermal aggregate emission, finite-temperature charge transport on a \(6\times6\) lattice, and internal conversion in aggregates of up to 100 molecules demonstrate the efficiency and versatility of TaChe in simulating complex molecular systems.

papers.intro:
Quantum many-body spectra and dynamical correlation functions connect quantum states to experimentally accessible observables. Their accurate calculation remains a central challenge in quantum chemistry, owing to the exponential growth of the many-body Hilbert space with system size. Tensor-network states exploit the entanglement structure of these states to reduce the cost of the many-body representation. Matrix product states (MPS), tree tensor network states (TTNS), and their associated density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) algorithms have consequently become useful tools for electronic structure and molecular quantum dynamics White (1992); Schollwöck (2011); Chan and Sharma (2011); Chan et al. (2016); Nakatani and Chan (2013); Baiardi and Reiher (2020).

(2016); Nakatani and Chan (2013); Baiardi and Reiher (2020).

A common approach to computing spectra is to propagate a quantum state in real time and Fourier transform the resulting time-correlation function. Time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) methods, including those based on the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP), have demonstrated broad applicability to electronic, vibrational, and vibronic Hamiltonians White and Feiguin (2004); Daley et al. (2004); Haegeman et al. (2011); Haegeman et al. (2016); Paeckel et al. (2019); Ronca et al. (2017); Ren et al. (2018); Baiardi and Reiher (2019); Baiardi (2021). However, accurate characterization of long-time dynamics and high-resolution spectral features remains computationally demanding. Frequency-domain methods address the same function through correction vectors, Krylov subspaces, or polynomial expansions Jeckelmann (2002); Dargel et al. (2012); Jiang et al. (2020); Lee et al. (2023). Chebyshev expansions are particularly useful because a single sequence of moments can determine both spectral functions and time orrelations Weiße et al. (2006); Holzner et al. (2011); Wolf et al. (2014); Wolf et al. (2015). Re-orthogonalized Chebyshev methods further use the generated tensor-network vectors to construct a reduced Hamiltonian for spectral reconstruction Xie et al. (2018); Jiang et al. (2021).

In conventional tensor-network implementations, repeated Hamiltonian applications increase the bond dimension, necessitating compression after each iteration to maintain a manageable representation. This compression, often performed through singular-value decompositions or variational optimization sweeps, can become a major computational bottleneck. Moreover, truncation errors disrupt the recurrence relations of iterative eigensolvers, therefore often requiring reorthogonalization or restarting, which further increases computational and memory costs Jiang et al. (2020); Wang et al. (2026); Xie et al. (2018). Tangent-space methods offer an alternative by representing variations in a linear space around a tensor-network reference, allowing the projected Hamiltonian to act directly on tangent-space coefficients without repeated compression. This framework underlies variational excitation methods, TDVP, and DMRG linear-response approaches Haegeman et al. (2011); Haegeman et al. (2012); Haegeman et al. (2013); Wouters et al. (2013); Dorando et al. (2009); Nakatani et al. (2014), and was further developed through the orthogonal projector formalism of Gleis, Li, and von Delft Gleis et al. (2022). More recently, tangent-space Krylov (TaSK) calculations exploited this strategy to compute MPS spectral functions using Lanczos iteration Kovalska et al. (2026). These advances are particularly attractive for tree tensor network states (TTNS), where the branching structure makes conventional variational compression more expensive than in MPS.

Here, we introduce the tangent-space Chebyshev method (TaChe) and formulate it within the TTNS representation. Unlike Lanczos methods used in TaSK, Chebyshev recursion is numerically more stable and does not suffer from the accumulation of roundoff errors, thereby eliminating the need for computationally expensive reorthogonalization procedures Silver and Röder (1997). Tree tensor networks allow strongly coupled degrees of freedom to be grouped into branches, naturally accommodating the molecular and vibrational structure of quantum-chemical Hamiltonians Nakatani and Chan (2013); Gunst et al. (2018); Larsson (2019). We construct both one-site and two-site tangent spaces and employ their projected Hamiltonians to generate scalar Chebyshev moments. By exploiting moment doubling, two Chebyshev moments are obtained per Hamiltonian application, while the three-term recurrence requires only a fixed number of tangent-vector buffers. Combined with GPU-accelerated tensor contractions and the reuse of reference environments, this approach avoids repeated tensor-network compression and reduces both computational overhead and memory requirements for spectral calculations.

papers.title: NOTREKS: Marginal Independence in Score-based Structure Learning
papers.abstract: Score-based structure learning estimates causal graphs by optimizing a data-dependent objective over structural equation models. We study how prior knowledge that selected pairs of variables are marginally independent can be incorporated into such causal discovery methods. Under faithfulness, marginally independent pairs cannot be connected by a trek, so the knowledge becomes a graphical no-trek constraint, which we call NOTREKS information. We introduce a power-series trek (PSTrek) penalty for gradient-based optimization and a trek constraint for order-based search, and we analyze why such information helps in finite samples and how it restricts the search space. Our numerical experiments illustrate to what extent NOTREKS information helps in causal discovery. In particular, using synthetic benchmarks with oracle NOTREKS information, we show that these constraints can improve both structural recovery and adjustment-based effect identification.

papers.title: Keeping Shielded Data-Driven Controllers Safe Under System Evolution via Model Consistency
papers.abstract: Cyber-physical systems (CPS) increasingly contain data-driven controllers, which raise safety concerns given their black-box nature. A common mitigation is to enforce system safety via a shield around the controller, which restricts the inputs based on assumptions about the physical system. However, these assumptions are usually fixed and may become invalid as the system evolves (during development or due to component degradation), possibly leading to unsafe behavior. We address this limitation in a model-driven approach that treats both the data-driven controller and safety shield as first-class models that are integrated into a virtual single underlying model (V-SUM) alongside system models. We describe system evolution as changes in the associated models, such that consistency checking yields a continuous assessment of safety guarantees. In case of inconsistencies, consistency-preservation rules automatically update the models and restore a valid safety shield. We evaluate our approach on a reach-avoid task for a unicycle system. The results show that consistency-driven evolution effectively maintains safety guarantees under system changes and provides a principled basis for evaluating and restoring performance.

papers.intro:
With the rising capabilities of machine learning, data-driven controllers, such as deep RL (RL) agents, are increasingly considered for complex control tasks in CPS Kiran et al., 2022. However, their black-box nature does not provide any guarantees on their behavior, which makes them unsuitable for safety-critical applications Alshiekh et al., 2018. Safety shields have been proposed to address this limitation Kasaura et al., 2023; Krasowski et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2025, by overriding unsafe actions of the controller at runtime based on a formal safety specification.

With the rising capabilities of machine learning, data-driven controllers, such as deep RL (RL) agents, are increasingly considered for complex control tasks in CPS Kiran et al., 2022. However, their black-box nature does not provide any guarantees on their behavior, which makes them unsuitable for safety-critical applications Alshiekh et al., 2018. Safety shields have been proposed to address this limitation Kasaura et al., 2023; Krasowski et al., 2023; Feng et al., 2025, by overriding unsafe actions of the controller at runtime based on a formal safety specification.

Figure 1 illustrates an example of the setting considered in this paper. An autonomous vehicle approaches a construction site. The learned controller proposes a steering command that would lead to a collision. Before execution, a safety shield corrects the proposed action. The main challenge is that the shield itself relies on assumptions about the physical system, such as braking capability or tire friction. These assumptions may change during system evolution, e.g., redesign or natural wear, causing the shield to become invalid. Similarly, the learned controller was trained under the original dynamics, and its performance may degrade when they shift Filos et al., 2020.

The main challenge is that the shield itself relies on assumptions about the physical system, such as braking capability or tire friction. These assumptions may change during system evolution, e.g., redesign or natural wear, causing the shield to become invalid. Similarly, the learned controller was trained under the original dynamics, and its performance may degrade when they shift Filos et al., 2020.

Both components can be hardened against such changes individually. For the shield, robust safety filters account for bounded disturbances and model uncertainty Jankovic, 2018. However, the bounds must be tight to avoid overly conservative behavior, hence they cannot account for large changes to the system. On the controller side, RL methods for non-stationary environments either train policies to be robust against a range of dynamics Moos et al., 2022 or adapt them to the change Padakandla, 2021. In both cases, the components remain isolated from the system models, so a known change to the system is not traced to the shield and controller that depend on it.

Tracing such changes across models is the goal of multi-model consistency management. Consistency is a weak form of correctness of the CPS, i.e., the overlapping system models are free of contradictions and are thus jointly realizable Spanoudakis & Zisman, 2001. Model-driven engineering approaches preserve consistency by relating models through explicit correspondences and propagating changes between them automatically Klare & Gleitze, 2019. We build upon Vitruvius Klare et al., 2021, which realizes this through the notion of consistency relations and preservation rules across heterogeneous models. These approaches require structurally and semantically well-defined models Knapp & Mossakowski, 2018. A safety shield can be defined this way, but the semantics of a learned controller are only observable through its behavior. Behavioral notions of consistency based on observable properties relax this requirement Färber et al., 2026, but do not explicitly address black-box models.

To ensure consistency of data-driven controllers, we treat both the safety shield and the learned controller as first-class models within a multi-model consistency framework. For the safety shield, consistency captures the validity of the underlying assumptions on the system and for learned controllers, consistency must be defined at the behavioral level. Thus, we distinguish mandatory safety consistency for the safety shield and behavioral consistency for the data-driven controller. We make the following contributions: (1) We extend multi-model consistency to learning-enabled CPS by treating the safety shield and the data-driven controller as individual first-class models; (2) We define safety consistency relations for safety shields, and behavioral consistency relations for learned controllers; (3) We propose corresponding consistency preservation rules to restore consistency under system evolution; (4) We demonstrate the approach on a reach-avoid task with unicycle dynamics controlled by an RL agent.

papers.title: Cwikel and Kato-Seiler-Simon estimates for commutators
papers.abstract:
We prove that the commutator $[a(X),b(-\mathrm{i}
abla)]$ belongs to the weak Schatten class $\mathcal{S}^p_{m weak}$ provided $
abla a\in L^p$ and $
abla b\in L^p_{m weak}$ for $\max\{1,2d/(d+2)\}<p<\infty$. This is an analogue of Cwikel's estimate, with a larger range of exponents. We also prove analogues of the Kato-Seiler-Simon and Birman-Solomyak-Simon estimates. Counterexamples show the necessity of the lower thresholds and the failure of the Lipschitz endpoint estimate.

papers.title: A Lions lift framework for gradient and Newtonian evolutions in Wasserstein spaces
papers.abstract: To analyze evolutions driven by functionals over the space of probability measures, one can opt for the extrinsic Lions lift approach or the intrinsic Wasserstein viewpoint with its abstract metric structure. While the latter has been a successful playground for the study of first-order gradient flows, it classically relies on $\lambda$-convexity, and has eluded attempts of extensions to second-order Newtonian-like dynamics. Motivated by these obstructions, we show that the extrinsic Lions lift has the full capabilities to carry out the first-order gradient-flow program, which is classically done intrinsically in the Wasserstein space. As illustrated in an example, this paves the way for a framework of gradient evolutions beyond the $\lambda$-convex case, which is classically demanded for energies in the Wasserstein space. Furthermore, our interpretation of the Lions lift enables the formulation of a notion of second-order Newtonian curves in the Wasserstein phase space. Such curves can be constructed through a second-order JKO-like scheme and, when applied to linear and interacting energies, naturally lead to Vlasov kinetic equations and existence of solutions thereof.

papers.title: What Survival Benchmarks Don't Tell You: Impact of Model Selection and Dataset Regimes
papers.abstract: Despite the proliferation of survival analysis methods, current benchmarks often operate under narrow conditions: they heavily rely on the concordance index (C-index) for evaluation and model selection, and frequently either exclude deep learning (DL) methods or underrepresent challenging dataset regimes. To address these limitations, we conduct a large-scale, neutral benchmark comparing 10 classical, tree-based, and DL methods across 49 diverse datasets. Crucially, we treat the model selection criterion (optimizing for C-index, Integrated Brier Score (IBS), or Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO)) as an independent experimental variable. Using Bayesian mixed-effects modeling, we demonstrate that evaluation design heavily dictates conclusions. For complex DL and tree-based architectures, selecting hyperparameters to optimize for IBS instead of C-index yields substantial improvements in probabilistic accuracy and calibration at a negligible cost to discriminative ranking. Furthermore, method performance (C-index, IBS, MAE-PO, and X-CAL) is fundamentally governed by dataset characteristics. While DL models scale exceptionally well with larger sample sizes, they suffer notable performance drops in high-dimensional feature spaces. Additionally, we expose a structural vulnerability where heavy censoring artificially inflates absolute calibration metrics, creating overly conservative tests. Ultimately, our findings challenge the utility of global single-number performance summaries and advocate for survival analysis results that transparently report the evaluation setup. Our code is available at: https://github.com/sdening/surv-bench-study

papers.intro:
The Cox proportional hazards model (Cox, 1972) has been a cornerstone method of survival analysis (time-to-event modeling) for over fifty years. While regularized extensions of it such as CoxNet (Simon et al., 2011) remain competitive today, the methodological landscape has rapidly expanded with, for instance, tree-based ensembles (e.g., (Ishwaran et al., 2008; Alberge et al., 2025)) and a recent wave of deep survival models (e.g., (Katzman et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Kvamme et al., 2019; Wang and Sun, 2022; Knottenbelt et al., 2025; Wiegrebe et al., 2024)). Yet, the evaluation practices used to compare these methods have not kept pace. Results are typically summarized through average ranks, winner counts on Harrell’s concordance index (Harrell et al., 1982) (or variants of it such as those by Antolini et al. (2005) and Uno et al. (2011); for ease of exposition, throughout the paper we abbreviate these collectively simply as the “C-index”, specifying a particular variant as needed) or mean metric values across datasets—a compression that obscures crucial method-level variation. This paper investigates what this standard evaluation process misses, demonstrating that the field has underestimated the nuances of model performance across different dataset regimes and especially across different model selection criteria.

Current neutral benchmarks for survival analysis generally converge on a stable consensus: no modern method consistently outperforms classical Cox-based methods (Chien et al., 2024; Burk et al., 2026; Herrmann et al., 2020; Birolo et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2022). However, this conclusion is drawn under evaluation conditions that leave large areas of the methodological space unexamined. As highlighted by Lillelund et al. (2026), survival analysis model evaluations overwhelmingly rely on the C-index, neglecting probabilistic accuracy, time-to-event accuracy, and calibration. Crucially, the model selection strategy (e.g., the choice of evaluation metric driving hyperparameter and checkpoint selection) is almost never varied. Papers introducing new models frequently select hyperparameters based on the C-index without exploring how other hyperparameter selection strategies might have performed (e.g., (Katzman et al., 2018; Lee et al., 2018; Kim et al., 2026)). Taken together, the conclusion that Cox remains competitive may hold under these narrow conditions, including datasets of small sample and feature size, but it has not been robustly tested in regimes where alternatives could plausibly excel.

A The Evaluation vs. Optimization Gap: Moving Beyond C-index Selection A.1 What Drives Performance Depends on the Metric: C-index typically varies little between methods within a dataset, but much more across datasets. Other metrics tell a different story: Probabilistic accuracy (IBS) and calibration (X-CAL), in contrary to C-index, show significant sensitivity to optimization and algorithmic choice. A.2 The Benefits of Proper Scoring Rules as Model Selection Criteria: Relying solely on the C-index for hyperparameter selection fails to regularize the predictive distributions of complex deep learning and tree-based methods. Shifting model selection to optimize a proper scoring rule like the Integrated Brier Score (IBS) yields significant gains in probabilistic accuracy and calibration, without significantly altering the model’s discriminative ranking. A.3 Time-to-event Accuracy Requires Direct Optimization: When models are tuned by optimizing C-index or IBS, their ability to improve Mean Absolute Error (MAE-PO) over a simple Kaplan-Meier (KM) baseline (Kaplan and Meier, 1958) is essentially a coin flip (50%). By instead tuning models to optimize MAE-PO, the models we benchmark outperform the KM baseline 72% of the time while reducing extreme temporal prediction outliers.

papers.title: Chebyshev Polynomial Zonotope Abstractions for Certified Reachability of Learning-Enabled Systems
papers.abstract: Nearly all current methods for computing reachable sets of nonlinear dynamics propagate them with truncated Taylor expansions plus rigorous remainders. The expansion is pointwise: once its argument is a whole set rather than a point, one polynomial must stay accurate across that set, and it reaches only as far as its disc of convergence. The limit binds hardest on the rational terms and sigmoid gates of modern controllers: smooth as these look on the real line, in the complex plane they blow up at points just off the real axis, closer as a gate sharpens, and those points cap the set width a Taylor expansion can cover, most tightly on the switching surface where the controller decides. We prove a dichotomy: no Taylor degree certifies sets wider than that cap, while a Chebyshev abstraction of equal degree, anchored to the whole set in the same polynomial-zonotope pipeline, has no cap and gains width at a geometric rate in degree. Measured walls match the formulas to between 89 and 94 percent. We give closed-form rigorous remainders, among them the first polynomial softmax transformer; existing sound treatments are linear relaxations. On closed loops, certificates survive where the Taylor ones diverge, and specifications flip from unknown to proven; on trained classifiers up to real MNIST digits, the Chebyshev frontier certifies input territory the Taylor basis surrenders. Every certified claim passed large Monte-Carlo harnesses with zero violations, and an applicability map states in advance where the basis provably cannot matter.
papers.intro:
Set-based reachability analysis asks whether all trajectories from a set of initial states satisfy a specification, which no finite batch of simulations can establish. The mature tools answer the question in the same way. Flow* [1], CAPD [2] and JuliaReach [3] propagate Taylor-model flowpipes; CORA polynomializes conservatively over (sparse) polynomial zonotopes [4, 5]; POLAR pushes polynomial arithmetic through neural-network loops [6]. In every case, the nonlinear functions on the current enclosure are replaced by a truncated Taylor expansion plus a rigorous remainder, and every tool that entered the ARCH-COMP nonlinear category in the last five years is Taylor-based [7].

The default is easy to defend. A truncated Taylor series is the best possible local model: exact to order NN at its expansion point, and unbeatable over a narrow enclosure. The mismatch appears when the enclosure is wide, because set propagation asks one polynomial to be accurate uniformly across the whole set, a different approximation problem from accuracy at a point, and one that a pointwise expansion answers only inside its disc of convergence. A Chebyshev expansion is anchored to the whole set instead of to its center, which is exactly the request set propagation makes. This paper is about the class of functions where that mismatch bites hardest, and about how little it costs to fix it. The class covers the rational expressions of vehicle and orbital dynamics (1/(1+x2)1/(1+x^{2})-type damping, μ/r3\mu/r^{3} gravity) and, more importantly for modern control, the gates, meaning the sigmoid and softmax nonlinearities that blend controller modes in gain scheduling [8], mixture-of-experts policies [9], and smooth approximations of switching logic. What all of these have in common is complex poles close to the real axis; for a gate, the pole distance shrinks in proportion to its sharpness.

papers.title: HydroMind: A Checkable Agent for Autonomous Hydrological Research
papers.abstract: General-purpose coding agents have written code for hydrological and Earth-system models. In these studies the researchers decided in advance how the model would be evaluated, for example the test period, the scoring function, and the standard the model had to meet. No study has tested what happens when the agent makes these decisions itself: how many of its claims are supported by its own data, code, and results, and whether readers can check them. Both may depend on the agent's harness, that is, the tools it can call and the written instructions it follows. We compared three harnesses: the agent's own harness; this harness plus the modeling tools of HydroMind, a hydrological modeling system we developed for general-purpose agents, which run every model through fixed commands and store its settings, trained model, and predictions; and both plus HydroMind's research procedure, under which the agent writes a research design before running any model and records every change to it. Under each harness, the same agent studied four open questions in hydrological model development and was given only the data. Under the three harnesses, the experiments submitted 23, 20, and 41 claims, each stating that one model or approach is better than, worse than, or similar to another. A claim does not hold if the difference recomputed from the experiment's own code and predictions disagrees with it, or if the code did not compare the two models or approaches the claim names. Under the three harnesses, 30%, 20%, and 5% of the claims did not hold. A statistical test, confidence interval, or decision rule that lets readers judge the stated difference was reported for 48%, 53%, and 83% of the claims. With the language model unchanged, changing only the harness reduced the share of claims that do not hold and increased the share that readers can check.

papers.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
papers.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

papers.intro:
The rise of powerful agentic AI coding tools, such as Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s codex, offers the possibility of quickly generating scientific results due to the speed at which they write functioning code. Moreover, these tools have been trained on a large body of text describing modern statistical techniques and the scientific literature in general, so they can often quickly “understand” a research problem. AI coding agents thus have the potential to dramatically improve research in the physical sciences. This shift could significantly change how modern science is practiced, which raises a host of practical, ethical, and philosophical concerns [11, see e.g., ] that will not be addressed here. This article instead describes a possible approach to developing, verifying, and archiving scientific code and data generated completely by AI models, including a brief presentation of a new software package called vaibify that can sequester and monitor AI agents while they write scientific code and analyze its output.

While the promise of large language models (LLMs) is great, they also demonstrate stochastic behavior [24], resulting in non-zero probabilities that code will be wrong [25], or, worse, critical files will be erased without authorization. Furthermore, scientists may trust the AI too much and not fully validate the numerical experiment, or not trust it enough to submit accurate and compelling research (an arguably worse outcome). Nonetheless, the speed at which they write useful code demands a consideration of how LLMs can be leveraged for cutting edge science, how their dangerous effects can be minimized, and how to maximize human trust in the code and data files they generate. When employing AI coding agents, the time bottleneck appears to be shifting from writing code to verifying code. These themes are explored in this article, leaving alone the harder (and perpetual) problem of properly interpreting results, i.e., evaluating if outcomes are accurate and/or publishable.

For now at least, the interpretation of cutting edge results remains a feature of science that cannot be fully outsourced to AI. Even efforts in which AI agents fully conceive, execute, and write scientific papers, such as Denario [37] and the AI Scientist [16], still rely on human evaluation of the results. The premise of this article is that AI agents are valuable enough today to integrate into most research projects, but that researchers still play a foundational role by verifying that the AI’s output is correct. papers.title: SWIMSS: An Open Multi-Center SwinUNETR Model for Multiple Sclerosis White Matter Lesion Segmentation
papers.abstract: Purpose: To develop and validate SWIMSS (SWInUNETR for Multiple Sclerosis white matter lesion Segmentation), a SwinUNETR-based deep learning (DL) model for reliable automated white matter (WM) lesion segmentation, in a large multicentric cohort of people with multiple sclerosis (pwMS). Methods: A real-world longitudinal dataset of 1,385 pwMS from seven Swiss clinical centers was used to train, validate, and test SWIMSS and two state-of-the-art DL architectures: UNETR and MSSegDiff. Inference results obtained with LST-AI were also compared. Preprocessed magnetization-prepared rapid acquisition gradient echo and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery MRI sequences, acquired with various MR systems and field strengths, served as model inputs. Model performance was evaluated using the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Results: SWIMSS achieved the highest performance, with a DSC of 81.37 (95% CI: 80.63-82.11), outperforming UNETR (79.06; 95% CI: 78.33-79.79), MSSegDiff (75.70; 95% CI: 74.97-76.43), and LST-AI (63.19; 95% CI: 62.08-64.30). Normalized DSC followed a similar trend, with SWIMSS reaching 84.88. Lesion detection F1 achieved 81.14. Statistical analyses confirmed its superior performance (p < 0.001). Conclusion: SWIMSS achieved state-of-the-art performance for WM lesion segmentation. By making this model publicly available, we enable broader access to high-quality segmentation tools, allowing smaller centers, often lacking large annotated datasets or computational resources, to benefit from a model trained on a diverse, large-scale cohort. This promotes more equitable access to advanced imaging analysis and supports reproducibility and standardization in MS research.

papers.title: JWST Observations of Starbursts: Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons in the NGC 253 Superwind
papers.abstract: We present the first spatially resolved study of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon (PAH) evolution in the galactic superwind of the nearby (d~3.5Mpc) galaxy NGC 253. Using JWST MIRI and NIRCam, we image ~$\pm$2kpc along the galaxy minor axis, capturing both sides of the starburst-driven wind at ~0.05''-0.375'' (~0.85-6.4pc) resolution and providing one of the most detailed views of the wind to date. We target PAH emission at 3.3um, 7.7um, and 11.3um, revealing PAH-bright filamentary streamers along the limb-brightened edges of the outflow cones out to at least a deprojected distance r~0.5kpc, beyond which they likely become confused with the spiral arms. In the southwest (SW) and northeast (NE) streamers, PAH intensity declines faster than $r^{-2}$, suggesting either PAH destruction or a decrease in gas column density or dust-to-gas ratio rather than a response to declining illumination alone. Band ratios trace changes in PAH properties, with the 11.3/7.7um ratio increasing with distance in the SW and northwest (NW) streamers and 3.3/7.7um and 3.3/11.3um decreasing in the SW and NE streamers, indicating larger, more neutral PAHs farther from the starburst. Given the thermal and dynamical properties of the gas in the SW streamer, cool gas is expected to survive acceleration in the outflow and enable PAH shielding. Compared with those of the prototypical starburst M82, the NGC 253 band ratios indicate faster evolution in PAH size. Thus, the NGC 253 wind may represent an earlier stage of outflow evolution in which small PAHs are destroyed near the starburst within the first few Myr.

papers.intro:
Galactic winds, or outflows, move baryons through and out of galaxy disks, and are crucial to galaxy evolution by regulating star formation and enriching the circumgalactic medium [95, 112, 114, CGM;]. Winds driven by stellar feedback are ubiquitous in high-star-formation-rate-density, high-pressure environments, which were common in cosmic noon galaxies (z∼2z\sim 2; Tacconi et al. 108) and today exist in local starbursts. Starburst-driven winds are multiphase, as supernovae and stellar feedback generate the hot (T∼107T\sim 10^{7} K) X-ray-emitting wind, which expands and entrains cold (T≲104T\lesssim 10^{4} K) gas and dust. The interface between the hot wind and colder gas produces a warm/cool (T∼105T\sim 10^{5} K) mixing layer of ionized material [54, 110]. Questions still remain about how cold gas and dust survive this hot-cold interplay as entrained clouds accelerate to the CGM. Radiative cooling [51, 52, 42, e.g.,] and acceleration by cosmic rays and magnetic fields [47, 100, 88, 3, 98] are possible solutions.

Dust is a prominent component of galactic winds. The smallest interstellar dust grains are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), which account for up to ∼20%\sim 20\% of the total IR luminosity in galaxies [99] by processing absorbed starlight, and produce complex spectral emission features in the infrared (IR) [111, 35, 24, 86, e.g.,]. The relative strengths of PAH features, which trace charge and size of PAHs, depend on the intensity and shape of the radiation field [34, 92, 7] and on environmental properties such as gas density, temperature, and metallicity [80, 2, 126, 123, 124, e.g.,].

In the Spitzer era, PAHs emerged as a tracer of cooler interstellar medium (ISM) phases [89, 12, 11, e.g.,]. Because PAHs cannot survive the initial shock and hot gas of galactic winds [80, 81], they trace the cool component [40, 79, 10, e.g.,]. With the improved spectral coverage, sensitivity, and resolution of JWST, PAHs and their band ratios are now powerful tools for observing cool material at parsec resolution in low-redshift galaxies [68, 96, 107, 23, 21, e.g.,]. For example, PAH band ratios revealed surprisingly minimal processing of the cool wind in the nearby starburst M82, with only minor changes in PAH charge and size, and no obvious change in abundance, with distance from its starburst [10, 29]. Correlations between PAH emission and CO, Hi, and Hα\alpha gas suggest that PAHs are protected underneath the ionized surfaces of cold entrained clouds [14, 43, 116, 117, 74, 32]. This protection may also explain observations in other galaxies where the cool phase traced by PAHs survives to the CGM [21] even out to long distances and timescales [115, ∼35\sim 35 kpc, tdyn∼100t_{\rm dyn}\sim 100 Myr;].

Like M82, NGC 253 is a nearby [90, 26, ∼3.5\sim 3.5 Mpc;] and highly inclined [79, i∼76∘i\sim 76^{\circ};] galaxy hosting a central starburst [83, 66, 67, star formation rate ∼3−5\sim 3{-}5 M⊙ yr-1;] that drives a large-scale outflow. Unlike the interaction-driven starburst in M82 [127], however, the NGC 253 starburst is fed by gas inflow along a bar [84]. NGC 253 is also more massive [69, M⋆∼4×1010M_{\star}\sim 4\times 10^{10} M⊙;], and its cool outflow is correspondingly more compact, with molecular streamers extending only ∼100−300\sim 100{-}300 pc in projection [15, 119]. The wind is also projected against the disk in the south and lies behind it in the north, making the northern side difficult to detect at optical wavelengths [28]. Nevertheless, the outflow has been measured in its cold molecular [104, 15, 119, 128, 61, 6], cold neutral atomic [16, 75, 62], warm/cool ionized [77, 122, 28], and hot X-ray [101, 102, 8, 73] phases. Cold molecular and neutral atomic gas constitute the bulk of the mass, as is typical for galactic winds [70, 61].

papers.title: Reference-Guided Data Curation for 3D Medical Vision-Language Pretraining
papers.abstract: Training 3D vision-language models (VLMs) on large medical imaging datasets collected across institutions is constrained by data quality. Vast, uncurated pools of image-report pairs are characterized by redundancy, class imbalance, and cross-institutional heterogeneity. We address this challenge of data curation for improving 3D VLM pretraining by proposing an offline, training-free, reference-guided data curation recipe. Our approach leverages a small, high-quality reference set to independently extract quality signals for each modality of a large, uncurated pool and merges them through a rank-aggregation step into a single ranking that guides sample selection. We validate this method on datasets comprising 35k 3D abdominal CT volume-report pairs from two institutions and 58k 2D chest X-ray image-report pairs. On 3D CT, using our reference-guided data curation strategy, our curated model matches the zero-shot disease classification performance of a state-of-the-art baseline (Merlin) while using $3.3\times$ less training data and a reference set of 5k samples. On 2D chest X-rays, our method yields a curated model that matches or exceeds the zero-shot disease classification performance of a model trained on the full pool while using up to $10\times$ less training data and a reference set of only 74 samples. Ablations show that the selection is stable under resampling of the reference, that smaller reference sets still outperform random sampling, and that label rebalancing does not improve performance. To support reproducibility, we release our code.

papers.intro:
Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are emerging as a promising technology in radiology, capable of performing complex downstream tasks such as findings classification, report generation, and cross-modal retrieval [21]. High-performing Computed Tomography (CT) VLMs typically require training on large datasets of paired volumes and reports [4], a demand supported by the steady growth of routinely acquired imaging data (with CT exam volumes increasing by 90% over a 16-year period) coupled with a shortage of radiologists [5]. Considering the growing data pool and large-scale datasets becoming accessible for pretraining [26, 15], achieving performant 3D VLM pretraining depends on effective data curation that filters redundancy and mitigates class imbalance, rather than on naive scaling.

Considering the growing data pool and large-scale datasets becoming accessible for pretraining [26, 15], achieving performant 3D VLM pretraining depends on effective data curation that filters redundancy and mitigates class imbalance, rather than on naive scaling.

Here, we consider two data regimes for future 3D VLM development: i) single-source, where the available data pool only contains in-distribution volume-report pairs from a single medical institution, and ii) heterogeneous, where large pools are formed by aggregating datasets from multiple institutions, introducing distribution shifts caused by varying scanner protocols, patient characteristics, and disease prevalence. In both regimes, the central challenge shifts from acquiring data to identifying a subset that maximizes performance and cross-distribution robustness. This shift motivates the exploration of data selection mechanisms for 3D CT VLM pretraining.

papers.title: Towards Cryogenic AI Hardware: Over 99% Precision In-Memory Computing at 4 K with 3-bit Ferroelectric Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 Capacitors
papers.abstract: High-accuracy cryogenic hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is demonstrated using Hf0.5Zr0.5O2 (HZO) ferroelectric capacitors (FeCAPs) as multilevel analog memories for capacitive compute in-memory (CIM) architectures. On the ISOLET spoken-word dataset, FeCAP-stored vectors achieve up to 92% classification accuracy at 4 K, while charge-domain matrix-vector multiplication (MVM) exhibits near-ideal behaviour with linearity of 1 and error probability below 1% for 4x4 and 4x8 configurations, operating below 3 V. Unlike the performance at 300 K, HDC and CIM at 4 K remains resilient to electric-field-cycling-induced fatigue, thanks to enhanced cryogenic device characteristics, including reduced state variability, strongly suppressed leakage current and stable retention, as well as 78% faster switching. Furthermore, these multibit FeCAPs exhibit endurance beyond 1E9 cycles with polarization degradation below 8%, preserving multilevel integrity. Benefits can also be observed at 300 K, following cooldown and wake-up pulsing at 4 K and subsequent warming up. These results establish multibit FeCAPs as a highly reliable, ultra-low-energy, and accurate analog CIM platform for future cryogenic AI-computing hardware.

papers.title: The Science and Technology of Broad-Band X-ray Astrophysics
papers.abstract:
Much of our understanding of high-energy astrophysical phenomena over the past decade has relied on coordinated observations extending from soft X-rays (<10 keV) to hard X-rays (>10 keV). While soft X-ray facilities remain abundant, focusing capabilities above ~10 keV are scarce, representing the primary gap for broad-band X-ray science. Simultaneous wide-band observations are essential to study thermal and non-thermal processes in extreme environments such as accretion discs, jets, and coronae. However, current high-energy observations remain limited by a lack of high angular resolution and sensitivity beyond Chandra's bandpass. With upcoming multi-messenger facilities set to dramatically increase variable and transient sources, a high angular resolution broad-band X-ray mission is critically needed.
  This report reviews the current landscape of high-energy facilities, outlines key science drivers, focusing on extragalactic accretion (the cosmic X-ray background) and Galactic compact objects, and examines the underlying technology landscape, including optics and detectors. Broad-band X-ray astrophysics is primed to address key questions from the Astro2020 Decadal Survey. While past focusing efforts have been limited to the Small Explorer class, technological advances now enable low-risk Probe- or Flagship-class architectures capable of delivering order-of-magnitude improvements in capabilities.

papers.title: Topological signatures of criticality: the Ising case
papers.abstract: Topological properties of microscopic configurations may provide additional insight into phase transitions beyond conventional thermodynamic observables. We investigate this idea in the two-dimensional Ising model on square and triangular lattices by associating cell complexes with the positive and negative spin domains and constructing an Euler-characteristic observable from their difference. We provide the expression relating this quantity to conventional observables of the Ising model. This derivation allows us to understand its expected behavior physically. As a byproduct, we show that at any finite positive temperature the expectation of the Euler characteristic exceeds a positive, lattice-size-independent bound, hence disproving a previously suggested conjecture. Monte Carlo simulations combined with multihistogram reweighting show that this spin-odd topological observable exhibits order-parameter-like behavior near the ferromagnetic transition. Finite-size scaling of its susceptibility yields pseudocritical temperatures that converge to the known critical temperature for both lattice geometries. On the square lattice, the leading-order estimate of the critical exponent obtained from the topological observable depends more strongly on the fitting range than the magnetization estimate. This behavior is consistent with stronger subleading finite-size corrections, as supported by fits including an additional correction term. On the triangular lattice, the corresponding estimate remains consistent with the theoretical Ising value. Our study suggests that topologically defined quantities such as the Euler characteristic can provide an alternative way to locate order-disorder phase transitions in the systems considered here. Since the definition of these observables is purely geometrical, they can provide useful insights in cases in which order parameters cannot be constructed.

papers.intro:
Equilibrium phase transitions are conventionally characterized by nonanalyticities of thermodynamic functions in the thermodynamic limit and, for continuous transitions, by the emergence of long-range correlations and universal scaling behavior [PelissettoVicari2002]. In many systems these changes are conveniently detected through an order parameter, such as the magnetization in a ferromagnet. A broader question, however, is whether structural properties of microscopic configurations can themselves provide useful signatures of a phase transition. In particular, topology offers a natural way of characterizing changes in the structural organization of microscopic configurations while remaining insensitive to detailed metric information.

Equilibrium phase transitions are conventionally characterized by nonanalyticities of thermodynamic functions in the thermodynamic limit and, for continuous transitions, by the emergence of long-range correlations and universal scaling behavior [PelissettoVicari2002]. In many systems these changes are conveniently detected through an order parameter, such as the magnetization in a ferromagnet. A broader question, however, is whether structural properties of microscopic configurations can themselves provide useful signatures of a phase transition. In particular, topology offers a natural way of characterizing changes in the structural organization of microscopic configurations while remaining insensitive to detailed metric information.

Topology has long been recognized as playing a central physical role in phase transitions. The paradigmatic example is the Berezinskii–Kosterlitz–Thouless transition, which is driven by the binding and unbinding of topological defects [KosterlitzThouless1973], but topological properties of extended structures are informative also for conventional order–disorder transitions. In the three-dimensional Ising model, the approach to the critical point is accompanied by a proliferation of handles on the interface between the two magnetized phases [Caselle:1993yu]; in two dimensions, the Euler–Poincaré characteristic of Fortuin–Kasteleyn clusters singles out the transition point of the Potts model [BlanchardFortunatoGandolfo2002], and the mean Euler characteristic and mean Betti numbers of the spin domains of Ising models with arbitrary spin display pronounced changes at the critical point [BlanchardEtAl2006].

A conceptually distinct line of work, usually referred to as the topological hypothesis, relates equilibrium phase transitions to changes in the topology of energy sublevel sets in configuration space. For smooth, finite-range and confining potentials with continuous degrees of freedom, such topology changes were originally shown to be necessary for a phase transition [FranzosiPettini2004]. However, this result was challenged by a counterexample involving the two-dimensional lattice ϕ4\phi^{4} model [KastnerMehta2011]. Subsequent work has refined the theoretical framework by accounting for topological changes emerging in the thermodynamic limit [GoriEtAl2022]. The scope and limitations of this approach are also discussed in Ref. [Kastner2008], and the framework has been extended to discrete spin systems, including the Ising model [CimasoniDelabays2019]. The advent of topological data analysis (TDA) [Edelsbrunner2002, ZomorodianCarlsson2005, Carlsson2009, ChazalMichel2021], and of efficient algorithms for persistent homology in particular [Edelsbrunner, Otter2017], turned these ideas into quantitative computational tools, first deployed on dynamically sampled configurations of the mean-field X​YXY and ϕ4\phi^{4} models [Donato2016].

In condensed matter and statistical systems, persistent-homology observables have provided interpretable order parameters and machine-learning-free detectors of criticality for Ising and other lattice spin models [Cole:2020hjx, Olsthoorn:2020xzs, Tran:2021wyg], and have yielded quantitative estimates of critical temperatures and exponents in two-dimensional X​YXY models [Sale2022]. In quantum field theory, the same strategy has been used to probe center vortices and deconfinement in S​U​(2)SU(2) gauge theory [Sale:2022qfn], confinement in non-Abelian lattice gauge theories [Spitz:2022tul, Spitz:2024bqh], ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} gauge theories [Sehayek:2022lxf], dense QCD effective models [Kashiwa:2021ctc], and monopole networks in compact U⁡(1)U(1) and S​U​(3)SU(3) Yang–Mills theory [Crean:2024nro, Crean:2026caz]. The present work follows this spirit: rather than studying energy sublevel sets in the full configuration space, we associate a cell complex with each individual spin configuration and ask whether its topology, summarized by the Euler characteristic of the spin domains, changes in a characteristic way across the phase transition.

papers.title: FairPGT: Partitioned Graph Transformers for Dual-Level Fair Graph Clustering
papers.abstract: Clustering on attributed graphs can produce demographically biased clusters, particularly when communities align with protected groups. Graph transformers can amplify this bias through same-group attention, while global attention limits scalability. We propose FairPGT, a partitioned graph transformer for fair graph clustering. FairPGT restricts attention to METIS partitions and connects them through routing tokens, which divides the quadratic cost of attention by the number of partitions. A graph-aware self-training target guides clustering, with a provably bounded deviation from the standard DEC target. Fairness is imposed at two levels: a mutual-information term promotes demographic parity in cluster assignments, while a normalized cross-group attention ratio (nCGAR) guides attention toward group neutrality through self-distillation. We prove that the nCGAR correction moves attention toward neutrality and establish a condition preventing overshooting. Across seven benchmarks, FairPGT achieves the best clustering performance and statistical parity on the three largest graphs (Credit, Pokec-n, Pokec-z), with a statistical-parity gap approximately ten times lower than DMoN, and is Pareto-dominated on only one dataset. On controlled stochastic block models, FairPGT attains 97% of the derived upper bound on NMI for exactly fair clustering when communities and protected groups coincide. These graphs further show that, under strong alignment, assignment-level fairness alone makes the attention group-heterophilous, whereas attention-level fairness alone improves neutrality without ensuring fair clusters. Code for reproducibility is available at https://github.com/SiamakGhodsi/FairPGT.

When a bank segments its customers or a platform groups its users, the resulting clusters decide who is offered what. Graph clustering, closely related to community detection, groups the nodes of a graph into structurally coherent communities and is a fundamental unsupervised task in network analysis, with applications in fraud analysis, bioinformatics, and recommendation [21, 46, 31, 18, 43]. When nodes carry protected attributes such as gender, age, or nationality, the communities a clustering finds can line up with demographic groups, and because clusters are used downstream, to target services or to segment users, such alignment can turn into biased decisions [5, 23]. The problem is hardest in unsupervised graph learning, where no label tells useful structure apart from structure that merely reflects the protected attribute.

Bias can enter a clustering pipeline at two points. First, at the representation level: node representations may encode group membership even when the protected attribute is removed from the input, because node features and graph structure act as proxies for it [19, 10]. In message-passing graph neural networks, aggregation over neighborhoods dominated by one group has been shown to amplify this signal [30, 41]. Similarly, graph transformers aggregate information through attention [37, 50, 11], and they are exposed to the same effect in a more flexible form: if attention concentrates on nodes of the same group, each representation becomes a summary of its own group. Moreover, at the assignment level, clusters can be demographically imbalanced even when the representations are reasonable; this is the level addressed by most classical fair clustering methods [14, 5, 35].

Figure 1illustrates both these levels concretely on a small graph with 45 nodes and depicts why balancing cluster assignments alone may be insufficient. In this toy graph, the protected groups are mixed within the communities, but group-correlated features draw attention toward same-group nodes and pull clusters away from the communities. Enforcing group proportions on the assignments balances the clusters while disrupting their community structure. Rebalancing attention alongside assignment-level fairness yields clusters that are both balanced and structurally cohesive.

Second, same-group attention has to be judged relative to the group composition of the attended nodes, because even group-agnostic attention gives more total mass to the larger group.

Existing methods cover parts of this picture. On the clustering side, fair clustering methods impose proportionality or individual-fairness constraints in spectral formulations [35, 27, 58, 20], or they add parity, adversarial, and contrastive regularizations to deep clustering models to remove protected information from learned representations [40, 63, 29]. In addition, our previous factorization-based models made the fairness–utility trade-off explicit at the assignment level [23, 22]. However, all of these methods act on the assignments or on the learned representations, and none of their encoders uses attention, so the group dependence of attention is neither measured nor controlled. In parallel, fair graph learning has developed adversarial, counterfactual, and graph-editing methods to debias graph neural network representations [15, 2, 17, 13, 59, 65], but mostly for supervised node classification. Closer to our setting, graph transformers have been used for attributed graph clustering, though without fairness considerations [64], while the two recent fair graph transformers of Luo et al., FairGT [45] and FairGP [44], still target supervised node classification: FairGT builds fairness-aware structural and multi-hop encodings, and FairGP restricts attention to graph partitions and removes attention across them. Consequently, no existing method measures and controls the group dependence of attention in unsupervised graph clustering. However, all of these methods act on the assignments or on the learned representations, and none of their encoders uses attention, so the group dependence of attention is neither measured nor controlled. In parallel, fair graph learning has developed adversarial, counterfactual, and graph-editing methods to debias graph neural network representations [15, 2, 17, 13, 59, 65], but mostly for supervised node classification. Closer to our setting, graph transformers have been used for attributed graph clustering, though without fairness considerations [64], while the two recent fair graph transformers of Luo et al., FairGT [45] and FairGP [44], still target supervised node classification: FairGT builds fairness-aware structural and multi-hop encodings, and FairGP restricts attention to graph partitions and removes attention across them. Consequently, no existing method measures and controls the group dependence of attention in unsupervised graph clustering. Finally, scalability is a further obstacle: full attention costs 𝒪⁡(n2)\mathcal{O}(n^{2}) per layer, which is prohibitive on the larger graphs of fair graph learning benchmarks.

papers.title: Redrock: Spectroscopic Classification and Redshift Fitting for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument
papers.abstract: Redrock is a software package for spectroscopic classification and redshift fitting, designed to use the full information from spectroperfectionism outputs: flux-calibrated spectra, uncorrelated errors, and a per-spectrum resolution matrix encoding the non-Gaussian wavelength-dependent spectral line-spread function. Redrock was originally developed for the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), but the Extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS) also used Redrock as their primary galaxy redshift fitter prior to DESI. This paper presents the algorithmic details of Redrock and its performance on DESI data. On spectra from DESI DR2, Redrock achieves a redshift recovery rate of approximately 98% for the Bright Galaxy Survey (BGS) and Luminous Red Galaxies (LRG), 95.9% for Emission Line Galaxies (ELG), and 92.6% for quasars (QSO), and it delivers unbiased stellar radial velocities with a precision of roughly 5 km/s.

The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument [33, 32, 28, 66, 78, DESI;] is a spectroscopic redshift survey designed to observe ∼\sim60 million galaxies and quasars over 17,000 deg2 with an 8-year observing program [82]. In addition to the sky-subtracted flux-calibrated spectra, a key output of DESI is the spectral classification (galaxy, quasar, star) and redshift of each observed object, included with the public data releases [31, 29]. Redrock is a spectral classification and redshift fitting code designed for the needs of DESI, while at the same time being open-source and generic enough to be applicable to other spectroscopic surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS).

In addition to the sky-subtracted flux-calibrated spectra, a key output of DESI is the spectral classification (galaxy, quasar, star) and redshift of each observed object, included with the public data releases [31, 29]. Redrock is a spectral classification and redshift fitting code designed for the needs of DESI, while at the same time being open-source and generic enough to be applicable to other spectroscopic surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS).

The algorithmic method in Redrock is similar to that used by SDSS [14]: selecting the χ2\chi^{2} minimum from Principal Component Analysis (PCA) template fits over a range of redshifts and template spectral types. It improves upon that method through updated templates, more rigorous error propagation, the use of wavelength-dependent non-Gaussian per-spectrum resolution modeling, and optional spectral archetype fits to avoid unphysical solutions [8]. The improvements in Redrock were significant enough that the SDSS-IV Extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS) switched to using Redrock for the final cosmology analyses instead of the original SDSS code [80].

Other previous methods for automated spectroscopic classification and redshift measurement include template Fourier cross-correlation [86], explicitly matching observed spectral peaks to sets of known emission lines [35, WiggleZ;], template fitting after subtracting a median-filtered spectrum [74, DEEP2;], and fitting flux-calibrated spectra to a library of archetype basis templates [25, PRIMUS;]. Redrock also uses flux-calibrated spectra — including the continuum — and fits templates across all observed wavelengths simultaneously without explicitly searching for and fitting individual emission or absorption features. This approach enables Redrock to use the full information available in the data. Since the PCA templates are derived from complete spectra, they implicitly encode correlations between line strengths, relative velocity offsets (for the quasar templates), and other line properties in addition to the relationship between these features and the underlying continuum shape. In principle, this offers an advantage over methods that rely on identification of individual features or groups of features: many low signal-to-noise emission and/or absorption lines can collectively contribute to achieving a secure classification and emission line confusion is discouraged. However, this approach is limited by the adequacy of the PCA templates, and reliant upon upstream processing to provide high-quality sky-subtracted flux-calibrated spectra with well-characterized errors as input.

Redrock comes with a set of templates for fitting stars, quasars (QSOs), and galaxies. The default templates are tuned to the primary populations targeted by DESI. For example, the default galaxy templates are derived from simulated spectra of nearby bright galaxies [42, BGS;], old metal-rich luminous red galaxies [93, LRG;], and active star-forming emission line galaxies [79, ELG;] while the quasar templates are designed to span the spectral diversity observed over the full targeted redshift range (z<3.5z<3.5) for cosmology [22]. papers.title: Risk-Controlled Correction for Frozen Multimodal Models under Missing Modalities
papers.abstract: A deployed multimodal predictor may face missing modalities after its weights can no longer be changed. This raises a question that training-time repair does not answer: what part of the resulting error is still correctable from the information that remains? We show that this part is characterized by the Bayes gap, the difference between the model's prediction and the Bayes prediction given the observed modalities. For cross-entropy and squared error, excess risk measures this gap in the geometry of the loss; ambiguity in the observed modalities cannot be removed. Thus, a badly degraded prediction is not necessarily a correctable one. Estimating the Bayes prediction normally requires labels. However, when a model observing more modalities is conditionally correct, averaging its outputs conditional on the remaining modalities recovers this target without retrieval labels; with the same fixed blend and neighbors, it is no worse in expected cross-entropy or Brier risk than averaging hard labels. Some such assumption is unavoidable: otherwise the target is not identifiable from unlabeled data alone. GUARD (Gated Utility-Aware Recalibration for Deployment) leaves the deployed predictor unchanged. It estimates a candidate correction by retrieval, learns from deployment-matched labeled data when correction is likely to help, and calibrates a threshold on a held-out split by conformal risk control. Under exchangeability, the marginal probability that GUARD applies a correction whose loss increase exceeds a prescribed tolerance is bounded by a preset level, regardless of the learned score. In controlled experiments, correction gain follows headroom rather than raw error; across nine frozen model-dataset pairs spanning six domains, GUARD retains most of blanket correction's gain within harm budgets that blanket correction often exceeds.

A diagnostic model trained on twelve-lead ECG (Wagner et al., 2020) may run where only a few leads are recorded (Reyna et al., 2021); an activity recognizer trained on a body-worn sensor array (Ordóñez & Roggen, 2016) may lose streams when sensors disconnect; an audio–visual model may receive only one of its two streams (Parthasarathy & Sundaram, 2020). Deployments may also fix the predictor because its weights are inaccessible (Sun et al., 2022). We assume query access to predictions and representations, without modifying the model. Output correction still requires validation and applicable change control (FDA, 2025).

papers.title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book
papers.abstract: Existing work suggests that markets can show volatility with paths rougher than those of Brownian motion. In theory this can happen when the order flow is close to instability with memory that decays as a power law. However, it is not fully clear how such order flow could arise from the predominantly algorithmic market making that characterizes order book dynamics. We show one such consistent mechanism. We treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. We assume that distinct desks do not act synchronously in time but act whenever new information relevant to their respective oracles arrives, which each desk samples over its own characteristic lookback horizon. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise. In the continuum limit this update rule makes the volume of the order book follow a conservative stochastic partial differential equation (the Dean--Kawasaki equation) whose fluctuations drive the order flow. The distinct horizons of the desks further induce a persistent memory in the order flow that decays as a power law. Standard scaling arguments then lead to rough volatility. We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. In liquid markets governed mainly by market makers, such as the perpetual futures of Binance, the order books are consistent with how our desks change the book.
papers.intro:
Empirical studies of many markets report volatility whose paths are rougher than those of Brownian motion [GJR18]. Such roughness can arise in theory when each order sets off very long chains of further orders whose influence fades as a power of the elapsed time. In a scaling limit the exponent of this power law sets the roughness of the order flow, which opposing buy and sell flows then carry into the price [EEFR18, JR16]. Such order flow has been argued to follow from the absence of arbitrage together with the splitting of large orders during execution [EEFR18, JR20]. These arguments rest on the behavior of traders. However, it is not a priori clear whether market makers that act purely on new information can produce such order flow through the order book on their own.

In a scaling limit the exponent of this power law sets the roughness of the order flow, which opposing buy and sell flows then carry into the price [EEFR18, JR16]. Such order flow has been argued to follow from the absence of arbitrage together with the splitting of large orders during execution [EEFR18, JR20]. These arguments rest on the behavior of traders. However, it is not a priori clear whether market makers that act purely on new information can produce such order flow through the order book on their own.

In this work we provide one mechanism that allows for this. To reflect algorithm-driven strategies, we treat each market maker as a desk that uses a first-order gradient rule to move the distances of its orders from the mid price toward target distances provided by an unknown oracle. As our model has no takers, we let the mid price move toward the side of the book with less volume near it. Each desk thus keeps correcting its orders against a moving reference. We next assume that each desk samples information over its own characteristic horizon [LdP18]. Since at each moment only the desks that have received new information take a step, order placements are asynchronous. Across all desks the rule therefore takes the form of stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with information-driven (mini-batch) noise.

As desks only redistribute volume, the volume of the order book is conserved irrespective of the nature of this noise. Rough volatility. Rough volatility was first documented in estimates from realized volatility [GJR18]. However, other works argue that such estimates could partly reflect estimation error [CD24]. In our work we provide a different route that relies purely on algorithmic market making, with roughness measured from the order count distributions that emerge from it.

Unlike other agent-based models [CI02, CB00, LM99], we use a gradient-based rule consistent with modern learning approaches and information-based sampling [LdP18] that guides the actions of fast-reacting desks.

papers.title: UCLIR: Unsupervised Continual Learning using Independent Representations
papers.abstract: In continual learning, regularization-based methods aim to mimic neuroplasticity by updating network weights to learn new tasks while constraining changes to parameters that are important for previously learned tasks through penalty terms. However, as the number of tasks increases, preserving knowledge from earlier tasks becomes less effective. This is mainly because updates for new tasks are distributed across the entire network, where parameters are highly interdependent due to the dense connectivity between neurons. Inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR), which states that the number of neural connections decreases with increasing physical distance, learning is naturally locally correlated while inter-area updates remain less task-dependent. Motivated by this principle, in this paper we demonstrate that applying weight regularization to multiple small and independently learned complementary representations is more effective than regularizing a single large shared representation. By decomposing the input into independently learned components, learning new tasks induces only localized parameter updates within specific representation, which limit interference and improve knowledge retention across tasks. We employ independent autoencoders that learn different parts of the input independently through unsupervised regularization. At inference time, a linear classifier is used for evaluation. The experimental results on a sequence of tasks using 5-Splits MNIST, sequence of 5-datasets, 5-Splits CIFAR-10, 10-Splits Tiny ImageNet shows competitive results with supervised and replay-based methods. Code is available.

papers.intro:
Recent advances in artificial intelligence have been largely driven by the availability of massive training datasets. However, regardless of data scale, modern deep models exhibit limited ability to generalize to unseen or unfamiliar scenarios due to the lack of dynamic learning mechanisms that enable continuous adaptation to new data. Since these models are typically trained in an offline manner using static datasets, their reasoning capability remains constrained by the diversity of the original training data. These limitations stem from architectural designs optimized for single-task learning with large datasets processed all at once, lacking the ability to continually learn new representations from a sequence of tasks without eliminating the previous learned representations. The inability of neural networks to preserve previously acquired knowledge while learning new tasks is known as catastrophic forgetting. This motivated the development of continual learning frameworks, which are generally categorized into replay-based Shin et al. (2017), architectural expansion Rusu et al. (2016), regularization-based approaches Kirkpatrick et al. (2017), or hybrid methods Yoon et al. (2018).

This principle lines up with regularization approaches that propose techniques to preserve previous knowledge by carefully updating the weights of the new task without significantly changing the weights of the neurons that contributed to the previous tasks Ahn et al. (3) When all tasks are encoded within a single latent space, task-specific features become highly correlated. This correlation causes interference and reduces the model’s ability to preserve diverse task knowledge over long task sequences.

This assumption is inspired by the Exponential Distance Rule (EDR) Ercsey-Ravasz et al. (2013) observed in the brain, which suggests that neural connections weaken as physical distance increases, leading to the hypothesis that learning primarily occurs through local synaptic updates, while interactions between distant regions are sparse and task-dependent. As a result, updating low-level layers often requires modifying later layers as well, which reduces the flexibility to learn new task-specific low-level representations without influencing existing high-level representations.

Within each task and each representation, weight regularization is applied to preserve the important weights of the previous tasks while learning a new task. At inference time, predictions are obtained using a linear classifier trained on top of the frozen representations.
