papers.title: Multi-epoch imaging observations of the Galactic Center with NIRCam and MIRI
papers.abstract: The center of the Milky Way is the densest and most extreme environment in our Galaxy, its most active star forming region, and the only galaxy nucleus where we can resolve stars down to about a solar mass on the main sequence. The Galactic Center (GC) contains a nuclear stellar disk, a nuclear star cluster, and a supermassive black hole, all embedded within the so-called Central Molecular Zone, which showcases conditions of the interstellar medium that are typically found in high-redshift star-forming regions. The GC hosts the highest concentration of massive stars in the Milky Way and hosts a large concentration of rare objects, such as Wolf Rayet stars and X-ray binaries. The GC is therefore an astrophysical target of outstanding importance. A multi-epoch JWST program enables novel science including the lifetime of planet-forming disks, the search for intermediate mass black holes, direct measurements of the multi-scale gravitational potential, and a deep measurement of the star formation history. Multi-epoch imaging observations with JWST's NIRCam and MIRI instruments will go far beyond Roman WFI surveys in terms of depth and astrometric and photometric precision because of its $3\times$ better resolution, and it expands spectral coverage in narrow bands and mid-infrared wavelength coverage. The proposed observations would correspond to a Treasury Program of about 420\,h, distributed over three epochs spaced three to five years apart.

papers.title: SPONGE: Sulphur, Phosphorus, Oxygen, Nitrogen, and carbon Galactic Evolution. I. CNOPS elements as probes of physical processes in stars and galaxies
papers.abstract: As fundamental bio-essential elements, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur (CNOPS) warrant a precise mapping of their cosmic origins. In this paper, we present the SPONGE project (Sulphur, Phosphorus, Oxygen, Nitrogen, and carbon Galactic Evolution), aimed at establishing a self-consistent galactic chemical evolution (GCE) framework capable of simultaneously reproducing local abundance benchmarks along with key observational constraints in external galaxies. Here, we focus on the Milky Way. We compile literature data and construct GCE models incorporating various single- and binary-star yields, taking stellar rotation and nova nucleosynthesis into account. Fast rotators are confirmed to be essential for primary 14N and 13C production at low metallicities. Although our homogeneous models do not reach the lowest 12C/13C ratios observed in some halo stars, this discrepancy should not be taken as a refutation of the model, as observational selection effects may apply. Predicted C and N isotopic ratios along the disc agree remarkably well with those inferred from radio observations of star-forming regions. Notably, our models explain Galactic P enrichment as originating predominantly from massive stars, without any ad hoc adjustment of the yields or the need for a significant nova contribution. Conversely, novae are required to synthesize non-negligible fractions of 13C and 15N. Optimizing GCE trajectories against a comprehensive CNOPS ensemble simultaneously, rather than single diagnostics one at a time, establishes a robust baseline for future work. Remaining open questions, such as the predicted overproduction of 12C at low metallicities and 34S along the disc, alongside the abundance scatter of some key elements, provide concrete targets for subsequent papers in this series.

papers.intro:
The first generations of stars (Population III stars, hereafter Pop III) formed from a pristine mixture of hydrogen, helium, and trace amounts of lithium (Bromm and Larson 2004; Klessen and Glover 2023). Their evolution and ensuing deaths initiated galactic chemical enrichment, forging the first metals and seeding the interstellar medium (ISM) for subsequent stellar generations. Since then, each stellar generation has further enriched the gas through stellar winds and supernovae, connecting the physics of individual stars to the formation and evolution of galaxies and galaxy clusters (Tinsley 1979; Pagel 1997; Matteucci 2021).

Their evolution and ensuing deaths initiated galactic chemical enrichment, forging the first metals and seeding the interstellar medium (ISM) for subsequent stellar generations. Since then, each stellar generation has further enriched the gas through stellar winds and supernovae, connecting the physics of individual stars to the formation and evolution of galaxies and galaxy clusters (Tinsley 1979; Pagel 1997; Matteucci 2021).

Tracing this enrichment process requires empirical probes across cosmic epochs. By measuring elemental abundances in long-lived, low-mass stars, we can reconstruct the life cycles of local galaxies, placing tight constraints on their star-formation histories, galactic-scale outflows, and mass assembly via coronal gas accretion and satellite mergers. Complementary gas-phase abundance determinations grant access to elements lacking measurable stellar spectral features, although they reflect only a snapshot of chemical enrichment at the time of observation.

Carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and sulphur (hereafter CNOPS) are fundamental to pre-biotic chemistry and the emergence of life as we know it. Multiple stellar generations are required to build a favourable chemical environment; tracking the evolution of CNOPS elements and their stable isotopes across cosmic time is therefore essential for both astrophysics and astrobiology. Addressing this question requires a multi-disciplinary approach combining empirical abundance measurements with detailed models of stellar and galactic chemical evolution (GCE). This is precisely the goal of the SPONGE (Sulphur, Phosphorus, Oxygen, Nitrogen, and carbon Galactic Evolution) collaboration.

Despite their crucial role, the Galactic evolution of CNOPS elements and their isotopes remains poorly constrained. In stars, CNO abundances can be derived from permitted and forbidden atomic lines, as well as molecular bands (C2\mathrm{C}_{2}, CH\mathrm{CH}, NH\mathrm{NH}, OH\mathrm{OH}, CN\mathrm{CN}, and CO\mathrm{CO}) in ultraviolet (UV), optical, and near-infrared (NIR) spectra (Barbuy et al. 2018; Randich and Magrini 2021). However, systematic differences between diagnostic methods yield conflicting abundances, even for the Sun (Caffau et al. 2009; Amarsi et al. 2019; Mashonkina and Ryabchikova 2024). Large spectroscopic surveys have provided C12{}^{12}\mathrm{C}, N14{}^{14}\mathrm{N}, and O16{}^{16}\mathrm{O} abundances for thousands of Galactic stars (Buder et al. 2019; Franchini et al. 2020; Franchini et al. 2021; Kisku et al. 2021; Li et al. 2024, e.g.), but these samples are largely restricted to giants, where atmospheric compositions are altered by evolutionary mixing processes. In contrast, the atmospheres of dwarf and unmixed subgiant stars retain their birth composition, making them excellent tracers of chemical enrichment on a Galactic scale.

Mapping chemical enrichment patterns across the entire Galactic disc requires probes such as classical Cepheids, open clusters, H ii regions, and molecular clouds (Wilson and Rood 1994; Milam et al. 2005; Arellano-Córdova et al. 2020; Colzi et al. 2022; Magrini et al. 2023; Yan et al. 2023; Bono et al. 2024, e.g.). Gas-phase tracers present distinct challenges. Molecular isotopologue ratios can be biased relative to true isotopic ratios by local physical processes such as isotope-selective photodissociation and chemical fractionation (Visser et al. 2009; Roueff et al. 2015; Colzi et al. 2020; Nomura et al. 2023, e.g.), which depend on the physical properties of the molecular cloud, such as density, temperature, or exposure to an external UV field. Similarly, abundances derived from the emission spectra of photoionized regions often rely on simplified assumptions that neglect thermal and spatial stratification (Marconi et al. 2024, e.g.) or dust depletion of refractory and semi-refractory species (Konstantopoulou et al. 2024; Psaradaki et al. 2024, e.g.). Nevertheless, these tracers are indispensable for probing regions where stellar spectroscopy is not feasible, including high-redshift emitters.

As the first paper in the SPONGE series, this study establishes a baseline for CNOPS evolution in galaxies by critically evaluating GCE model predictions for the Milky Way against state-of-the-art observational data, highlighting key discrepancies and missing ingredients in current nucleosynthesis prescriptions. Section 2 outlines the assumptions of the adopted homogeneous chemical evolution model. Section 3 describes the observational dataset, followed by a comparison with model predictions in Sect. 4. Our findings are discussed in Sect. 5, where we also draw our main conclusions. Extensions to other galaxies and high-redshift environments are deferred to future papers.

papers.title: The 7th International Verification of Neural Networks Competition (VNN-COMP 2026): Summary and Results
papers.abstract: This report summarizes the seventh International Verification of Neural Networks Com- petition (VNN-COMP 2026), held as part of the Symposium on AI Verification (SAIV) co-located with the International Conference on Computer-Aided Verification (CAV) at FLoC 2026 in Lisbon, Portugal. The goal of the competition is to provide an objective comparison of the state-of-the-art methods in neural network verification, in terms of scal- ability and speed. Along this line, we used standard formats (ONNX for neural networks and VNNLIB for specifications), standard hardware (all tools are run by the organizers on AWS), and tool parameters provided by the tool authors. This report summarizes the rules, benchmarks, participating tools, results, and lessons learned from this competition.

papers.title: PatchAdaNet: Unsupervised class incremental learning using local patches and global adapters
papers.abstract: Biological learning systems acquire knowledge incrementally through broad, reusable representations established early and kept largely stable, while integrating new experience with minimal interference with previously learned knowledge. Replay-based methods approximate this by storing samples or features from previous tasks and mixing them into the current task. However, memory buffers grow with the number of tasks and may retain task-specific noise that reduces generalization. To address these limitations, we propose PatchAdaNet (Patch Adapter Network), an unsupervised class-incremental learning method for image classification that continually updates feature representations using autoencoders. Since images share structural features such as edges, corners, and shapes, we first divide each image into patches and train independent autoencoders on external data to reconstruct each patch. The layers of all patch encoders are aggregated into global frozen layers that generalize across tasks and remain fixed throughout learning. Learnable adapters then build global image representations from these features to reconstruct the entire image. To prevent feature drift without storing data, we introduce the Global Feature Centroid (GFC), a fixed-size running average of adapter outputs updated after each task to penalizes representation drift. Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is applied to the learnable layers to preserve previously learned features by constraining important weights. Finally, a linear classifier is trained on the frozen latent representation and GFC for class-incremental evaluation. We evaluate PatchAdaNet in both CNN and Vision Transformer settings on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, miniImageNet and 5-Datasets, providing a comparative study of the two architectures under identical class-incremental settings. Code is available.

papers.intro:
When a neural network is trained sequentially, the parameter updates required to fit the current task conflict with the weight configurations that encode knowledge of previous tasks, a fundamental and largely unsolved challenge in deep learning known as catastrophic forgetting. This problem is especially severe in class-incremental learning (CIL), where the model must classify all classes seen so far without access to task identity at inference time. Existing continual learning methods address forgetting from several perspectives. Regularization methods constrain parameter updates by penalizing changes to weights identified as important for prior tasks Kirkpatrick et al. (2017); Zenke et al. (2017); Aljundi et al. (2018). For example, Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) Kirkpatrick et al. (2017) measures weight importance through computing Fisher information and adds a quadratic penalty on parameter drift. Synaptic Intelligence Zenke et al. (2017) estimates importance online during training, without requiring a separate importance estimation pass after each task. Architectural expansion methods allocate new, task-specific parameters for each task, either by instantiating an entirely new set of layers per task Rusu et al. (2016) or by selectively retraining and expanding only the neurons relevant to each new task Yoon et al. (2018). Replay-based methods store or generate examples from previous tasks and incorporate them with current-task training Lopez-Paz and Ranzato (2017); Shin et al. (2017). Knowledge distillation methods use a frozen copy of the model from the immediately preceding task as the teacher, transferring its soft predictions to constrain the student trained on the current task Li and Hoiem (2017); Wen et al. (2024).

(2024).

Despite this progress, several limitations remain across existing approaches: 1) regularization methods such as EWC operate purely in weight space, applying a single importance estimate uniformly across all layers. This merges task-specific and shared representations within the same parameters, making it difficult to isolate what should change and what should be preserved. 2) architectural expansion methods introduce parameter or memory costs that scale with the number of tasks. 3) replay-based methods require a growing memory buffer to retain samples or features from previous tasks, and the retained data often carries task-specific noise that reduces generalization to new tasks. 4) knowledge distillation methods depend on keeping a copy of the previous model as a teacher, which doubles the memory requirement, and the distilled features tend to become increasingly task-specific as the sequence grows, losing the general representations needed for class-incremental classification. 5) Supervised continual learning methods require the classifier to be restructured each time new classes arrive, binding representation learning directly to the evolving label space and limiting flexibility in open-ended scenarios.

This merges task-specific and shared representations within the same parameters, making it difficult to isolate what should change and what should be preserved. 2) architectural expansion methods introduce parameter or memory costs that scale with the number of tasks. 3) replay-based methods require a growing memory buffer to retain samples or features from previous tasks, and the retained data often carries task-specific noise that reduces generalization to new tasks. 4) knowledge distillation methods depend on keeping a copy of the previous model as a teacher, which doubles the memory requirement, and the distilled features tend to become increasingly task-specific as the sequence grows, losing the general representations needed for class-incremental classification. 5) Supervised continual learning methods require the classifier to be restructured each time new classes arrive, binding representation learning directly to the evolving label space and limiting flexibility in open-ended scenarios.

To address each of the previous limitations, we propose PatchAdaNet (Patch Adapter Network). To tackle the entanglement of shared and task-specific representations, PatchAdaNet explicitly separates the two through a two-stage design. In the first stage, which is performed once before sequential training begins, each image is divided into non-overlapping patches and an independent autoencoder (PatchAE) is trained to reconstruct each patch, where each PatchAE is assigned to a specific patch position index and trained across all pretraining images at that index. The layer-wise features of the patch autoencoders are then aggregated to form global frozen layers that serve as a domain-agnostic feature generalizer across tasks and remain unchanged throughout the entire learning process, without neither weight updates nor regularization, making them immune to forgetting by construction. In the second stage, learnable adapter layers refine the shared frozen aggregated features to learn task-specific global image representations capturing only what is novel to the current task while preserving the shared structure already encoded in the frozen layers. The resulting task-specific representations are then decoded by a decoder to reconstruct the full input image. To address the limitations of replay, PatchAdaNet maintains no memory buffer. Instead of storing past samples or features, it maintains the Global Feature Centroid (GFC), a proposed compact fixed-size running average of adapter output layers updated after each task. The GFC serves as feature regularizer anchor to penalize representational drift away from the accumulated shared representation across tasks without retaining any data. EWC is applied exclusively to the adapter layers rather than to the frozen layers to keep the weight-space regularization target narrow and well-defined rather than spread across the full network, which reduces parameter interference. GFC derive its regularization signal entirely from the model’s own training process, without storing past samples or features, or relying on a separate teacher model. The representation is learned without any supervision, and a linear classifier is trained on the concatenation of the frozen bottleneck encoder output and the GFC features after each task, ensuring that feature learning remains independent of the expanding class label space. In addition, we provide a comparative analysis of class-incremental learning performance under the same framework using two different model architectures, CNN and Vision Transformer autoencoders.

papers.title: Constellation Shaping for OFDM-ISAC Systems: A Systematic and Experimental Comparison
papers.abstract: Emerging integrated sensing and communications (ISAC) systems reuse the communications signal for radar-like sensing to provide environmental awareness. However, this integrated design imposes conflicting constraints on the modulation format, as communications systems use higher-order modulation formats while sensing systems use unit-modulus signals, making constellation shaping a key performance driver in ISAC systems. This paper develops a unified analytical and experimental framework for constellation shaping in monostatic orthogonal frequency division multiplexing ISAC systems and systematically analyzes its interaction with the three canonical sensing channel estimators (SCEs): the matched filter, the reciprocal filter, and the Wiener filter (WF). We begin by deriving constellation-dependent image signal-to-interference-and-noise ratio (ISINR) expressions for the SCEs that account for practical effects such as windowing and multi target scenarios. Based on this, we derive the corresponding entropy-maximizing channel input distributions. We generalize an autoencoder framework to optimize geometric, probabilistic, including conventional and generalized low-complexity probabilistic amplitude shaping (PAS), and joint constellation shaping across all three SCEs. Extensive simulations and hardware-in-the-loop experiments validate the derived ISINR and show that sensing performance is governed by the SCE choice, while communications performance is dominated by the shaping method. Notably, the WF combined with joint shaping achieves the best ISAC trade-off. Low-complexity PAS variants closely approach this performance, offering a flexible trade-off and outperforming legacy modulation formats.

Therefore, next-generation communications systems are envisioned to integrate sensing capabilities by reusing the OFDM communications signal in a radar-like manner [2, 1], improving energy, hardware, and spectral efficiency compared to operating two separate systems.

This degradation depends on the SCE employed at the sensing receiver to remove the information-bearing transmit symbols. Common SCE include the MF (MF), which maximizes the output SNR (SNR) at the cost of signaling-induced interference, the RF (RF), which avoids this interference but introduces noise enhancement, and the WF, which balances both effects by minimizing the channel estimation MSE (MSE), while attenuating the target peak [3]. Accordingly, different intermediate metrics have been used to characterize the individual degradation mechanisms. For example, the EISL (EISL) quantifies signaling-induced sidelobes but does not account for noise enhancement or the attenuation of the target peak. In contrast, the output SNR captures the target power relative to noise but neglects signaling-induced interference. While the MSE captures target attenuation, noise enhancement, and signaling-induced interference, it describes them as estimation error and does not compare the power of the target to the resulting image noise-and-interference floor [4]. This limits its ability to compare the considered SCE [4].

Since the modulation format fundamentally determines both SC performance [7], constellation shaping has emerged as a practical tool to govern the SC trade-off inherent in ISAC systems and to outperform legacy modulation formats such as QAM. Constellation shaping can be broadly categorized into (i) geometric shaping, which optimizes the constellation symbol locations assuming equal probabilities of occurrence; (ii) probabilistic shaping, which optimizes the probabilities of occurrence of the symbols under fixed constellation symbol locations (e.g., for QAM); and (iii) joint shaping, which jointly optimizes both the symbol locations and their probabilities of occurrence.

While AE (AE)-based constellation optimization is well established in communications [8, 9], its extension to ISAC is recent. Prior work has studied probabilistic shaping for the MF and compared geometric, probabilistic, and joint shaping, showing that joint shaping achieves the best overall SC performance [10, 11, 12]. So far, constellations optimized for ISAC [4, 13] are designed for specific sensing constraints. However, practical ISAC systems must dynamically adapt their modulation to varying SC requirements. While a codebook of offline-optimized constellations may be stored for a discretized set of SC requirements, a fine sensing constraint grid increases the memory requirements, whereas coarse quantization may either sacrifice communications performance or violate the sensing requirement and online training is computationally impractical. This motivates continuously adaptive constellations [14] for ISAC that can generate a constellation for the currently required sensing constraint without online retraining or the storage of a densely sampled constellation codebook. For the WF, such an adaptation is particularly relevant since the constellation additionally depends on the sensing scenario.

So far, only specific combinations have been explored, such as geometric [5] or probabilistic [4, 15] shaping for the RF or probabilistic shaping for the WF [4]. In particular, [4] fixes the constellation points and restricts the design to probabilistic shaping, while employing an MSE-based sensing constraint to obtain a convex optimization problem. Hence, neither is a comparable image domain metric optimized directly, nor is the SC trade-off achievable by jointly optimizing geometric and probabilistic shaping explored. Therefore, the literature lacks a unified comparison of geometric, probabilistic, and joint shaping across different SCE.

papers.title: Boundaries of groups with compact-by-amenable decomposition
papers.abstract: We look at the Liouville property (triviality of harmonic functions) of topological groups G relative to a compact subgroup K. We show that Gelfand pairs have this property. Furthermore, we show that this property holds if and only if G admits a product decomposition G = K S for an amenable subgroup S. We identify the Poisson and Furstenberg boundaries of these groups. This applies in particular to reductive algebraic groups over local fields.

papers.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
papers.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.
papers.intro:
We study open-ended lifelong learning as a continuing process in which agents autonomously generate goals, accumulate knowledge from interaction, and reuse that knowledge to acquire new capabilities. Unlike learning toward a fixed terminal task, this process is not organized around a predefined endpoint. A suggestive image comes from The Wild Robot: cast ashore on an unfamiliar island with only her built-in directives, Roz learns to coexist with the wildlife and, by raising an orphaned gosling, comes to belong to the island. Future autonomous agents may likewise enter physical or digital worlds carrying only system-level directives, and must confront unfamiliar phenomena, discover new things to do, and devise new strategies without human intervention.

Unlike learning toward a fixed terminal task, this process is not organized around a predefined endpoint. A suggestive image comes from The Wild Robot: cast ashore on an unfamiliar island with only her built-in directives, Roz learns to coexist with the wildlife and, by raising an orphaned gosling, comes to belong to the island. Future autonomous agents may likewise enter physical or digital worlds carrying only system-level directives, and must confront unfamiliar phenomena, discover new things to do, and devise new strategies without human intervention.

Toward this vision, substantial progress has been made in enabling agents to learn and act in open worlds. Reinforcement and imitation learning support long-horizon control (Baker et al., 2022; Hafner et al., 2023), while LLM-based agents combine planning, memory, and reflection to tackle increasingly complex tasks (Zhu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025; Shinn et al., 2023). Systems such as Voyager, Optimus-1, and AriGraph further demonstrate how reusable skills, structured experience, and knowledge graphs can support knowledge accumulation and reuse (Wang et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Anokhin et al., 2025). Despite these advances, much of the research remains organized around predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. Although systems such as Voyager support autonomous exploration, an individual agent still learns primarily from its own interactions, limiting the range of experience available to guide its development. Open-endedness research does generate new challenges rather than fixing them, by co-evolving environments with their solvers or by asking a foundation model which tasks are interesting (Wang et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2023), but this concerns what a single learner pursues next. Knowledge acquired by one agent does not automatically become available to others. This motivates moving beyond individual learning toward agent-group evolution, where experience acquired through diverse interactions can contribute to a shared, growing body of knowledge.

Learning from others offers a natural route from individual learning to collective improvement. CAMEL and MetaGPT enable agents to collaborate through role-based communication and structured workflows (Li et al., 2023; Hong et al., 2024), while Generative Agents combines memory, reflection, and social interaction to support information diffusion and coordination (Park et al., 2023). More directly, Group-Evolving Agents (GEA) shares evolutionary traces across agents and turns them into framework-level improvements through reflection (Weng et al., 2026). Memory systems such as G-Memory and LLMA-Mem keep shared memory across LLM agents (Zhang et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026), and selective-sharing methods pass only chosen experiences or policy modules between agents (Gerstgrasser et al., 2023; Nath et al., 2026). These approaches demonstrate different ways for agents to benefit from one another, from coordinating actions to improving their own implementations or sharing memory and experience, though most are evaluated with tasks given in advance. For open-ended lifelong learning, we focus on a complementary challenge: how to turn knowledge acquired through individual interactions into a shared resource that supports continued exploration and capability acquisition across the group. This calls for distinguishing memories tied to an agent’s particular circumstances from experience that can be reused by others, and continually consolidating the latter as agents explore and learn.

To this end, we introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning (Figure 1). OpenKAGE enables agents to autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. Two mechanisms underpin this process. First, a two-layer knowledge representation separates private situated memories from transferable experience and skills, retaining the applicability conditions needed for reuse across agents. Second, a knowledge-sharing mechanism semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim and remain maintained by their authors. We evaluate OpenKAGE in Minecraft, where agents must survive, explore, and develop increasingly advanced capabilities through sustained interaction with an open world. Starting with empty knowledge stores, agents accumulate and share knowledge acquired through their own exploration. Across four backbone models, OpenKAGE supports sustained exploration and progression to advanced technological milestones, obtaining obsidian on all four and entering the Nether on three, while reducing deaths relative to the planner-only control; on the default backbone it also outperforms Voyager and an Echo baseline, neither of which reaches obsidian or the Nether within the evaluated horizon. Furthermore, knowledge accumulated by one group can be transferred to a newly initialized group using a different backbone model, substantially improving its survival and exploration progress. Together, these results show that knowledge accumulated through individual interactions supports continued learning within a group and capability acquisition by new agents.

papers.title: Delay Mismatches Shape the Spectra of Three Synchronized Semiconductor Lasers
papers.abstract: We study a network of three synchronized chaotic lasers and the radio frequency spectra of the intensity fluctuations. The position and morphology of the peaks are significantly different depending on the set of lasers being synchronized. The lasers and coupling paths are similar but not identical in all parameters, including their feedback and coupling delay times. The inverse of the delay mismatch between each pair of lasers introduces characteristic frequencies that shape the spectral response of the synchronized system. By studying two different three-laser configurations, we find that peaks appear whenever multiple harmonic contributions overlap in frequency, resulting in constructive enhancement of the spectral power. Numerical simulations performed with the same delay configurations show a clear agreement with the experimental measurements, reproducing both the peak positions and the overall spectral structure. These results indicate that the frequency content of the synchronized dynamics is largely determined by the delay-mismatch network and its harmonics.

papers.title: Radio emission from a local Little Red Dot: a challenge to the ionized cocoon scenario
papers.abstract: Several scenarios have been proposed to explain the properties of Little Red Dots (LRDs), invoking either heavy obscuration by dense neutral gas, super-Eddington accretion, or an ionized gas cocoon that produces electron scattering. Radio observations can distinguish between these scenarios. Radio emission is largely unaffected by neutral gas and dust obscuration, whereas free-free absorption can suppress it in the presence of large free electron columns. Here, we investigate the origin of radio emission from the local LRD J1047. We jointly analyze its radio data and the broad H$\alpha$ emission from optical spectroscopy to test the predictions of different physical scenarios. We find that the observed radio luminosity must have an AGN origin, and it is consistent with that of a standard radio-quiet AGN obscured by dense neutral gas. Pure super-Eddington accretion underpredicts the radio luminosity by a factor of $\sim 30$, although a combination of super-Eddington accretion and obscuration remains viable. Interestingly, the statistically preferred model for the H$\alpha$ profile is an exponential fit, which is often associated with electron scattering in LRDs. This interpretation implies an electron column density of $N_e=2.4\times10^{24}\rm~cm^{-2}$ and a strong free-free absorption ($\tau_{\rm ff,5GHz}\sim 10^6$), incompatible with the radio detection. This tension suggests that the exponential profiles of J1047 more likely trace a stratified broad line region rather than electron scattering, with potential implications for virial black-hole mass estimates also in high-$z$ LRDs. Less likely, the radio emission may escape through a partially covering ionized medium or originate outside the putative scattering cocoon.

papers.intro:
One of the most exciting results of the first years of JWST operations is the discovery of Little Red Dots [67, LRDs,], a population of compact, broad-line AGN characterized by a distinctive V-shaped spectral energy distribution (SED) [see 36, for a recent review]. Many LRDs exhibit narrow absorption features in their broad Balmer lines [44, 68, 43], rare among AGN discovered before JWST [41, 34, 113]. Despite the evidence for accreting black holes (BHs) provided by their broad emission lines and luminosities, LRDs are remarkably X-ray weak, with stringent upper limits up to ∼\sim2-3 dex below standard Type I AGN expectations [18, 27, 117, 2, 66, 72]. Several scenarios have been proposed to explain these peculiar properties (see Inayoshi and Ho 36). In one scenario, dense neutral gas surrounding the central BH, with densities of n∼109−10​cm−3n\sim 10^{9-10}\ \rm cm^{-3} and potentially high covering factors, produces the observed optical emission and Balmer features, while absorbing the intrinsic X-ray emission [37, 39, 45]. Alternatively, the X-ray weakness may be intrinsic, resulting from super-Eddington accretion, which can suppress and collimate the X-ray emission through the formation of a slim disk and a weak corona [80, 55, 63, 50, 108]. In this scenario, the optical properties of LRDs can be reproduced when they are observed through the equatorial Broad Line Region (BLR) and dusty torus distribution [65, 27, 55].Many LRDs also exhibit non-Gaussian broad-line profiles, well reproduced by exponential fits [93, 78, 23]. These profiles have been interpreted as the result of Thomson scattering by free electrons in an ionized hydrogen layer [93, 107, 19, 68, 100, 26]. If so, these broad components would no longer trace the BLR dynamics, implying BH masses up to 1-2 dex below standard virial estimates and correspondingly higher accretion rates [93, 13, 14, 36].

Conversely, the large free-electron columns invoked by the scattering scenario may produce strong free-free absorption (FFA), particularly at low frequencies, and alter the radio spectrum [112, 71, 93].

papers.title: TechReport: Implementing CHERI in gem5
papers.abstract: Despite countless mitigation efforts, memory safety issues still prevail. The recently discovered security issues in PHP underline this fact. One of the most promising approaches to solving this problem is the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI). There is a well-developed ecosystem of ISA simulators, compilers, operating systems, and hardware designs that support CHERI. However, the lack of a simulator modeling microarchitectural detail hinders efficient and fast design space exploration for CHERI-enhanced designs means the performance impact of CHERI remains understudied. Therefore, we present gem5-CHERI: a CHERI-enhanced adaptation of the gem5 simulator that can boot the CheriBSD operating system and run custom workloads. The simulator is available open-source on GitHub.

In recent years, the concept of Capability Hardware Enhanced RISC Instructions (CHERI) [9] is gaining traction as one of the most promising and holistic approaches to architectural memory safety. CHERI’s main concept are so called Capabilities that extend ordinary pointers by appending meta data encoding the bounds and permissions plus an additional tag bit, at the cost of effectively doubling the original size. CHERI extends customary Instruction Set Architectures (ISAs) such as ARM and RISC-V with additional instructions to handle and manipulate these capabilities.

papers.title: New Heuristics for Large-Scale Joint Order Selection, Allocation, Batching, and Picking
papers.abstract: Manual order picking in warehouses plays an important role in modern e-commerce fulfillment. In this work, we consider a warehouse fulfillment model recently introduced by researchers at Zalando, a leading fashion e-commerce company. It simultaneously models the hierarchy of decision stages in a very large-scale setting with a semi-online order set, where only a certain number of items have to be fulfilled in each time interval. For their base model, we present both new and improved algorithms together with comprehensive performance evaluation. We further extend the model to a setting with multiple phases, which more closely represents the situation observed in real warehouses, and adapt the algorithms to this setting, including new variants that incorporate multi-phase specific features. We demonstrate that this extension allows us to model, control, and optimize for certain parameters such as order age which play an important role in managerial considerations with the growing importance of next or even same day delivery.

papers.intro:
In the age of ever-growing e-commerce, manual order picking in large-scale warehouses still plays an important part in the fulfillment supply chain. While semi- or fully-automated warehouses are seeing increasing use, manual order picking is still seen in a majority of warehouses [7]. In a typical setting, items are distributed on shelves throughout the warehouse and pickers collect them individually. The cost of order picking is often cited to make up more than 50% of the total cost of the warehouse operation. Pickers, on average, spend around half of their time traveling between their assigned items to pick or the drop-off stations [36]. This implies that there are major cost-saving opportunities just through optimization of this part of the supply chain. In this work we focus on a setting recently introduced by researchers working at Zalando, one of the largest e-commerce fashion retailers in Europe [3]. Their setting combines a multi-layered decision process with a very large-scale setting, with tens of thousands of pending orders at any given point in time.

Their setting combines a multi-layered decision process with a very large-scale setting, with tens of thousands of pending orders at any given point in time.

A multitude of variants of order picking problems in real warehouses exist and an even larger amount of settings has been studied from a theoretical perspective. Several recent surveys provide a comprehensive overview over the current state of the art [7, 22, 28, 12, 4]. While some publications discuss the optimization of the warehouse layout itself, most works consider a fixed layout which has been determined during the warehouse’s initial design phase. Commonly studied layouts are rectangular shelf arrangements with one or more cross-aisles, fishbone configurations and V-shaped rack configurations [32, 11, 37, 5]. Items are spread across the shelves throughout the warehouse. Unlike in settings such as spare parts management for big industrial machines, in e-commerce often many items of a specific article (SKU) are stocked inside of the warehouse. It has been shown to be beneficial to spread these items throughout the warehouse instead of keeping all at the same location, as this enables routing synergies when collecting items [25], so modern warehouses typically support such storage policies. This strategy is called scattered or explosive storage.

This strategy is called scattered or explosive storage.

In our setting, we focus on a pure picker-to-parts model, where humans, possibly with the help of some form of cart, walk throughout the warehouse and collect the items. Some other variants have been studied where the pickers are assisted by technological tools such as automated guided vehicles which deliver picked orders to the depots or rideable “cobots” which enable pickers to travel across large distances more quickly [21, 35]. The pending demand is usually specified by a list of orders, each of which consists of one or several articles contained in the warehouse. While some low throughput systems exist where each order is individually collected by a single picker, in larger warehouses with high order volume the task is typically spread amongst several pickers who each pick articles belonging to different orders. For each picker, an efficient route from the depots through the warehouse has to be calculated. The picked items are then combined into the respective orders in a later step of the logistics process, which we do not consider here. This setting and closely similar ones have been studied by many authors. Focusing on the picklist route step, results in [31, 29, 8, 26] have shown polynomial time solvability of this subproblem for certain restricted warehouse layouts. Settings which combine batching/assignment and routing have been studied in works such as [6, 2, 34] and are usually computationally hard.

While not every one of Zalando’s warehouses contains all of the products, we model several hundred thousand distinct articles with a million total items contained in our instances spread across 100100 zones with 100×100100\times 100 locations each. papers.title: Biases and Limits of AlphaFold Predictions for Non-Globular Proteins
papers.abstract: AlphaFold has transformed protein structure prediction, making structural models accessible across the life sciences. We explore experimentally validated cases of non-globular proteins to uncover where predictions diverge from biologically relevant structural states and how molecular context shapes these discrepancies, guiding a more informed interpretation of AlphaFold models.

papers.title: Data-Driven Factored Abstractions of Stochastic Systems
papers.abstract: Formal verification and correct-by-design policy synthesis for stochastic dynamical systems face significant scalability challenges due to the curse of dimensionality. These challenges are exacerbated when the system dynamics are unknown and abstractions must be constructed from data. This paper introduces a data-driven framework for constructing factored interval Markov decision process (fIMDP) abstractions from noisy transition observations. Assuming conditional independence of successor coordinates and known coordinate-wise Lipschitz bounds on the dynamics, the framework estimates marginal transition probabilities rather than joint probabilities, resulting in an exponential reduction in the number of probability entries to be estimated and stored. We establish finite-sample confidence guarantees that the abstraction captures the concrete transition probabilities uniformly over each abstract region, enabling certified lower bounds on satisfaction probabilities for $\omega$-regular specifications. Experiments on benchmark systems, including pendulum swing-up, unicycle control, and a four-dimensional planar robot model, demonstrate improvements in certified satisfaction probability lower bounds of up to 25 percentage points compared with a state-of-the-art flat IMDP abstraction method. Our framework required up to 23x less memory and was consistently faster in constructing the abstraction.

papers.intro:
Stochastic dynamical systems operating in uncertain environments require rigorous guarantees on safety and task satisfaction (Alur, 2015; Baier and Katoen, 2008). Formal abstractions support verification and correct-by-design policy synthesis by representing continuous-state dynamics through finite-state models with quantified guarantees. When the dynamics or noise distributions are unknown, constructing such abstractions requires reasoning from observations while accounting for the uncertainty introduced by finite data. Data-driven formal abstraction methods provide a principled basis for this task; see, e.g., (Jackson et al., 2021; Kazemi et al., 2024; Nazeri et al., 2025b) and the recent survey (Samari et al., 2026).

Despite recent progress, scaling data-driven abstractions to high-dimensional state spaces remains challenging. In a flat abstraction, (bounds on) the transition probability must be estimated and stored for each abstract state and action over the full abstract state and action space, leading to many probabilities to estimate, which in turn requires much data, and substantial storage requirements. Factored representations exploit conditional independence between successor-state components to represent these transitions through marginal distributions. For continuous-state stochastic systems, this structure has been used to construct formal abstractions represented as dynamic Bayesian networks from a given model (Soudjani et al., 2015; Soudjani et al., 2017). Subsequent developments have exploited structured representations for abstraction-based control synthesis (Van Huijgevoort et al., 2023; Mathiesen et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). These results motivate the construction of factored abstractions from observations when the underlying dynamics and noise distributions are unknown.

papers.title: DRIFT: Detachable Reasoning for Runtime-Flexible and Efficient End-to-End Driving
papers.abstract: The integration of vision-language models (VLMs) into end-to-end (E2E) autonomous driving has demonstrated strong potential by providing scene description and reasoning capabilities. However, VLMs are computationally expensive, and switching language reasoning on and off at runtime without hurting closed-loop performance has not been demonstrated, which hinders practical adoption. To address these issues, we propose DRIFT, an E2E autonomous driving framework that integrates a lightweight language model (LM) for visual question answering and action commentary. By efficiently projecting intermediate driving representations into the language embedding space, we demonstrate that a compact LM (<150M parameters) can achieve strong scene description and action commentary. Furthermore, we introduce a runtime-flexible planning module that is trained on surrogate reasoning features distilled from the LM and can be conditioned on either the LM or the surrogate reasoning features at inference. This design enables bypassing the LM entirely when required by deployment constraints, without sacrificing driving performance. With only 255M parameters, DRIFT reaches up to a Driving Score (DS) of 97.03 and a Success Rate of 89.39% (mean over three runs) on Bench2Drive by interleaving its LM and surrogate reasoning at a chosen reasoning rate. This is on par with the strongest non-language models while being far more compact than existing VLM-based models. DRIFT further achieves competitive results on the real-world NAVSIM and AlpaSim benchmarks at significantly lower computational cost than existing VLM-based approaches. papers.intro:
End-to-end (E2E) driving models [13, 16] achieve promising driving performance, but they lack interpretability and high-level semantic reasoning. To address these limitations, recent works have integrated vision-language models (VLMs) into the driving pipeline, enabling visual question answering (VQA) [32, 34] and language-guided reasoning [32, 8]. Despite their success, existing VLM-based E2E methods typically improve language performance by scaling up the language models (LMs), incurring substantial computational overhead. Approaches such as DriveVLM [34], ORION [8], and AdaThinkDrive [25] employ models exceeding 7B parameters, making real-time deployment on edge hardware increasingly challenging. This motivates us to study how strong language reasoning can be achieved with a significantly smaller LM.

To address these limitations, recent works have integrated vision-language models (VLMs) into the driving pipeline, enabling visual question answering (VQA) [32, 34] and language-guided reasoning [32, 8]. Despite their success, existing VLM-based E2E methods typically improve language performance by scaling up the language models (LMs), incurring substantial computational overhead. Approaches such as DriveVLM [34], ORION [8], and AdaThinkDrive [25] employ models exceeding 7B parameters, making real-time deployment on edge hardware increasingly challenging. This motivates us to study how strong language reasoning can be achieved with a significantly smaller LM.

A second limitation is that these frameworks couple language reasoning tightly to the driving pipeline, requiring LM inference throughout deployment. To reduce this cost, some models run separate fast (standard E2E) and slow (VLM-based) branches and switch between them at runtime [30, 10, 41], while others switch a single VLA between thinking and non-thinking modes [25, 45], but most of them still rely on a large model in complex scenes. Others distill the LM into the driving model, such as DiMA [11], VLM-AD [38], and VERDI [7], but language only shapes the planner during training, and the planner cannot take reasoning as input at inference. papers.title: The GECKOS Survey: deriving bar properties in edge-on galaxies from molecular gas kinematics
papers.abstract: The characterisation of disc-connected structures such as bars and nuclear rings is a difficult task in edge-on galaxies. We present a simple method to derive bar position angles and lengths in edge-on galaxies using molecular gas kinematics from ALMA observations. Our approach exploits the geometry of bar-driven gas flows: assuming that cold molecular gas settles into an elliptical nuclear ring oriented orthogonally to the bar, the line-of-sight velocity of the nuclear ring varies predictably with bar viewing angle. Using only the observed nuclear ring velocity and a circular velocity derived from Multi-Gaussian Expansion (MGE) stellar mass models, we construct a grid of bisymmetric bar flow models spanning a range of radial and transverse velocities to constrain the bar position angle. We validate this methodology on a toy model and an isolated galaxy hydrodynamical simulation snapshot, demonstrating that the technique reliably distinguishes three viewing angle brackets: side-on (0{\deg} - 35{\deg}), intermediate (35{\deg} - 65{\deg}), and end-on (65{\deg} - 90{\deg}). Applying this method to six GECKOS Survey galaxies hosting boxy-peanut bulges with ALMA CO observations, we find four bars oriented side-on, one at an intermediate angle, and one end-on case (IC 1711), the latter confirming predictions from stellar kinematics alone. Derived nuclear ring sizes and deprojected bar lengths are broadly consistent with measurements from more face-on literature samples. This method offers a practical and computationally inexpensive means of constraining bar properties in edge-on galaxies, complementing full dynamical modelling approaches.

papers.intro:
Bars are well-known to impart a profound effect on their host galaxies. By focusing disc stars primarily into elongated (x1x_{1}) orbits, they act as galactic gas highways, funnelling gas along them and depositing it into the central regions (Spinoso et al., 2017, e.g.). This gas often settles into a star-forming nuclear ring at or near the inner Lindblad resonance (Kim et al., 2012; Li et al., 2015; Sormani et al., 2018, ILR; e.g.), whose new stars in turn build a nuclear stellar disc (Cole et al., 2014; Bittner et al., 2020, e.g.). Both the nuclear ring and nuclear stellar disc are expected to be somewhat ellipsoidal (Comerón et al., 2010, e.g.), with their position angle orthogonal to that of the bar (Contopoulos and Papayannopoulos, 1980; Athanassoula, 1992a, e.g.). Bars, bar-built nuclear stellar discs and nuclear rings are therefore closely linked galactic structures, with their formation and evolution entwined (Schultheis et al., 2025, for a recent review, see).

Somewhat counterintuitively, edge-on galaxies constitute an ideal testbed to study bars in disc galaxies. In spite of challenges with visual identification owing to their high degree of inclination, the maximal component of velocity from the line-of-sight projection can be recovered, allowing dynamical studies to place constraints on the role of bars to drive gas, stars and angular momentum redistribution in galaxies. Despite difficulties with geometry and dust obscuration, the signature of a nuclear stellar disc dynamically-decoupled from the main galactic disc is readily observable in the plane of edge-on galaxies as a small region of anti-correlation between the third (h3h_{3}, skew) and first (V⋆V_{\star}, mean velocity) moments of the stellar line-of-sight velocity distribution (Chung and Bureau, 2004, LOSVD; e.g.). Additionally, the region of influence of the bar (and its projected structure, a boxy-peanut bulge) frequently display coherent regions of h3h_{3}-V⋆V_{\star} sign matching often extending 11 – 22 kpc off the plane of the disc (Bureau and Athanassoula, 2005; Iannuzzi and Athanassoula, 2015; Li et al., 2018; Fraser-McKelvie et al., 2025, e.g.). The nuclear disc can also be demarcated by a radial peak in the ratio of V⋆/σ⋆V_{\star}/\sigma_{\star} (Gadotti et al., 2020, e.g.), where σ⋆\sigma_{\star} is the line-of-sight velocity dispersion, or through identifying a star-forming ring at its edge (van den Bosch and Emsellem, 1998; de Sá-Freitas et al., 2025, e.g.).

Through stellar kinematics alone it is difficult to place constraints on key bar physical parameters such as the bar viewing angle and bar length in edge-on galaxies, due in part to dust obscuration and continuum signal-to-noise ratio requirements. Even in deep and highly spatially resolved nearby galaxy samples such as the GECKOS11 1 GECKOS: Generalising Edge-on galaxies and their Chemical bimodalities, Kinematics, and Outflows out to Solar environments (van de Sande et al., in prep.; Fraser-McKelvie et al. 2025). survey, extinction due to dust in the plane of the galaxy, measurement uncertainties, and a lack of diagnostic criteria all contribute to the lack of feasibility. The bar viewing angle (which we will refer to as the bar position angle throughout) is a vital parameter to determine the deprojected bar length, key to properly characterise a galaxy’s mass distribution and important for some methods of bar pattern speed measurement (Tahmasebzadeh et al., 2022; Dattathri et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025, e.g.).

A path forward involves turning to the gas flowing along bars and settling into orbital resonances. Despite the depth of the GECKOS observations, the relatively low spectral resolution of the Multi Unit Spectroscopic Explorer (MUSE) instrument (R∼2500R\sim 2500 or ∼50​km​s−1\sim 50\penalty\ \rm{km}\penalty\ \rm{s}^{-1} at Hα\alpha) coupled with dust obscuration makes kinematic extraction of multi-component ionised gas emission lines difficult and the separation of bar orbits in position-velocity space impossible for the GECKOS MUSE sample. However, the dynamically cold nature of molecular gas coupled with a knowledge of the discrete resonance features that it aggregates in means that observations of sufficient spectral resolution can be used to fit non-axisymmetric flow patterns induced by bars and derive useful parameters (Spekkens and Sellwood, 2007; Hogarth et al., 2024, e.g.). Full dynamical modelling with sophisticated treatment of bisymmetric flows (Sormani and Barnes, 2019; López-Cobá et al., 2022; Hogarth et al., 2023, e.g.) is however time-consuming and thus challenging to apply to large galaxy surveys. A simpler method to derive bar properties in edge-on galaxies using molecular gas data is therefore warranted.

The key to our model is the assumption that cold gas in the bar-dominated region is located within resonance rings, one of which (the inner ring) is roughly at the end of the stellar bar, the other (the nuclear ring) at the edge of the nuclear disc and inside the ILR (Ruiz-García et al., 2024; Sormani et al., 2024, e.g.), though note that some discrepancy still exists with hydrodynamical simulations (see Fragkoudi et al., 2021, for a summary). The (periodic) orbits supporting the gas flows are elliptical (Athanassoula, 1992a), particularly near the edge of the nuclear disc, and hence the magnitude of the velocity component along the line of sight varies perceptibly with bar (and nuclear ring) position angle.

papers.title: On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models
papers.abstract: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by $+2.42$ points on RULER, $+1.08$ on LongBench, and $+0.76$ on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only $0.72$--$3.57$ GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.

papers.intro:
Hybrid attention models retain full attention in only a few layers and use linear attention elsewhere, preserving long-context modeling capabilities and precise retrieval (Arora et al., 2024a; Jelassi et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a), while substantially reducing computation and KV-cache memory usage (Katharopoulos et al., 2020; Sun et al., 2025b; Sun et al., 2025a). Owing to this favorable trade-off between performance and efficiency, hybrid attention has been adopted in a growing number of production-scale large language models (LLMs) (Li et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Cao et al., 2026; Team, 2026; Team et al., 2026). To avoid the prohibitive cost of pretraining from scratch, existing approaches reuse the weights of pretrained LLMs and replace a subset of full attention layers with linear attention, achieving Transformers-to-hybrid conversion. Model quality is then recovered through distillation and continued training (Kasai et al., 2021; Bick et al., 2024; Lan et al., 2025; Goldstein et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Bick et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025). A central challenge in this conversion process is determining which full attention layers to retain under a given budget. As the only layers in the resulting hybrid model that can directly access the entire context, their placement largely determines how much of the original model’s capability can be recovered (Li et al., 2026a; Chen et al., 2026; Lan et al., 2026).

Exhaustively evaluating all possible layer combinations is prohibitively expensive, motivating existing work to explore a variety of layer-selection strategies. Beyond fixed uniform interleaving patterns, PostNAS (Gu et al., 2026) performs supernet-based architecture search, KL-LS (Li et al., 2026a) ranks layers by the KL reduction from per-layer restoration and distillation, and HALO (Chen et al., 2026) uses replacement-based sensitivity scoring. More recently, FlashMorph (Lan et al., 2026) jointly optimizes layer-wise gates to learn a global hybrid configuration. Each layer interpolates between aligned full- and linear-attention branches through a continuous gate, which is then discretized under a given full-attention budget. FlashMorph preserves strong long-context recall and general benchmark performance while substantially reducing layer-selection cost.

Limitations. FlashMorph’s layer-selection process still suffers from two forms of off-policy mismatch. (L1) Off-policy computation: The forward computation used during layer selection differs from that of the candidate discrete model. Continuous mixing allows the full- and linear-attention branches to complement each other, while each layer operates on teacher-forced hidden states. At deployment, only one branch is retained per layer and hidden states are generated by the hybrid model itself. Consequently, complementarities observed under continuous mixing may not transfer to the final discrete architecture, and the resulting layer-importance estimates may fail to capture error accumulation and cross-layer compensation. (L2) Off-policy weights: The weights used for layer selection are inherited from the original model and remain frozen during gate optimization, without adapting to the hybrid architecture induced by the selection policy. Layer selection therefore cannot account for the cross-layer co-adaptation of model weights during subsequent recovery, which may alter the layer-importance ranking observed before recovery.

Our Method. We introduce FlashMorph2, which improves upon FlashMorph by bringing the on-policy principle into its layer-selection process. papers.title: DiWALI: Diffusion Policy Learning in World Models via Latent Action Inference from Human and Robot Play
papers.abstract: Learning robot manipulation is constrained by the availability of action-labeled robot data, for both imitation and world models. Humans can demonstrate skills in seconds, but their demonstrations lack the required robot actions. We introduce DiWALI, a framework that learns and improves diffusion policies within a world model trained on human and robot play. DiWALI infers latent actions from consecutive frames using an inverse dynamics model, enabling world model training without action labels, and grounds them in robot commands through a decoder trained separately on robot play. Skill policies are trained over latent actions from action-free human demonstrations and improved with reinforcement learning in imagination. On the CALVIN benchmark, DiWALI policies trained solely from human demonstrations substantially outperform baselines trained with robot demonstrations. Incorporating human play into the world model training also yields stronger policies after fine-tuning than using the same amount of robot play alone. Experiments on a physical robot show that skills learned primarily from human demonstrations are further improved in imagination with a world model trained on human and robot play. Together, these results demonstrate that human experience can support both manipulation skill acquisition and subsequent policy improvement, reducing reliance on action-labeled robot data. Videos, dataset and code are available at https://diwali.cs.uni-freiburg.de.

papers.title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics
papers.abstract: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior. We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.
papers.intro:
Aerodynamic drag and lift coefficients govern vehicle range, stability, and fuel economy. Design engineers evaluate hundreds of geometries against these coefficients before converging on a design. Drag and lift are surface integrals of the pressure and wall shear stress. Computing these quantities requires numerically solving the Navier-Stokes equations around the vehicle, which is a task traditionally done by high-fidelity CFD solvers. A single simulation can take hours to converge. Neural surrogates have emerged as computationally efficient alternatives. Given a vehicle geometry, these surrogates can predict surface and volume flow fields in milliseconds to seconds (Wu et al., 2024; Adams et al., 2025; Ranade et al., 2025; Choy et al., 2025; Nabian et al., 2024), which makes wide design sweeps tractable (Ananthan et al., 2024; Ashton et al., 2024c; Ashton et al., 2024a; Elrefaie et al., 2024). This speedup comes at an upfront cost. Each surrogate has to be trained on many CFD runs of the vehicle class, and every new class, e.g., a different body style, segment, or program, requires repeating this expensive training process.

This generalization is critical in practice since each new target domain typically comes with only a handful of CFD runs. Generating more simulations is precisely the cost that pretraining is meant to avoid (Zhang et al., 2026).

In this work, we adopt them as our transfer learning testbed and aim to answer the following question: How can a pretrained aerodynamic surrogate adapt to a new vehicle class from a few simulations while keeping its accuracy on the source dataset? Answering this question raises three challenges. (i) Attribution. Improvement after fine-tuning mixes the value of pretraining with the value of the target simulations themselves. A credible comparison must hold the architecture, data, and selection protocol fixed. (ii) Coverage versus physics. A target geometry close to the source can still differ in solver, mesh, and flow conditions, so geometric similarity alone does not determine transfer. (iii) Conflicting source updates. Source information that helps one target can hurt another, so adaptation must detect when a source update opposes the target objective.

papers.title: Analytic guiding center formulas for bounce-transit motion in a concentric circular, finite inverse aspect ratio tokamak geometry
papers.abstract: Bounce-transit motion in concentric circular magnetic geometry is typically analyzed in the limit that the inverse aspect ratio, $\varepsilon$, is small. We prove that this approximation is not necessary to study a concentric circular geometry by deriving new analytical formulas while retaining a non-zero $\varepsilon.$ We use these formulas to demonstrate that the approximation is robust for $\varepsilon \lesssim 0.3.$

papers.title: Time-Varying Bayesian Optimization and Extremum Seekingfor Drift-Tube Linac Tuning at LANSCE
papers.abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) has emerged as a promising machine learning approach to accelerator tuning. It has the advantage of being able to incorporate prior information, including simulation and historical data, and explicitly model measurement noise. However, standard implementations can produce large, abrupt parameter updates that are undesirable and potentially unsafe in accelerator operation. They may also spend excessive time exploring less promising regions of the search space. We address these limitations by imposing soft and hard step size limits. We evaluate these methods by adjusting the radio frequency settings of the drift tube linac (DTL) at the Los Alamos Neutron Science Center (LANSCE) to maximize the particle count at the end of the linac. We first test the methods in simulation with constant exogenous parameters, then repeat the tests with drifting exogenous parameters. Under drifting conditions, progressively reducing the BO step size limit improved convergence. We also find that an initial BO segment followed by extremum seeking (ES), an approach we call BO-ES, combines BO's use of prior information and sample efficiency with ES's effectiveness in local optimization and drift tracking. Finally, tests on the LANSCE accelerator with BO-ES demonstrate an approximately $25\%$ reduction in losses at the end of the linac across different configurations of historical and simulation data.

The DTL operating point varies over time due to temperature fluctuations, magnetic hysteresis, component replacement, and gradual wear, among other effects, such that settings that are optimal at one time may be suboptimal later. These variations occur on both long timescales (e.g., across operating periods) and short timescales (e.g., within a single run).

Vanilla Bayesian optimization is also for static situations. Modifications must be made to deal with dynamic situations. While there are methods to deal with these dynamic situations, some of which we examine, there is another algorithm, bounded extremum seeking (ES) [35], which is very well-suited for the task [31, 29, 32, 36]. ES works locally and is model-independent, therefore it is robust for quickly time-varying conditions with large distribution shifts for which memorizing prior information can be misleading and can degrade performance.

papers.title: Solid-state formation of H$_2$CS and CH$_3$SH in molecular clouds: Carbon-initiated reactions with atomic and molecular hydrogen
papers.abstract: The solid-state formation pathways of thioformaldehyde (H$_2$CS) and methanethiol (CH$_3$SH) in dense molecular clouds remain poorly constrained. We investigate carbon-initiated reactions in hydrogen sulfide (H$_2$S) ice in the presence of atomic or molecular hydrogen. We co-deposited H$_2$S, ground-state atomic carbon, and H or H$_2$ at 10 K under ultra-high vacuum. We monitored the reaction products using reflection absorption infrared spectroscopy (RAIRS) and characterized their thermal desorption using temperature-programmed desorption (TPD) with quadrupole mass spectrometry. Gas-phase ab initio calculations were used to assess pathways to CH$_3$SH formation. Atomic carbon reacted with H$_2$S at 10 K to form H$_2$CS, detected as both monomers and H$_2$CS-derived oligomers. With atomic H, successive H addition to H$_2$CS leads to CH$_3$SH. With molecular H$_2$, CH$_3$SH also forms efficiently. The results support an alternative pathway in which C reacts with H$_2$ to form CH$_2$, which abstracts H from H$_2$S. The resulting CH$_3$ and SH radicals can then recombine to form CH$_3$SH. The infrared bands and TPD fragmentation patterns support the formation of H$_2$CS and CH$_3$SH in the ice at 10 K. These findings expand the set of viable solid-state pathways to sulfur-bearing molecules and constrain models of sulfur chemistry in prestellar environments.

papers.intro:
The detection of molecules in the interstellar medium provides fundamental constraints on the physical and chemical evolution of star- and planet-forming regions. Molecular inventories, abundance ratios, and spatial and thermal distributions encode the history of formation, processing, and transport of matter, making the origin of simple and complex species a central question in astrochemistry (Herbst and van Dishoeck, 2009; Öberg and Bergin, 2021; Cuppen et al., 2024, e.g.,). Although most of the more than 350 molecules11 1 https://cdms.astro.uni-koeln.de/ identified in interstellar and circumstellar environments have been detected in the gas phase through their rotational spectra, many abundant H-rich species are thought to form efficiently on icy grain surfaces such as H2O, CH4, NH3, and CH3OH (Ioppolo et al., 2008; Dulieu et al., 2010; Qasim et al., 2020a; Fedoseev et al., 2015b; Watanabe and Kouchi, 2002; Fuchs et al., 2009).

Laboratory solid-state experiments under dense molecular cloud conditions have shown that complex organic molecules (COMs) can form via non-energetic atom-addition and abstraction chemistry, without requiring thermal diffusion of heavy radicals. Instead, reactive intermediates generated in close proximity can undergo prompt, non-diffusive radical-radical recombination reactions (Fedoseev et al., 2015a; Chuang et al., 2016b; Chuang et al., 2020, e.g.,). This mechanism has since been incorporated into modern astrochemical models (Jin and Garrod, 2020; Garrod et al., 2022; Borshcheva et al., 2025). Consistent with this picture, infrared observations, including recent JWST results, show that these ices are chemically rich, containing both simple molecules and signatures of O-bearing complex species (Boogert et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2022; McClure et al., 2023).

Sulfur-bearing molecules have been detected in a wide range of environments, from cold cores to hot cores, hot corinos, and Galactic Center molecular clouds, and include both simple species, increasingly complex organosulfur molecules and sulfur-bearing carbon chains (Agúndez et al., 2014; Cernicharo et al., 2021). papers.title: A lepto-hadronic perspective on the properties of the candidate neutrino-emitter blazar 5BZQ J0808+4950
papers.abstract: The role of active galactic nuclei in the production of high-energy neutrinos has been highlighted by the association of the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 with IceCube neutrino events. In particular, blazars, with their powerful jets, are potential sites of neutrino production via (photo-)hadronic interactions. The gamma-ray bright blazar 5BZQJ0808+4950 is consistent with a spatial anisotropy in the IceCube neutrino all-sky maps. An individual high-energy neutrino event, IC110929A, was also reported in the direction of this blazar. Although the correlation between the gamma-ray bright blazars and the neutrino production remains inconclusive, 5BZQ J0808+4950, with a luminous accretion disk serving as a photon field for the photo-hadronic interactions, offers the opportunity to test the relation between neutrino production and the radiative output of the blazar jet. We compile available multi-wavelength data and analyze the gamma-ray light curve of 5BZQ J0808+4950, leading us to define six contemporaneous epochs to model the source's spectral energy distribution and its evolution over time. We use a lepto-hadronic, time-dependent framework to model 5BZQ J0808+4950, taking into account external photon fields. We find that the solutions corresponding to the different states the source exhibits are explained mostly by a change in the particles' injection properties. The correlation between the predicted X-ray and the neutrino luminosity in this source is stronger than the correlation between gamma-ray and neutrino luminosity. We predict that the rate of neutrinos detectable by IceCube for this blazar ranges from $\sim 10^{-3}$ to $\sim10^{-1}$ neutrinos per epoch. Assuming Poisson statistics, the predicted neutrino number contemporaneous with the interval in which the high-energy neutrino event IC110929A was detected, is compatible with the detection of one neutrino.
