papers.intro:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN), powered by accretion onto a central supermassive black hole, have since long been considered to be good candidates for the acceleration of (ultra-) high-energy cosmic rays (Hillas, 1984). If AGN jets are able to accelerate hadrons to sufficient energy, these particles can interact with photon fields (p​γp\gamma interactions; see Mücke et al., 1999, for an application to astrophysical environments) and in turn produce neutrinos (Mannheim and Biermann, 1989; Stecker et al., 1991; Stecker et al., 1992; Mannheim, 1993; Szabo and Protheroe, 1994; Mannheim, 1995; Mastichiadis, 1996; Protheroe, 1999; Atoyan and Dermer, 2001; Mücke and Protheroe, 2001; Atoyan and Dermer, 2003; Mücke et al., 2003; Dermer et al., 2009; Dermer et al., 2012; Dimitrakoudis et al., 2012; Böttcher et al., 2013; Halzen, 2013; Murase et al., 2014; Dermer et al., 2014; Mastichiadis, 2016; Gao et al., 2017; Murase et al., 2018; Oikonomou et al., 2019, see e.g.). Non-jetted AGN are also considered as possible neutrino emitters, invoking hadronic interactions (p​ppp interactions) taking place at the core of the AGN (Murase et al., 2016; Inoue et al., 2019; Inoue et al., 2021; Kheirandish et al., 2021; Fiorillo et al., 2024; Karavola et al., 2025; Neronov et al., 2025, see e.g.). In both cases, neutrinos are the smoking-gun signatures of hadronic interactions.

The current most sensitive detector for high-energy (≳\gtrsim TeV) astrophysical neutrino searches is the IceCube Neutrino observatory, located at the South Pole (IceCube Collaboration, 2013; Aartsen et al., 2013; Aartsen et al., 2014; Aartsen et al., 2015a; Aartsen et al., 2015b). As of today, only a few high-energy neutrino events detected by IceCube are spatially consistent with astrophysical sources that are thought to be capable of producing them. Currently, the strongest astrophysical neutrino signal originates from the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068 – a non-jetted, low-luminosity AGN – (IceCube Collaboration et al., 2022). papers.title: Exploiting Common Volatility Dynamics in High-Dimensional Portfolio Selection
papers.abstract: We study how commonalities in monthly realized stock volatilities can be exploited for high-dimensional covariance forecasting and portfolio selection. We compare latent factor models with ARMA models that pool dynamic parameters within pre-specified groups of stocks. We show that pooled ARMA models admit an exact dynamic factor representation with group-specific dynamics and stock-specific loadings. The implied static factor representation involves group-specific factors that need not be pervasive. Combining volatility forecasts with realized dynamic conditional correlations and nonlinear shrinkage, we evaluate out-of-sample minimum variance portfolios of S&P 500 constituents. Pooling-based approaches consistently outperform the alternatives across portfolio constraints and model specifications.

papers.title: Stafford's conjecture on cyclicity of torsion modules
papers.abstract: We prove that over a Weyl algebra over a field of characteristic zero $A_n(k)$, every nonzero $d\in A_n(k)$ admits $F,R,S\in A_n(k)$ such that $1=dR+FdS$, a conjecture Stafford proposed in 1978. As a consequence, every finitely generated torsion right $A_n(k)$-module is cyclic. The proof maps $d$, by a symplectic change of variables, to a normal form $\tilde d$ and shows that the cyclic module $Q=A_n(k)/(\tilde dA_n(k)+x_1^N\tilde dA_n(k))$ vanishes. We first show that right multiplication by $x_1$ is surjective on $Q$. A comparison of lengths of localized modules over the associated graded ring then gives $\operatorname{gr}Q=x_1\operatorname{gr}Q$, so that the characteristic variety of $Q$ is disjoint from the hyperplane $\{x_1=0\}$. Finally, Gabber's involutivity theorem together with an argument about conormal directions at infinity from algebraic geometry shows that such a characteristic variety must be empty and therefore, $Q = 0$.

papers.title: ProvCards: Artifact-Oriented Provenance for Heterogeneous Scientific Workflows
papers.abstract: Reproducibility in scientific workflows is hindered by heterogeneous components and execution environments, as well as fragmented provenance capture. Although existing approaches offer established semantics and workflow-specific solutions, provenance remains difficult to capture, exchange, and compose across workflow boundaries. We present ProvCards, an artifact-oriented approach that treats provenance as a first-class artifact grounded in the W3C PROV Data Model. Individual workflow components can generate cards that are stored, exchanged, reused, and composed independently of any workflow system or centralized execution context. ProvDecks group related cards into portable scopes while preserving their identities. ProvGraphs provide derived views for provenance reconstruction, querying, visualization, and analysis. Together, these representations support coherent, task-specific provenance views across heterogeneous components, facilitating traceability, reuse, and reproducibility. We implement ProvCards using a graph-based infrastructure and evaluate them in a scientific data-processing workflow. The results demonstrate independent provenance capture at the component level, composition across component boundaries, and reconstruction for querying and analysis. ProvCards provide a portable, composable, and incrementally extensible foundation for provenance management in heterogeneous scientific workflows.

papers.intro:
Provenance is increasingly important for verifying data and reproducing computational results. Modern scientific data processing, however, commonly spans databases, files, scripts, notebooks, workflow engines, external services, and distributed execution environments (Goble et al., 2020; Gaignard et al., 2020). Since no single system controls or observes the complete processing lifecycle, the provenance of a result is typically distributed across multiple technical and organizational boundaries. The participating systems already generate provenance-relevant information by design. Logs, execution traces, catalogs, and metadata records contain input and output references, commands, parameters, timestamps, software versions, responsible actors, and execution status. Yet this evidence is represented in system-specific formats and remains tied to the components that generated it. It therefore cannot readily be exchanged or composed into consistent end-to-end provenance. Existing approaches provide standardized provenance semantics, workflow-integrated capture, provenance processing, or workflow-level packaging, but they lack an independently manageable unit for incrementally capturing and composing provenance across heterogeneous components.

A ProvCard is an independently manageable unit of provenance capture and exchange. Each card represents a provenance-relevant entity, activity, or agent and can refer explicitly to elements captured by other components. ProvCards can be generated incrementally during or after execution and can be identified, stored, retrieved, and exchanged independently of a shared workflow environment. Their contribution lies not in introducing new provenance semantics, but in providing a portable operational unit for provenance that remains usable when no single system controls the complete data-processing lifecycle. Within this layered model, ProvCards form the atomic elements. Collections of related cards, called ProvDecks, establish portable scopes for composing and exchanging provenance while preserving the identity of the individual cards. ProvGraphs provide derived graph representations for reconstructing, querying, visualizing, and analyzing the relationships captured by the cards.

papers.title: RoboDx: Repair and Diagnosis of Faults in Robot Software
papers.abstract: A patch to a robot's navigation software can pass every unit test and still drive the robot off its path. Checking how the repaired robot drives catches such patches. It does not show that the agent found everything that was wrong. We introduce RoboDx, a generator of repair tasks for simulated robot navigation software with known injected faults. A hidden verifier marks a repair as verified only if the robot then drives correctly in hidden scenarios, which the agent never sees. A second track hides the code and asks the agent to pick the cause from a list of hypotheses. A task with two faults can contain a quiet fault, a fault that makes no hidden scenario fail unless the other fault is also present. On our set of 100 tasks, RoboDx-Hard-100, almost every repair by Claude Opus 5.5 with standard coding tools is verified. We analyse 94 of the tasks, 44 with one fault and 50 with two. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of Opus's 49 verified repairs remove both injected edits. Most faults left behind are configuration constants whose correct value the task's documentation does not state. Opus names both faults on 10/50 of these tasks when it cannot see the code. We then give four current models the same measurements of each faulty robot, picked so that, in the simulator, only the true cause produces all of them. The models name the cause on at most 38 of 94 tasks. They are right on almost all when they also get the simulator's output for every hypothesis. Their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain. On 97 tasks from real bug-fix pull requests, Claude Haiku 5.5, the weakest model on the generated tasks, scores lowest, and the other three models are not ordered.
papers.intro:
A coding agent is asked to repair a robot that drives off its route. The robot’s navigation software has two faults. One line sets the heading gain ten times too low. The heading gain controls how hard the robot steers back toward its route, so the robot now turns sluggishly and misses waypoints, the points along its route. The other fault is a deleted speed cap. Without the cap the robot no longer slows down while it turns. With a correct heading gain the robot turns quickly, so alone the missing cap makes no test mission fail. The agent restores the gain. The robot then completes every test mission, and the repair counts as solved. The speed cap is still missing from the code (Figure 1).

The robot then completes every test mission, and the repair counts as solved. The speed cap is still missing from the code (Figure 1).

Robot software holds much code like the speed cap. Speed caps, timeouts and safety stops do nothing until something else fails, so a check of the robot’s behaviour can miss them. Coding agents are now applied to robot software [34, 37, 72], and finding the cause of a robot’s misbehaviour is a research problem of its own [46, 44, 58]. The closest benchmark for robot repair holds 33 real defects [104]. With real defects only the reported fault is known, so a fault that a repair leaves behind cannot be counted.

RQ1: Does a verified repair remove every injected fault? A verified repair often leaves a fault in place. With standard tools, Opus has a verified repair on 98 of the 100 tasks. On the 50 two-fault tasks, only 17 of its 49 verified repairs remove both faults (Section 4.1). RQ2: Can agents name the cause without the code? Opus often does on single-fault tasks and rarely on two-fault tasks. It names both faults on 10/50 of the two-fault tasks. A reference procedure that picks its measurements at random, and is given the simulator’s output for each hypothesis, is right on 47/50 (Section 4.2). RQ3: What do agents lack when they miss the cause? Our evidence suggests that they lack the simulator’s output for each hypothesis. Adding that output raises them to 89 to 94, and their own predictions of that output give no detectable gain (Section 4.3). RQ4: Do real bug-fix tasks separate the same agents? papers.title: MAIC-2 v2.3: A Fortran program for simulating the surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation of the planet Mars
papers.abstract: The Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler MAIC-2 is a computationally efficient, zonally-averaged model designed to simulate Martian surface temperature, atmospheric water transport and surface glaciation over timescales of 10^5 to 10^7 years. While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs) provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere, their high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution. MAIC-2 addresses this gap by utilizing physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations, including a Local Insolation Temperature (LIT) scheme and a mass balance engine driven by free-convection and instantaneous mixing physics. Version 2.3 introduces a fully modularized Fortran architecture that improves maintainability and ensures that the software remains entirely self-contained, requiring no external numerical libraries or specialized data formats for execution. Demonstrated through a 20-million-year transient simulation, the model successfully reproduces the primary characteristics of the Martian polar layered deposits. MAIC-2 provides the planetary science community with a versatile, open-source tool for investigating the long-term climatic impacts of orbital variations on the Martian surface.

papers.intro:
Understanding the history of the Martian climate and surface glaciation requires simulating processes over paleoclimatological timescales (10510^{5} to 10710^{7} years). While sophisticated General Circulation Models (GCMs), such as the Mars Planetary Climate Model (Forget et al. 1999, Forget et al. 2022, Millour et al. 2024, PCM;) and the NASA Ames MGCM (Haberle et al. 2003, Kahre et al. 2023, Kahre et al. 2024), provide high-resolution simulations of the Martian atmosphere for the present, other time-slices or short periods of time, they are computationally intensive because they solve the full equations of fluid dynamics and thermodynamics. This high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution.

This high computational cost makes them largely unsuitable for studies covering millions of years of orbital evolution.

MAIC-2 (Mars Atmosphere-Ice Coupler Version 2) addresses this need by providing a computationally efficient model specifically designed for long-term paleoclimate studies. It simplifies the complex descriptions of the Martian climate found in GCMs by utilizing a set of physically-based, zonally-averaged parameterizations. This approach allows the model to bridge the gap between high-fidelity atmospheric simulations and the multi-million-year timescales required to investigate the evolution of surface ice and polar layered deposits. In Section 2, we sketch the development history of the model, starting in the mid-2000s as a module of the 3D dynamic/thermodynamic ice-sheet model SICOPOLIS (SICOPOLIS Authors 2026, SImulation COde for POLythermal Ice Sheets,), later evolving into a standalone program, and culminating in the current, thoroughly modernized version 2.3 with a fully modularized design. In Section 3, we discuss a previously unpublished simulation of the Martian glaciation from 10​Ma10\>\mathrm{Ma} ago until 10​Ma10\>\mathrm{Ma} into the future, driven directly by the zonally averaged insolation computed from time-dependent orbital parameters (obliquity, eccentricity, and solar longitude of perihelion) provided by a numerical model of the solar system (Laskar et al. 2004). Section 4 concludes the paper.

papers.title: VESPA: Verifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation for Safe Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Safe reinforcement learning (RL) aims to prevent agents from taking actions that are dangerous or destructive to their environment. This is especially important for safety-critical domains, such as robotics or autonomous driving. Formal verification can be used to prove agent safety through safety constraints. However, in practice, many policies do violate safety constraints, and thus are verified to be unsafe. Since the goal is to obtain a safe policy, we would need to retrain a new policy from scratch and then verify it again until a candidate happens to pass. Both training and verification are usually not cheap, which makes this process inefficient. We introduce VESPA ($\textbf{VE}$rifiable $\textbf{S}$ymbolic $\textbf{P}$olicy $\textbf{A}$daptation), a framework for targeted fine-tuning of decision tree policies. We show that using counterexamples for policy adaptation can make existing unsafe policies safe, or at least make considerable progress towards safety. Targeted fine-tuning of the existing policy on those counterexamples enables it to learn how to avoid violating safety constraints. We thus use the result of a formal verification as a training signal for fine-tuning. On CartPole, VESPA raises the mean number of verified safe steps from 63.8 to at least 92.7, reaching after two iterations what the same loop without counterexamples reaches after ten. On MountainCarContinuous, VESPA turns an unsafe policy into a safe policy in 53 of 60 runs. We conclude that counterexamples from a verifier are an effective training signal, which can be utilized to systematically improve the safety of policies. Our implementation is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/VESPA-Submission/
papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved remarkable progress in the areas of robotics and control (Tang et al. 2025). Generally, both the training and evaluation of RL algorithms are based on expected return. However, solely optimizing the expected return for a given task is inadequate for safety-critical applications, because the environment or agent can impose safety constraints which must not be violated. For instance, in robotic applications it is insufficient to evaluate solely on average task performance. Instead, we need to guarantee that unsafe behaviors, such as a humanoid robot falling over, never occur. RL does not give such guarantees by default.

Instead, we need to guarantee that unsafe behaviors, such as a humanoid robot falling over, never occur. RL does not give such guarantees by default.

In the area of safe RL, numerous approaches have been proposed to overcome this problem. As discussed by Zhao et al. (2023), some approaches provide proofs of safety, while others give probabilistic safety guarantees. We argue that any form of probabilistic safety guarantee is insufficient for deploying RL in safety-critical domains. In environments with high risks, a formal verification for the deployed policy is needed. Safety can either be enforced at runtime, during training or inference, as in shielding (Alshiekh et al. 2018), or verified offline as a one-time proof for a fixed policy. Reachability analysis (Althoff, Frehse, and Girard 2021) is a versatile approach to offline verification, and issues a final verdict (either safe or unsafe) once for a fixed policy.

Formal verification only returns the verdict safe or unsafe. Since the final goal is to create a safe policy, one must train and verify many independent candidates, which is inefficient and in some cases infeasible.

To overcome this challenge, we introduce VESPA (VErifiable Symbolic Policy Adaptation) and show how to fine-tune a given policy based on the result of a formal verification. We focus on symbolic tree-based policies (Marton et al. 2025, SYMPOL,), since their axis-aligned splits make them amenable to reachability analysis. For policies with an unsafe verdict, we natively obtain counterexamples, i.e., states that are reachable by the policy and violate the safety constraints. Those are then traced back to some predecessor state region and used as start states for fine-tuning the policy. This targeted policy adaptation teaches the policy to steer away from the unsafe counterexamples. In this way, VESPA utilizes the output of the reachability analysis as a training signal to fine-tune the current policy and obtain the next candidate policy. papers.title: The Partially Saturated Cells Method for Complex Moving Geometries in Turbulent Flow Conditions
papers.abstract: We present four application cases to test and validate fluid-structure-interaction models based on the Lattice Boltzmann and the Partially Saturated Cells method (PSM) for turbulent flow conditions. For a flow around a stationary sphere we compare the PSM with direct mapping boundary conditions and achieve good agreement to reference data for Reynolds numbers up to one million. In particular, the model predicts the drag crisis for this case with good accuracy. papers.title: On the thermal behavior of composites embedding extended general interfaces
papers.abstract: In heterogeneous materials, surface roughness, chemical incompatibility, mechanical mismatch or manufacturing defects result in imperfect bonding between the constituents. Such imperfections introduce a finite-thickness interphase zone between the constituents that possess a graded or inhomogeneous micro-structure. It is virtually impossible to resolve the behavior of such interphases. Instead, a well-established approach is to replace the interphase by a zero-thickness interface endowed with its own energetic structure. Conventional interface models define the interface temperature as an average of the temperatures of the surrounding bulk phases. However, this assumption is only adequate to represent uniform homogeneous interphases and it fails to accurately capture the behavior of graded or inhomogeneous interphases. In this work, we address this limitation by allowing for unequal contributions of the surrounding bulk phases to the interface temperature. We systematically revisit the resulting balance equations and present the computational framework for the finite element implementation of the model. We further incorporate the proposed model within the homogenization framework and derive closed-form analytical expressions for the effective thermal conductivity of fiber- and particle-reinforced composites, accouting for the influence of the extended general interface. Finally, through a series of numerical examples, we demonstrate the capabilities of the proposed model and investigate the influence of its parameters on the size-dependent thermal behavior of composites.

papers.intro:
Over the past few decades, composites have emerged as key engineering materials owing to their exceptional mechanical and thermal properties. The overall behavior of a composite is governed not only by the properties of its constituents, but also by microstructural features such as the orientation, distribution, volume fraction, and shape [8, 54, 9, 81, 13, 89]. Predicting the behavior of composites becomes more complex when the bonding between the matrix and the reinforcing phases is imperfect due to surface roughness, chemical incompatibility, mechanical mismatch, or manufacturing defects [67, 68, 69]. Such imperfections give rise to interphase regions which significantly influence the mechanical and thermal behavior of the composite.

Over the past few decades, composites have emerged as key engineering materials owing to their exceptional mechanical and thermal properties. The overall behavior of a composite is governed not only by the properties of its constituents, but also by microstructural features such as the orientation, distribution, volume fraction, and shape [8, 54, 9, 81, 13, 89]. Predicting the behavior of composites becomes more complex when the bonding between the matrix and the reinforcing phases is imperfect due to surface roughness, chemical incompatibility, mechanical mismatch, or manufacturing defects [67, 68, 69]. Such imperfections give rise to interphase regions which significantly influence the mechanical and thermal behavior of the composite.

A well-established approach for capturing the influence of a finite interphase is to replace it with a zero-thickness interface characterized by discontinuities in temperature and heat flux [80, 73], leading to the notion of thermal interface models. Seminal studies by Hashin [37, 38] established the link between interphase properties and interface jumps, highlighting size-dependent effects that become pronounced at small scales. Thermal interface models can be classified based on the continuity conditions they impose on temperature and heat flux across the interface. (i) The Perfect interface model assumes ideal thermal contact between the constituents, in that both the temperature and the normal heat flux remain continuous across the interface [77, 28, 40, 70, 29, 30]. Analysis of composites with perfect interfaces is, in principle, identical to classical homogenization. A vast body of literature has been devoted to predicting the effective conductivity of heterogeneous media with perfect interfaces [77, 28, 40, 70, 29, 30]. (ii) The lowly conductive (LC) interface model is classically described by Kapitza’s model of thermal resistance [51]. This formulation is consistent with the second law of thermodynamics and allows for a discontinuity in temperature across the interface while enforcing continuity of the normal heat flux. Sanchez-Palencia [80] demonstrated that a highly resistant interphase of vanishing thickness gives rise to a temperature jump at the interface. Several micromechanical approaches were developed to quantify the impact of LC interfaces on the effective thermal properties of composites. Benveniste and co-workers [3, 4] generalized classical homogenization schemes, including the generalized self-consistent method and the Mori–Tanaka theory, to account for LC interfaces and showed that temperature jumps systematically reduce the effective conductivity. Further advances were made through both analytical and variational methods. Chiew and Glandt [12], Hasselman and Johnson [42], Hasselman et al. [41], and Every et al. [17] incorporated interfacial resistance into modified classical models and linked size effects to Kapitza-type barriers. See [75, 15, 76, 55, 46, 6] for further studies on LC interface model. (iii) The highly conductive (HC) interface model is characterized by continuous temperature across the interface and a discontinuity in the normal heat flux, arising from in-plane heat conduction along the interface. The model was first formalized by Pham-Huy and Sanchez-Palencia [73], who showed that for a superconducting interphase of vanishing thickness, the flux jump is proportional to the surface Laplacian of the interfacial potential. Subsequent studies established theoretical bounds and dualities between HC and LC interfaces [63, 64, 11, 65]. Miloh and Benveniste [71] and Chen [10] extended HC interface model for ellipsoidal and circular inclusions with spatially varying interface properties, while Duan and Karihaloo [14] unified HC and LC descriptions through a multiple-scattering framework. Le-Quang et al. [61] extended Eshelby’s solution to anisotropic phases with HC interfaces, showing uniformity of the thermal tensor fields in contrast to earlier studies. See [7, 61, 58, 47] for further studies on HC interface model. (iv) The general interface model allows for discontinuities in both temperature and the normal heat flux across the interface. This broader formulation includes the lowly conducting and highly conducting interfaces as special cases. Seminal work of Hashin [39] established the theoretical foundation of this interface model in the context of elasticity. Variational estimates and bounds for composites with imperfect interfaces were developed by Lipton and Talbot [66]. These works was followed by important theoretical refinements. Gu and co-workers [25, 26, 27] developed coordinate-free derivations and closed-form estimates for the size-dependent effective conductivity of composites with spherical inclusions. These models have since been embedded in homogenization schemes such as Mori–Tanaka and self-consistent methods, and extended to anisotropic and spheroidal composites [59, 60, 56, 62, 53]. Higher-order asymptotic analyses further refined the modeling of curved and finite-thickness interphases, leading to interface conditions of arbitrary order accuracy [1, 31, 82, 57, 83, 84, 16, 32]. A thermodynamically consistent formulation of general imperfect interfaces, allowing simultaneous jumps in temperature and normal heat flux, was developed by Javili et al. [48], together with a unified finite-element framework. Kaessmair et al. [50] extended this formulation to thermomechanically coupled coherent interfaces. For further computational approaches on thermal interface problems, see [32, 91, 92].

papers.title: Investigating the Impact of SAX J1808.4-3658's Very Bright Thermonuclear X-ray Burst on the Accretion Disc with NICER
papers.abstract: We analyse a bright thermonuclear X-ray burst from the accreting millisecond X-ray pulsar (AMXP) SAX J1808.4-3658, the brightest burst detected by \textit{NICER} to date, to explore interactions between thermonuclear burst radiation and the accretion disc. This burst features a remarkable soft (<1.5 keV) excess in its spectra. For the first time, we simultaneously detect a reflection signal and the signature of an evolving persistent component, with our fits producing a peak persistent scaling factor $f_{a,1} = 59.6\pm0.6$. We find a high peak reflection fraction ($f_{r,1} = 0.82\pm0.15$) and a peak bolometric burst blackbody flux below Eddington (0.68$L_{\mathrm{Edd}}$) despite signatures of photospheric radius expansion. We detect a raised $N_\mathrm{H}$ ($\approx$34% above persistent emission) and raised disc blackbody temperature ($\approx$15% above persistent emission) during the burst's tail. This is the first time that spectroscopic evidence consistent with burst-induced disc heating has been found. We interpret that disc heating could cause the disc to puff up and inhibit burst photons, explaining the high reflection fraction and below-Eddington burst luminosity during the burst peak. We find an increasing count rate starting from $\approx$150s before the burst onset. Spectral analysis revealed a thermal component that evolves towards hotter temperatures closer to the onset of the burst. This is the second detection of this phenomenon from an AMXP. Lastly, we find that both the double-peaked structure and the "pause" in the rise are energy-dependent.

Thermonuclear (type-I) X-ray bursts (hereafter “X-ray bursts" or “bursts") are sudden increases in X-ray emission from accreting neutron star low-mass X-ray binary systems. Material accreted from a solar-mass companion star will spread across the surface of the neutron star, where it is compacted by intense gravity. Once the matter reaches a critical density, a runaway thermonuclear explosion is ignited (see, Lewin et al., 1993; Strohmayer and Bildsten, 2006; Galloway and Keek, 2021, for reviews). X-ray bursts last tens to hundreds of seconds, typically having a short (≤1−10\leq 1-10 s) rise followed by a roughly exponential decay (Galloway et al., 2008b, e.g.,). X-ray burst emission is well-described by a blackbody spectrum, where peak blackbody temperatures of 1−31-3 keV have been found (Galloway et al., 2020, e.g., MINBAR11 1 https://burst.sci.monash.edu/minbar).

This standard approach assumes that both the spectral shape and intensity of the persistent emission remain unchanged during an X-ray burst. This standard approach assumes that both the spectral shape and intensity of the persistent emission remain unchanged during an X-ray burst. Observations have shown, however, that a burst spectrum is not always accurately described by this standard approach (van Paradijs and Lewin, 1986; Galloway et al., 2008a; Güver et al., 2012, e.g.,).

In cases where the standard approach is not a good description of the data, a simple way to fit the typical residuals found is by scaling the persistent emission’s intensity by a factor greater than 1 (Worpel et al., 2013; Worpel et al., 2015; in’t Zand et al., 2013; Güver et al., 2022a, faf_{a}-method;). This phenomenological tool allows us to parameterise changes in the persistent emission which would be challenging to capture by varying the persistent component parameters directly during the burst. This enhancement of the persistent flux captured by the faf_{a}-method is often attributed to an increased accretion rate during the burst. This may be caused by the burst photons exerting Poynting-Robertson (PR) drag on the material in the inner accretion disc, making this material more easily accreted (Walker and Meszaros, 1989). Recent simulations by Fragile et al. (2020) and Speicher et al. (2023) support the interpretation that PR drag plays a significant role in burst-disc interaction. Fragile et al. (2020) confirms the expected effect of PR drag whereby the orbital angular momentum of the inner disc material is reduced on burst timescales, and Speicher et al. (2023) show that prograde spin of the neutron star does not minimise the effects of PR drag. Whilst the significance of PR drag during a burst has been supported by these simulations, the historic association of the faf_{a}-method with an increased accretion rate caused by PR drag has been questioned in a recent study by Speicher et al. (2024), who suggest that the faf_{a} factor more reliably characterises changes in disc temperature due to irradiation from the burst than mass accretion rate.

papers.title: Infrared spectrum of the Type Iax supernova remnant Pa30
papers.abstract: The central star of Pa30 and its nebulosity offer one of the best opportunities to study a SN Iax explosion and its remnant. Pa30 is thought to be the product of the historical supernova explosion of 1181. No infrared spectroscopy of its extremely hot central star has hitherto been reported. Here, we present a 0.75-5 $\mu$m spectrum taken by the Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer (SPHEREx), together with ground-based infrared spectra, at higher resolution, covering the 0.8-2.5 $\mu$m region. The spectra contain very broad lines, which we have attempted to identify and model using the codes CMFGEN and CLOUDY. The CMFGEN modelling suggests that most of the lines are due to OVI. However, CLOUDY modelling, using expected theoretical abundances for the bound remnants of SN Iax explosions, provides evidence for the presence of coronal lines of Si, S, Mg, and Al arising from a shocked gas. This strengthens the suggestion that Pa30 is indeed the remnant of a SN Iax explosion.

papers.intro:
Patchick 30 (hereafter Pa30; also known as IRAS 00500+6713, 2MASS J00531123+6730023, IPHAS J005311.21+673002.1, WISE J005311.24+673002.4, Gaia DR3 526287189172936320) has been identified as the remnant of the “guest star” widely observed in China, Japan and Egypt in 1181 August (Kronberger et al., 2014; Ritter et al., 2021; Fischer et al., 2025). It was first identified as the remnant of a putative SN Iax explosion by Oskinova et al. (2020), using X-ray data, and data from the Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer (Wright et al., 2010, WISE;). Earlier optical spectroscopy (Gvaramadze et al., 2019) revealed emission lines of O vi and C iv; these authors also concluded that the stellar remnant has a luminosity 104.610^{4.6} L⊙L_{\odot} and a high effective temperature (211,000 K). Gvaramadze et al. suggested that the properties of Pa30 and its nebula are consistent with the merger of two massive white dwarfs (WDs) that resulted in a super-Chandrasekhar-mass remnant. However, Lykou et al. (2023) argue for a final mass in the range 1.2–1.45 M⊙M_{\odot}. The widths of the O vi lines suggest a wind velocity of 16,000 km s-1, likely magnetically driven (Gvaramadze et al., 2019). Gvaramadze et al. deduced a magnetic field of 2×1082\times 10^{8} G; however, Lykou et al. (2023) deduced an upper limit of 2.5×1062.5\times 10^{6} G, based on the absence of Zeeman splitting in the O viii lines.

papers.title: Atomic-scale assembly of sulfur vacancy complexes for tailored in-gap states in monolayer WS$_{2}$
papers.abstract: Atomic-scale defects in two-dimensional semiconductors are quasi-isolated quantum systems with promise for emerging technologies. Although their potential as spin qubits, quantum sensors and single-photon emitters has been demonstrated experimentally, creating them deterministically and identifying them chemically remains challenging, which limits control over their electronic states. In this work we assemble sulfur vacancies in monolayer WS$_{2}$ into complexes of different sizes and geometries using the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope. We study their electronic properties by a combination of scanning tunneling spectroscopy and density functional theory, revealing the intricate influences of geometry, underlying point group symmetries and spin-orbit coupling on hybridized states. Among the realized sulfur vacancy complexes, we characterize two configurations that are candidates for bright single photon emitters. Our findings demonstrate an atomic-scale method for engineering quantum states within the band gap of two-dimensional semiconductors.

papers.intro:
Point defects in monolayers of semiconducting transition-metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) have a wide range of properties relevant to the emerging field of quantum nanotechnology [50, 36, 33, 8]. Their surface accessibility is envisioned to allow creation and manipulation of tailored hybrid orbitals in the band gap of their host. Optical transitions involving these localized orbitals can give rise to antibunched single-photon emission (SPE), first observed in 2D semiconductors more than a decade ago [14, 39, 45, 4].

Their surface accessibility is envisioned to allow creation and manipulation of tailored hybrid orbitals in the band gap of their host. Optical transitions involving these localized orbitals can give rise to antibunched single-photon emission (SPE), first observed in 2D semiconductors more than a decade ago [14, 39, 45, 4].

Although SPE of defects in semiconducting TMDs is experimentally well established in far-field optical studies, the nature of the defects remains strongly debated as these measurements lack atomic resolution. Single chalcogen vacancies have long been the prime candidates for the narrow photoluminescence (PL) emission lines observed experimentally [23, 34, 17, 10], which were shown to exhibit SPE characteristics [2, 24, 3]. However, near field optical measurements probing photon emission from the tunnel junction of a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) only observed electroluminescence [38] with no exciton emission lines emerging at sulfur vacancy sites [19], questioning single chalcogen vacancies as SPE sources. This observation is in line with a weak optical transition dipole calculated for single sulfur vacancies in WS2\mathrm{WS_{2}} [43], which only becomes comparable to the direct band-to-band transitions of the pristine 2D semiconductor under application of strain [15].

Recently, complexes comprising two or more chalcogen vacancies have been proposed as alternative SPE candidates [43, 5, 11]. Depending on size, structure and symmetry, these complexes are predicted to give rise to shallow defect states close to the conduction band minimum (CBM) in density functional theory (DFT) calculations. The enhanced hybridization between defect state and CBM increases the optical transition dipole and thus activates the defect’s optical activity. However, experimental proof for the existence of these states, their proximity to the conduction band of the 2D host, and their responsibility for SPE is so far lacking.

Here we deterministically create sulfur vacancy complexes in monolayer WS2\mathrm{WS_{2}} with the tip of a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) and subsequently manipulate their configuration via tip-induced sulfur diffusion. This serves as a powerful technique to study the effects of system size, geometry and underlying symmetries on electronic in-gap states, as well as their link to optical properties. Various complexes comprising up to four vacancies are characterized using a combination of low-temperature scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) and DFT. In sulfur vacancy dimers, we observe strong hybridization of defect states as a function of vacancy separation and relative orientation to the host lattice. Overall, we experimentally observe the existence of a shallow in-gap state for two vacancy clusters: the lateral nearest-neighbor dimer as well as the vacancy trimer in hollow-centered triangle configuration, thereby confirming theoretical predictions [43].

papers.title: Learning Trajectories Leave Decodable Traces in Neural Network Weight Space and Internal Representations
papers.abstract: Neural networks trained on the same task develop related weight-space structures, yet remain distinguishable after learning. Do these differences merely reflect alternative solutions, or do they preserve information about individual learning histories? We tested whether final weights reveal initialization, task order, and earlier trajectory states. Training reorganized the ensemble: initial pairwise distances did not consistently predict final distances. Nevertheless, all 30 trained networks were correctly matched to their initial weights among ten candidates per dataset. Networks sharing an initialization also developed recognizable final hidden representations across different batch schedules, although direct comparisons with initial activity did not recover identity. Learning order remained readable as well. A linear probe decoded the order of two earlier tasks with 100% accuracy on 80 held-out networks after ten epochs of a common final task. Earlier intermediate weight states were partly predictable, but individual initial weights could not be reliably reconstructed. Final weights thus retain selective historical information rather than a complete trajectory record. Perturbed networks recovered classification performance without returning to their unperturbed training paths. This separation persisted across datasets, intervention times, and network layers. Moreover, 2,157 of 2,160 aligned endpoint pairs showed no positive loss barrier at sampled interpolation points, indicating low-loss connections between distinct solutions rather than convergence to one weight vector. Together, these findings show that a shared task constrains networks to related successful solutions without erasing their individual histories. Final weights reflect not only what a network has learned, but also where learning began and how it unfolded.

papers.intro:
Can a trained neural network reveal its own past? Its present weights support a learned computation, but they were also produced by a particular initialization and a particular sequence of updates. Training could erase those individual beginnings as different networks adapt to a shared task. Alternatively, the solutions could retain recognizable traces of how they developed. Distinguishing these possibilities changes what we can learn from a final model: its structure may describe both the problem it solves and the history that produced it.

Our preceding study showed that independently initialized networks form dataset- and task-dependent clusters in weight space after hidden-neuron permutations and positive ReLU rescalings are taken into account (Krauss et al., 2026). Related structure emerged in their internal representations, and a fixed-input comparison showed that changing the target rule redirected the organization. The separation began early, while displacement from initialization was still small. Nevertheless, networks solving the same problem did not collapse onto a common weight matrix. These findings established reproducible organization at the level of tasks, while leaving the origin of the remaining individual differences unresolved.

These differences could be incidental variations among functionally equivalent solutions. Alternatively, they could retain traces of the initial conditions and learning experiences that shaped each network. Distinguishing between these possibilities would reveal whether the geometry of weight space reflects only what a network has learned, or also how it learned it. This perspective extends our work on class separability, neural successor representations, and linguistic constructions (Schilling et al., 2021; Stoewer et al., 2022; Ramezani et al., 2025). Those studies characterize internal organization beyond predictive performance; the present study adds the history through which that organization develops.

Several forms of historical persistence must be distinguished. The distances among networks might preserve their ordering from initialization to the end of training. Alternatively, that ensemble geometry might be reorganized while each network retains an individually recognizable origin. Historical influence may also survive without direct resemblance to an earlier state: two copies of the same initialization might learn related final representations even when neither resembles its initial representation particularly closely. Finally, an endpoint might reveal a past event without containing enough accessible information to reconstruct the intervening sequence of weights. These possibilities require different tests.

Comparisons in weight space also require a definition of equivalence. Hidden neurons can be relabeled, and incoming and outgoing weights can be reciprocally rescaled in ReLU networks without changing their function. Permutation-aware matching makes it possible to compare organization beyond these coordinate freedoms (Ainsworth et al., 2023; Krauss et al., 2026), while representation-based measures such as centered kernel alignment provide a complementary view of the responses to common inputs (Kornblith et al., 2019; Krauss et al., 2026). Importantly, the geometry of weight space and the geometry of internal representations are not interchangeable. Differences in weight configurations do not necessarily imply corresponding differences in neural activations, nor do differences in internal representations necessarily imply differences in the underlying weights. papers.title: The Elephant in the Question: Unified Models Picture the Concepts Behind Their Answers
papers.abstract: Visualizing intermediate representations could help us inspect the reasoning steps underlying a model output. Unified multimodal models offer this opportunity by combining understanding and generation in one architecture. Their image generators can access representations formed while processing text. We introduce the V-lens, which uses this connection to visualize a chosen token's hidden state without training a decoder. Across four diffusion-based and two purely autoregressive unified models, the resulting images reveal key intermediate concepts that connect a question to its answer even when the concepts are never named explicitly. Controlled tests show how this content changes with context, token position, and depth. We then introduce lens tuning, which supervises selected hidden states with pictures through the V-lens. Across BAGEL, SenseNova-U1, and HunyuanImage-3.0, the rate of correct visualizations of pronoun referents rises from 2-11% to 86-94%. Surprisingly, such visual supervision also improves text answers without supervising the answer tokens directly. Code is available at https://github.com/multimodal-ai-lab/V-lens.

papers.title: Low Moments, Small Balls and Star Discrepancy
papers.abstract: Let $D_P$ be the discrepancy function of a configuration $P$ of $N$ points in the $d$-dimensional unit cube, and let $\|D_P\|_q$ be its $L^q$ discrepancy. We prove that for all fixed $d\ge2$ and $0<q\le1$ the $L^q$ discrepancy of every configuration of $N\ge2$ points is at least $c_{d,q}(\log N)^{(d-1)/2}$ with a constant $c_{d,q}>0$. This bound is sharp; together with the classical results for $q>1$, it determines the minimal order of the $L^q$ discrepancy for every $0<q<\infty$ in every dimension $d\ge2$, and for $q=1$ it answers Chen's problem on the sharp lower bound for the $L^1$ discrepancy in dimension $d\ge3$. We prove the small ball inequality for Haar functions in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$ and for arbitrary real coefficients with the conjectured power of $n$, up to a polylogarithmic factor; here $2^{-n}$ is the smallest volume of the dyadic boxes involved. The method also extends to a class of piecewise polynomial mother functions. For the $L^\infty$ discrepancy $\|D_P\|_\infty=ND^*(P)$, where $D^*(P)$ is the star discrepancy, we prove the conjectured lower bound $c(\log N)^{3/2}$ in dimension three, and the lower bound $(\log N)^{d/2}$ up to a power of $\log\log N$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge4$. Finally, we construct $N$-point sets whose $L^\infty$ discrepancy is $O_d((\log N)^{d-1-1/16})$ in every fixed dimension $d\ge3$; this disproves the conjectured optimality of the order $(\log N)^{d-1}$ of the classical constructions.

papers.title: The Impact Of Multitasking In Video Meetings On Meeting Outcomes: Initial Results
papers.abstract: Multitasking in video meetings is a ubiquitous phenomenon. While extant literature has investigated the circumstances under which people multitask in video meetings, little is known about the impacts of multitasking on meeting outcomes. Building on the findings of previous studies investigating the impact of multitasking in individual non-video meeting work setups and threaded cognition theory, we present a research model that suggests that multitasking may have negative effects on meeting outcomes such as process loss and team meeting outcome satisfaction. We tested the research model in an incentivized within-subject laboratory experiment with n=72 participants. Results suggest that multitasking has a negative effect on process loss and team meeting outcome satisfaction compared to non-multitasking. We plan to further investigate the mediating role of cognitive user states and neurophysiological activations and ultimately aim to contribute with a deeper understanding of the impacts of multitasking.

papers.title: Spontaneous emission of atomic systems near metallic and semiconducting atomic chains
papers.abstract: We investigate the spontaneous emission of a quantum emitter placed near finite atomic chains described by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. By tuning the chain from a metallic to a semiconducting character through dimerization, we analyze how the electronic structure of an atomic-scale scatterer, together with the illumination profile, determines the strength, bandwidth, and spatial structure of the spontaneous emission enhancement. The resonant enhancement depends on both spectral matching and the emitter position relative to the induced charge and field patterns. In metallic chains, the nearly harmonic energy spectrum leads to overlapping optical transitions and strong resonances. For semiconducting chains, dimerization opens a gap and leads to a modified density of electronic states, redistributing the response over a broader spectral range and reducing its peak intensity. Coulomb interactions affect the optical resonances through blueshift or modification of their spatial character, and act differently on collective and single-particle-like excitations. Finally, we show that the same mechanisms demonstrated in atomic chains persist in realistic quasi-one-dimensional systems, including trans-polyacetylene chains and graphene nanoribbons. Our findings indicate a general direction for engineering light-matter interactions at the atomic scale, and may offer design principles for tunable nanoscale photonic and quantum-optical devices.

papers.title: Plug-and-Play Sensor Evolution in Software-Defined Vehicles through Asset Administration Shells
papers.abstract:
Software-defined vehicles (SDVs) promise continuous software evolution, but sensor integration in deployed vehicles still depends on manual configuration, hardware-specific drivers, and repeated application-side adaptation. Existing standards address only parts of this problem. AUTOSAR standardizes selected sensor interfaces, the Vehicle Signal Specification (VSS) standardizes signal semantics, and Asset Administration Shells (AAS) standardize digital asset descriptions. However, these building blocks are rarely combined into an end-to-end onboarding path for sensors attached after vehicle deployment.
  This paper presents an AAS-driven plug-and-play sensor integration framework for safety-supervised sensors. Each sensor is represented by an AAS that combines hardware identification, interface metadata, VSS mappings, and references to containerized driver and optional application software. After physical connection, an edge gateway identifies the device, retrieves the matching AAS, deploys the referenced software, and publishes the resulting data under stable vehicle signal paths. A prototype on a resource-constrained edge gateway connected to an RR100 UGV demonstrates automated integration of a USB camera and an ultrasonic sensor. Across repeated integration cycles, the prototype reaches operational state in about 2s, shows no failed events, and keeps applications independent of hardware-specific interfaces. The results indicate that the introduction of AAS as an executable onboarding contract enables automated runtime deployment of sensor drivers in SDV environments.

papers.title: Evaluation of tracking plane pitch and xenon-helium gas mixtures for the NEXT experiment
papers.abstract: NEXT is an experimental program to search for neutrinoless double-beta decay ($\beta\beta 0\nu$) in high-pressure xenon gas using electroluminescent time projection chambers. A key feature of the NEXT technology is the reconstruction of MeV-scale electron tracks, which plays a key role in identifying $\beta\beta 0\nu$ events. This work presents a Monte Carlo study aimed at determining the optimal configuration for NEXT detectors employing SiPM-based tracking planes. The simulations are carried out in the NEXT-100 detector geometry, and to classify the events as signal or background, we use a Sparse Convolutional Neural Network. We find that topological rejection power improves by approximately a factor of two at the lower pressure studied (5 bar) compared to the baseline design (13.5 bar). A finer pitch also offers consistent improvement, where reducing pitch from 15 mm to 5 mm decreased the accepted background fraction by a factor of approximately 1.4 at 13.5 bar for a fixed signal efficiency in the different configurations studied. The addition of helium to reduce electron diffusion provides a comparable enhancement, reducing the accepted background fraction by up to a factor of 1.5 at 13.5 bar. We highlight two key practical configurations at 13.5 bar pressure: the present NEXT-100 (pure Xe with a 15 mm tracking plane pitch) and an upgraded NEXT-100 (a Xe-He gas mixture and a 10 mm tracking plane pitch). These results provide quantitative guidance for the design and optimisation of future NEXT detectors, balancing physics performance with technical and financial constraints.

The observation of neutrinoless double-beta (β​β​0​ν\beta\beta 0\nu) decay is still one of the highest-priority goals in particle physics. Its discovery would prove that the neutrino is Majorana in nature (its own antiparticle), establish the violation of lepton number conservation, and provide some insight into the absolute neutrino mass scale Avignone III et al. (2008); Dolinski et al. (2019); Gómez-Cadenas et al. (2023). The search for this decay requires ultra-low background experiments with large isotopic masses and excellent energy resolution to distinguish a potential signal peak from background events at the Q-value of the decay (Qβ​βQ_{\beta\beta}).

The planned NEXT-HD apparatus Adams and others (2021) will further scale the mass to about several tons at 15 bar.

Optimising the design of these future large-scale detectors requires a scalable method to evaluate their topological discrimination power. Double beta decay events, consisting of two energetic electrons emitted from a common vertex, produce a track topology that is notably different from that of one-electron events produced by gamma ray backgrounds. We choose to employ a Sparse Convolutional Neural Network (SCN) Graham and van der Maaten (2017), given the sparse nature of the energetic electron tracks in xenon gas, which can be trained on simulated datasets to separate signal (β​β​0​ν\beta\beta 0\nu) and background (one-electron) events. This follows previous work carried out within NEXT employing neural networks, in particular Kekic and others (2021), in which an SCN was trained on simulated events and applied to experimental data from the NEXT-White detector. Various other experiments have used the SCN, such as MicroBooNE Abratenko and others (2021), NOvA Shmakov et al. (2023), and DUNE simulation studies Abed Abud and others (2023), for event classification and segmentation. Here we use the SCN to quantify the ability of the detector to distinguish between signal and background events of the same energy under various configurations of tracking plane pitch, pressure, and electron diffusion.

The principle of operation of an HPXe-EL TPC is based on several distinct properties of xenon: a) xenon scintillates (with an average wavelength of 172 nm, well into the VUV spectrum) due to the formation and decay of short-lived excimers, when a charged particle excites the gas. Therefore, the primary scintillation produced by the charged particle, denoted as S1S_{1}, is not re-absorbed by the gas and can be observed; b) xenon is a noble gas, and therefore xenon atoms have a closed electron shell, so drifting electrons are not captured by neutral atoms. Given sufficiently high gas purity, electrons can be drifted over long distances of up to meters by a moderate (several hundred V/cm) electric field. As a consequence, a track of ionisation electrons can be transported with minimal attachment losses towards the TPC anode, where it crosses a region of higher electric field (the EL region); c) in the EL process, electrons gain enough energy to excite xenon atoms but not enough to cause further ionisation. The number of excitations produced is proportional to the width of the EL region, and therefore the resulting scintillation produced by de-excitation, which we call S2S_{2}, amplifies the ionisation signal with sub-Poissonian fluctuations, yielding excellent energy resolution.

The number of excitations produced is proportional to the width of the EL region, and therefore the resulting scintillation produced by de-excitation, which we call S2S_{2}, amplifies the ionisation signal with sub-Poissonian fluctuations, yielding excellent energy resolution.

The EL region is defined by two transparent grids separated by ∼\sim10 mm, the anode itself, held at ground, and the gate, which is held at a voltage that produces a reduced electric field in this region on the order of 2 kV/cm/bar. In typical operations, 100-1000 photons are emitted per ionisation electron. Photons emitted in the direction of the anode intersect a plane, called the tracking plane, equipped with an array of light-sensitive detectors (SiPMs), separated at some pitch in the X and Y dimensions. Tracks are reconstructed combining the information of the SiPMs and the timing information provided by the TPC. This ability to reconstruct tracks is a distinctive feature of the NEXT technology, which provides a strong handle to suppress backgrounds.

papers.title: Towards Reliable Scaling Laws for Tabular Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Scaling laws are widely used to predict foundation model performance and guide compute allocation. However, tabular foundation models (TFMs) differ from conventional foundation models in that they are pretrained on virtually unlimited synthetic data from configurable distributions, while ultimately being evaluated on real-world datasets. We investigate whether scaling laws for TabPFNv2-style models reliably extrapolate to larger compute budgets and generalize across evaluation settings. Our analysis reveals differences between synthetic and real-world scaling behavior and shows that accurately fitting a scaling law does not necessarily yield reliable prescriptions on unseen datasets. In particular, selecting configurations using too few evaluation datasets leads to systematically over-optimistic performance estimates. We further demonstrate that compute-optimal scaling requires expanding the range of synthetic pretraining dataset sizes alongside model size and training compute. Increasing the maximum numbers of rows and features sampled during pretraining improves performance and produces more predictable scaling trends. These insights guide the training of more efficient TabPFNv2-like models, using the open-source training pipeline of nanoTabPFN.

papers.intro:
Tabular data underpins predictive tasks across diverse domains, including healthcare, finance, and scientific discovery (borisov2022deep; priorlabs2026awesome). Unlike conventional models that require dataset-specific training, tabular foundation models (TFMs) achieve state-of-the-art performance on small- to medium-sized datasets without dataset-specific parameter updates (erickson2026tabarena; purucker2026beyond; jager2026tabpfn). Models such as TabPFN (hollmann-nature25a; jager2026tabpfn), TabICL (qu2025tabicl; qu2026tabiclv), LimiX (zhang-2025limix), and Mitra (zhang2025mitra) learn to perform in-context prediction by pretraining on synthetic datasets sampled from task priors.

The success of TFMs has motivated extensions to time-series forecasting (hoo2026from), causal effect estimation (robertson2025dopfn), survival prediction (bohm2026survpfn; qi2026survivalpfn), and hyperparameter optimization (muller-icml23a; rakotoarison-icml24a). These applications motivate experimentation with task-specific priors and model architectures, increasingly facilitated by open-source implementations such as TabICL (qu2026tabiclv) and TFM-Playground (pfefferle2026tfmplayground). However, while such experimentation is feasible at small scales, evaluating promising configurations at competitive compute budgets remains expensive, especially as models scale to hundreds of millions of parameters (kong2026tabfm). Scaling laws, widely used to predict performance and guide compute allocation in language modeling (kaplan-arxiv20a; hoffmann-neurips22a), offer a framework for bridging this gap.

Previous studies have investigated scaling relationships for TFMs (zhang-2025limix; ma2025tabdpt; zhang2025mitra), but accurately fitting observed performance does not guarantee reliable extrapolation to larger compute budgets. In particular, unconstrained scaling-law formulations can yield predictions outside the valid range of evaluation metrics, such as ROC AUC (zhang-2025limix). Finally, the synthetic prior design and sampling contain many degrees of freedom that yield vastly different data mixtures while remaining finely controllable. This makes the prior itself a scaling axis for the compute-optimal performance of TFMs. We investigate these challenges using over 6,0006{,}000 training runs spanning model sizes, compute budgets, synthetic prior configurations, and training hyperparameters. papers.title: Old Experience, New Lessons: Relabeling Autonomous Robot Rollouts in Interactive Imitation Learning
papers.abstract: Interactive imitation learning enables robots to learn from human interventions during deployment. These interactions naturally produce sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Yet existing methods either leave this experience unused for action supervision or imitate historical robot actions, which can reinforce suboptimal behavior. To address this limitation, we propose Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA), a framework that learns from autonomous robot experience through set-valued supervision of policy relabels. Later policy checkpoints relabel this experience, and agreement across checkpoints filters the relabels. Since agreement does not guarantee correctness, SeRA constructs desired action sets around accepted relabels. Following Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP), it trains an action-chunking diffusion policy to increase the probability of actions within these sets. A step-masked denoising loss combines accepted relabels with available human corrections in partially supervised chunks. Experiments across five simulated manipulation tasks in online and offline settings show that SeRA improves policy performance over SDP and outperforms baselines that imitate historical robot actions or exact relabels. On a real-robot tomato-picking task, SeRA achieves 80% success, compared with 40% for SDP, using the same human feedback and training budget. These results demonstrate that relabeled autonomous robot experience can complement human corrections to improve policy performance.

papers.intro:
Learned manipulation policies remain vulnerable to failures around contacts, task bottlenecks, and states outside the demonstration distribution. Interactive imitation learning (IIL) addresses these failures by allowing a human teacher to intervene during deployment and provide corrections [1, 2]. These interactions naturally produce two streams of data: sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Learning only from the corrections leaves this experience unused for action supervision. We instead treat it as unlabeled data and seek to learn from it alongside human corrections.

Learned manipulation policies remain vulnerable to failures around contacts, task bottlenecks, and states outside the demonstration distribution. Interactive imitation learning (IIL) addresses these failures by allowing a human teacher to intervene during deployment and provide corrections [1, 2]. These interactions naturally produce two streams of data: sparse human corrections and abundant autonomous robot experience without human action labels. Learning only from the corrections leaves this experience unused for action supervision. We instead treat it as unlabeled data and seek to learn from it alongside human corrections.

Prior work has sought to exploit autonomous robot experience by retaining historical robot actions as imitation targets. IWR imitates these actions alongside human corrections [3]; CEILing uses additional evaluative feedback to select useful behavior [4]; and Sirius downweights pre-intervention actions using intervention context [5]. However, autonomous actions need not be optimal, even when they do not trigger an intervention or occur in a successful trajectory. Retaining them as targets can therefore reinforce suboptimal behavior. This raises a central question: how can autonomous robot experience support policy learning without imitating imperfect historical robot actions?

However, autonomous actions need not be optimal, even when they do not trigger an intervention or occur in a successful trajectory. Retaining them as targets can therefore reinforce suboptimal behavior. This raises a central question: how can autonomous robot experience support policy learning without imitating imperfect historical robot actions?

Our key insight is that later policies incorporate additional human corrections and may generalize these corrections to observations collected earlier. We use the latest policy to relabel autonomous robot experience and accept these relabels based on agreement across later policy checkpoints. Yet agreement alone does not guarantee correctness: multiple checkpoints can share the same error. Directly imitating even these accepted relabels can reinforce prediction errors through confirmation bias [6]. Learning from this experience therefore requires supervision that tolerates imperfect relabels.

In this work, we introduce Set-valued Relabeling of Autonomous experience (SeRA),33 3 Webpage: https://sera-webpage.github.io/ a framework that combines policy relabeling with set-valued supervision for action-chunking diffusion policies. Building on Set-Supervised Diffusion Policy (SDP) [7], we supervise each accepted relabel with a desired action set: a region of action space centered at the relabel, whose radius is scaled by its distance from the historical robot action. papers.title: OpenGNS: An Open Dataset of the Gradient Noise Scale across Vision, Language, and Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: The Gradient Noise Scale (GNS) metric measures the signal-to-noise ratio of gradients in stochastic gradient descent and, as shown by McCandlish et al. (2018), can be used to approximate the Critical Batch Size (CBS) during neural network training. Despite its appearance in technical reports of frontier models, no open dataset of GNS measurements across modern architectures exists, limiting systematic study of the metric. We close this gap by releasing OpenGNS, a dataset of more than 400 GNS measurement trajectories spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets, autoregressive language modeling with Generative Pre-trained Transformers (GPTs), and image synthesis with Diffusion Transformers (DiTs), covering models from 11M to 1B parameters trained under Maximal Update Parameterization (muP) with dense batch-size and learning-rate sweeps. Building on this dataset, we study how the GNS depends on hyperparameters, scale, and training progress, and how it relates to the CBS. We find that the GNS behaves as a consistent "temperature of training", remaining stable across model sizes under muP at equivalent loss, and our results suggest task-dependent biases in its relation to the CBS: a tendency to overestimate the CBS for classification and to underestimate it for generative tasks, consistent in direction across common CBS definitions. The dataset is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/olympique-marcel/OpenGNS

papers.intro:
The GNS (GNS), introduced by McCandlish et al., (2018), provides a principled approach to understanding the trade-offs inherent in stochastic gradient descent. Intuitively, the GNS quantifies the noise in the stochastic gradient: When gradient noise is high, larger batch sizes are beneficial, as averaging over more samples yields a more accurate approximation of the true gradient. When noise is already low, additional samples merely increase computational cost per update without improving gradient quality. This intuition connects the GNS to the CBS (CBS), which is the batch size that balances runtime and computational effort required to reach a given loss level, and is therefore highly relevant to the AutoML community.

Understanding and accurately estimating the CBS has become increasingly important in the era of foundation models. Pre-training autoregressive LLM and diffusion models from the CV (CV) domain consumes substantial computational resources, often distributed across thousands of GPU (Singh et al.,, 2025; Grattafiori et al.,, 2024; NVIDIA et al.,, 2025). Making pre-training more efficient, therefore, reduces energy consumption and cost, and helps democratize AI (AI) research for academic laboratories that lack industrial-scale compute. In the data-parallel training setting, the global batch size directly determines how many GPU can be utilized in parallel, making batch-size selection a critical decision that affects training efficiency, resource utilization, and final model quality.

We close this gap with OpenGNS, an open dataset of GNS measurements spanning three domains: image classification with ResNets on CIFAR-10, autoregressive language modeling with GPT on FineWeb, and image synthesis with DiT on ImageNet. The dataset covers eleven model configurations from 11M up to 1B parameters under muP, trained over dense batch-size and learning-rate grids. Such a dataset is also directly relevant to the AutoML community. Full hyperparameter sweeps over batch size and learning rate are prohibitively expensive at the scale of modern foundation models, and methods that rely on cheap proxies (smaller models or shorter runs) depend on the assumption that low-fidelity behavior transfers to higher fidelities. Per-step trajectories of loss and GNS across a dense grid of model sizes, batch sizes, and learning rates provide a quantitative basis for studying this assumption and for informing HPO (HPO) strategies for batch-size and learning-rate selection without re-running the underlying experiments. Alongside the dataset, we present an empirical study that demonstrates its utility and yields insights that can inform more efficient allocation of computational resources in large-scale training runs. In summary, we make the following three contributions: • The OpenGNS dataset: We release GNS measurements together with training and validation losses for more than 400 training runs spanning three domains, eleven model sizes, and dense batch-size/learning-rate grids under muP. To our knowledge, this is the first open dataset of its kind. • GNS across hyperparameters: The measurement of the GNS depends strongly on the batch-size and learning-rate configuration. However, when both hyperparameters are jointly well-tuned, training runs exhibit consistent GNS trajectories, validating the notion of the GNS as a temperature of training (McCandlish et al.,, 2018) also for modern Transformer architectures. • GNS across loss and model size: Empirical tests examine how well the GNS approximates the CBS across different learning tasks, extending experiments from McCandlish et al., (2018) on CIFAR-10 to GPT-style architectures and DiT. The results suggest systematic differences depending on the task type: Overestimation for classification and underestimation for generative tasks. Scaling up model size under muP, both metrics remain consistent across model sizes, enabling transfer of CBS recommendations across widths at the same loss.

papers.title: About the occurrence of Akhmediev breathers in dispersive systems
papers.abstract: Akhmediev breathers are spatially periodic solutions of the NLS equation which are localized in time. We prove a new NLS approximation result for dispersive wave systems, showing that there are solutions to these systems where Akhmediev breathers in the lowest order approximately modulate the underlying wave packet. Since the solutions of the original wave system are quasi-periodic in space, the main challenge is to find an appropriate function space to estimate the approximation error.

papers.title: A unified Sobolev framework for long-wave limits of the Gross-Pitaevskii equation
papers.abstract: We present a unified justification of the KdV, Airy, inviscid Burgers, and Whitham approximations for the one-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii equation in Sobolev spaces. Using energy estimates for its Madelung formulation, we establish quantitative error bounds on the natural time scales of the respective approximations. The analysis covers different long-wave scaling regimes within a single framework.

papers.intro:
We consider the one-dimensional Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equation i∂tq=−∂x2q+2(|q|2−1)q,i\partial_{t}q=-\partial_{x}^{2}q+2(|q|^{2}-1)q, (1) with x,t∈ℝx,t\in{\mathbb{R}} and q⁡(x,t)∈ℂq(x,t)\in{\mathbb{C}}. We are interested in the description of the dynamics near q=1q=1 by amplitude equations in various long wave limits. For sufficiently small amplitudes, linear dispersion dominates and leads to the Airy equation. At the critical scaling, dispersion and nonlinear transport balance, yielding the KdV equation. For larger but still asymptotically vanishing amplitudes, nonlinear transport dominates, resulting in the inviscid Burgers equation. When the amplitude remains fixed in the long-wave limit, the coupled evolution is described by Whitham’s modulation equations. We prove the validity of these approximations within a unified Sobolev framework.

We prove the validity of these approximations within a unified Sobolev framework.

papers.title: Learning to Interact in Multi-Agent Self-Play for Controllable Autonomous Driving Scenario Generation
papers.abstract: Large-scale, multi-agent self-play trains robust driving policies effectively in simulation, but controlling these models to generate specific, safety-critical edge cases remains a key challenge. Existing goal-conditioned self-play frameworks rely primarily on static map-location goals and fail to reliably produce complex agent interactions such as aggressive tailgating or adversarial cut-offs. These agent interactions are necessary for rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing. To address this, we present an extended multi-agent self-play framework that introduces agent-relative dynamic goals. By conditioning policies on this extended goal representation, our framework enables targeted, controllable scenario synthesis. We demonstrate that our approach successfully generates interactive driving behaviors that static-goal baselines cannot simulate, providing a flexible tool for long-tail scenario generation in AV testing.
papers.intro:
Rigorous autonomous vehicle (AV) testing depends on being able to simulate long-tail driving scenarios with agents that react to the vehicle under test rather than ignore it. Recent advances have shown that large-scale, multi-agent self-play can be used to train such agents [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. In contrast, the common alternatives for simulation agents (log replay, hand-scripted actors, and rule-based car-following models [7]) fail to produce realistic interactive behavior.

Recent advances have shown that large-scale, multi-agent self-play can be used to train such agents [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. In contrast, the common alternatives for simulation agents (log replay, hand-scripted actors, and rule-based car-following models [7]) fail to produce realistic interactive behavior.

Gigaflow [1] is the clearest demonstration of this, where copies of one policy control every traffic participant. This policy is trained against copies of itself in large-scale simulation to optimize a parameterized reward function, with each agent receiving different parameters sampled during training. Agents observe a local view of the map, goal locations, their own state, nearby agents, and their reward parameters. From this setup, and without any human driving data, the policy learns generalist, robust, and human-like driving. Conditioning on the reward parameters allows the agent’s behavior to be controlled at inference time (e.g. to create harder simulations by making agents more aggressive).

Simulation agents are used to test an AV system. During validation, challenging agent interactions such as cut-offs, tailgating, and brake checks are of particular interest; nominal driving behavior is simply not very useful for testing advanced AV systems. What we want is an agent that can reliably produce these interactions in simulations with the AV driving system. The standard self-play recipe, however, cannot achieve this. As demonstrated below, the reward parameters and static goals used to condition these agents are insufficient to get the agent to perform these key interactions with another agent. This begs the question: how can we modify the multi-agent self-play training recipe to add support for agent interactions while preserving all the positive attributes of this recipe?
