In this work, we improve the multi-agent self-play recipe of Gigaflow by adding support for agent-relative goals through an extended goal interface. These agent-relative goals are defined with respect to another reference agent and therefore move along with that reference agent. These new goals allow us to simulate specific agent interactions that otherwise cannot be expressed with the previous static goals. For example, we can command a red agent to cut-off the blue agent by placing the red agent’s goal in front of the blue agent (Figure 1). Because the goal is agent-relative, it moves with the blue agent. The only way for the red agent to reach its goal is to get in front of the blue agent.

papers.title: The geometry of neural network decision boundaries
papers.abstract: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) are built using well-understood mathematical operations, yet their complex nature poses significant challenges to intuitively understanding their decision-making processes. This work introduces a method for visualizing and measuring ANN decision boundary geometry directly in the high-dimensional input space, avoiding distortions found with traditional projection-based techniques. We analyze boundary curvatures and distances in diverse inputs, architectures, and training methods. Boundary distances grow smoothly and slowly with consistent curvature as the size of the subspace increases, suggesting that decision boundaries are close to input samples within large, continuous subspaces. We also quantify how much boundary distances and curvatures reduce near dataset samples after adversarial training. Training methodology has a significantly stronger impact on boundary distance and curvature than architecture or test-set accuracy. These findings are contextualized within prior work, supporting or refuting several previously proposed theories of boundary behavior. Our analytically and empirically supported methodology lays the foundation for future studies to improve network interpretability and understanding.

papers.title: Rethinking Contrastive Targets in Radiology Language-Image Pretraining
papers.abstract: CLIP-style contrastive image-text pretraining is widely used in radiology data, where each image is paired with one report and every other report in the batch is treated as a negative. Under this recipe, two failures appear, neither of which is systematically addressed by existing contrastive learning theory: zero-shot evaluation peaks then degrades while training loss keeps decreasing, and training fails to learn from large batches. We hypothesize the cause is structural rather than radiology-specific: many unpaired reports share clinical findings with a given image, so CLIP's paired-identity target is systematically biased, not merely noisy. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology, a synthetic testbed that preserves only this overlapping-fact structure and reproduces both failures. With evidence that the structure is sufficient to reproduce the failures, we develop a target-misspecification theory that explains both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size, and use it to motivate a minimal compatibility-based correction, CorLIP: text is treated as positive whenever its clinical assertions agree with the image, with no architecture changes. Beyond benchmark improvements, CorLIP largely removes the post-peak degradation, makes large-batch training succeed where it previously collapsed, substantially amplifies the gains from more data, and is the only configuration that remains stable up to B=2048. The correction transfers from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.

papers.intro:
Contrastive language–image pretraining (CLIP) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for learning general-purpose visual representations from paired image–text data [1], and the same contrastive objective is widely used in radiology vision–language pretraining (VLP) across imaging modalities, including X-ray [2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], CT [8, 9, 10], MRI [11] and multi-modality images [12, 13]. These systems usually inherit a paired-identity assumption from CLIP: within a batch, the paired text is the only positive for an image, and every other text is treated as a negative. This assumption is approximately correct for web image–caption data, where captions and image content are less likely to overlap, but its validity on radiology image–report data has not been systematically examined. Prior work tends to attribute medical CLIP’s difficulties to a broad medical-vs-general domain gap [14, 15, 16]. We argue this gap has a precise and identifiable structure that helps explain why the standard recipe is systematically biased.

We argue this gap has a precise and identifiable structure that helps explain why the standard recipe is systematically biased.

We systematically study the training dynamics of medical CLIP and document two failure modes that current contrastive theory does not address. First, the rise-then-fall dynamic: zero-shot performance rises, peaks, and then degrades while training loss decreases monotonically, even though a supervised classifier on the identical backbone shows no late-training drop, ruling out generic overfitting. Second, large-batch collapse: training fails to learn (AUC near random, loss near log⁡B\log B) at batch sizes that are routinely beneficial for general-domain CLIP [1, 17, 18]. Existing literature has noted pieces of these phenomena without systematic analysis [19, 20, 21, 10] or attributed the rise-then-fall pattern to overfitting [22], but neither failure has a unified explanation. Together, these upstream failures cap downstream performance and prevent medical CLIP from leveraging the growing scale of image–report data.

Second, large-batch collapse: training fails to learn (AUC near random, loss near log⁡B\log B) at batch sizes that are routinely beneficial for general-domain CLIP [1, 17, 18]. Existing literature has noted pieces of these phenomena without systematic analysis [19, 20, 21, 10] or attributed the rise-then-fall pattern to overfitting [22], but neither failure has a unified explanation. Together, these upstream failures cap downstream performance and prevent medical CLIP from leveraging the growing scale of image–report data.

These observations point to a single suspect: the contrastive target. We hypothesize that both failures arise from a structural property of the data rather than from medical-specific appearance, language, or annotation. Specifically, radiology image–report pairs share what we call a shared-schema fact-bundle structure: anatomy is the same across images (lungs, heart, mediastinum, pleura), each anatomical region carries a finding state drawn from a small clinical vocabulary (e.g., effusion present or absent, cardiomegaly present or absent), and each report bundles assertions about many such states simultaneously. Under this structure, multiple unpaired reports can match a given image on most asserted findings, so paired identity is systematically biased rather than merely noisy. The hypothesis is falsifiable: any data sharing the same three ingredients should fail in the same way, regardless of domain. To test this, we construct CLEVR-Radiology [23], a synthetic testbed that retains the three ingredients but strips every radiology-specific factor such as image appearance, clinical jargon, annotation noise, and scale. Both failures recur identically on CLEVR-Radiology, supporting the hypothesis that the structure, rather than radiology-specific artifacts alone, can drive the failures. We then formalize this as a target-misspecification theory that derives both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias amplified by batch size.

The correction generalizes across radiology modalities, from chest X-ray (CXR) to 3D CT.

Contributions. (i) Diagnostic. We identify two failures of medical CLIP (rise-then-fall, large-batch collapse) and isolate their cause as structural via CLEVR-Radiology, a controlled synthetic testbed. (ii) Theory. A target-misspecification theory derives both failures from a single deterministic gradient bias, with two verified predictions: a quantitative loss-floor match and a mechanistic shortcut heatmap drift. (iii) Correction. We propose CorLIP11 1 Project repository: https://github.com/yhygao/CorLIP, a minimal compatibility-based correction, which requires no change to architecture or optimizer, and only changes the batch target matrix constructed with an offline fact parser. Beyond benchmark improvements on chest X-ray classification and grounding, CorLIP recovers scaling regimes that do not work with vanilla medical CLIP: large-batch training succeeds where it previously collapsed (stable up to B=2048B{=}2048), additional data delivers substantial rather than marginal gains, and the correction generalizes from chest X-ray to 3D CT modalities.

papers.title: Skill Roulette: Measuring Skill Invocation Rate Across LLM Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Agent skills package procedures for large language model (LLM) coding agents. An agent selects a skill from its name and description before reading the procedure. It may complete the task without invoking a relevant skill. We investigate how reliably coding agents invoke relevant skills and which factors affect that decision. We estimate invocation rates by repeating trials with identical inputs; invocation rate is the proportion of trials in which the agent invokes the relevant skill. We test 9 non-directional hypotheses about skill metadata, competing skills, contextual instructions, and task wording and composition. Eight concern invocation; the ninth tests whether making a skill available changes the occurrence of an action that the task does not request. We use tasks from 4 software engineering categories in a synthetic repository, running each of 4 coding-agent harnesses with 2 models. The planned 20,400 trials include 60 repetitions per Baseline category and configuration, 60 more per category in Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5 that admit each category's task and skill, and 10 per experimental condition. Comparisons are specified before collection and evaluated within each model and harness configuration using Boschloo's exact test.

An agent skill is a file containing a procedure that a large language model (LLM) coding agent should follow for a class of tasks. The agent first reads the skill’s name and description, assesses its relevance, and decides whether to load the body (Anthropic, 2026e). The procedure can guide the agent only after the skill body loads (Figure 1).

The agent first reads the skill’s name and description, assesses its relevance, and decides whether to load the body (Anthropic, 2026e). Successful task completion does not establish whether an agent invoked a relevant skill or followed its procedure. A trace can establish whether the skill was invoked, but deciding whether it should have been invoked requires an assessment of its relevance. When a missed invocation matters, a developer can supply the procedure directly or require the agent to invoke the skill. Understanding when such omissions occur is a prerequisite for detecting and correcting them in autonomous workflows.

papers.title: Neural Network-Based In-Contact Task Segmentation of Demonstrated Robot Motions via Hand Guiding
papers.abstract: Intuitive robot programming approaches, such as Programming by Demonstration, enable non-experts to teach robots tasks through hand-guided demonstrations. However, for in-contact tasks requiring force control for parts of the motion, automated segmentation of motion types is crucial for improving usability. Considering the related work, this work proposes a neural network-based segmentation method categorizing motion into three fundamental types using input data of cartesian twists and wrenches at the end effector. We collect demonstration data using a 7-axis robot with a wrist-mounted force torque sensor and generate ground truth labeling by hand. While still in development, our research direction aims to enable non-experts to program in-contact tasks more intuitively.

papers.intro:
The shortage of skilled workers significantly affects the economy, making automation a key strategy to enhance work efficiency [1]. As more affordable robot models enter the market [2], cobots are also becoming accessible to small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). Nevertheless, hiring a robot expert to program such systems is often not affordable for SMEs. Intuitive robot programming approaches focus on simplifying robotic systems and minimizing this problem by enabling non-experts to program them [3].

Intuitive robot programming approaches focus on simplifying robotic systems and minimizing this problem by enabling non-experts to program them [3].

Programming by Demonstration (PbD) provides an intuitive solution by allowing users, for example, to move the robot along the desired path via hand guiding [4, 5]. However, the robot’s trajectory alone is sometimes not sufficient to achieve all the goals intended by the user. For some tasks, the interaction force with the environment is also required (e.g., during surface treatment or assembly). Therefore, these so-called in-contact or contact-rich tasks require a specification of position and force over time. To enable non-experts to program such tasks, we extend an existing intuitive programming framework [6, 7] for pick-and-place tasks to in-contact tasks. For this, we developed an intuitive visualization and force input method via a touch GUI in our previous work [8, 9]. To further extend our approach, measuring the interaction forces with the environment directly during the user’s demonstration would be beneficial. Often, a wrist-mounted force torque sensor [10, 11] or a sensor attached to the environment [12] is utilized.

The user typically demonstrates a task of different motion segments during the programming process. For example, when wiping a whiteboard with an already gripped sponge, the segments are approaching, wiping, and departing the whiteboard (see Fig. 1). Segmenting and labeling the recorded path data is a lengthy and complex task that exceeds non-experts’ capabilities. Therefore, automating this procedure is necessary for an intuitive workflow. The advantages of such segmentation are, for example, extraction of the end condition of the segment, optimization of the movement (acceleration, adaption through machine learning models), or visualization in the programming system.

While previous literature has proposed various labeling approaches (see Sect. II), we aim for a method segmenting a robot motion into universally applicable motion types related to the fundamentals of force-controlled actions [13, 14]. To achieve this, we categorize motion segments into three distinct types: (a) Guarded motion, which terminates upon reaching a predefined force/torque condition (Fig. 1(a)); (b) Compliant motion, where interaction with the environment continues until a specified trajectory is completed (Fig. 1(b)); (c) Free space motion, where the robot moves without external contact (Fig. 1(c)). A key advantage of such a segmentation approach is its generality, as these three motion types allow for a complete and assumption-free decomposition of any demonstrated task.

Early segmentation methods relied on rule- and threshold-based techniques [15, 16], which limit adaptability across various tasks, application areas, and robotic systems. To overcome these limitations, we propose a research direction exploring machine learning-driven segmentation. By training a model to classify motion segments, we aim to eliminate the need for predefined thresholds, creating a more adaptive and parameter-free method. Our goal is to enable non-expert users to intuitively program general in-contact tasks, enhancing the accessibility of robot programming. We start by reviewing related work with a focus on machine learning approaches (Sec. II), followed by our proposed method (Sec. III), and conclude the extended abstract in Sec. IV.

papers.title: On the Beauville Dimension of Finite Abelian Groups
papers.abstract: Unmixed Beauville manifolds of general type are rigid quotients of products of compact complex curves of higher genus by free diagonal actions of finite groups. Their biholomorphism classes are encoded by equivalence classes of group-theoretic data. For a finite abelian group $G$, we characterize when these data exist and determine the unmixed Beauville dimension $\mathrm{d}_{\mathcal{U}}(G)$, the minimum dimension of such a manifold arising from a diagonal action of $G$. We prove that $\mathrm{d}_{\mathcal{U}}(G)<\infty$ if and only if $\exp(G)$ is odd and greater than $3$, and the largest invariant factor of $G$ occurs at least twice. In that case, \[ \mathrm{d}_{\mathcal{U}}(G)=\max\{\mathrm{rk}(G),\mathrm{rk}_3(G)+2\}. \] Specializing to $\mathrm{d}_{\mathcal{U}}(G)=2$ recovers the classical result of Bauer, Catanese and Grunewald: the finite abelian Beauville surface groups are precisely $(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^2$ with $n>1$ and $\gcd(n,6)=1$. Although the Beauville dimension has a geometric origin, our proof is entirely group-theoretic and combinatorial.

papers.title: A Hierarchical Onboard Vision-Language-Navigation Framework for Aerial Robots in Complex Environments
papers.abstract: Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are expected to achieve semantic reasoning, intelligent decision-making, and long-horizon navigation under strict onboard constraints. While recent foundation-model-driven approaches have shown promising progress toward this goal, existing methods remain limited by challenges in 3D data availability, trajectory feasibility, long-horizon reasoning, and computational efficiency in complex environments. To bridge these gaps, we propose VLN-AR, a hierarchical vision-language-navigation (VLN) framework for aerial robots. VLN-AR decouples multimodal reasoning and low-level control, enabling structured prediction of 3D pose commands and navigation intentions that are translated into dynamically feasible actions. In addition, a lightweight cognitive agent improves long-horizon reasoning via memory-aware task decomposition. Existing UAV navigation datasets are often limited to outdoor environments with coarse visual features and insufficient fine-grained structural details, resulting in sim-to-real domain gaps. • Mismatch between 3D action representation and safety-aware control. UAV navigation requires safe and reliable control. End-to-end continuous commands derived from foundation models often fail to guarantee safety or satisfy dynamical constraints, while semantically discrete action representations offer limited maneuverability. Balancing 3D maneuverability, control stability, and collision avoidance remains a core challenge. • Insufficient reasoning for long-horizon embodied navigation. Existing VLN/VLA methods typically rely on single-frame or short-term reasoning, making it difficult to integrate historical observations in complex indoor environments. Long-horizon aerial navigation requires spatial grounding, conditional inference, and sequential task decomposition, which cannot be sufficiently supported by single-step prediction schemes. • Prohibitive onboard computational constraints. State-of-the-art foundation models are computationally intensive, making real-time deployment on small UAVs with strict size, weight, and power (SWaP) constraints challenging [11]. Practical onboard deployment therefore requires preserving strong inference capability while significantly reducing computational and memory overhead.

papers.title: H3Remover: Reinforcing Video Object Removal without Paired Data
papers.abstract: Pretrained video editors possess rich removal and completion priors, yet may retain targets or alter unrelated content. We present H3Remover, which reinforces MiniMax-H3 Base Ref2VA for video object removal without paired object-free training targets. To discourage superficial edits such as recoloring, a target-removal reward favors calibrated depth changes consistent with revealing farther content. To limit unintended scene changes, a background-geometry reward encourages preservation of relative depth ordering. To preserve background appearance without retaining unwanted shadows or reflections, an appearance reward constrains RGB changes in source-derived protected regions while exempting targets and estimated effects. Frozen HPSv3 complements these constraints with perceptual-quality feedback for synthesized content. Evaluation regions remain fixed across candidates, and DiffusionART optimizes LoRA adapters with the backbone frozen. Experiments show substantial reconstruction gains over original H3, with qualitative comparisons demonstrating more effective object removal and better preservation of surrounding scene content.

papers.intro:
Video object removal aims to erase unwanted objects and reconstruct the scene behind them while retaining the content that should remain unchanged. Beyond filling masked pixels, this task requires a careful balance between modifying the target and preserving the surrounding scene. Flow-guided propagation and spatiotemporal transformers provide effective tools for video inpainting [22, 53, 57], while diffusion-based approaches introduce generative priors for recovering missing content [21, 1, 58]. However, the region that needs modification may extend beyond an object’s visible silhouette: shadows, reflections, and other associated effects can remain after the object itself disappears [29, 31, 7]. A useful removal model must therefore learn both what to change and what to preserve.

Beyond filling masked pixels, this task requires a careful balance between modifying the target and preserving the surrounding scene. Flow-guided propagation and spatiotemporal transformers provide effective tools for video inpainting [22, 53, 57], while diffusion-based approaches introduce generative priors for recovering missing content [21, 1, 58]. However, the region that needs modification may extend beyond an object’s visible silhouette: shadows, reflections, and other associated effects can remain after the object itself disappears [29, 31, 7]. A useful removal model must therefore learn both what to change and what to preserve.

Obtaining paired supervision for this task is challenging: a clean target video must remove both the object and its associated effects while preserving the remaining scene and temporal alignment. Existing efforts construct such pairs through synthetic rendering or controlled real-world capture [31, 7]. Rendering depends on curated assets and simulated interactions, while real-world capture requires carefully matched scene conditions, lighting, and camera motion. These requirements make data construction costly and constrain coverage of diverse real-world scenes and effects. This motivates adapting a capable pretrained editor without requiring paired object-free target videos.

Our first two rewards use estimated geometry to distinguish desirable target changes from undesirable background changes. When an opaque foreground object is removed, the newly revealed surface is typically farther from the camera than the object it replaces. We use this observation to define a target-removal reward: after calibrating source and edited depth predictions to a comparable scale, we reward target pixels whose estimated depth increases. This signal serves as a proxy for revealing the scene behind the object, rather than a semantic certificate of successful removal. To constrain the surrounding scene, a complementary background-geometry reward penalizes changes in the relative depth ordering of background pixel pairs. Inspired by the use of depth ranking in SparseNeRF [44], this term encourages consistent near–far relationships instead of requiring identical absolute depth predictions. Both rewards use a frozen Video Depth Anything estimator [6], encouraging targeted geometric change while constraining the scene outside the target regions.

papers.title: Beyond Stars: MTTX Brings Developer Responsiveness to Dependency Decisions, from Dashboard to IDE to GitHub Actions
papers.abstract: Modern software reuses open-source packages as dependencies, and developers often choose among candidate packages with cheap signals, such as GitHub stars and download counts. However, such signals are easy to fake, so developers need signals that represent "observed behavior," such as how quickly the developers of a package respond to new dependency releases and to security fixes. Prior work computed these responsiveness metrics, MTTU (Mean Time To Update) dependencies and MTTR (Mean Time To Remediate) vulnerable dependencies, but only with a research prototype for a fixed set of packages. Therefore, developers cannot easily benefit from them or integrate them into their workflow. We present MTTX, an open-source tool that computes MTTU and MTTR with accurate historical dependency resolution for any package and given time window, and brings them into different phases of developer workflow. MTTX resolves each version constraint of npm, PyPI, and Cargo packages as of a past date, with data from the native registries or deps.dev and vulnerability data from OSV. We validated MTTX with 328 automated tests, and for 90 packages from prior work, we manually verified its dependency resolution at each historical release point and its MTTU and MTTR computation. Developers can use MTTX in an interactive web dashboard, an IDE extension, and a GitHub Action, which are all available from the project homepage at https://imranur-rahman.github.io/dependency-update-metrics/. We envision that package registries (e.g., npm) and metadata aggregators and intelligence platforms (e.g., deps.dev) will display these values on the package page, alongside download counts and stars, to make them easier for developers to access. A demo video is at https://youtu.be/MZqjDnJ8bEQ.

papers.title: automodel: A Skill for Agentic Model Discovery
papers.abstract: The search for better models, whether expressed as analytical equations or neural architectures, has increasingly shifted from manual design toward data-driven automation. While a multitude of algorithms exist, ranging from exhaustive search to AlphaEvolve, recent advances in general-purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex raise the question: could providing such systems with a "model discovery recipe" be enough to discover or improve models? We present automodel, an agent skill for general model discovery. With case studies in astrophysics, cardiovascular dynamics, precision agriculture, traffic flow, and vehicle tire dynamics, we show how commercial agents equipped with automodel can successfully identify novel and scientifically-relevant models. Our findings suggest that encoding model-discovery methodology as a portable agent skill can provide a simple, interactive, powerful and broadly applicable alternative to domain-specific automated discovery pipelines. The skill is available at: https://github.com/unlayer-ai/automodel.

Since the 20th century, advances in computational power and algorithms have made it possible to automate many steps in this process. Heuristics for discovering models as physics laws from data emerged before the 1990s [1], predating the subsequent development of genetic programming-based symbolic regression, where compositions of operators, variables, and constants that fit the data are evolved [2, 3]. In 2009, Schmidt and Lipson used symbolic regression to demonstrate that Hamiltonians, Lagrangians, and other known physical laws could be recovered automatically from observational data [4]. Today, modern symbolic regression algorithms range from evolutionary to deep learning approaches, and have proven capable of discovering new candidate laws, for example in astrophysics [5, 6].

papers.title: Convergence of replicator-mutator particle systems via bounded Wasserstein distance
papers.abstract: Interacting particle systems with selection and mutation mechanisms arise in biological modeling, evolutionary optimization, and particle filtering methods. In this work we will consider the paradigmatic replicator-mutator PDE, which combines a diffusive component with a source term that depends on an external potential. We derive quantitative error estimates for the distance between the empirical measure of an unweighted particle system and the solution of the PDE. The proof uses a Wasserstein-1 distance with a bounded ground cost, which allows us to treat unbounded potentials on an unbounded state space. The key tools are the optimal coupling of newly resampled particles and, for the time-continuous limit, the use of a discrete-time killing resampling.

papers.title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
papers.abstract: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.

papers.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
papers.abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

Hardware specialization can improve datacenter performance, energy, and cost efficiency (Ranganathan et al., 2021; Abali et al., 2020; Sriraman and Dhanotia, 2020). Specialization can take several forms, from new instructions and dedicated execution units within a CPU to tightly coupled or detached accelerators (Zhang and Sanchez, 2019; Kanev et al., 2017; Karandikar et al., 2021; Stojkovic et al., 2026). By tailoring hardware to recurring computations, designers can avoid the overheads of executing those computations on general-purpose processors. At datacenter scale, even modest application-level improvements can translate into substantial savings.

By tailoring hardware to recurring computations, designers can avoid the overheads of executing those computations on general-purpose processors. At datacenter scale, even modest application-level improvements can translate into substantial savings.

However, deciding which computations warrant specialized hardware is difficult because datacenters run diverse services built from large, continuously evolving software stacks (Kanev et al., 2015; Ayers et al., 2019; Gonzalez et al., 2023). Their execution spans application logic, runtime systems, and many layers of libraries. Across services, cycles spread over many functions, each contributing only part of the total cost. Hence, a locally expensive function does not necessarily provide a useful specialization target. Hardware vendors must consider whether a target’s aggregate benefits justify the design, integration, and deployment costs.

Successful specializations often begin with clearly identified targets. ML provides good examples: GPUs and custom accelerators such as Google’s TPU (Jouppi et al., 2023), Meta’s MTIA (Krishnamurthy and Bland, 2026), and Microsoft’s Maia accelerate widely used AI/ML kernels (Guthrie, 2026). Beyond ML, researchers have identified a datacenter tax: recurring infrastructure work, such as memory allocation, serialization, and compression, that supports many services (Kanev et al., 2015; Sriraman and Dhanotia, 2020). Researchers proposed numerous accelerators to address these overheads (Kanev et al., 2017; Karandikar et al., 2021; Abali et al., 2020; Pourhabibi et al., 2020). Even commercial platforms, such as Intel’s Sapphire Rapids (Mulnix, 2022) and Microsoft’s Cobalt 200 (Bilgin and Stemen, 2025), now incorporate related capabilities through integrated on-chip accelerators. Specialization also appears within processor instruction sets, including AVX for vector operations and AMX for matrix operations (Intel, 2026).

For example, a small character-classification unit could accelerate a shared step across multiple serialization and parsing functions. However, the same computation can appear in different forms. One implementation may compare characters explicitly, while another uses a lookup table. Therefore, identifying shared computations requires reasoning about what the code computes across different implementations. This is difficult to perform manually at datacenter scale.

However, these approaches miss shared computations when their algorithms differ. LLM agents offer a way to connect these implementations via semantic reasoning. They can interpret new code, investigate relationships between implementations, and revise their conclusions using analysis tools (Yang et al., 2024; Trae Research Team et al., 2025). However, applying them directly to datacenter software introduces challenges in both scale and reliability. Large software stacks exceed their analysis capacity, and their conclusions can incorrectly group code with different behavior. Hence, reliable automation requires a compact representation of executed code and independent correctness checks on the agents’ semantic claims.

To address these challenges, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that discovers shared computations across workloads and translates them into hardware specialization candidates. Lodestone makes semantic analysis scalable through compact representations of frequently executed code regions. Then, agents reason about what these code regions compute and group implementations of the same computation into a computational family, even when their code structure differs. Independent agents challenge these matches and search for overlooked relationships. To check the resulting claims, Lodestone tests each piece of code against a set of provided reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions.

For selected families, Lodestone next proposes hardware implementations and the software changes needed to invoke them. These candidates include ISA extensions in the core, near-core units beside it, and detached accelerators. Lodestone chooses among them based on the amount of work per invocation, memory-access patterns, and the cost of invoking the hardware. For example, Lodestone discovers hash-table probes across database engines and proposes a parameterized instruction that accommodates their different table layouts. In key-value stores, it identifies recurring hash-mixing operations across five algorithms and proposes a near-core unit that supports those algorithms. In AI agents, it discovers escaped-length calculations across JSON encoders and proposes an instruction that handles their different character policies. Human experts then assess these proposals to determine if the benefits across implementations justify the hardware and software integration costs.

papers.title: A Fast, Programmable GPU-to-CPU Invocation Layer for GPU-Initiated Communication
papers.abstract:
Modern GPU workloads increasingly rely on device-initiated communication to let GPU kernels communicate directly without synchronizing with the host at kernel boundaries. Existing libraries commonly favor placing transport control on GPU threads, an approach known as GPUDirect Async (GDA), and treat reverse offload to host proxy threads as a slower fallback. We argue that reverse offload can outperform GDA and should be a first-class communication path. We further propose exposing reverse offload as a programming interface that lets users define workload-specific communication operations.
  We present KIWI, a programmable reverse-offload framework that achieves sub-microsecond one-way device-to-host latency and hundreds of millions of operations per second. We address practical challenges of scaling reverse offload, including contention on shared queues, polling overhead, and load imbalance across proxies. KIWI-P2P, a SHMEM-like library built on KIWI, outperforms state-of-the-art GDA implementations in both latency and bandwidth. More importantly, KIWI-EP redesigns low-latency mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine kernels around workload-defined operations, lowering expert-parallel communication latency by up to 2.3x over the best existing backend on AMD GPUs and time per output token in vLLM by up to 29%. The source code of KIWI is available at https://github.com/AMDResearch/kiwi.

GPU cores favor bulk-parallel computation and data movement, whereas the NIC-facing control path is a sequence of dependent scalar steps of protocol selection, descriptor enqueueing, and doorbell ringing. On a GPU, these steps require branches, global-memory accesses, and system-scope fences. The weak sequential performance of a GPU thread thus limits the communication primitives and patterns that GDA can express efficiently. Moreover, a GPU furnishes far more parallel execution resources than a NIC provides independent communication endpoints. A GDA runtime therefore allocates many NIC endpoints, such as InfiniBand queue pairs, to reduce contention, yet GPU threads still outnumber them and must synchronize to share them. Both synchronization and large endpoint counts limit GDA scalability.

papers.title: Grounding Radiology Reports in 3D Chest CT: Results of the ReXGrounding Challenge
papers.abstract: Segmenting each reported finding in a radiology scan would allow findings to be measured and tracked over time and let AI systems generate reports that are verifiable, but so far AI models have performed poorly at this task. To advance this task, we organized the ReXGrounding Challenge at MICCAI 2026, the first challenge dedicated to it. Given a non-contrast chest CT scan and the set of findings from its report, participants trained models to produce the corresponding set of 3D segmentations. The challenge used 2,992 training and 200 validation scans from the ReXGroundingCT dataset, and evaluated methods on a held-out test set of 300 scans with 582 findings, exhaustively annotated by board-certified radiologists. In total, 48 teams from 15 countries made 760 submissions, and the best method reached a Dice of 0.375 and a hit rate of 0.77, matching agreement between two independent radiologist groups (Dice 0.32, hit rate 0.76, on a 50-scan subset). On the 100 scans of the pre-challenge benchmark, the winner reached a Dice of 0.390, against 0.285 for VoxTell, the best model before the challenge, which five of the six best teams fine-tuned. Non-focal findings remained far harder to segment than focal ones, instance F1 stayed below inter-reader agreement (0.34 vs. 0.47), and models sometimes segmented the right abnormality in the wrong location. Top methods thus match radiologist agreement in Dice, but non-focal findings, findings with multiple instances, and adherence to the anatomical location described in the text remain open problems.

papers.intro:
Radiology reports describe the location of each finding only in words, such as a “5 mm nodule in the posterior segment of the right upper lobe”, without marking it on the scan, so a reader has to find it again before it can be measured, compared with prior studies or checked. Grounding each finding, that is, segmenting the region a sentence describes, would let findings be measured and tracked over time and make reports, whether written by radiologists or generated by AI, verifiable against the image (Bannur et al., 2024; Baharoon et al., 2026a). This matters all the more as AI systems for medical image interpretation advance quickly, because their use in clinical practice depends on more than accuracy: their outputs must also be explainable and verifiable (Rajpurkar and Lungren, 2023; Silcox et al., 2024; Abgrall et al., 2024). The need is greatest in chest CT, which is performed in large volumes (about 20 million examinations a year in the United States alone (Smith-Bindman et al., 2025)) and in which a single scan often contains many co-occurring findings, from small nodules to diffuse emphysema.

Existing datasets, models and challenges do not support this task. Large chest CT datasets pair scans with reports but lack voxel-level labels (Hamamci et al., 2026b), and grounding datasets either link sentences to anatomical regions rather than to findings (Zhang et al., 2025a), have fewer than 250 cases (Bai et al., 2024), or focus on 2D modalities such as chest X-ray with bounding boxes instead of segmentation annotations (Boecking et al., 2022; De Castro et al., 2025). Current text-promptable segmentation models, trained mostly on short category-level prompts, fail on the descriptive findings written in radiology reports (Zhao et al., 2025c; Zhao et al., 2025a; Zhao et al., 2025b; Du et al., 2024; Subramanian et al., 2026; Baharoon et al., 2025). papers.title: MetacouplingLLM: Integrating geographic adjacency, flow indicators, and LLM-assisted analysis
papers.abstract: The metacoupling framework examines interactions within coupled human and natural systems and between adjacent or distant systems, but its application is constrained by inconsistent geographic classifications and limited standardized quantitative workflows. We present MetacouplingLLM, an open-source Python package integrating adjacency databases, reproducible flow indicators, and large language model (LLM)-assisted qualitative analysis. The databases combine administrative boundaries, hydrography, and fixed-crossing evidence, with configurable adjacency policies and optional country-level maritime adjacency. Metacoupled Flow Shares, Metacoupled Flow Evenness, and the Metacoupled Flow Concentration Index characterize flow composition, balance across coupling types, and partner concentration within each type. The qualitative workflow combines literature retrieval, optional web evidence, and geographic checks to draft structured analyses. Applications to global marine fishing and Indonesian palm oil demonstrate these capabilities; the fisheries reanalysis reveals differing partner concentration among regions with similar telecoupled flow shares. MetacouplingLLM facilitates consistent framework application and comparative sustainability research.

papers.title: Sharp boundary regularity for planar minimal graphs with analytic Dirichlet data
papers.abstract:
We study the boundary behavior of generalized (BV) solutions of the Dirichlet problem for the minimal surface equation over a bounded set \(\Omega\). Such a generalized solution is always the graph of a smooth function \(v\) inside \(\Omega\), but might carry a vertical part over \(\partial\Omega\), which records the gap between the prescribed Dirichlet datum \(g\) and the boundary trace \(h\) attained by \(v\). When \(\Omega\) is a bounded real-analytic planar domain and \(g\) is real analytic we prove that \(h\) is Lipschitz, right and left differentiable at every point, of class \(C^1\) on \(\partial\Omega\setminus\Sigma\), and real analytic on \(\{h\neq g\}\setminus\Sigma\), where \(\Sigma=\{\kappa=0\}\) is the zero set of the curvature of \(\partial\Omega\). Also, at each point \(p\in\Sigma\cap\{h\neq g\}\), the two one-sided branches extend real analytically across \(p\).
  The proof recasts the vertical part near a contact point as a scalar obstacle problem with a possibly degenerate right-hand side, whose model case is \(\Delta v=H\,\id_{\{v>0\}}\) with \(H\ge0\) a polynomial. These results are optimal: for merely smooth data the trace may be discontinuous, while in the real-analytic case there are examples where corners do occur.

papers.title: Target-Clamped Contrastive Learning in Nonlinear Resistive Networks with Monotone Elements
papers.abstract: In the pursuit of energy-efficient hardware for machine learning, nonlinear resistive networks trained via local learning rules are emerging as promising alternatives to digital neural networks. Learning in these physical systems is often achieved with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), which compares a "free" state to a "nudged" target-driven state to perform gradient descent on an objective defined by an explicit cost function. In contrast, Target-Clamped Contrastive Learning (TCCL) "clamps" output nodes directly to exact target values, performing gradient descent on an implicit contrastive function - an objective whose properties have long remained unknown. Focusing on nonlinear networks composed of resistors with monotonically increasing current-voltage characteristics (such as Ohmic resistors and diodes), our contribution is twofold. First, we establish rigorous convergence guarantees for TCCL. We prove that the contrastive function is convex for nonlinear resistive networks without hidden nodes, and demonstrate that this property does not hold in general for the objective function optimized by EP. For these networks, TCCL converges to a global minimum of the contrastive function under suitable assumptions on the learning rate. In the presence of hidden nodes, the contrastive function is not convex, but we show that TCCL still converges to a stationary point on a subsequence. We also reveal cases where such stationary points are global minimizers of the contrastive function. Second, we characterize the representational capacity of these circuits. We establish a novel function approximation theorem demonstrating that any continuous, monotonically non-decreasing, and shift-equivariant function can be approximated to arbitrary precision, proving that these properties are the sole limitations on the network's computational expressivity.

papers.intro:
The escalating energy demands of modern machine learning have driven a resurgence of interest in analog computing paradigms and the development of training methods dedicated to such platforms [34]. By replacing the digital von Neumann architecture with analog compute-in-memory substrates, these systems promise substantial improvements in energy efficiency for both inference and training. Among these alternative platforms, resistive networks have attracted special interest.

By replacing the digital von Neumann architecture with analog compute-in-memory substrates, these systems promise substantial improvements in energy efficiency for both inference and training. Among these alternative platforms, resistive networks have attracted special interest.

A resistive network is an electrical circuit comprised of (linear or nonlinear) resistors, with nodes typically partitioned into input, hidden and output sets. In such a network where computation is driven by the circuit’s physics, the input node potentials are clamped to specific values, while the output node potentials serve as the network’s prediction. Conductances of variable resistors serve as the trainable parameters, and the objective is to find parameter configurations that implement a desired input-output mapping. It is well-known that the hidden and output potentials of a linear resistive network minimize the total dissipated power; in nonlinear resistive networks—those containing nonlinear one-port resistive elements—the hidden and output potentials extremize a more general notion known as the co-content [32], also referred to as “pseudo-power” [27]. This property allows resistive networks to function as energy-based models where the co-content acts as the energy function. For such systems, energy-based learning rules have been developed which adjust conductances based solely on local voltage measurements, allowing decentralized training [27, 17, 3, 24]. On the hardware side, small-scale prototypes have successfully demonstrated self-learning capabilities on toy tasks [17, 16]. On the simulation side, SPICE-class simulations of modest-size nonlinear resistive networks have been performed on MNIST [27, 51], while recent methods exploit the co-content minimization formulation to achieve speedups of several orders of magnitude [43, 37], paving the way for large-scale simulations.

To rival artificial neural networks, resistive networks must demonstrate representational capacity, and learning capabilities. Learning in resistive networks was initially formalized by [27] through Equilibrium Propagation (EP), an energy-based learning framework that enables gradient descent on an arbitrary cost function [40]. EP is part of a broader class of energy-based learning methods [41] that optimize parameters by comparing the network in two different states: the inference state (called free state), and a perturbed state where outputs are clamped or nudged towards a target. Other energy-based learning rules differ from EP in the way the perturbed state is defined. In particular, the Contrastive Learning (CL) algorithm of [24] (adapted from [35, 41]) clamps output nodes to exact target values in the perturbed state, effectively performing gradient descent on a nonnegative contrastive function whose minimum of zero is attained precisely when the network outputs match the target output. In [24], it was shown that the contrastive function is convex for linear networks without hidden nodes, establishing the convergence for a range of step sizes. These results were also recently extended to linear resistive-capacitive networks in [23]. On the representational capacity front, [42] showed that nonlinear resistive networks can approximate arbitrary continuous functions, provided they incorporate two-port elements like voltage-controlled voltage sources (VCVSs).

In this paper, we establish mathematical foundations for learning and representation in nonlinear resistive networks constructed exclusively from one-port elements. This deliberately precludes the VCVSs utilized by [42]. We assume all circuit components possess strictly monotonically increasing current-voltage characteristics, which encompasses Ohmic resistors and diodes, and yields a strictly convex network co-content. Within this framework, we answer two fundamental questions: under what conditions does learning reliably converge, and what is the network’s representational capacity?

While [24] proved the convergence of the CL algorithm with clamped outputs, their analysis was limited to linear networks without hidden nodes. Our first main contribution extends their framework to nonlinear networks. We prove that the contrastive function is convex for nonlinear networks without hidden nodes, guaranteeing convergence of the parameters to a global minimum. This is in contrast with the EP objective function, which is in general non-convex, even without hidden nodes. For the more expressive and general case that includes hidden nodes, the contrastive function is no longer convex, but in this case, we prove that the learning dynamics converge on a subsequence to a stationary point. Interestingly, any of such stationary points in the interior of the constraint set is shown to be a global minimum of the contrastive function.

papers.title: Asgard/NOTT: L-band nulling interferometry at the VLTI IV. Prospects for characterising hot exozodiacal dust
papers.abstract: Near-infrared interferometric surveys have revealed extended emission around the photosphere of $\approx 40$ main-sequence stars, attributed to the presence of hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD). A promising technique for investigating this phenomenon is nulling interferometry. The Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI) nulling interferometer NOTT (Nulling Observations of exoplaneTs and dusT) is designed to characterise exoplanets and HEZD in the $L'$ band ($3.5-4.0\,\mu$m). We aim to assess NOTT's potential for the detection and characterisation of HEZD with various instrumental and model parameter configurations. We model the HEZD as an optically thin dust ring, using the nearby Sun-like star $\tau$ Ceti with HEZD as a reference model. Applying the end-to-end nulling tool SCIFYsim to model the instrumental response of NOTT to simulated HEZD brightness distributions, we evaluate how variations in HEZD and instrumental parameters affect NOTT's key observables: the photon flux rate and the null depth. We demonstrate that NOTT is capable of disentangling stellar and dust contributions to the signal and detecting HEZD. The null depth and photon flux rate are sensitive to the HEZD geometry, with inclination, position angle, and ring location having the strongest impact on the signal. Although the detailed temporal signatures are target-specific, the results can be generalised to other systems. NOTT has the potential to deliver unprecedented sensitivity for HEZD observations, granting access to detailed information through spectral dispersion, beam-combination schemes, and exploitation of sky rotation. This enables more sensitive HEZD detections than is possible with current instruments, and improved spatial constraints on the dust, as well as variability studies.

papers.intro: High-precision long-baseline interferometric observations of nearly 200 main-sequence stars, achieving angular resolutions of approximately 1010 mas, have revealed an interferometric signature in the near-infrared (NIR) photometric HH and KK bands for ≈40\approx 40 of these targets (e.g., Absil et al. 2006; Absil et al. 2013; Absil et al. 2021; Ertel et al. 2014; Ertel et al. 2016; Nuñez et al. 2017). This signature is interpreted as the spatially extended radiation originating from hot exozodiacal dust (HEZD) and translates into an excess over the stellar photospheric emission of at most a few percent. The observed NIR signature has been detected around stars spanning spectral types from G to A and is inferred to originate from regions close to the sublimation radius of the host star (Di Folco et al. 2007). Although these NIR excesses are commonly explained by submicron-sized grains (Kirchschlager et al. 2017), larger particles may also influence the observational appearance of HEZD (Stuber et al., 2023). Since submicron-sized grains are subject to rapid destruction via sublimation or ejection by radiation pressure (e.g., Backman & Paresce 1993), the persistence of HEZD around main-sequence stars presents a puzzling problem. To resolve this, models invoke either short-term replenishment through exocometary and planetesimal fragmentation (e.g., Bonsor et al. 2012; Bonsor et al. 2014; Faramaz et al. 2017; Sezestre et al. 2019) or grain trapping mechanisms facilitated by gas or magnetic fields (e.g., Lebreton et al. 2013; Su et al. 2013; Rieke et al. 2016; Stamm et al. 2019; Kimura et al. 2020; Pearce et al. 2020; Pearce et al. 2022). Furthermore, silicate grains are unlikely to be a dominant component, as their characteristic mid-infrared (MIR) spectral features would conflict with the faint MIR excess observed (Absil et al. 2006; Akeson et al. 2009; Kirchschlager et al. 2017; Stuber et al. 2023). Beyond its intrinsic physical properties, HEZD provides critical insights into the broader architecture of planetary systems (Kral et al. 2017). However, its presence also poses a potential challenge for future exo-Earth imaging missions, such as HWO (Habitable Worlds Observatory; Ertel et al. 2025) or LIFE (Large Interferometer for Exoplanets; Quanz et al. 2022). Specifically, HEZD can induce coronagraphic leakage or parasitic signals, elevate photon noise levels within the habitable zone, and complicate the polarimetric characterisation of close-in exoplanets (Ollmann et al. 2023). Detecting HEZD requires isolating faint circumstellar emission from the dominant stellar flux at small angular separations. Nulling interferometry (Bracewell 1978) addresses this challenge by explicitly suppressing the on-axis light. By adjusting the phases of incoming beams, the technique places a destructive interference fringe (the "null") directly onto the star so that the off-axis radiation from the circumstellar environment is revealed, with its transmission modulated by the specific geometry of the interferometric fringe pattern. The most productive ground-based nulling interferometers to date have operated in the NN band, including KIN (Keck Interferometer Nuller; Serabyn et al. 2012; Colavita et al. 2013) and LBTI (Large Binocular Telescope Interferometer; Hinz et al. 2016; Isbell et al. 2024). These instruments are particularly sensitive to warm habitable-zone dust and have enabled major surveys (KIN: Millan-Gabet et al. 2011; Mennesson et al. 2013; Mennesson et al. 2014; LBTI: Ertel et al. 2020) as well as detailed characterisations of individual systems (Lebreton et al. 2013; Lebreton et al. 2016; Defrère et al. 2021; Garreau et al. 2025). Moreover, KIN data have also been used to constrain the properties of HEZD (Kirchschlager et al. 2017; Stuber et al. 2023). The NOTT (Nulling Observations of exoplaneTs and dusT; Defrère et al. 2018; Defrère et al. 2022) is a high-contrast visitor instrument for the Very Large Telescope Interferometer (VLTI; Schoeller et al. 2003; Haubois et al. 2020). NOTT employs nulling beam-combination techniques in the L′L^{\prime} band (3.5−4.0​μ3.5-4.0\,\mum) to characterise exoplanets and HEZD. By combining either the four 8.2 m UTs (Unit Telescopes) or the four 1.8 m ATs (Auxiliary Telescopes) over baselines of up to 200 m, the nulling interferometric approach provides a significant sensitivity improvement for the detection of circumstellar emission compared to FLUOR (Fiber-Linked Unit for Optical Recombination; Coudé du Foresto et al. 1997) and PIONIER (Precision Integrated-Optics Near-infrared Imaging ExpeRiment; Le Bouquin et al. 2011). As part of the Asgard suite (Martinod et al. 2023), NOTT relies on the high-precision fringe tracker HEIMDALLR (High-Efficiency Multiaxial Do-it ALL Recombiner; Ireland et al. 2018; Taras et al. 2024) and the Baldr wavefront sensor (Courtney-Barrer et al. 2024) to reach its target performance. In addition, it operates alongside the beam combiner BIFROST (Beam-combination Instrument for studying the Formation and fundamental paRameters of Stars and planeTary systems; Kraus et al. 2022) and the Solarstein laser alignment calibrator (Taras et al. 2024). In the L′L^{\prime} band regime, the relatively low thermal background from the atmosphere and telescope optics compared to the NN band creates favourable conditions for detecting young giant planets and HEZD via their enhanced contrast against the host star relative to the HH and KK bands. Of the two HEZD studies in the LL band (Kirchschlager et al. 2020; Ollmann et al. 2025), a clear detection was reported only by Kirchschlager et al. 2020, with a dust-to-star flux ratio up to a factor of five higher than typical HH band values, where most detections have been made using constructive long-baseline interferometry. Combined with the tenfold improvement in contrast achieved through nulling interferometry, NOTT L′L^{\prime} band observations are expected to reach an overall sensitivity to HEZD that is approximately 50 times higher than that of previous HH band observations (Defrère et al. 2022). The performance of NOTT for detecting exoplanets has already been well-characterised (Defrère et al. 2024). The beam combination mode used for these observations, however, is primarily sensitive to asymmetric brightness distributions, whereas the HEZD distribution is expected to exhibit a high degree of symmetry, although its extent is currently unknown. To simplify the modelling, we therefore assume a symmetric HEZD distribution, which reduces the number of free parameters compared to an asymmetric model. To explore the potential of NOTT to detect and characterise HEZD, we introduce, for the first time, alternative beam combination schemes that are sensitive to such symmetric dust geometries. From this analysis, we identify one configuration that combines a strong reduction of unwanted instrumental and atmospheric contributions with sensitivity to symmetric structures, making it the most promising option for HEZD detection. Specifically, we investigate NOTT’s primary observables (the photon flux rate and the corresponding null depth) as a function of the hour angle for selected HEZD and instrumental parameters to identify characteristic geometric signatures of HEZD and assess which model parameters can be constrained through their impact on the temporal modulation of the expected signal. The paper is structured as follows: In Sect. 2, we outline the theoretical foundation of NOTT’s observables, introduce our stellar and HEZD model and present the assumed observing strategy. In Sect. 3, we analyse the behaviour of these observables under varying dust and instrumental configurations. We discuss the implications of our results in Sect. 4 and summarise our findings in Sect. 5.

papers.title: Predicting Process-Level Behavior: A Benchmarking Study
papers.abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) typically forecasts the future of individual process instances, hence operating on trace level. Process managers, however, typically operate on process level, e.g., when assigning staff or calculating KPIs. The question is how well such process-level managerial decisions are supported by existing approaches, given that PPM research has so far not focused on process-level predictions. We answer this question through a comprehensive benchmarking study of two process-level prediction tasks: concurrent trace prediction and average throughput time prediction. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare statistical and machine-learning-based methods, foundation models, business process simulation, and, importantly, established trace-level PPM approaches, aggregating their predictions to the process-level. We assess which modeling paradigms are most suitable for predicting process-level behavior and whether existing trace-level PPM can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show substantial variation in performance across approaches. Notably, aggregated trace-level predictions cause errors to compound on process-level, reducing accuracy and highlighting process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that warrants dedicated research.

papers.intro:
Predictive process monitoring (PPM) is a branch of process mining that aims to forecast the future behavior of business processes, enabling proactive process management (Ceravolo et al., 2024). Most PPM approaches thereby operate on trace level, predicting the future of individual process instances (Di Francescomarino and Ghidini, 2022). This supports trace-level decisions, such as escalation. Other process management decisions, however, concern the process as a whole. For example, managers may adapt staffing levels to handle increasing workloads or remove activities to reduce throughput time. Such decisions require process-level predictions: forecasts of aggregate process behavior, captured through key performance indicators (KPIs) such as workload or throughput time (Folino et al., 2015; Cuzzocrea et al., 2018). Whereas trace-level predictions support interventions for individual traces, such process-level predictions can thus support higher-level decisions concerning capacity, resources, and process design.

Whereas trace-level predictions support interventions for individual traces, such process-level predictions can thus support higher-level decisions concerning capacity, resources, and process design.

Despite their practical relevance, process-level predictions are underexplored in PPM research, leaving the suitability of approaches unclear. Some works have shown that aggregate process behavior can be forecast in the form of throughput time (Leribaux et al., 2025), constraint violations (Folino et al., 2015; Cuzzocrea et al., 2018), or work in progress (Mehrdad Bibalan et al., 2024), but they each focus on one specific prediction target and a particular model family. Importantly, it is also unclear to what extent existing trace-level PPM approaches can be leveraged for process-level predictions. In principle, those approaches can predict process-level KPIs based on collections of traces. However, the efficacy and accuracy of such aggregated predictions has not yet been investigated.

Against this background, we present a comprehensive benchmark of approaches for predicting process-level behavior. We consider two complementary prediction tasks: Concurrent Trace Prediction (CTP), forecasting the number of simultaneously active traces, and Throughput Time Prediction (TTP), forecasting the average completion time of traces. Across synthetic and real-life event logs, we compare a broad spectrum of prediction paradigms for process-level prediction: (1) approaches also used in existing work on process-level KPI forecasting from statistical and machine learning (ML) methods, (2) recently emerged tabular and time series foundation models, which appear promising for process-level prediction, (3) process simulation approaches, which provide an alternative means of projecting future behavior, and (4) established trace-level PPM approaches, with individual predictions aggregated to the process level. This broad comparison allows us to assess which methods are most suitable for process-level prediction and, in particular, whether existing trace-level approaches can be effectively repurposed for this task. Our results show that trace-level approaches consistently underperform, mainly because they underestimate long-running traces, causing errors to accumulate at the process level. This indicates that trace-level approaches are not necessarily suitable for forecasting process-level behavior. Though usually better, the approaches that directly forecast process-level KPIs are also often inaccurate, underscoring the need to treat process-level prediction as a distinct predictive task that requires tailored solutions.

papers.title: Asymptotic probabilities in random Latin squares
papers.abstract: We introduce some new general techniques for studying asymptotic probabilities in random Latin squares. Using these techniques, we obtain an asymptotic formula for the probability that a given 'small' partial Latin square $H$ is present in a uniformly random $n\times n$ Latin square (as conjectured by Divoux-Kelly-Kennedy-Sidhu). As applications, we determine which configurations are likely to appear in random Latin squares (resolving a conjecture of Allsop-Morris), we determine the asymptotic distribution of the number of $3\times 3$ Latin subsquares in a uniformly random $n\times n$ Latin square (resolving conjectures of McKay-Wanless and Kwan-Sah-Sawhney), and we show that the first two rows of a random $n\times n$ Latin square are statistically indistinguishable from a random derangement (answering a conjecture of Cameron and Cavenagh-Greenhill-Wanless).

papers.intro:
An n×nn\times n Latin square is an n×nn\times n array filled with nn different “symbols” (usually taken to be the set of integers [n]={1,…,n}[n]=\{1,\dots,n\}), with the property that each symbol appears exactly once in each row and each column. For example, the multiplication table of a group is always a Latin square; in general, Latin squares can be interpreted as multiplication tables of a class of algebraic structures called quasigroups. See for example [36] for an introduction to this vast subject.

See for example [36] for an introduction to this vast subject.

While groups have very rigid structure, a growing body of research is showing that Latin squares can have almost arbitrary structure. This is exemplified in the study of random Latin squares: by now the field has accumulated a range of theorems (and substantial numerical evidence) showing that the behaviour of random Latin squares can be very accurately predicted via various naïve heuristics (e.g., by considering the model where each row is independently taken to be a uniformly random permutation, or where the symbol in each position is chosen independently and uniformly at random).

This is exemplified in the study of random Latin squares: by now the field has accumulated a range of theorems (and substantial numerical evidence) showing that the behaviour of random Latin squares can be very accurately predicted via various naïve heuristics (e.g., by considering the model where each row is independently taken to be a uniformly random permutation, or where the symbol in each position is chosen independently and uniformly at random).

However, the field is severely lacking general theorems and methods to rigorously justify these types of heuristics; in fact it is surprisingly difficult to rigorously prove anything nontrivial about uniformly random Latin squares, or even to study them empirically. The main issues are that Latin squares do not enjoy any neat recursive structure, and they are very “rigid” objects, in the sense that there are only very limited ways to make a “local perturbation” to change a Latin square into another one. To highlight the difficulties here, we remark that (despite some very ambitious conjectures; see [2, Section 4.1]) we still have a rather poor understanding of the total number of n×nn\times n Latin squares (the best known upper and lower bounds differ by exponential factors; see [51, Section 17]), and there is no rigorously justified way to efficiently sample a uniformly random Latin square (there are certain ergodic Markov chains on the space of n×nn\times n Latin squares [47, 32], but these are not known to be rapidly mixing). Almost every new theorem in this area has required the development of ingenious new techniques, which have all had quite severe limitations. We discuss the history of this topic in Section 1.4.

papers.title: ALIVE: Bring Foundation Features to Life with Events
papers.abstract: Visual foundation models provide powerful representations for diverse tasks, but their features become stale as visual content changes between image observations. Refreshing them requires new frames and repeated runs of a computationally expensive image encoder. We introduce ALIVE, an event-based method that incrementally updates native foundation model features between image observations. Given an anchor image, ALIVE uses subsequent events to transport and correct existing multi-layer features extracted by a frozen DINOv3 encoder. Its lightweight updater is trained end-to-end using only synthetic data, without downstream task supervision, and transfers directly to real-world event streams without any adaptation. Across three real-world datasets and five task-dataset settings spanning object detection, semantic segmentation, and depth estimation, ALIVE outperforms all evaluated event-based methods in every metric. On DSEC, when the anchor frame is 200,ms old, ALIVE improves over anchor-image predictions by 30.9,mAP in detection, 11.6,mIoU in segmentation, and 15.9% in depth AbsRel. Compared with image re-encoding, ALIVE reduces FLOPs by 82.4% and latency by a factor of 2.5.

papers.intro:
Visual foundation models (VFMs) provide general-purpose features that a single frozen backbone can share across many tasks through lightweight heads [33, 29, 21, 37]. However, these features are computed from a single image and describe the scene only at the moment it was captured. Between frames, they stay fixed while the scene keeps changing, and every prediction derived from them grows stale. This staleness limits applications that must respond quickly, such as autonomous driving and robotics [13, 23].

This staleness limits applications that must respond quickly, such as autonomous driving and robotics [13, 23].

With a conventional camera, one must choose between two unsatisfactory options. At a low frame rate, predictions remain stale until the next image arrives, and at a high frame rate, the VFM must run on every image at a high computational cost. Event cameras offer a way out of this dilemma. They report per-pixel brightness changes asynchronously with microsecond resolution [11]. Paired with a frame camera, either on the same chip [6, 2, 22, 17] or as a separate sensor [14, 49, 50], they observe precisely the interval in which VFM features go stale.

The question then becomes how to use events to keep perception up to date. Most event-based methods train dedicated networks with task labels, e.g., detection [31, 16, 18], segmentation [1, 38], or depth estimation [12]. Event-guided feature propagation [43, 41] keeps the features of task-specific networks up to date between frames but is likewise trained with task supervision. Each new task thus requires new labels and new training. Task-agnostic alternatives avoid task labels, but each falls short in efficiency or accuracy. Reconstructing images, from events alone [35, 9] or from events and frames [48], and encoding them with the VFM brings back the cost of running the VFM on every image. Warping features with event-based optical flow [15, 25] only moves existing content and cannot account for changes that motion does not explain. Mapping events directly into the feature space of a VFM [8, 32] discards the rich visual information already captured by the latest frame. What remains missing is a task-agnostic update that builds on the latest frame, accounts for changes beyond motion, and costs only a fraction of re-encoding.

Our key insight is that such an update should act on the features of the frozen VFM and can be supervised by the VFM itself. These features are the common input of all heads, and updating them refreshes all predictions at once. Encoding a later frame with the same VFM yields the features that the update should produce. The update can therefore be learned without any task label. Based on this insight, we propose ALIVE, a lightweight event-driven updater that keeps the features of a frozen VFM up to date between frames (). We instantiate it with DINOv3 [37]. Starting from the multi-layer features of the latest frame, ALIVE updates them with each incoming packet of events (Fig. 2): it moves existing content along the motion observed by the events and corrects the changes that motion cannot explain. At inference, parameter-free moment matching aligns the updated features with the statistics of the latest frame.

papers.title: DAL: Dynamic Angular Loss for Imbalanced Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: Class imbalance remains a major obstacle in medical image classification, where rare but clinically important classes are often overshadowed by majority categories. Although current strategies for reducing bias, including angle-based softmax (ABS) losses, offer strong discriminative features, their behavior in settings with a small number of severely imbalanced classes remains insufficiently understood. Previous approaches that estimate the intrinsic parameters of ABS rely on the assumption of many classes, which does not hold in medical settings. We derive data-driven upper and lower bounds for the scale parameter and an upper bound for the angular margin using negative-angle statistics, and use these to drive a batch-adaptive angular margin (BAAM), which we combine with dynamically-weighted cross entropy (DWCE) to define our dynamic angular loss (DAL). Across four highly imbalanced medical image classification benchmarks spanning dermatology, ophthalmology, and gastrointestinal endoscopy, our method consistently achieves superior balanced accuracy and the lowest coefficient of variation of per-class recall. Although this entails a small performance reduction on majority classes, the gains on minority categories are substantial, yielding a reliable and equitable overall classifier. Our source code is available at: https://github.com/msalman95/DAL.

papers.intro:
Analysis of medical images is a central component of contemporary diagnostic workflows, supporting disease identification, early detection, and follow-up assessment across dermatology, ophthalmology, and other clinical domains. These tasks frequently require the interpretation of subtle and heterogeneous visual patterns, where diagnostic distinctions depend on fine structural and textural cues. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) assists medical practitioners to identify known diseases. While some of these diseases appear regularly and many practitioners are able to identify them, the importance of CAD systems comes at highlighting rare cases that practitioners might not be familiar with. Therefore, CAD systems should particularly focus on detecting rare cases, while still recognize common cases reasonably.

Many modern CAD systems are based on deep learning, due to its ability to learn task-specific representations directly from raw clinical images (Esteva et al., 2017; Yu et al., 2018). Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and related architectures have demonstrated strong performance on large-scale benchmarks, including dermatologist-level skin-cancer classification (Esteva et al., 2017) and high-performing diabetic-retinopathy (DR) detection (Gulshan et al., 2016). However, disease distributions typically reflect population prevalence and clinical datasets are rarely balanced. Therefore, models operate under pronounced class disparities that influence learned representations (Johnson and Khoshgoftaar, 2019).
