Therefore, models operate under pronounced class disparities that influence learned representations (Johnson and Khoshgoftaar, 2019).

Handling such class imbalance is a long-standing challenge in machine learning. It is well-known that predictive models are biased toward majority classes, distort decision boundaries, and – most severely for their practicability – undermine minority-class recognition (Sun et al., 2009; Krawczyk, 2016; Rudd et al., 2016). These issues become more pronounced in medical imaging, where minority categories often represent clinically meaningful but infrequent findings, e.g, melanomas occur notably less often than benign lesions, and exhibit substantial intra-class variability alongside high visual similarity to non-malignant categories (Gessert et al., 2019). This often leads to reduced performance on minority classes, limiting the applicability of deep-learning systems in scenarios requiring reliable detection.

A variety of strategies for handling imbalanced data have been proposed, including class weighting, cost-sensitive learning, over- or undersampling, and data augmentation. Angular margin-based softmax formulations provide a mechanism to improve representation discriminability by imposing geometric constraints on the embedding space. Notably, ArcFace (Deng et al., 2022) introduces an angular margin that encourages compact intra-class clusters and stronger inter-class separation. Although these methods achieve strong results in large-scale benchmarks, they are generally developed under relatively balanced class distributions and rely on fixed global margin behavior. In highly imbalanced medical image settings, uniform angular constraints may be insufficient to maintain adequate separation for minority categories, allowing majority classes to dominate the learned embedding geometry.

In this work, we analyze the behavior of angular-margin losses under class-imbalanced medical distributions and address this methodological gap. We derive data-driven upper and lower bounds for the scale parameter ss used in angular softmax formulations, providing principled guidance when the assumptions underlying prior adaptive scaling strategies Zhang et al. (2019) are violated. Additionally, we derive a theoretical upper bound for the margin parameter mm. Based on this analysis, we introduce a dynamic angular loss (DAL) that integrates a batch-adaptive angular margin (BAAM) with dynamically weighted cross-entropy (DWCE) to improve robustness under long-tailed medical regimes. To assess performance equity, we additionally quantify variability across classes using the coefficient of variation (CoV). Experiments on ISIC Codella and others (2018); Combalia et al. (2019), APTOS Karthik et al. (2019), and Hyper-Kvasir Borgli et al. (2020) demonstrate consistent improvements in balanced accuracy and minority-class sensitivity.

papers.title: Data-driven control of polynomial systems using implicit methods
papers.abstract: While conventional behavioral data-driven control represents linear time-invariant (LTI) systems directly from data, extending these data representations to nonlinear systems remains an open challenge. We address this gap for general polynomial systems, characterizing their finite-length trajectories as a real algebraic variety defined by implicit polynomial relations rather than explicit equations. First, we provide conditions on measured data under which these data can be used to represent the system. Building on this representation, we formulate data-driven simulation and predictive control problems that are equivalent to their model-based counterparts, and solve the resulting polynomial systems globally using homotopy continuation. Numerical case studies confirm the effectiveness of this approach by successfully simulating a stiff Van der Pol oscillator in situations where explicit models fail. Furthermore, these data-driven simulation and control methods are illustrated on a Duffing oscillator, demonstrating that our method outperforms Koopman-based approaches in predicting long trajectories.

papers.intro:
Data-driven predictive control based on behavioral systems theory has become popular for linear systems (Coulson et al., 2019; Berberich et al., 2020; Dörfler et al., 2022). The behavioral approach describes a system by the set of its trajectories rather than by a particular representation through equations. For linear time-invariant (LTI) systems, the set of trajectories is a subspace, and this geometric viewpoint allows for a direct data representation of the behavior by the Fundamental Lemma (Willems et al., 2005; Markovsky and Dörfler, 2023). For nonlinear systems, the set of trajectories is not a linear subspace, and extending such direct data representations is an open problem, as also highlighted in the reviews by Markovsky and Dörfler (2021); Berberich and Allgöwer (2025). In this work, we focus on polynomial systems, for which this set is a real algebraic variety, and we show that it can be represented directly by data, enabling data-driven simulation and control.

In this work, we focus on polynomial systems, for which this set is a real algebraic variety, and we show that it can be represented directly by data, enabling data-driven simulation and control.

Related work: in the data-driven control literature, nonlinear systems are often described by explicit models in discrete-time, such as nonlinear state-space or nonlinear ARX (NARX) equations (Martin et al., 2023; De Persis et al., 2023; Bonassi et al., 2022). While powerful, these explicit descriptions treat variables asymmetrically by isolating the future state or output, which often fails to capture the nonlinear geometry of the system. On the other hand, the behavioral approach preserves the geometric structure by treating all variables symmetrically, enabling implicit descriptions, see Section 2.1 for an illustration. Data-driven methods inspired by the Fundamental Lemma have also been extended to nonlinear systems (Berberich and Allgöwer, 2025). Many of these extensions are restricted to specific system classes, such as Volterra (Rueda-Escobedo and Schiffer, 2020), Hammerstein and Wiener (Berberich and Allgöwer, 2020), or generalized bilinear systems (Markovsky, 2022), while others address general nonlinear systems through NARX models (Mishra et al., 2021; Fazzi and Chiuso, 2024), basis functions (Lazar, 2024), kernel methods (Huang et al., 2023), or local linearization (Berberich et al., 2022). Most importantly, all these methods rely on explicit equations, which forgoes the main advantage of the geometric, representation-free viewpoint.

Koopman operator methods lift the state by a dictionary of observables and fit a linear model in the lifted space (Williams et al., 2015; Korda and Mezić, 2018; Mezić et al., 2026). This general framework is suitable for describing implicit relations in the data. In practice, however, the lifted state is propagated by the linear model and mapped back to the state by a linear decoder (Mezić et al., 2026), so nonlinear relations between the observables are typically lost along the prediction. Reprojection onto the set of lifted states restores this consistency (van Goor et al., 2023; Mezić et al., 2026), but the predictions remain approximate unless the observables span a Koopman-invariant subspace, which can be infinite-dimensional even for polynomial dynamics.

Beyond data-driven control, relevant approaches also exist in the learning and system identification literature. For instance, the SINDy framework identifies nonlinear dynamics by regressing the time derivative of the state on a library of candidate functions with sparse coefficients (Brunton et al., 2016). While Mangan et al. (2016); Kaheman et al. (2020) propose implicit variants of the SINDy algorithm, they aim at identifying continuous-time dynamics, and therefore require measuring or estimating time derivatives, which can be restrictive. This same limitation applies to Guo et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2025) that design controllers for continuous-time polynomial systems via sum-of-squares programs. Finally, manifold learning methods also exploit that the data lie on a low-dimensional manifold, learned together with the dynamics on it (Floryan and Graham, 2022) or via a diffusion model (Kharitenko et al., 2026), but these approximations lack conditions on the data that guarantee an exact representation.

We represent these relations directly by data, and solve the resulting polynomial equations instead of relying on linear methods. Specifically, our contributions are as follows. • We motivate implicit data-driven methods through the example of simulating continuous-time systems from sampled data, and propose a pragmatic implicit behavioral description for polynomial systems, defined by the zero set of multiple, multivariate polynomials. • We provide conditions on the data (akin to the generalized persistency of excitation for LTI systems) enabling a direct data representation of polynomial behaviors with bounded degree. papers.title: Combinatorial Properties of The Giant Under Supercritical Percolation
papers.abstract: We study combinatorial properties, such as diameter and long paths and cycles, of the giant component of percolated graphs. Such combinatorial properties are well studied for classical graphs such as pseudo-random graphs and the hypercube. We aim to obtain similar results for extensive families of $d$-regular $n$-vertex graphs. Specifically, assuming expansion properties of the host graph, we show a typical vertex expansion by a factor of $1/d\log d$ in the giant component of the percolated subgraph. As a consequence, we obtain bounds on various combinatorial properties of the giant component. For example, a bound of $O\left(d\log^2 d+\log n\right)$ on the typical diameter of the giant component of the percolated subgraph. In addition, we construct graphs with very good vertex and edge expansion, but having large diameter, showing that the diameter of the percolated subgraph is not necessarily typically logarithmic in the number of the vertices of the graph. We also present good expanders such that their percolated subgraph typically contains a bad expanding set.

papers.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
papers.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

papers.title: The Gas-Phase Metallicity and Nitrogen abundances in typical galaxies at $z\sim5$
papers.abstract: The relation between stellar mass and gas-phase metallicity (MZR) is a key tracer of the baryon cycle in galaxies. JWST now gives access to rest-optical emission lines at z > 3, enabling unprecedented constraints on the chemical enrichment and the conditions of the interstellar medium of galaxies in the early Universe. In this work, we present the MZR at $z=3.8-6.6$ from stacked NIRCam/grism spectra of 1748 H$\alpha$-selected star-forming galaxies compiled over an area of 320 arcmin$^2$. The simple H$\alpha$ flux-limited selection allows us to measure representative [NII]$\lambda$6584/H$\alpha$ and [SII]$\lambda\lambda$6716,6731/ H$\alpha$ ratios in stacks spanning $\rm log(M_\star/M_\odot)=8-10.2$, extending the upper mass range of previous high-redshift MZR measurements by $\sim1$ dex. Gas-phase metallicities are derived from these ratios using strong-line calibrations recently derived from high-redshift galaxies. The[NII]-based MZR has a slope $\gamma = 0.42^{+0.10}_{-0.07}$ and $12+\rm log(O/H) = 7.94^{+0.06}_{-0.09}$ at $\rm log(M_\star/M_\odot) = 9$, in broad agreement with recent empirical studies and hydrodynamical simulations. The [SII]-based relation yields a consistent slope and a $\sim0.3$ dex higher normalization, within the systematic uncertainties of strong-line calibrations. From the resolved [SII] doublet we infer a median electron density of $n_e = 184^{+226}_{-169}\,\rm cm^{-3}$. Combining [NII] and [SII], we indirectly estimate the N/O ratio and find that it follows the trend expected from primary and secondary nitrogen production, with no evidence for nitrogen enhancement in the HII region emission that dominates our galaxies. Our results provide a benchmark for the chemical enrichment and ISM conditions of typical star-forming galaxies at $z\sim5$ across a wide mass range.

papers.title: Game2Player: Scaling Gameplay Experience for Visual Agents through Environment-Player Co-Development
papers.abstract: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

papers.intro:
Visual agents powered by vision-language models (VLMs) have made rapid progress on computer-use and embodied tasks [37, 67, 25, 53, 43]. Video games pose a broader challenge for visual intelligence [46, 52, 39, 58, 47, 28]: each game brings its own visuals, rules and controls, which an agent must infer from the screen while reasoning over a changing scene and acting with precise timing. This diversity makes gameplay experience a valuable source of training data for general-purpose visual agents. We therefore aim to collect gameplay data at scale across diverse games for visual agent training.

This diversity makes gameplay experience a valuable source of training data for general-purpose visual agents. We therefore aim to collect gameplay data at scale across diverse games for visual agent training.

A central bottleneck is obtaining such gameplay experience at scale: learning requires trajectories that pair actions with explicit goals and reliable signals of success. Human gameplay recordings [16, 80, 23, 34, 19] are expensive to collect, and online gameplay videos lack actions, which have to be recovered with inverse-dynamics or latent-action models [2, 41, 9, 73]; in both cases, goals and outcomes are annotated after the fact [3, 56, 74, 39]. Interactive game environments provide all three natively [32, 77, 20, 33, 30, 79, 1, 27], but each new game demands game-specific engineering, which limits their coverage.

Coding agents could automate both the environment building and gameplay needed for data collection. They can synthesize verifiable environments from code repositories and websites [66, 5, 51, 60], write games from scratch [72, 36], and develop executable policies for playing games [52]. Adapting existing web games for such data collection requires locating their internal state in engine-specific code and using it to define task initialization, progress measures and success checks. However, the resulting environment may pass the coding agent’s own tests even when a task is impossible to complete, its progress measure fails to update, or its success check triggers too early. Such defects may only become apparent when an agent actually plays the task. This motivates environment–player co-development: environments and the players that test them are developed together, each improving the other through play.

Building on this principle, we present Game2Player, a framework in which a Builder agent and two players, a VLM Player and a Coding Player, co-develop verifiable environments from in-the-wild web games (Fig. 2). The Builder sets up each game in a sandboxed, reproducible runtime, exposes its internal state, and defines tasks whose progress and success are read from that state, guided by engine-specific skills. The players then attempt every task: the VLM Player plays from screenshots, pausing the game while it reasons, whereas the Coding Player writes a Python policy over player-visible state, runs it in real time and refines the code from the recorded outcomes. When a failure traces back to the environment, the players report it, either as a defect, such as a key with no effect or progress that never moves, or as a request for on-screen information that the policy cannot read. The Builder checks each report against the recorded episode before repairing the environment, and accepts an environment once the players’ episodes confirm its own evaluation (Sec. 3.2).

The Builder checks each report against the recorded episode before repairing the environment, and accepts an environment once the players’ episodes confirm its own evaluation (Sec. 3.2).

Once an environment is accepted, the players turn from testing it to collecting experience in it, and every recorded episode is paired with its task instruction and a dense, state-based progress signal. The two players are complementary teachers, offering efficient demonstration collection and visually grounded action explanations, respectively. A code policy can be rerun without any model calls, supplying high-quality demonstrations quickly and at scale. The VLM Player acts on the same screenshots that the trained agent will see and explains each action in a short note, so its episodes show how to approach a game even when they fall short of the goal. We distill both sources into one pixel-based agent with progress-weighted SFT, which up-weights actions that advance task progress.

As verifiable game benchmarks remain limited in both number and diversity, we also use it to construct PlayerBench, 50 held-out games with 287 tasks for evaluating game agents on unseen games. papers.title: WaveView: The Novel View Is in the Noise
papers.abstract: Generative novel view synthesis (NVS) employs a diffusion model to render a static or dynamic scene from a target camera view. Explicit warp methods complete a reprojection of the source with video diffusion models, and implicit methods encode the camera parameters or 3D cues. Both add inference overhead, and the generated layout often drifts from the ground truth. We present WaveView, which injects the warped source into the phase of the initial noise of a pretrained generator. The Dual-Tree Complex Wavelet Packet Transform (DT-CWPT) allows local and anisotropic phase injection. The generator is thus constrained less in disoccluded regions and along the epipolar line. WaveView keeps the architecture and adds negligible overhead. On the DL3DV benchmark, it outperforms all baselines in every overlap bin. In the hardest bin, it gains 0.84 dB PSNR on the covisible region over MetaView, which shares its generator, while running 2.1 times faster. For dynamic NVS, fine-tuning AnyView with the same noise raises its zero-shot PSNR on AnyViewBench from 11.58 to 12.35 dB.

papers.intro:
Novel view synthesis from a single image asks for a scene as seen from a camera view that was never observed. When the camera moves far, little of the target view is visible in the source, and a generative model has to complete it. Two requirements then hold at once: the originally visible content must land where the geometry places it, and the completed content must look plausible.

When the camera moves far, little of the target view is visible in the source, and a generative model has to complete it. Two requirements then hold at once: the originally visible content must land where the geometry places it, and the completed content must look plausible.

Explicit warp methods reproject the source with an estimated depth and let a video diffusion model complete the warp [50, 27, 16]. The warp fixes the layout. But the generator is not told which pixels of the warp can be trusted, so depth errors, stretched surfaces, and the ragged borders of disocclusions are carried into the output. These methods also often generate a video to obtain a single view, making them 3.6 to 27 times slower than ours (see Sec. 5.2 for a comparison).

These methods also often generate a video to obtain a single view, making them 3.6 to 27 times slower than ours (see Sec. 5.2 for a comparison).

Implicit methods omit the warp and provide the camera, and in some cases implicit geometry features, as a pose or in the positional encoding of the source tokens [1, 4], relying on the learned distribution of the generator. Their outputs are clean, but their layout drifts as the viewpoint change grows. Fig. 1 shows both failures on one example: ViewCrafter [50] distorts the geometry, and MetaView [4] places the hall off the layout that the warp could have provided. For both, generation starts from Gaussian noise.

The noise does not have to be neutral, however. Phase-preserving diffusion shows that a pretrained generator follows the structure carried by the phase of its initial noise, while the magnitude remains Gaussian [52, 37]. The noise can therefore guide the layout of a novel view. Phase fixes where structure lies, while the random magnitude leaves the generator free to correct it.

In this paper, we go one step further and challenge isotropy. We present WaveView, which injects a geometric prior of the novel view into the initial noise of a pretrained generator. A depth warp places the source at the target view, and the noise takes its phase from this warp and its magnitude from a Gaussian sample. The phase is not trusted uniformly: an error in depth moves a pixel only along its epipolar line. We therefore release the phase along that line as the depth uncertainty grows and keep its information across the line. An isotropic floor absorbs the error of the warp itself, and disoccluded regions remain pure noise.

papers.title: Joint extreme-value asymptotics for the radius and centre of smallest enclosing balls
papers.abstract: We study the joint extreme-value behaviour of the radius and centre of the smallest ball containing an i.i.d.\ spherically symmetric sample. In the Gumbel and Weibull regimes, we obtain joint limit theorems and show that the enclosing ball is asymptotically supported by exactly $d+1$ sample points, thereby resolving an open support problem in the Gumbel case. In the Fr\'echet regime, the limit is given by the smallest enclosing ball of an extremal Poisson cloud. For planar Gaussian samples, we derive an explicit joint limit law from Daniels' finite-sample formula and show that this law is universal throughout the planar Gumbel domain. In the bounded-support Weibull regime, we additionally obtain uniform tail bounds, moment convergence and an explicit limiting density, while the uniform-ball case admits an interpretation in terms of a Poisson zero cell.

papers.title: Construction of a Deployable Hard-Constrained Turbulence Closure
papers.abstract: We present a framework for constructing deployable hard-constrained turbulence closures of unclosed terms in the transport equations of Reynolds stresses and turbulent dissipation rate. The framework is built from modules, each performing a single task. The closure module represents the closure with a small network, while the state module represents the flow state during training. The closure network is coupled to the state network through the governing equation residuals, allowing the closure to be learned without reference closure values being supplied as training data. The coordinate module learns monotone input coordinates that help both networks resolve sharp changes. Within the network architecture, the boundary condition (BC) module imposes boundary values exactly using the Theory of Functional Connections, and the realizability module keeps the closure realizable. We apply the framework to decaying homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) with experimental and direct numerical simulation trajectories. Here, the state module is a Deep Operator Network (DeepONet), the BC module imposes the initial state and the closure's low and high Reynolds number limits, and the realizability module ensures growth of the Taylor microscale. Across ten random seeds, the framework reduces root-mean-square seed-to-seed closure variation by about 95\% relative to the unconstrained model over the training and held-out range. The deployed 18-parameter closure network requires only the Taylor scale Reynolds number and can be exported as a standalone C function.

Turbulence closures model the unclosed terms in the averaged Navier–Stokes equations and in the associated Reynolds stress and dissipation rate transport equations. Classical models combine theoretical analysis with experimental and numerical data, while accounting for invariance, realizability, and known limiting behavior (Launder et al., 1975; Pope, 1975; Lumley, 1978; Launder, 1989; Speziale et al., 1991; Jovanovic et al., 2003). Data-driven models allow more flexible closure relations, but they must still satisfy these physical requirements.

Data-driven models allow more flexible closure relations, but they must still satisfy these physical requirements.

These requirements can be incorporated into closure modeling using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) (Raissi et al., 2019; Karniadakis et al., 2021). They commonly enforce constraints through loss penalties (Wang et al., 2021; McConkey et al., 2025), but these do not guarantee exact satisfaction. Architectural constraints can instead enforce specific properties, such as tensor invariance and total energy conservation, by construction (Ling et al., 2016; van Gastelen et al., 2024). Boundary conditions can be enforced exactly using trial functions that combine a term satisfying them with a free function that cannot alter them (Lagaris et al., 1998). The Theory of Functional Connections (TFC) provides a general construction of such functions, and Deep TFC uses a neural network as the free function (Mortari, 2017; Leake and Mortari, 2020).

The closure relation is learned jointly with the state representation through governing equation residuals, without prescribing an analytical closure model a priori or supplying reference closure values as training data. Separate modules handle the state representation, closure, input coordinates, and physical constraints. The framework enforces boundary conditions and physical constraints exactly, while learned monotone input coordinates reduce sensitivity to training initialization. papers.title: Evaluating Governed LLM-Driven ML Experimentation: Lifecycle, Provenance, and Failure Metrics
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents that run ML experiments are usually judged by the best score they reach. That score says nothing about how it was reached: whether the agent stayed within the files it was allowed to edit, whether failed trials were kept or silently dropped, and whether each keep or discard decision can be traced to its evidence. We propose evaluating such systems on their experimental process as well as their outcome, and we build a governed harness that makes this possible. A control plane, not the LLM that proposes changes, owns each trial's lifecycle, checks its edit scope, decides keep or discard, and appends one record per trial to an append-only ledger. Governance metrics such as the invalid-action rate, the repeated-bad rate and provenance completeness are computed from that ledger. Across six ML tasks, from synthetic logistic regression to language-model training, and 1,445 trials, the same contract applied unchanged. The ledger exposed failures that a task score hides: a no-memory arm in which all 120 trials failed, a benchmark adapter whose bounded proposals ran out, and a reset failure that reproducibility hashes revealed, after which the affected campaigns were rerun. In a matched counterfactual, a loop that logs only successful trials left no record of 43 of 50 trials, while the governed ledger recorded all 50. Memory ablations show that memory's effect on repeated bad proposals depends on the task. We release the ledgers of all 1,445 trials, so that every number reported for them can be recomputed.

papers.intro:
Suppose an LLM agent that tunes a training script reports that validation AUC rose by 0.05. The score does not say how the gain was obtained. The agent may have edited a file it was not supposed to touch, a run that crashed may have been dropped from the record, or the same bad idea may have been tried many times before one variant worked. For scientific ML, where an experiment is only as useful as the evidence behind it, these questions matter as much as the score: an autonomous experiment needs auditability, a traceable and reproducible record of every decision and its evidence.

What is missing is a way to measure the experimental process itself, and a record of that process that the agent does not control.

Following the view of an agent as a model plus a harness (Trivedy, 2026), which together form a compound AI system (Zaharia et al., 2024), we separate three roles. papers.title: Strongly Suppressed Cosmic-Ray Diffusion in a Wind-Blown Cavity Environment of SNR G21.8-3.0
papers.abstract: We report the discovery of a GeV $\gamma$-ray source spatially offset from SNR G21.8-3.0, while no significant high-energy emission is detected from the remnant itself. Using 16 yr of \emph{Fermi}-LAT observations together with $^{12}$CO ($J=1-0$) data, we show that the GeV emission is spatially associated with a localized molecular cloud located just outside a gas cavity whose boundary closely follows the SNR shell. This configuration supports a scenario in which cosmic rays (CRs) escaping from the remnant propagate through a progenitor-carved low-density cavity and illuminate nearby dense gas. Modeling of the cloud emission requires a diffusion coefficient suppressed by a factor of several tens relative to the canonical Galactic value, indicating strongly inhibited CR transport around the remnant. Rather than serving as a simple low-density escape channel, the wind-blown cavity appears to regulate CR propagation through local magnetic structure and enhanced turbulence. This system therefore provides evidence that circumstellar structures can control the escape and early transport of CRs around supernova remnants.

papers.intro:
Massive stars can profoundly reshape their surrounding interstellar medium through stellar winds and ionizing radiation before exploding as supernovae [14, 47]. These feedback processes may excavate low-density cavities surrounded by dense gas, thereby modifying both the gas distribution and the subsequent transport of cosmic rays (CRs) released by the supernova remnant (SNR) [16, 38]. In the standard escape scenario, CRs accelerated at SNR shocks diffuse into nearby dense gas and produce γ\gamma-ray emission displaced from the remnant itself [17]. As interactions between SNRs and molecular clouds are widely observed in the Galaxy [23], well-known examples such as W28 and W44 have shown that spatially offset γ\gamma-ray emission can trace nearby molecular material illuminated by escaped CRs [5, 44]. Some systems show bright γ\gamma-ray emission from both the SNR and nearby molecular clouds, with the external emission interpreted as arising from escaped CRs [31, 32, 30]. However, systems in which the SNR shell is faint in high-energy γ\gamma-rays while only localized external dense gas is bright remain comparatively rare [33]. Such sources are particularly valuable because they probe not only CR escape from the shock, but also how the circumstellar environment regulates the early propagation of CRs.

papers.title: MobileWeave: Program-First Synthesis of Dependency-Linked Tasks for Training Mobile GUI Agents
papers.abstract: Native mobile GUI agents require large-scale training trajectories covering both individual app functions and multi-goal workflows within and across apps, which makes automatic task synthesis a promising way to scale training data. Existing synthesis pipelines, however, produce each task as free-form text, leaving implicit how its subgoals depend on one another. This matters because composition is a skill in its own right: a policy may complete each subtask of a workflow on its own, yet fail to chain these subtasks into the complete workflow. We present MobileWeave, which instead synthesizes every task as an executable program derived from the app implementations of a controllable simulator. MobileWeave abstracts each app into a typed capability graph with semantic types shared across apps, composes atomic programs into single- and cross-app composite programs through explicit value and object dependencies, and verifies each program by native execution, deriving both its instruction and its completion check from the same program. Trained on teacher trajectories collected for these tasks and on recovery supervision at the policy's own stalls, MobileWeave-8B improves its base model by 26.7 points on MobileGym and by 8.6, 21.3, and 17.6 points on AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, and MobileWorld, with comparable gains at 4B. Beyond these gains, we find that composition is learnable from task structure: explicit dependencies between subgoals act as a training signal that teaches a policy to compose skills it already masters. We release data, model, and code at https://maxxnotmarx.github.io/MobileWeave/ .

Native mobile GUI agents complete tasks in interactive applications by mapping user instructions and screenshots directly to GUI actions [15, 30, 32, 25, 28, 18]. They are typically post-trained with supervised fine-tuning on interaction trajectories, often followed by online reinforcement learning [15, 30, 32, 25], so what a policy learns is bounded by the tasks it is trained on. To obtain an agent that handles the breadth of everyday mobile use, these tasks must be abundant [15, 11, 25, 8, 21, 17]. Each task, in turn, is useful only when its goal, initial environment state, completion criteria, and executed actions are mutually consistent [17, 24]. Yet, authoring these components by hand is costly, and covering multi-goal workflows in this way is particularly difficult [9]: the possible combinations grow combinatorially with apps and functions, and each one needs an initial state in which all subgoals are jointly feasible and a check that covers every one of them.

To reduce this cost, a growing body of work synthesizes GUI tasks and trajectories automatically [20, 23, 12, 11, 4, 9]. These methods typically provide a language model with some form of environment information, such as GUI screenshots [12, 23, 9], previously collected interaction trajectories [20, 11], transitions between interface states [4, 27], or descriptions of application functionality [19, 27], as a basis for proposing tasks, thereby improving their realism and diversity. From the app code and app state of MobileGym, it first abstracts each app into a typed capability graph, whose nodes are types of objects and values shared across apps and whose edges are app functions. It then specifies every task as a small program over this graph: atomic programs instantiate single functions, and composite programs weave them within and across apps so that later subgoals consume the values and objects returned by earlier ones. The program carries the goal structure: it is executed natively to verify feasibility, and both the instruction and the completion check are derived from it, so dependencies it specifies are enforced by the check. papers.title: Cardiac MRI-informed electrocardiography enables biologically grounded cardiomyopathy detection
papers.abstract: Precise myocardial phenotyping at population scale is limited by the cost and accessibility of cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), whereas electrocardiography (ECG) is widely available but reflects electrical rather than structural and functional information. Here we develop MyoECG, a cross-modal representation learning framework that distils myocardial structural and functional knowledge from CMR into standard 12-lead ECGs, enabling imaging-informed cardiomyopathy detection and subtype classification from ECGs alone. MyoECG was pretrained on 45,241 paired ECG-CMR examinations from UK Biobank and a tertiary cardiovascular centre, then developed and validated across more than 1.8 million ECGs from seven independent datasets. Across internal and external datasets spanning prevalences of 0.2-54.7%, MyoECG outperformed five pretrained ECG foundation models, with AUROCs of 0.800-0.974 for cardiomyopathy detection. In a multi-reader study of six cardiologists, MyoECG assistance improved mean sensitivity by 0.109 (95% CI, 0.041-0.175; P = 0.009) and specificity by 0.056 (95% CI, 0.004-0.108; P = 0.040). In 41,128 UK Biobank participants, the MyoECG score showed genetic correlations with cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.409) and dilated cardiomyopathy (rg = 0.371), genome-wide associations at four loci, including regions mapped to NFIA and KCNQ1, and associations with 69 circulating proteins related to myocardial stress, cell adhesion, vascular biology and metabolism. The cardiomyopathy correlation attenuated to non-significance after adjustment for 27 measured CMR traits (rg = 0.131; P = 0.143), indicating that the score captures CMR-derived information rather than dataset-specific shortcuts. MyoECG offers a scalable route to CMR-informed cardiomyopathy assessment and a strategy for transferring knowledge from resource-intensive imaging to widely deployable physiological signals.

papers.title: TrajWAM: Trajectory-Conditioned Future Learning for Vision-Language Driving
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) connect future scene prediction with action planning for autonomous driving. Each driving record pairs an executed ego trajectory with its observed future, providing a factual outcome for learning this connection. We present TrajWAM, a trajectory-conditioned WAM that improves vision-language driving through auxiliary bird's-eye-view (BEV) future learning. An ego-trajectory query conditions DINOv3-aligned BEV predictions from shared planner representations. Training combines factual reconstruction under the executed trajectory with one-sided feature separation under an unlabeled perturbed trajectory. Together, these objectives train the shared planner to generate driving waypoints. Native inference directly generates waypoints and bypasses the auxiliary future-prediction branch. On all 220 Bench2Drive routes, TrajWAM achieves 91.53 Driving Score and 75.45% Success Rate, exceeding a schedule-matched planning-only fine-tuning baseline by 5.31 Driving Score points and eight successful routes.

Autonomous driving requires recognizing the current scene and anticipating its evolution under ego actions. World Action Models (WAMs) connect observations and actions with future scene representations [27, 32]. Driving systems learn video, latent, or bird’s-eye-view (BEV) futures to support planning [28, 11, 13, 40]. When future prediction and planning share parameters, observed futures also supervise the driving policy during training. This coupling supports direct waypoint generation at deployment.

Native inference retains the fixed future-query tokens and directly generates reasoning and waypoints.

papers.title: Calibration of LHAASO-WCDA Energy Scale using Cosmic Ray Moon Shadow
papers.abstract: Cosmic-ray particles in the TeV range, originating outside the solar system, are partially blocked on their way to Earth by the Moon, producing a deficit in their flux known as the Moon shadow. This work presents a precision measurement of the westward shift of the Moon's shadow using 3.4 years of data from LHAASO's Water Cherenkov Detector Array (WCDA). We use this direct physical measurement, combined with four cosmic-ray composition models, each divided into five mass groups, to calibrate the detector's absolute energy response in the range of 4 - 37 TeV. We quantify the fractional deviation between the calibrated and simulated energy scales by determining a best-fit scale shift parameter of $\epsilon$ =-0.04 $\pm$ 0.03. This yields a 95% confidence interval of -9% to +0.2% for the systematic energy scale deviation. Complementing the simulation based on hadronic interaction model, this geomagnetic calibration provides a data-driven physical validation of the simulated WCDA energy response, effectively bounding systematic uncertainties and refining the overall energy scale.

papers.intro:
The cosmic ray Moon shadow refers to a reduction in the observed cosmic ray flux in the direction of the Moon. As the Moon obstructs incoming cosmic ray particles, detectors located on Earth or in space measure a diminished cosmic ray flux in its vicinity, resulting in a “shadow” effect. The shadow is, however, slightly displaced westward due to the deflection of primary particles by the Earth’s magnetic field. Since the deflection is energy dependent, the phenomenon can be used to calibrate the energy scale of cosmic ray detectors along with estimating their angular resolution. It is particularly important for ground-based detectors, in which the atmosphere acts as a calorimeter, and only a fraction of secondary cosmic ray particles produced by a primary through an extensive air shower (EAS) are detected. Energy calibration is therefore an essential aspect of cosmic ray physics with ground-based detectors, playing a crucial role in precise measurements of energies of primary cosmic ray particles.

The first experimental observation of the Moon and Sun shadow of cosmic-rays, which achieved the significance of 4.9σ\sigma and an angular resolution of 0.75−0.09+0.130.75_{-0.09}^{+0.13}, was reported in 1991 [6]. The ARTEMIS (Antimatter Research Through The Earth Moon Ion Spectrometer) experiment used its Imaging Atmospheric Cerenkov telescope to search for the Moon’s shadow in TeV cosmic rays; however, atmospheric fluctuations constrained its sensitivity, preventing detection of a percent-level antimatter component [28]. Using the Soudan 2 experiment with a depth of 2090 mwe (meter water equivalent), the Moon’s shadow was observed in the underground muon flux at a significance of 5σ\sigma, revealing an angular resolution better than 0.3 degrees and confirming the detector alignment stability within 0.15 degrees over ten years [16]. The MACRO experiment observed the Moon shadow with 6.5 σ\sigma significance and the Sun shadow with 4.6σ\sigma significance, and established an upper limit of 48% on the antimatter flux in cosmic rays around 10 TeV, using muon flux data collected from 1989 to 2000 [7]. Using the L3+C muon spectrometer at CERN, the shadowing effect of the Moon of cosmic rays was observed with 9.4σ\sigma significance, revealing a strong geomagnetic field (GMF) effect and setting an upper limit of 0.11 on the antiproton-to-proton ratio with 90%C.L. at 1 TeV [1]. With the Tibet-III air shower array, the Moon’s shadow was observed with 40σ\sigma significance, exhibiting a 0.23 degrees westward shift caused by GMF, and providing a 90%C.L. upper limit of 7% on the multi-TeV anti-proton-to-proton flux ratio [8]. The Main Injector Neutrino Oscillation Search (MINOS) detector observed the Moon’s shadow at 5.6σ\sigma and the Sun’s shadow at 3.8σ\sigma, establishing an absolute pointing of 0.17±0.12∘0.17\pm 0.12^{\circ} and revealing hints of interplanetary magnetic field effects in both shadows [2].

The ARGO-YBJ experiment observed the cosmic-ray Moon shadow effect in the multi-TeV energy region with 55σ\sigma significance, using its westward shift from the GMF to calibrate the primary energy scale and its shape to determine the angular resolution and pointing accuracy. Furthermore, the shadow was studied to investigate the effects of the solar wind through day/night comparisons and demonstrated as a comprehensive tool for characterizing the performance of an air-shower array [9]. In addition, three years of IceCube observations further establish the cosmic-ray Moon and Sun shadows as high-significance calibration tools, with both shadows detected at greater than 12σ\sigma across different detector configurations [11]. Extending this Moon-shadow study, ARGO-YBJ disentangle composition dependence in absolute-energy scale calibration using Moon-shadow data dominated by the light component, yielding a 17% energy scale error from 3 TeV to 50 TeV and validating the technique against the light component cosmic-ray spectrum over the same energy range [10]. LHAASO-KM2A has recently published cosmic-ray Moon shadow measurements that precisely confirm its Monte Carlo detector energy response over the 20-260 TeV range, yielding an energy scale uncertainty of 14% to 17% at a confidence level of 95% [13].

Cosmic ray air shower experiments like the Tibet ASγ\gamma, HAWC (High Altitude Water Cherenkov Observatory) and LHAASO (Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory) are designed to observe a cascade of secondary cosmic ray particles using an array of ground-based detectors. These experiments use different detection techniques, including water Cherenkov detectors, scintillation counter, and air Cherenkov telescopes, to measure the arrival times, directions, and energies of cosmic ray showers. A Moon shadow study was carried out using LHAASO WCDA data from March 2021 to December 2022, in which cosmic-ray Moon shadows were analyzed for events with compactness C << 10 and C >> 10. The results reveal that shadow shifts decrease and shadows become more compact with increasing energy, providing support for detector calibration, event selection, and understanding of cosmic-ray trajectories in the GMF [27]. The absolute energy scale of primary cosmic rays observed by the Wide Field-of-View Cherenkov Telescope Array (WFCTA) is calibrated using the Moon’s westward shift measured for nine months of data by WCDA-I of LHAASO and propagated to WFCTA through commonly triggered events, producing consistent median energies around 21-23 TeV [5]. The present work builds directly on the previous single pond calibration (WCDA-I) Although that work was limited to eight months of data, this analysis extends the data set to 3.4 years and incorporates all three WCDA ponds (WCDA-I, WCDA-II and WCDA-III). The primary focus remains the observation of the Moon shadow using LHAASO-WCDA and its application to calibrate the detector’s energy scale, but now with significantly increased statistics and temporal coverage.

papers.title: Mining the time axis with TRON. IV. MeerKAT detects a radio burst from a nearby M~dwarf
papers.abstract: We report the detection of a minute-timescale, highly circularly polarised ($\sim100\%$) radio burst from an active M dwarf (spectral type M1Ve), PM J14111$-$6155, located 19.6 pc from the Sun. Identified in the 1.28 GHz SMGPS using 8-second integrations from the TRON-pipeline, the burst peaked at 7.7 mJy. Visibility-based dynamic spectra reveal a drifting, band-limited emission feature ($\sim$300 MHz FWHM) with a maximum cut-off near 1.65 GHz, associated with electron cyclotron maser instability (ECMI), implying the existence of large-scale magnetic topologies ($B_* \approx 0.59$ kG). A non-detection ($3\sigma$ upper limit) four hours later points to intermittent or rotationally modulated beamed emission. An analysis of both TESS and ground-based survey data failed to recover an unambiguous rotational period for the optical counterpart. Follow-up SALT spectroscopy confirms its active chromospheric state, exhibiting prominent emission in the Ca {\sc ii} infrared triplet, Balmer lines, and persistent double-peaked H$\alpha$ emission ($44.6\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ peak separation) attributable to optically thick self-absorption. This discovery demonstrates that the coordinated use of time-series optical photometry, high-resolution spectroscopy, and high-cadence spectropolarimetric radio imaging enables direct probing of coherent radio emission from the magnetically active atmospheres of nearby M dwarfs.

papers.intro:
Flaring activity from magnetically active low-mass stars is observed across the electromagnetic spectrum, from radio wavelengths to X-rays (Benz and Güdel, 2010). At radio frequencies, both incoherent gyrosynchrotron emission and coherent bursts are detected, the latter often driven by the electron cyclotron maser instability (ECMI) (Linsky, 2017; Vedantham et al., 2020). ECMI provides a sensitive probe of energetic particle dynamics and magnetic field strengths in stellar magnetospheres. In density-depleted regions, anisotropic electron populations propagating along converging magnetic field lines can excite the ECMI (Wu and Lee, 1979; Treumann, 2006), producing circularly polarised (∼100%\sim 100\%) radiation at frequencies near the local electron gyrofrequency. Although ECMI emission can occur across a wide frequency range determined by the local magnetic field strength (fcyc≈2.8​B​MHzf_{\mathrm{cyc}}\approx 2.8\,B\,\mathrm{MHz}), detecting these beamed, polarised bursts is observationally challenging due to narrow beam geometries and low duty cycles (Hallinan et al., 2006; Hallinan et al., 2008).

While periodic coherent emission is frequently observed in ultracool dwarfs (Rea et al., 2026, e.g.), serendipitous detections of isolated, highly circularly polarised radio bursts provide vital diagnostics of transient magnetic reconnection and particle acceleration in active stellar coronae (Osten et al., 2006). Because such bursts are governed by narrow beaming geometries and low duty cycles, unravelling their emission mechanisms requires high-cadence spectropolarimetry coupled with optical characterisation. Coherent radio bursts of this type trace strong large-scale magnetic fields and electrodynamic coupling within the system (Zarka, 1998; Treumann, 2006; Ferrario, 2026), providing direct diagnostics of stellar dynamos and magnetic topology in low-mass stars (Morin et al., 2010).

Wide-field high-sensitivity interferometers, such as the South African MeerKAT array (Jonas and MeerKAT Team, 2016), the Australian SKA Pathfinder (ASKAP; Johnston 2007), and the LOw Frequency ARray (LOFAR; van Haarlem 2013), now enable systematic searches for these events directly in the image plane. The TRON pipeline has demonstrated sensitivity to various radio time-domain phenomena, including the recovery of known millisecond pulsars (Smirnov et al., 2025b) and additional discoveries (Blecher et al., 2026), as well as distant stellar flare activity in wide-field radio interferometric data (Smirnov et al., 2025a).

Building on this capability, we report the discovery of highly polarised narrowband emission from the nearby active M dwarf PM J14111-6155, identified while reprocessing the SARAO MeerKAT Galactic Plane Survey (Goedhart et al., 2024, SMGPS;). Detecting ECMI in this star constrains the emission geometry and duty cycle, probing its active magnetospheric structure (Hess et al., 2014). We combine the radio transient detection from the MeerKAT with follow-up high-resolution optical spectroscopy from the Southern African Large Telescope (SALT), multi-sector Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) light curves, and archival eROSITA X-ray data (Predehl et al., 2021), providing a comprehensive multiwavelength characterisation of the star’s magnetic and coronal activity.

papers.title: An inspiral of a star inside a common envelope with its giant companion
papers.abstract: The formation of compact stellar binaries requires rapid orbital tightening of their progenitor binary stars. This is theorized to happen via Common Envelope Evolution (CEE), when the stars orbit in a loosely bound, shared convective envelope, triggering an inspiral due to frictional drag. However, this inspiral in such a system has never been observed directly. Here, we present observations of AT 2025abao, a transient eruption in the Andromeda Galaxy, that originates from the CEE of a ~7M$_{\odot}$ asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star with its companion. Extensive pre- and post-eruption spectroscopy is best explained as a ~0.7M$_{\odot}$ companion inspiraling within the convective AGB envelope that powers a seven year period of gradual brightening - the first direct observations of frictional drag energy dissipation induced by CEE. The subsequent merger of the companion with the primary core within a few (<10) orbits powers the ejection of the outermost ~10% of the stellar envelope at speeds ~10x the primary escape speed, and empirically constrains the fraction of dissipated orbital energy available to unbind the convective common envelope, $0.01\lesssim \alpha \lesssim 0.4$. This end-to-end characterization using multi-survey observations demonstrates a path towards mapping the landscape of CEE outcomes with upcoming surveys.

papers.title: Auditable Clinical Support with Decision Agents
papers.abstract: Clinicians reviewing a diagnostic work-up will ask what was considered at each step and why the assessment changed. Agents powered by free text can reach physician-level diagnostic accuracy, but their written reasoning does not always reflect the factors that went into the decision. Here, we present Decision2Care, a decision agent that works up the acutely ill patient without producing any text. A decision model assigns a probability to each permitted EHR action, and fixed rules carry out the most probable one. We evaluated Decision2Care on the records of 546 emergency admissions across 12 diseases. Decision2Care reached a diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, compared with 86.1% for the MIRA-v2 agent, and required a median of 2.2 s per work-up, compared with 92-100 s. Each work-up tracked which options Decision2Care was considering at each step. In 10 of the 12 diseases, the differential diagnosis changed most at the test on which the guideline bases the diagnosis. Where Decision2Care was most confident after a single work-up, all but four of its diagnoses were correct (98.5%). We traced each of these four errors back to a single imaging report. Three of them were corrected when that report was removed. The same kind of decision was used to select the treatments, and Decision2Care's drug orders were judged guideline-adherent more often than MIRA-v2's. In emergency patients, its prediction of death was comparable to that of three intensivists on the same cases. In five of the eight intensive care cohorts, it exceeded the best of the three 24-h severity scores within 2-6 h of records. Our results show that decision agents can carry out clinical work-ups while recording the options, probabilities, and execution rules behind each action for audit.

papers.intro:
At morbidity and mortality conferences, clinicians review missed diagnoses by asking what was known at each step and why a test was or was not done[1, 2]. A patient with right upper abdominal pain shortly after cholecystectomy may first be investigated for an abdominal complication. The cause may instead be pulmonary embolism (PE), one of the most commonly missed diagnoses[3], which can be overlooked if the investigation stops at the first plausible diagnosis[4]. To review such a case, clinicians must know which options were considered and which results changed the assessment.

Evaluations of large language models (LLMs) in medicine have progressed from the initial phase of assessing them on clinical vignettes[5] to examining them in the context of diagnostic conversations[6], work-ups using patient records[7, 8, 9] and actions within the electronic health record[10]. In a work-up scenario, an LLM agent can request the patient’s examination findings, laboratory results, and imaging before reaching a diagnosis and treatment plan. Ferber et al.[8] found that one such agent (MIRA, the Medical Intelligence for Reasoning and Action) was at least as good as a physician at diagnosing emergency cases given the same information. If such agents are to order tests in a real clinical setting, their workups must be auditable.

Current LLM agents[7, 8, 9] produce their reasoning and tool calls as text[11]. The transcript shows what the agent did, but its explanation may omit the findings that led to a particular decision[12]. Confidence measures are also costly. In MIRA-v2[9], the best-performing measure requires five work-ups of the same case. DeepRare [13] links its diagnostic reasoning to medical sources, but source attribution alone does not establish how individual patient findings affect a decision. Earlier reinforcement learning agents selected from a pre-defined set of actions for symptom inquiry[14] and sepsis treatment[15]. Each of those was trained on a single task using structured input. None of these agents record, at each step, the options they weighed in a form that can be quantified and re-run.

Here, we present Decision2Care, a clinical agent for the patient in the emergency department (ED) and intensive care unit (ICU) that generates no decision as text. It does the work-up via typed decisions (e.g. choosing a diagnosis from a list, deciding whether to order a test). In each case, the decision model returns a probability for every option. A controller then applies fixed rules to those probabilities: It executes the most probable action, and orders a test when its probability reaches 0.5. We call an agent constructed this way a decision agent. The same architecture is used to select treatment and to estimate mortality risk, and the controller can use different decision models. Decision2Care records the probabilities of all the options at each step, so a reviewer can see which options were considered. The work-up takes a few seconds, so we can remove or replace a result, re-run the work-up and check which result changed the decision.

To test whether a decision agent can still do the work of an LLM, we ran Decision2Care on 546 emergency admissions to Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center spanning 12 diseases, taken from MIMIC-IV. Decision2Care reached a mean diagnostic accuracy of 86.5%, within the range of MIRA-v2 with the three LLMs, while a work-up took a median of 2.2 s instead of 92–100 s and cost less than a fifteenth as much. Its work-ups could be followed step by step. For example, in the patient described above, the probability of PE in the differential diagnosis was 0.45 after abdominal computed tomography (CT) and 0.96 after chest CT. When we left out the lipase and amylase results and repeated the diagnosis, accuracy in pancreatitis admissions decreased by 54 percentage points, whereas removing the imaging reports or the routine blood tests left it unchanged. The confidence score derived from a single work-up distinguished correct from incorrect diagnoses about as well as the agreement among five repeated MIRA-v2 work-ups, and the 49.3% of admissions in which Decision2Care was most confident were diagnosed with 98.5% accuracy. The drug orders of Decision2Care were judged guideline-adherent more often than those of MIRA-v2 and the documented first-day care. Using about half of the available records, it predicted death in emergency patients as well as three intensivists who had all of them. In the ICU, its predictions from 12 h of records were as good as or better than three severity scores computed at 24 h. In records from Stanford Health Care, the prediction reached AUROCs of 0.81 in 555 patients with PE and 0.77 in 78 with pneumonia, similar to those at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center. These results indicate that a decision agent can perform a clinical work-up, including treatment and prognosis, without generating text, and that each step is auditable.

papers.title: Two Faint Tidal Disruption Events Discovered in a Pilot Search with the Wide Field Survey Telescope
papers.abstract: We report the discovery of TDE 2025alrm/WFST250129blnve and TDE 2025amkg/WFST251021dbmwk in the first six months of the wide-field survey (WFS) performed by the 2.5-meter Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST). Both events are apparently faint among known optical tidal disruption events (TDEs), with peak magnitudes of $g \sim 20.0$ and $g \sim 19.6$, respectively. Blackbody fits to the multi-band photometry yield roughly constant temperatures of $\sim 10^{4}$ K for both sources, with peak bolometric luminosities of $10^{43.6}$ erg s$^{-1}$ and $10^{43.8}$ erg s$^{-1}$, respectively. Optical spectra obtained during the declining phase display characteristic broad Balmer, He II, and N III emission lines, classifying both sources as H+He TDEs. Host-galaxy SED fitting suggests stellar masses on the order of $10^{9} M_{\odot}$ and black hole masses of $\sim10^{6} M_{\odot}$, which are typical of optically selected TDE hosts. The pilot discovery of these two faint TDEs along with dozens of candidates, demonstrates the capability of WFST to discover TDEs, owing to its exceptional survey depth. Furthermore, these events highlight the value of the $u$ band in multi-band surveys for TDE selection, particularly for distinguishing TDEs from supernovae at early phases. With continued operations, WFST is expected to substantially expand the known TDE population, especially by uncovering nearby low-luminosity events and high-redshift TDEs, both of which remain poorly explored.

papers.intro:
It is widely believed that supermassive black holes (SMBHs) reside at the centers of most galaxies. When a star approaches an SMBH closely enough, it can be tidally disrupted as the black hole’s tidal forces overcome the star’s self-gravity, an event known as a tidal disruption event (TDE) [46]. Part of the stellar debris subsequently falls back onto the black hole and forms an accretion disk. This process generates a luminous flare in the UV/optical and X-ray bands, providing a powerful way to detect quiescent black holes. Thanks to wide-field time-domain surveys over the past decade, the discovery and study of TDEs have advanced significantly [19]. In particular, the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF; Masci et al. 41) has dramatically increased the TDE discovery rate, enabling systematic studies of TDEs based on large samples (e.g., van Velzen et al. 55, Hammerstein et al. 26, Yao et al. 65). These systematic studies have revealed substantial spectroscopic diversity among TDEs. Their optical spectra are typically characterized by a blue continuum accompanied by broad hydrogen and/or helium emission lines, based on which they are commonly classified as TDE-H, TDE-H+He, or TDE-He. Some TDEs exhibit nearly featureless blue continua with weak or absent broad emission lines and are classified as TDE-featureless.

Optically selected TDEs typically exhibit a set of characteristic photometric properties that have become the basis for identifying TDE candidates in optical time-domain surveys. These events are generally characterized by blackbody temperatures of (1CLOSE(1–OPEN5)×104​K5)\times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}, resulting in persistently blue optical colors (e.g., g−r<0g-r<0) with little temporal evolution. Most TDEs rise to peak brightness on timescales of about one month, reaching peak blackbody luminosities of 104310^{43}–104610^{46} erg s-1, followed by a power-law decline lasting months to years [36, 26, 65]. However, the optical/ultraviolet spectral energy distributions (SEDs) of TDEs generally show no evidence of a turnover at the blue end [38, 69], suggesting that the SED peak likely resides in the extreme-ultraviolet (EUV) band. This is independently supported by infrared echo observations of several TDEs. The dust heating energy inferred from the infrared emission exceeds that directly observed in the optical/UV band, implying a substantial contribution from unobserved EUV radiation (e.g., Wu et al. 62). Therefore, photometric observations in bluer bands, such as the uu band, are expected to be more effective for identifying TDEs than observations at redder wavelengths.

The currently known TDE population is largely confined to the low-redshift Universe (z≲0.5\text{z}\lesssim 0.5) and is dominated by intrinsically luminous events ( Lbb≳1043\text{L}_{\text{bb}}\gtrsim 10^{43} erg s-1 ) [65]. Expanding the census toward fainter TDEs, either intrinsically underluminous or located at higher redshifts, will be a key focus of future TDE searches. With its large field of view of 6.5 deg2\text{deg}^{2}, deep single-exposure limiting magnitude of r∼23r\sim 23, and high-cadence multi-band imaging including the uu band over a wide area, the Wide Field Survey Telescope (WFST; Wang et al. 57) is well suited to meet this requirement and to substantially expand the TDE sample toward both lower luminosities and higher redshifts [37]. Here we report the discovery of TDE 2025alrm (WFST250129blnve, z=0.179z=0.179) and TDE 2025amkg (WFST251021dbmwk, z=0.180z=0.180), two apparently faint TDEs identified by the Wide Field Survey (WFS) Program of WFST. Under this program, WFST will perform daily two-band observations: during dark or gray nights, it uses the uu band together with an additional optical band; during bright nights, it observes in the gg and rr bands. The survey covers approximately 3500 deg2\text{deg}^{2} with a cadence of 3–4 days and will reach a total surveyed area of 8000 deg2\text{deg}^{2} within one year. This observing strategy enables the discovery of large numbers of faint transients while providing sufficiently dense temporal sampling to robustly characterize their light-curve evolution, including both the rise and decline phases. With observed peak magnitudes of g∼20g\sim 20 and g∼19.6g\sim 19.6, TDE 2025alrm and TDE 2025amkg are among the faintest TDEs discovered to date in terms of apparent magnitude. Moreover, the well-sampled and complete optical light curves obtained by WFST demonstrate its capability to both detect and characterize faint TDEs, highlighting its power in probing the faint end of the TDE population.

papers.title: Multifrequency deep radio continuum VLA observations toward OMC-2/3
papers.abstract: We present multiwavelength (0.7-5 cm) Very Large Array continuum observations of high sensitivity (3 $\mu$Jy beam$^{-1}$), reaching an angular resolution of $0.4''$ (154 au) toward the Integral Shaped Filament in Orion. We image a field of $12.5'$ in diameter, containing the whole OMC-2 region and the southernmost $2.5'$ of OMC-3. We report the positions, flux densities and spectral indices of 47 radio sources, and discuss their nature. We conclude that, out of the 57 radio sources in the field of view, 36 (63%) are very likely tracing YSOs, 4 are tracing jet/outflow knots, and 6 are extragalactic sources; the nature of the remaining sources is unclear. We identify the driving sources of the 9 previously reported molecular outflows in our field of view. Four of them show a clear elongated radio jet morphology. We detect free-free emission from two potential photoevaporating discs associated with Class III YSOs. We find variability in 11 radio sources, 7 of which are also variable at shorter wavelengths. We find 7 pairs of radio sources with projected separations of 150-3000 au, which are potential binary systems; we identify a total of 17 potential multiple systems within this separation range when taking into account sources detected at other wavelengths. This work highlights the potential of deep VLA observations to uncover a large population of weak radio sources and study their diversity, serving as a guide for future surveys with the SKA and ngVLA.

papers.intro:
The Orion Molecular Cloud complex, with reported distances ranging from 380 to 450 pc (Menten et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2008; Stutz and Gould, 2016; Kounkel et al., 2017; Kounkel et al., 2018; Großschedl et al., 2018), is one of the nearest active star-forming regions, where young stellar objects (YSOs) of both low and high luminosity coexist. The complex is composed of two elongated giant molecular clouds, Orion A and B, with a total mass exceeding 2×105​M⊙2\times 10^{5}M_{\odot} (Wilson et al., 2005), roughly aligned in the north-south direction (see fig. 1 of Megeath et al. 2012). Toward the northern end of the Orion A cloud, Mezger et al. (1988); Mezger et al. (1990) and Chini et al. (1997) identified several bright millimeter sources, aligned along an Integral Shaped Filament (Bally et al., 1987; Peterson and Megeath, 2008; Stutz and Gould, 2016; Kainulainen et al., 2017, ISF,). Most of these sources were later associated with YSOs (e.g., Adams et al. 2012, Furlan et al. 2014, and references therein; Furlan et al. 2016, and references therein; Osorio et al. 2017, and references therein). Outstanding among them are the bright FIR 3 and FIR 4 sources, which are associated with the Class I HOPS 370 and the Class 0 HOPS 108 YSOs, respectively. In this paper, we analyze the protostellar content toward the Orion Molecular Clouds 2 and 3 (OMC-2/3), two of the richest molecular clouds in protostars and prestellar cores, located in the northern part of the ISF.

The Orion complex has been intensively observed in the infrared spectral range with surveys carried out with the Spitzer Space Telescope (Megeath et al., 2012; Megeath et al., 2016) and the Herschel Space Observatory. In particular, 330 protostars have been studied in great detail as part of the open-time key program Herschel Orion Protostar Survey (HOPS, e.g., Stanke et al. 2010; Fischer et al. 2010; Fischer et al. 2017; Fischer et al. 2020; Manoj et al. 2013; Stutz et al. 2013; Furlan et al. 2014; Furlan et al. 2016; González-García et al. 2016). For these objects, identified with HOPS numbers, Furlan et al. (2016) modeled their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) from near-IR to submillimeter wavelengths allowing them the determination of fundamental properties such as their luminosity and the envelope mass, as well as their classification in terms of evolutionary stage. However, in some cases, the SED was contaminated by emission from nearby sources, due to the relatively low angular resolution of those observations. Therefore, observations at other wavelength ranges and with higher angular resolution can help to better understand the nature of these sources. papers.title: QuantAtlas-OM: Taming Neural Spectral Bias in Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Ocean Dynamics
papers.abstract: Autoregressive neural networks exhibit spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal prediction. As rollouts progress, high-frequency details decay, blurring the predicted fields and destabilizing long-range forecasts. Ocean dynamics offer a particularly stringent test because kinetic energy is concentrated in mesoscale eddies and fronts spanning tens of kilometers. This degradation stems from coupling large-scale phase evolution and small-scale energy retention in a shared feature space. Evolution on a coarse grid smooths out high-wavenumber eddies, whereas evolution on a fine grid amplifies small-scale phase errors and triggers rollout instability. We introduce QuantAtlas-OM (QuantAtlas Ocean Model), a scale-spectral decoupling framework that confines deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for long-term stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through an outer bypass to the decoder. Across physical regimes, the evolution core pairs non-local attention with resolution-invariant dilated spatial gating. Across three western boundary currents, QuantAtlas-OM retains $43.7\%$ to $86.5\%$ of mesoscale spectral energy along the $k^{-3}$ cascade at Day $120$, sustains anomaly correlation coefficients of $0.81$ to $0.88$ at Day $60$, and reaches $0.66$ at Day $120$ in the Kuroshio ($2.5\times$ to $7.7\times$ the best baselines). Trained at $0.25^\circ$, QuantAtlas-OM transfers zero-shot to a global $0.125^\circ$ grid ($0.81$ Day-$10$ spatial correlation) and leads global $0.25^\circ$, $23$-level 3D ocean simulations ($120$ days) and coupled ocean-atmosphere forecasts ($60$ days), ranking first on $15$ of $16$ metrics and cutting $60$- to $120$-day salinity RMSE by $13\%$ to $27\%$ across global ocean basins.

papers.intro:
Autoregressive prediction over long horizons is a central problem in spatiotemporal physical modeling [26, 3, 30]. Starting from the current state, a model recursively predicts future states over tens of days or months [18, 1, 5, 12, 13]. Yet autoregressive models consistently encounter a fundamental limitation as rollouts progress and the predicted fields become increasingly blurred [6, 22, 31]. Fine-scale structures disappear first, followed by frontal weakening and eventual large-scale flow distortion [5]. A primary driver of this degradation is the spectral bias of neural networks [24, 6], since networks preferentially fit low-frequency components and attenuate high-frequency modes. Such high-frequency losses remain subtle in single-step prediction [22]. Over tens or hundreds of closed-loop steps, however, each prediction feeds into the next step [26, 1, 36], and high-frequency attenuation compounds exponentially across extended rollouts.

Ocean dynamics brings this challenge into sharp focus. Unlike the atmosphere, the ocean has a Rossby deformation radius of only tens of kilometers [7], with most kinetic energy concentrated in fine-scale fronts and mesoscale eddies [8, 27]. As Figure 1 shows, sea surface temperature in the Kuroshio and Oyashio transition region decomposes into a smooth low-wavenumber background in the upper panel that captures basin-scale temperature patterns, and high-wavenumber frontal and eddy residuals in the lower panel. These residuals are far from negligible perturbations. Their temperature variations reach approximately ±7∘​C\pm 7\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}, comparable to the temperature contrasts in the background field, yet their spatial extent is only about 100​km100\,\mathrm{km}, equivalent to just a few grid cells at 0.25∘0.25^{\circ} resolution. These high-frequency residuals govern ocean heat transport, cross-scale mixing, and extreme events such as marine heatwaves [11, 2]. Under spectral bias, however, neural networks fit the smooth background in the upper panel while progressively erasing the high-frequency frontal and eddy residuals in the lower panel across multi-month autoregressive rollouts [5, 22].

A direct attempt to preserve eddies spanning only a few grid cells is to evolve features directly on high-resolution maps. Our experiments, however, reveal a spectral dilemma when evolution resolution alone changes. Downsampling the fields for temporal evolution on a coarse grid truncates high-frequency residuals during encoding, irreversibly blurring eddies and fronts. Conversely, long-horizon evolution directly on a fine grid amplifies small-scale, high-frequency phase errors through autoregressive steps and propagates them toward larger scales, destabilizing the flow field. On a single feature manifold, coarse-grid evolution preserves stability at the expense of high-frequency detail, whereas fine-grid evolution retains detail at the cost of long-term rollout stability and physical consistency.

The decomposition in Figure 1 points to a clear structural resolution. Because the smooth background and high-frequency residuals differ fundamentally in spatial scale and dynamical behavior, a single deep evolution module should not carry both. Based on this insight, we propose QuantAtlas-OM (QuantAtlas Ocean Model), a framework for scale and spectral decoupling (Figure 2). The encoder separates the ocean state into two orthogonal pathways. A pathway through a coarse latent grid filters out high-frequency truncation noise through strided downward projection and applies deep temporal evolution exclusively to the low-wavenumber background flow, anchoring long-term phase stability. Unlike multiscale U-Net architectures that inject intermediate skip connections into deeper layers and reintroduce high-frequency perturbations into temporal evolution, we retain only a single outer bypass at full resolution. This bypass routes frontal and eddy residuals around the entire evolution bottleneck and directly to the decoder, where the evolved large-scale flow guides their local realignment and refinement. To match the computational and transfer requirements of different ocean regimes, the latent evolution core provides two spatial mixing operators. papers.title: Expand & Reduce: a Framework Bridging Branch-and-Reduce and Dynamic Programming
papers.abstract: We introduce expand-and-reduce, a framework that augments classical reduction rules with a new type of optimality-preserving operation, called an expansion rule. While a reduction rule in practice typically makes the instance smaller, an expansion rule may enlarge the instance yet still making progress towards a solution. We present a simple expansion rule called edge expansion for the Maximum Weighted Independent Set (MWIS) problem. It encodes the joint choice of two non-adjacent vertices by adding an edge between them and creating a new vertex representing their union. We prove that the number of edge expansions needed to transform a graph into a clique equals the number of independent sets in the graph minus the number of vertices. We demonstrate that expand-and-reduce, using edge expansion and just two well-known reduction rules, has greater reduction power than a set of 22 commonly used reduction rules for MWIS. Therefore, it can significantly simplify methods that depend on reduction rules. To highlight the practical potential of the expand-and-reduce framework further, we provide an implementation and preliminary results showing that a simple implementation outperforms a far more advanced method for MWIS preprocessing. Moreover, expand-and-reduce can simulate both branching and dynamic-programming-style state construction, yielding exact and fixed-parameter algorithms with matching asymptotic running times. By that, expand-and-reduce offers a unified and conceptually clean perspective on techniques that are usually considered incompatible.
