papers.title: Study of the intra-pixel timing resolution of planar silicon sensors using the TDCpix ASIC
papers.abstract: A study of the intra-pixel timing resolution in planar silicon detectors, bonded to the TDCpix Application Specific Integrated Circuit (ASIC), is performed using the TimePix4 telescope. Spatial non-uniformities in the timing resolution, arising from the weighting field, are measured for the first time in an experimental environment. The results are validated using simulation and discussed in the context of future Research and Development (R&D) goals.

papers.title: Gaia Science Alerts microlensing events with mass estimates verifiable in Gaia Data Release 4
papers.abstract: Gaia Science Alerts provide an all-sky stream of photometric transients, including events consistent with gravitational microlensing. For such events, forthcoming epoch astrometry from the Gaia mission offers the possibility of testing photometric lens mass predictions. While microlensing parallax inferred from the photometric light curve can constrain the event geometry, a direct lens mass measurement additionally requires the angular Einstein radius, which may be accessible through astrometric microlensing. We aim to construct a pre-Data-Release-4 (DR4) sample of Gaia microlensing events for which the available photometry provides a measurable microlensing-parallax signal. This allows us to derive statistical predictions for the lens mass and distance. We forward-modelled these events to predict the detectability of the astrometric microlensing signal in Gaia DR4. We identify 56 Gaia Science Alerts microlensing events with 71 point-source point-lens solutions with annual parallaxes that satisfy our fit-quality, posterior-boundedness, and parallax-significance criteria. Lens masses and distances were inferred using two prior-based frameworks, pyLIMASS and the Besan\c{c}on Galaxy Model, which combine the measured microlensing parameters and Gaia source information with stellar-population and Galactic models. These inferred parameters were used to simulate Gaia DR4-like along-scan astrometry and estimate the detectability of the astrometric microlensing signal. The inferred lens masses and distances remain strongly prior-dependent without a direct angular Einstein radius measurement. Among the 284 event-solution-prior branches, 47 are classified as high-confidence astrometric detections using Gaia DR4-like simulations. These predictions can be tested once epoch astrometry is released in Gaia DR4.

Gravitational microlensing occurs when a foreground lens passes sufficiently close to the line of sight of a background source, producing transient magnification (Paczyński, 1986; Gould, 2000). Because the signal is gravitational rather than radiative, microlensing is sensitive to lenses regardless of their luminosity and, therefore, provides a unique probe of faint or non-luminous objects. This includes low-mass stars, isolated stellar remnants (Sahu et al., 2022), planets, and free-floating planetary-mass objects.

This includes low-mass stars, isolated stellar remnants (Sahu et al., 2022), planets, and free-floating planetary-mass objects.

Since the first detections in the early 1990s, microlensing has been driven primarily by photometric monitoring: first by surveys such as MACHO, EROS, and OGLE (Alcock et al., 1993; Aubourg and others, 1993; Udalski et al., 1993), and later by dedicated high-cadence Galactic-bulge surveys such as OGLE, MOA, KMTNet, and PRIME (Udalski et al., 2015; Bond et al., 2001; Kim et al., 2016; Sumi et al., 2025). This is complemented by wide-field transient surveys such as ASAS-SN, ATLAS, Gaia, VVV, and ZTF (Shappee et al., 2014; Tonry et al., 2018; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016; Minniti et al., 2010; Bellm et al., 2019). In the coming decade, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will further transform the field. The Rubin observatory will provide wide-field optical monitoring across much of the southern sky, while the Roman telescope will conduct high-precision near-infrared time-domain observations through the Roman Galactic Bulge Time Domain Survey and the Roman Galactic Plane Survey, delivering large new samples of microlensing events (Ivezić et al., 2019; Penny et al., 2019).

Additional constraints can be obtained from annual or satellite microlensing parallaxes, finite-source effects, lens-flux constraints, spectroscopic characterisation of the source star, high-resolution imaging, interferometric observations, and astrometric microlensing. In particular, combining the microlensing-parallax amplitude with the angular Einstein radius yields the lens mass directly through ML=θE/(κ​πE)M_{\rm L}=\theta_{\rm E}/(\kappa\pi_{\rm E}) (Gould, 2000). Astrometric microlensing produces a displacement of the centroid of light of the combined unresolved lensed images relative to the unlensed source position. Because the amplitude of this displacement is proportional to θE\theta_{\rm E}, modelling the astrometric trajectory provides a measurement of the angular Einstein radius (Dominik and Sahu, 2000). Combining photometric and astrometric microlensing measurements can therefore constrain the lens mass and distance and break degeneracies inherent in photometric-only models.

Gaia is uniquely suited to studying microlensing events. The mission combines homogeneous all-sky photometry with high-precision astrometry and spectroscopic information for over two billion sources (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2016). The Gaia Science Alerts (GSA) system has identified and published ongoing photometric transients in near real time, enabling ground-based follow-up while transients continue to evolve (Hodgkin et al., 2021). For microlensing, Gaia is particularly complementary to ground-based bulge surveys because it covers the Galactic disc and higher-latitude fields, where events can be bright, appear relatively nearby, and favour astrometric lensing (Belokurov and Evans, 2002). Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3) has already delivered the first all-sky catalogue of Gaia microlensing candidates (Wyrzykowski et al., 2023) with multiple dark lens candidates (Kruszyńska et al., 2024).

Gaia photometry has contributed to a diverse set of microlensing discoveries, including planetary events such as Gaia22dkvLb (Wu et al., 2024), AT2021ueyLb/Gaia21dnc (Ban et al., 2025), and Gaia23bra b (Harris et al., 2026), long-timescale dark-lens candidates such as Gaia18cbf (Kruszyńska et al., 2022) and Gaia18ajz (Howil et al., 2025), high-magnification events with a complementary space-parallax signal such as Gaia19bld (Rybicki et al., 2022), and binary-lens events with full Keplerian orbital solutions such as Gaia16aye (Wyrzykowski et al., 2020) and Gaia20fnr (Wicker et al., 2026). Gaia data have also contributed to the identification of very short-timescale events associated with free-floating or wide-orbit planetary-mass lenses, such as KMT-2024-BLG-0792/OGLE-2024-BLG-0516 (Dong et al., 2026). For Gaia DR3-ULENS-001, the anomalous Gaia DR3 astrometric parameters are consistent with the astrometric microlensing signal predicted by simulations based on the photometric model. This agreement suggests a nearby isolated white dwarf as the lens (Jabłońska et al., 2022). Many more such events are expected in Gaia Data Release 4 (DR4)11 1 Expected 2 December 2026, where epoch astrometric and photometric data will be available for all sources. The long Gaia astrometric time series, paired with photometric data from other surveys or follow-up observations, makes Gaia sensitive to long-timescale microlensing events, such as those from isolated black holes (Rybicki et al., 2018).

papers.title: LEMUR: A Searchable Web Archive of Deep Chandra Images of Galaxies and Galaxy Clusters
papers.abstract:
We present LEMUR, a publicly accessible archive of uniformly reduced, deep Chandra images of 2,569 galaxies and galaxy clusters (including groups), comprising 5,505 ACIS observations and 138.8 Ms of exposure. By combining the publicly available imaging observations of each target, we provide background-subtracted, exposure-corrected images in broad, soft, and hard bands at the native ACIS pixel scale of 0.492 arcsec. Our primary goal is to make the wealth of archival Chandra observations accessible to researchers without requiring specialized expertise in X-ray data reduction.
  Each observation is reprocessed with CIAO, filtered for background flares, and reduced with settings chosen to preserve faint diffuse emission; the merged images are exposure corrected and background subtracted using the ACIS blank-sky backgrounds in a broad (0.5-7.0 keV), a soft (0.5-2.0 keV), and a hard (2.0-7.0 keV) band. For every object, we measure an X-ray center at the peak of its diffuse emission, and we provide a morphological similarity search based on embeddings from the AstroCLIP foundation model, in which nearest neighbors share cool-core status in 73% of matched cluster pairs, compared with 51% by chance.
  Photometry of 275 point sources agrees with the Chandra Source Catalog to within 3% in the broad band. The images, along with their counts images, background models, exposure maps, and quick-look stamps, are available through a searchable web archive at https://lemur-archive.lemur-xray.workers.dev/. The catalog tables are archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24351915), and all code is open source at https://github.com/crhea93/Lemur.

papers.intro:
Over the past 25 years, Chandra has been instrumental in our understanding of the hot, diffuse gas in galaxies and galaxy clusters (White et al. 2009). Through using the Chandra archive, astronomers have discovered the presence of cold fronts in the intra-cluster medium (ICM) of galaxy clusters (Owers et al. 2009), studied the statistics of X-shaped radio galaxies (Hodges-Kluck et al. 2010), and verified the existence of hot, X-ray emitting gas in dwarf galaxies (Ott et al. 2005; Pandya et al. 2016). While these studies have advanced our understanding of X-ray emitting sources, the full potential of the Chandra archive remains unrealized, in part because few systematically reduced, merged images of these objects are available.

While these studies have advanced our understanding of X-ray emitting sources, the full potential of the Chandra archive remains unrealized, in part because few systematically reduced, merged images of these objects are available.

Chandra archival data is widely available through a web-based data portal, the Chandra Data Archive (CDA). The portal offers calibrated data products for each archival Chandra observation, including level-1 and level-2 processed event files, exposure files, and observational reports, but not reduced images that combine the observations of a target. Other archives, such as the Archive of Chandra Cluster Entropy Profile Tables (Cavagnolo et al., 2009, ACCEPT) and its recent successor ACCEPT 2.0 (Donahue et al., 2026), provide uniformly derived thermodynamic properties of galaxy clusters. ACCEPT 2.0 expands the original sample to 532 clusters, providing radial density, temperature, and entropy profiles, along with integrated X-ray properties. LEMUR11 1 LEMUR is not an acronym: the archive is named after the first author’s cat, Lemur, who in turn is named after her ringed tail. complements these efforts by focusing on uniformly processed, deep, merged X-ray imaging products for a broader sample of galaxies and galaxy clusters. The CXO also provides tools for a ‘‘quick look’’ at observations (Chandra Fast Image22 2 https://cda.harvard.edu/pop/dispatchQuick) and cleaned data from individual observations (Chandra Footprint Service33 3 https://cxcfps.cfa.harvard.edu/cda/footprint/cdaview.html); however, no service provides merged images of the many targets observed more than once (744 of the 2,569 objects in LEMUR).

Several other catalogs draw on the X-ray archives, but none provides deep, merged images of individual extended sources. The Chandra Source Catalog (Evans et al., 2010; Evans et al., 2024, CSC) combines overlapping Chandra observations to detect sources and reports their positions, fluxes and spectral properties; its stacked images combine only observations whose pointings lie within about an arcminute of each other, and its detection is designed for point-like and compact sources rather than emission extending over arcminutes. The Chandra Galaxy Atlas (Kim et al., 2019) provides uniformly reduced, merged images and spatially resolved spectral maps of 70 early-type galaxies. The first eROSITA all-sky survey (Merloni et al., 2024, eRASS1;) and its catalog of galaxy clusters (Bulbul et al., 2024) cover half of the sky uniformly, but with exposures of a few hundred seconds and an angular resolution of roughly half an arcminute, far shallower and coarser than a deep Chandra pointing. The XMM Cluster Survey (Romer et al., 2001; Mehrtens et al., 2012, XCS) searches the XMM-Newton archive for serendipitously detected clusters and measures their properties, while ACCEPT and ACCEPT 2.0 provide entropy and temperature profiles for a sample of well-observed clusters. LEMUR is complementary to these efforts. For every galaxy and galaxy cluster observed with Chandra ACIS under the CDA’s ”normal galaxies” and ”clusters of galaxies” science categories, it combines all available observations into a single, background-subtracted and exposure-corrected image reduced to preserve faint diffuse emission, measures the position of that emission, and makes the result searchable, including by morphological similarity to other objects in the catalog.

In this manuscript, we present an archive of deep, merged images of galaxies and galaxy clusters, reduced with a pipeline optimized for the detection of faint diffuse emission. The primary aim of this catalog is to make available the deepest Chandra reduction of galaxies and galaxy clusters for non X-ray astronomers and X-ray astronomers alike; therefore, it improves the dissemination of Chandra data products. To make the final data products widely accessible, we have created a modern web-based catalog and provide all code for the construction of the data products and website at https://github.com/crhea93/Lemur.

papers.title: Synthesis-route-dependent state selection in the frustrated spinel ZnV$_2$O$_4$
papers.abstract: The emergent properties of strongly correlated materials can be highly sensitive to how they are made, yet synthesis pathway is rarely treated as a fundamental variable governing their ground states. The spinel ZnV$_2$O$_4$ provides a model system in which to test this idea: its pyrochlore lattice of antiferromagnetically coupled V$^{3+}$ $S=1$ moments hosts competing spin and orbital degeneracies, while different synthesis routes yield markedly different low-temperature behaviour. Here, we show that changing the solid-state synthesis pathway reproducibly selects a distinct structural and magnetic ground state. Microwave-assisted solid-state synthesis (MASS) stabilises the cubic spinel structure to low temperature, suppressing the conventional cubic-to-tetragonal transition and preserving the highly frustrated $S=1$ pyrochlore lattice. Combining high-resolution diffraction, magnetometry and inelastic neutron scattering, we find a magnetic ground state exhibiting persistent spin-liquid-like dynamics together with partial spin freezing. Our results establish synthesis pathway as an experimental variable for selecting between competing emergent states in strongly correlated materials, revealing a route to accessing ground states not realised by conventional synthesis.

papers.title: A Universal Diffusion Model for the Quantum Position Operator
papers.abstract: The quantum position operator and its response to perturbations underpin the functional properties of insulating materials. In the modern theory of polarization, Wannier charge centres encode Berry-phase polarization, while their structural derivatives determine key response functions. Here we introduce a universal diffusion model based on E(3)-equivariant graph neural networks for moments of the position operator, with the first moment defining Wannier centres and the second central moment their real-space localization. We demonstrate the framework for liquid water, amorphous silicon and crystalline BaTiO$_3$, and train a universal model that generalizes to 100 unseen crystals spanning a 67-species chemical space. The predicted centres reproduce infrared spectra in large liquid and amorphous cells beyond routine first-principles reach and enable finite-difference calculations of Born effective charges and piezoelectric tensors. This framework provides a scalable route to electronic polarization and localization in complex materials, supporting high-throughput screening and finite-temperature simulations.

papers.title: Towards modelling redshift uncertainties in the photometric void size function
papers.abstract: We present an extension of the theoretical formalism for the Void Size Function (VSF) to incorporate photometric redshift uncertainties, combining the excursion set with the theory of Lagrangian density peaks. Photometric redshift scatter induces anisotropic line-of-sight smoothing of the density field, which modifies the variance of the field and suppresses the abundance of large voids. We model this effect by damping the variance of the smoothed density field in the theoretical model, and we test it on AbacusSummit halo lightcones with true redshifts and with mock photometric redshifts generated with a Gaussian scatter. The predicted damping of the variance agrees with the one measured in the halo distribution to 1% and the suppression of the VSF due to photometric redshift scatter is well reproduced by the modified model, with recalibrated barrier parameters, for sigma_z <= 0.015 and for voids larger than 40 Mpc/h (about 2.5 mean tracer separations). This work is a first step towards modelling the VSF in modern photometric surveys such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time and the Euclid mission.

papers.intro:
The large-scale structure of the Universe contains a wealth of cosmological information to be captured by summary statistics. The statistical distribution of over-densities in the initial matter density field, the Lagrangian space, has been extensively studied and successfully modelled using robust theoretical formalisms such as the excursion set [5] or the theory of Lagrangian density peaks [2]. On the other hand, the statistical analysis of under-dense regions, called cosmic voids, presents a greater challenge as their formation cannot be reduced to the same simple collapse picture that describes haloes. Their evolution is instead driven by the expanding shell-crossing mechanism [31], and, unlike haloes, voids remain sensitive throughout their evolution to both the initial conditions and the environmental dynamics around them [29]. In this work, we focus on the modelling of the void size function (VSF), which describes the number density of voids as a function of their radius.

The VSF measured from spectroscopic data recently provided its first ever constraints [7], reaching Ωm=0.29±0.06\Omega_{m}=0.29\pm 0.06 (about 21% precision) and σ8=0.79−0.08+0.09\sigma_{8}=0.79^{+0.09}_{-0.08} (about 10% precision), independent of and complementary to the constraints from standard cosmological probes. Its power from current and upcoming spectroscopic surveys is forecasted in several studies [20, 24, 25, 9, 19, 39, 33]. Nevertheless, the study of the VSF from photometric data remains limited [22], as a proper modelling of the VSF in photometric data is still missing. Photometric surveys have so far mostly been exploited to identify voids in projection, through two-dimensional void catalogues [27], rather than through a full three-dimensional treatment of the VSF such as the one we present here. The redshift uncertainty in photometric data introduces an important smearing effect along the line of sight (LOS), distorting the tracer density field and suppressing structures on all scales. While the impact of photo-zz uncertainties has already been studied for the galaxy power spectrum [4], galaxy lensing tomography [15], and galaxy angular correlations [1], its impact on the VSF remains unexplored, and to date no analytical model exists that predicts the VSF directly from the linear power spectrum in the presence of photo-zz scatter.

Our study is an extension of the theoretical formalism presented in G. Verza et al. [37] (hereafter V24), which combines the excursion-set framework with peak theory, for both halo and void statistics, and models statistics such as the multiplicity function, the abundance of collapsed or under-dense structures as a function of their size, and the VSF. The accuracy of the model in constraining cosmological parameters with spectroscopic data has been demonstrated in a forecast on a galaxy mock that mimics the expected features of the Roman High Latitude Wide-Area Spectroscopic Survey (HLWASS) [40] for the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [39]. The extension presented in our work is motivated by the advent of current and upcoming surveys producing photometric data, such as the Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time [14, LSST;] and the Euclid mission [12]. Although the extension we propose is general and can be adapted to various barrier formalisms, we focus here on its implementation in the original formalism of V24. We test it on halo lightcones from the AbacusSummit suite of NN-body simulations [16]. In this work, our main objective is to test whether the photometric-redshift VSF can be recovered by our extended formalism through the modification of the variance term, and to test whether our formalism predicts the amplitude and radius dependence of the suppression of the VSF at large radii RR in photometric data compared to the true redshift case, i.e. the case with no redshift error. Section III describes the extension, introducing the anisotropic window function and the resulting modifications to the variance and barrier function. In Section IV we test our formalism on mock halo catalogues and finally make our conclusions and present future improvements in Section V.

papers.title: A Batched Discrepancy Principle for Stochastic Landweber-Kaczmarz Iteration and its Application to EIT
papers.abstract: We consider an inverse problem given as ill-posed system of possibly nonlinear operator equations between Hilbert spaces. To solve the problem we use a stochastic mini-batch Landweber-Kaczmarz method, drawing uniformly a subset of equations in each step. As an a posteriori stopping rule, we introduce a batched version of the discrepancy principle, in which only the residual of the selected batches is monitored. Under the tangential cone condition, we establish the convergence of the iterates for exact data, the convergence of the regularized iterates for noisy data under an a priori choice of the stopping index, and the convergence of the method when it is terminated by the proposed batched discrepancy principle. Numerical experiments for the electrical impedance tomography problem illustrate the theoretical results and demonstrate the performance of the method for different batch sizes.

papers.title: Efficient Implementation of Diagonally Implicit Runge-Kutta Methods for Model Predictive Control
papers.abstract: In direct shooting methods for nonlinear optimal control, one of the major computational costs is simulation of the system and calculation of sensitivities. These costs are particularly steep when the stiffness of the controlled system prescribes the use of implicit integrators, amongst which, implicit Runge-Kutta schemes are most popular. These methods require the use of Newton's method to solve a moderately sized system of nonlinear equations with a dense Jacobian, the computation of which grows cubically with the number of stages, that is, the number of abscissa. To mitigate this we investigate the use of the family of Diagonally Implicit Runge-Kutta (DIRK) methods whose Butcher tableaux are lower triangular. We describe the structure exploiting linear algebra required to make the DIRK methods competitive with fully implicit methods, including efficient sensitivity calculations. Finally, we evaluate the performance of DIRK methods on several example systems, and show that the efficient implementation yields Pareto optimal integration schemes. The fixed step size integrators are provided as part of the acados package and use high-performance linear algebra provided by BLASFEO.

In order to formulate the linearized dynamics, numerical integration schemes which can provide sensitivities are required. In many applications, the continuous time DAE is in fact a non-stiff Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE) and can be easily handled via explicit integration schemes such as the famous fourth order explicit scheme RK4. However, when the dynamics are numerically stiff, such explicit schemes are inefficient and implicit schemes must be used [3]. In these cases it is often suggested [4] that practitioners use members of the Gauß-Legendre or Radau-IIA classes of methods, which are both Fully-Implicit Runge-Kutta (FIRK) methods. This is because these methods are of the order proportional to twice the number of stages, and thus offer good efficiency regarding the trade-off between accuracy and evaluation cost.

The field of numerical integration using Runge-Kutta methods has, however, spent many decades developing schemes with Butcher tableaux [5] with exploitable structure. These include a zoo of Diagonally Implicit Runge-Kutta (DIRK) methods [6, 7, 8], along with the Singly Implicit Runge-Kutta (SIRK) methods [9, 10]. These structured tableaux allow for more efficient solving of the nonlinear systems of equations by accelerating the factorization of the associated linearizations, when applying Newton’s method [8]. These structured methods are, however, only rarely used in NMPC contexts [11, 12, 13], and we are unaware of any efficient open-source implementations tailored for NMPC. An alternative approach for structure exploitation in the Runge-Kutta equations is to detect and exploit linear dependencies in the model equations. This is also implemented in acados [14] and might even be combined with a structured-tableau approach.

In this paper, we discuss the efficient implementation of fixed-step-size SDIRK integrators in the open-source optimal control and MPC software acados. The implementation provides the capability for simulation as well as forward sensitivities, adjoint sensitivities, and symmetric Hessian propagation [15]. We discuss inexact Newton schemes and structure-exploiting calculations which allow for significant theoretical, and, as we verify, practical, speedups over FIRK methods of equivalent order. Finally, we compare our implementation on several system models and hardware platforms, both of which show the practical benefits of high-order SDIRK methods. In particular, we evaluate our implementation on compute constrained embedded hardware typical of NMPC applications.

papers.title: Data-driven simulation of the brain's response to stimulation: a system identification approach for closed-loop neuromodulation, piloted in adaptive deep brain stimulation
papers.abstract: Closed-loop neuromodulation uses a physiomarker to control stimulation. Developing such controllers requires exploring a large space of strategies and parameters, which is often not feasible with the human-in-the-loop. Simulation environments offer an alternative. Adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS) for Parkinson's disease is a stereotypical application: while physiomarker identification progresses rapidly, clinically available control is limited to threshold and proportional strategies. We propose to identify dynamical models of the brain with and without deep brain stimulation (DBS) using the sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics (SINDy) framework. Identified ex post from existing recordings, such models are a middle ground between abstract bottom-up models and the realistic but difficult-to-access human-in-the-loop. Forecasting neural activity from real initial conditions, the models create a simulation environment for "what if" analyses of DBS changes. In a proof-of-concept with EEG data from a single subject, we train and evaluate threshold, proportional, proportional-integral-derivative (PID), and proximal policy optimization (PPO) control, aiming to have the simulated data classified as DBS ON at minimal energy. SINDy models fitted on spatially filtered EEG maintained DBS condition-specific characteristics. All aDBS controllers delivered DBS more efficiently than continuous DBS (cDBS), with up to 20.2% energy reduction. Proportional control yielded a small but significant gain over threshold control. PID and PPO achieved a comparable reward advantage over cDBS, with PPO stimulating more conservatively and PID saving the most energy. The approach thus proved feasible, and within this simulation environment, PID control is a strong a-priori choice, while the benefit of deep reinforcement learning may only emerge with richer physiomarker signals.

papers.intro:
Closed-loop neuromodulation adapts stimulation based on a physiomarker which is informative about the need for stimulation. Examples range from adaptive deep brain stimulation (aDBS) [1, 2, 3] over responsive neurostimulation in epilepsy [4, 5] to closed-loop spinal cord stimulation [6, 7, 8]. Common to all of these is the need for a control strategy (controller), which decides how to stimulate given the physiomarker. Designing and tuning such controllers requires exploring a large space of strategies and parameters, which is often not feasible with a human-in-the-loop setup, as experimental time with patients is limited and each evaluation is costly.

On a high level, an aDBS system comprises three components: 1) a sensor with (near) real-time recording and streaming capabilities, 2) a decoding algorithm which extracts a physiomarker from sensor data, 3) a control algorithm which decides how to stimulate based on the physiomarker’s current state, and a neuro-stimulator which allows (near) real-time adjustment of the stimulation parameters. Steps 1) and the neuro-stimulator of step 3) are mainly driven by hardware advances, the others are predominantly algorithmic/software bound. The algorithmic development in identifying physiomarkers is progressing quickly and producing various candidates [1, 9, 10, 11, 12], converging to the need for patient specific evaluation [13, 14]. The development of control strategies which make it to the final evaluation with a human-in-the-loop is progressing more slowly. Central challenges are the limited interaction time when applying DBS on externalized leads, or the limited hardware and streaming capabilities when working on implanted systems. From a clinical perspective [3], aDBS control is mainly associated with threshold [15, 1] and proportional control [16, 17], as these are available on certified aDBS-ready implantable pulse generator (IPG) from Medtronic (Minneapolis, MN, USA) and Newronika (Milan, Italy).

[30] fitted autoregressive models with exogenous input (ARX models) of the tremor band power measured with an inertial measurement unit under DBS ON and OFF conditions. The ARX models were then used to optimize a model predictive controller. Yang et al. [31] proposed a system identification framework based on linear state-space models (LSSM), and identified a stochastic stimulation pattern for an optimal identification of the input-output system. The framework was later applied to local field potentials (LFP) of non-human primates, where model-based closed-loop control [32] was then simulated. Wang et al. [33] used existing LFP data from rodents to fit an ARX model with DBS ON/OFF as input on a theta-band marker, and evaluated a closed-loop controller. These approaches either require dedicated experiments (specific stimulation sequences), are based on animal data, or model behavioral instead of neural signals. In all cases, the models enabled a simulation environment for evaluating the controllers.

With this work, we propose to derive such a simulation environment ex post from human electroencephalogram (EEG) data, which were recorded under different DBS conditions. Instead of treating DBS as an exogenous input, we use system identification [34] to model the neural signal dynamics within each DBS condition. Like the approaches above, it is a middle ground between using the actual human-in-the-loop system and the abstract computational bottom-up models. Specifically the latter are often tuned to produce group level phenomena, such as beta synchrony [35], that might not be present in the individual [13] or might not be susceptible to DBS in individual cases [36]. We apply this approach on a proof-of-concept, using a regularized form of Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy) [37, 38] on data of a single patient from a previously published EEG dataset [11, 36, 39]. Combined with preprocessing for an optimized DBS contrast, we create models describing the inherent dynamics of the DBS ON and OFF regimes. The models are used with numeric integration to build a novel simulation environment in which we optimize and evaluate threshold, proportional, proportional-integral-derivative (PID) and proximal policy optimization (PPO) based aDBS control. While this proof-of-concept is specifically done in the domain of aDBS, the approach in and of itself is more generally applicable for any offline data set with recordings of at least two different conditions.

papers.title: One size does not fit all: session-specific effects of deep brain stimulation on hand-motor kinematics in Parkinson's disease
papers.abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) effectively treats motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease (PD), but it is unclear whether it changes fine hand movements in the same way for every patient. We analyzed 35 sessions of 19 patients with PD from a multi-center cohort performing the CopyDraw task, a drawing task designed to overcome the subjectivity and limited granularity of clinical assessments. Besides standard kinematics (mean velocity, acceleration, jerk, and drawing accuracy), we derived higher distributional moments and non-linear complexity measures, for 38 features in total. DBS effects were quantified with linear mixed models at the group level and with residualized regression and a random-effects meta-analysis per session. The DBS state was decoded per session with regularized linear discriminant analysis to compare feature sets as behavioral labels for deriving physiomarkers for adaptive DBS (aDBS). DBS modulated all 38 features at the group level, most strongly velocity-related features. However, for every feature, the between-subject variability of the DBS effect exceeded the group-level effect. Only one feature, the detrended fluctuation analysis of the distance to the template, showed a significant mean effect across sessions, and it is not a standard kinematic feature. In six sessions without any significant modulation of standard features, complexity measures were modulated instead. For decoding, standard features alone were the best choice in ten of 35 sessions, but combining all 38 features yielded the highest average area under the ROC curve (0.700 vs. 0.677), with the largest gains in sessions that were hard to decode from standard features. DBS effects on hand-motor behavior are individual. Deriving neural markers for aDBS from behavior therefore requires session-specific analyses with individualized features beyond standard kinematics and group-level effects.

papers.intro:
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder [2] caused by the loss of dopaminergic cells in the substantia nigra pars compacta. PD affects over 10 million people worldwide [3], with a rapid rise in prevalence over the last 20 years [4]. Its characteristic motor symptom is bradykinesia, in combination with rigidity, resting tremor, and/or postural instability [5]. These symptoms are linked to a broad range of motor deficits affecting the entire body [6]. Fine motor execution of the hand is one such domain that is heavily impacted by the disease. These impairments significantly restrict patients’ independence in activities of daily living [7], which in turn negatively impact overall quality of life [8].

Because of the highly sensitive nature of fine motor control, handwriting and continuous drawing capabilities were found to be impaired already at a prodromal stage [9]. As such, hand-motor control is used for the early identification of PD and for the comparison of PD vs. healthy controls [10]. Two prominent clinical examples are the assessment of micro- or dysgraphia [11] and the Archimedes spiral drawing task [12, 13]. Micrographia, in its progressive form, describes an amplitude decay observed during a continuous writing task. Similar continuous, rhythmic movements are analyzed during the spiral drawing task, which captures spatial trajectories, motor arrest, and tremor frequency [14]. Consequently, both tasks have been used as behavioral proxies to capture symptom severity and to monitor disease progression in interventional studies [15, 16, 17, 18]. Such interventions primarily comprise dopamine replacement therapies [19] and/or deep brain stimulation (DBS) [20, 21, 22]. The comparison of treatment conditions in the hand-motor context (e.g., medication ON/OFF and DBS ON/OFF) mostly focuses on spatial and temporal kinematics—such as velocity, acceleration, and fluency—enabled by the use of digitizing tablets [23]. Additionally, measures of spatial complexity and dynamic irregularities have been analyzed [18, 24].

papers.title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
papers.abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

papers.title: Where Global Context and Weight Sharing Work in Compact Vision Backbones
papers.abstract: Compact convolutional backbones such as EfficientNet achieve strong parameter efficiency through local depthwise separable convolutions, yet two structural questions remain central to hybrid design: where does global self-attention improve recognition over pure convolution, and can repeated blocks share weights without losing representational capacity? We investigate both questions on ImageNet-1k (50,000-image validation) using controlled EfficientNet-B0 experiments. First, we show that wrapping a classification backbone in multi-scale feature pyramids (BiFPN) fails to outperform a plain MBConv trunk (69.99% - 71.81% vs. 72.86% plain B0) until paired with stage attention (73.15%). In contrast, keeping the MBConv trunk intact and inserting lightweight zero-gated residual self-attention adapters at stages P3 (28x28 windowed), P4 (14x14 global), and P5 (7x7 global) reaches 74.02% standalone and outperforms a bit-for-bit matched plain-B0 control by +0.954 percentage points (73.88% vs. 72.92%) across an 88-epoch stateless replay schedule, with learned attention amplitude rising monotonically with semantic depth (27.2% at P3 -> 45.4% at P4 -> 66.3% at P5). Second, we evaluate recurrent weight sharing across repeated MBConv blocks with pass-specific BatchNorm statistics (+1,536 parameters per pass). While post-hoc kernel averaging degrades accuracy to 17.03% and single-template stage tying (-27.6% parameters) plateaus at 66.10%, alternating two shared block templates ([B1, A, B, A]) in Stage 6 cuts total model parameters by 10.9% (582K weights) and recovers by +10.82 points in a single epoch to 70.92% (-1.84 points vs. unshared control).

papers.title: Attention Is Not Relevance: Challenging the Causality of Attention in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: Attention has become one of the most widely adopted solutions for estimating the relevance of surrounding objects and interpreting an autonomous vehicle's driving decisions. However, its ability to capture the causal impact of individual input elements on an AI model's output has long been discussed in the literature, particularly in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain. This work brings this discussion into the autonomous driving domain by analyzing the accuracy of attention in estimating the impact of an input object on an autonomous vehicle's driving, i.e., its relevance. To this end, we compare different attention-based relevance estimation methods against a causal reference of object relevance obtained through counterfactual analysis. We perform our analysis on more than 80,000 synthetic driving scenes using an autonomous vehicle based on PlanT 2.0, a state-of-the-art Transformer-based model for object-level planning. Results show that attention provides a correlational rather than causal indication of object relevance. Attention-based relevance estimation methods do not consistently identify all relevant objects and tend to incorrectly classify as relevant objects with little or no impact on the vehicle's driving. In particular, results show that attention can effectively identify relevant objects in simple single-lane, straight-road scenarios, but its accuracy degrades in more complex settings, such as multi-lane roads and intersections. These findings highlight the limitations of attention as a proxy for object relevance, calling for novel methods able to accurately capture the causal impact of individual objects on the vehicle's driving and distinguish it from correlational associations.

papers.title: Let a Small Model Read First: Faster Prefill for Long Interleaved Image-Text Inputs
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages and collections of hundreds of images, but they are slow to start: on inputs of about 100K tokens, the prefill takes most of the wait for the first output token. A common approach prunes the input by scoring its tokens with the target model itself or with a small model of the same family that first writes an answer. However, this scoring takes much of the time that pruning saves. We find that the evidence for a question lies in a few whole units (images or paragraphs), and that a small hybrid model finds them with one attention head of an early layer, even at half image resolution. Based on these findings, we propose SkimPrefill, which lets the small hybrid model read the whole input first, up to that early layer, with images at half resolution. Most layers of the small hybrid model (Qwen3.5-0.8B) run in linear time, so this pass is short. SkimPrefill then ranks every unit with that head and gives the target the top units as an ordinary shorter prompt. One untrained selector serves targets of different model families. Extensive experiments on MMLongBench at 128K tokens, with 19 datasets of five task types, show the effectiveness of SkimPrefill. With 10% of the input tokens kept, SkimPrefill speeds up the prefill of Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3-VL-32B by 3.7 times, 11.6 time and 8.2 times while maintaining their average accuracy.

Vision-language models (VLMs) [1, 12, 31] answer questions about long interleaved inputs, such as documents of many pages [27] and collections of hundreds of images [46, 47], but respond slowly. A key source of this delay is the prefill [22], which passes every token of these inputs, up to 128K [46], through every layer before the first output token. However, a question usually depends on a small part of such an input. Token pruning [5, 58, 53, 60] therefore shortens the target’s prefill by dropping tokens that are redundant or that the answer does not need.

Most existing VLM pruning methods score the input with the target or with a small model of its family, but they keep individual or merged tokens [53, 58] instead of a whole image or a whole paragraph (Tab. 1). FastV [5] ranks visual tokens by the attention of an early layer of the target and prunes them inside it. This is cheap, but one early layer ranks tokens poorly at small budgets [60]. The training-free form of FlexSelect [59] takes the attention of a deeper reference layer instead, so the target reads the whole input up to that layer before it selects. Small-VLM-Guided Pruning (SGP) [60] lets a small model of the target’s family write an answer first and sums its attention over all layers. IF-Prune [37] moves beyond this answer-driven attention: it fine-tunes a small model that scores each visual token in one pass and serves larger models of the same architecture. SGP and IF-Prune pass token positions to the target, so their small models serve only targets of their own family.

papers.title: Zippers and Twisters II: The lopsidedness of satellite systems around local massive galaxies emerges from a shifting cosmic web landscape
papers.abstract: We investigate the role of the cosmic web on the origin and strength of lopsidedness in the distributions of luminous dwarf satellites around massive galaxies analogs in the high-resolution hydrodynamic simulation NewHorizon. Using common lopsidedness estimators, we find that $>25\%$ of our sample display ``statistically significant" lopsidedness incompatible with expectations for dark matter sub-haloes. The NewHorizon sample is generally skewed towards being more lopsided than naive expectations. This cautions against using dark matter or under-resolved hydrodynamic simulations as a null-hypothesis to compare to real systems. We find broad, hemispheric lopsidedness to be much more prevalent than narrow lopsidedness inherited from group infall. Across all systems, the dividing plane between the richest and emptiest hemispheres is systematically aligned with a nearby intermediate-scale cosmic filament. Further analysis reveals that the lopsidedness of systems is largely inherited from that of the network of filaments feeding them. The most populated side almost systematically contains the highest number of filaments. Such anisotropies of local filament networks are often indicative of on-going or recent zippers (filament merger $<2$ Gyr). Converging filamentary structures therefore funnel satellites preferentially onto one side of host halos, naturally generating lopsided configurations without requiring galaxy mergers. Twister remnants (of high orbital momentum mergers of filaments) are also found on the richest hemisphere of our systems, perhaps reminiscent of vorticity preventing mergers hence causing satellites' pooling. These results suggest that lopsidedness is primarily an outcome of the evolution of the intermediate-scale cosmic web. This highlights the need for increased hydrodynamic resolution in simulations.

papers.title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
papers.abstract: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $\Theta(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $\alpha d$ coordinates, $0<\alpha<1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $\Theta(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leq\alpha d$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0<\alpha<2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.

A model fitted to pairwise marginals sees independence; a model that uses the cycle can learn their joint law (Section 2.2). We use this family to quantify how learning and query costs differ from circuit approximation costs.

Tractable marginals need not imply compact positive circuits: Martens and Medabalimi (2015, Theorems 36–37) prove this for spanning-tree laws, including limits of fixed-size circuits. Zhang et al. (2020, Theorems 3–4) use the same law to separate determinantal point processes from nonnegative decomposable circuits. Approximate lower bounds at small TV tolerance hold for deterministic decomposable circuits (Leland and Choi, 2025, Theorem 4.1). Zhao et al. (2026) analyze separation rank under a fixed vtree and derive a separation when two functions need different vtrees for compact representation. Our approximation bounds also apply without a fixed vtree. Our circuit lower bounds adapt balanced decompositions for nonnegative circuits (Martens and Medabalimi, 2015, Theorem 38) and Boolean circuits (Bova et al., 2016, Theorem 6). Within structured-decomposable circuits, monotone and squared representations are incomparable (Wang and Van den Broeck, 2025). Tensor networks also have unbounded size gaps between nonnegative and squared factorizations (Glasser et al., 2019). Mixtures of separable flows use correlated Gaussian bases (Yalavarthi et al., 2026), and squared circuits allow negative or complex parameters (Loconte et al., 2026). Our circuit bounds do not cover these classes.

papers.title: Improved Bounds for Online TSP on the Half-Line
papers.abstract: In the open online traveling salesperson problem, requests appear over time at different positions of a metric space. A single agent traveling at unit speed must serve all requests, by visiting their positions, with the objective of minimizing the completion time. We propose online algorithms for this problem for the case that the metric space is the half-line. First, we present a $2$-competitive algorithm in which the server always either moves at unit speed or remains stationary, which improves on the previously best-known ratio of $2.04$. We further observe that algorithms must sometimes move slower than unit speed to achieve competitive ratios below $2$. We introduce a second algorithm that beats the barrier of $2$ by carefully modulating its speed, and prove a tight bound of $1.75$ on its competitive ratio. Finally, we slightly strengthen a known lower bound on the best-possible competitive ratio on the half-line from $1.627$ to $1.646$.

We study the online traveling salesperson problem (TSP) on the half-line. In this problem, requests of the form r=(t,p)r=(t,p) are revealed over time, where t∈ℝ≥0t\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} denotes the release time and p∈ℝ≥0p\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} the position of the request. A single server, initially located at the origin and moving at speed at most 11, must serve every request by visiting position pp at some time not earlier than time tt. In the online setting, the algorithm only learns about a request at its release time, whereas an offline algorithm knows the entire request sequence from time 00. The objective is to minimize the makespan, i.e., the time when all requests are served. Note that the offline setting does not coincide with the classical TSP, as the offline algorithm is still restricted to serving a request after its release time. Furthermore, we consider the open version of the problem, where, in contrast to the closed version, the server does not need to return to the origin.

Online TSP models dynamic routing scenarios arising, for instance, in robotic maintenance, cleaning, or collection tasks where jobs appear over time. In many such settings, the depot lies at the boundary of a one-dimensional operating region, such as inspection along a track, pipeline, or corridor, so that the underlying metric space is the half-line, making it a natural case to study. While the online TSP has been extensively studied in many variants [3, 4, 5, 13, 19, 20, 21, 26], in particular for the underlying metric space being the real line ℝ\mathbb{R} or higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, we focus here on algorithms tailored specifically to the half-line ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. Although this setting appears simple at first glance, obtaining optimal strategies turns out to be surprisingly challenging. The half-line has fundamentally different structural properties due to the lack of symmetry around the origin, and it seems that optimal strategies cannot be obtained by simple adaptations of known algorithms. For instance, we will see that, unlike any algorithm previously proposed for online TSP, an optimal online strategy on the half-line must already start moving before the first request is revealed.

papers.title: Early spectra of AT2017gfo from scaled 3D merger ejecta: mass--velocity distribution, 3D structure, and treatment of line opacity
papers.abstract: We present ARTIS radiative transfer calculations for neutron star merger ejecta with line-by-line opacities, wavelength-calibrated lanthanide data, and time-dependent r-process compositions and thermalisation, testing how the early kilonova depends on the mass-velocity distribution, dimensionality, and line treatment. We rescale 3D dynamical ejecta from a merger simulation in density and velocity to approximate AT2017gfo. Mass scaling alone provides good agreement with the bolometric light curve but inconsistent spectra. With velocities additionally halved, the model also reproduces the observed spectra at 1.4, 2.4, and (albeit less accurately) 3.4 days. The Sr II triplet contributes most to the 10500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ peak, and La III and Gd III to the 13500 $\mathring{\mathrm{A}}$ shoulder. Although hydrodynamically not fully self-consistent, this model is to our knowledge the first kilonova model based on calibrated atomic data that reproduces the light curve and main spectral features of the early AT2017gfo, suggesting that total (dynamical plus post-merger) ejecta with higher mass, lower velocity, and similar composition compared to our dynamical ejecta could explain AT2017gfo. A 2D azimuthal average mixes lanthanide-poor with lanthanide-rich regions, smooths the density, and makes the averaged model three times fainter at 1 day and redder throughout than the 3D model, highlighting the importance of 3D modelling. We compare the line-by-line macroatom treatment with expansion-opacity and line-binned schemes with thermal redistribution, using identical atomic data. Luminosities agree to $\lesssim 10$ per cent after 1 day, but the expansion-opacity scheme, unlike converged line-binned schemes, overestimates the spectral flux by up to 20 per cent, which can bias inferred abundances.

papers.intro:
A kilonova is a rapidly evolving transient that follows a compact object merger and is powered by the radioactive decay of newly synthesised heavy nuclei (Metzger et al., 2010; Metzger, 2019, e.g.,), produced through rapid neutron capture (the r-process). To date, the most complete observed sequence of spectra of a kilonova is that of AT2017gfo (Coulter et al., 2017; Smartt et al., 2017; Pian et al., 2017), the electromagnetic transient associated with the gravitational-wave signal GW170817 (Abbott et al., 2017), which originated from a neutron star merger (see Margutti and Chornock, 2021, for a review). These spectra carry signatures of freshly synthesised r-process elements (Pian et al., 2017; Smartt et al., 2017; Watson et al., 2019, e.g.,), which merger ejecta are expected to produce (Lattimer and Schramm, 1974; Lattimer et al., 1977; Freiburghaus et al., 1999; Goriely et al., 2011; Korobkin et al., 2012; Fernández and Metzger, 2013; Wanajo et al., 2014; Perego et al., 2014; Just et al., 2015; Radice et al., 2018, e.g.,).

An outstanding goal of recent kilonova modelling efforts is to reproduce the observations from AT2017gfo accurately enough to infer, ideally in an unambiguous manner, the multidimensional mass–velocity distribution and composition of the ejecta. While individual properties of AT2017gfo can be reproduced using models that are simplified in one way or another, models that agree in both the light curve and spectral features (and their time evolution) pose an enormous multi-disciplinary challenge, because they require accurate knowledge of atomic data for the photon opacities as well as nuclear data for the composition and radioactive heating of the ejecta, and computationally expensive numerical hydrodynamics and radiative transfer simulations that link ejecta properties to observables. Each of these modelling ingredients is still beset with significant uncertainties. A particularly important aspect for spectral modelling is to calibrate theoretically obtained atomic lines to experimentally known values, which is necessary for a faithful association of observed spectral features with specific ions (Ryabchikova et al., 2015; Kurucz, 2018; Domoto et al., 2021; Domoto et al., 2022; Gillanders et al., 2022; Flörs et al., 2023; Flörs et al., 2026, e.g.,). So far no fully self-consistent 3D hydro-plus-kilonova model using calibrated atomic data has been shown to reproduce both the light curve and spectral features of AT2017gfo during its early photospheric phase.

Kilonova calculations that treat thermalisation of radioactive decay energy in detail (Hotokezaka and Nakar, 2020; Andalman et al., 2026, e.g.,) or use wavelength-calibrated line lists (Gillanders et al., 2022, e.g.,) have mostly used simplified ejecta models, such as 1D density profiles with parameterised compositions. Multidimensional radiative transfer studies have likewise often adopted parameterised or spatially averaged ejecta distributions (Wollaeger et al., 2018; Kawaguchi et al., 2018; Bulla, 2019; Wollaeger et al., 2021, e.g.,). Such averaging removes any small-scale structure of the merger ejecta, such as angular variations of the composition, dense clumps, and low-density channels between them. 3D radiative transfer calculations that keep this structure have been presented for the ejecta of neutron star mergers (Tanaka and Hotokezaka, 2013; Collins et al., 2023; Shingles et al., 2023b; Neuweiler et al., 2023; Collins et al., 2026; Kiuchi et al., 2026) and of black hole–neutron star mergers (Tanaka et al., 2014; Darbha et al., 2021; Kawaguchi et al., 2024). Such calculations indicate that the 3D structure can be important for predicting synthetic observables. For example, in Shingles et al. (2023b), we showed that a sequence of spectra similar to that of AT2017gfo can be obtained from a model that includes the 3D merger structure while a model from a 1D spherical average had strongly suppressed flux below ∼\sim8000 Å (and different luminosity), which is less consistent with the observed spectral series. However, the model used by Shingles et al. (2023b) was too faint and evolved too rapidly, probably because its mass was low. It was based on a simulation that ended 20 ms after the merger and thus contained only the dynamical ejecta (matter that tidal forces and shocks expel during the first milliseconds of the merger) with no post-merger ejecta. As such, its mass of 0.005 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot} is well below the total ejecta mass estimated for AT2017gfo, which is 0.03–0.05 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot} as inferred from its light curve (Smartt et al., 2017), and up to ∼\sim0.08 M⊙\mathrm{M}_{\odot} as suggested by multicomponent fits (Kasen et al., 2017; Villar et al., 2017). The spectral features of that model were also at shorter wavelengths than those of AT2017gfo, which suggested that the expansion velocities of the model were too high. Of the 3D calculations listed above, Kawaguchi et al. (2024) and Kiuchi et al. (2026) include the post-merger ejecta, but they present no synthetic spectra and use wavelength-calibrated data for only eight ions.

Kilonova models also differ in how they treat the line opacity. A line-by-line treatment evaluates the optical depth of each line individually in the Sobolev approximation (Sobolev, 1960) and follows the emission after each absorption, for example with the macroatom method of Lucy (2002); Lucy (2003). To reduce the computational cost, many kilonova calculations instead combine the lines of each wavelength bin into one binned opacity, either an expansion opacity (Karp et al., 1977; Eastman and Pinto, 1993) or a line-binned opacity (Fontes et al., 2020). Codes that use binned opacities typically also assume thermal redistribution, in which the re-emitted radiation has a spectrum set by the local temperature and opacity of the gas, with no memory of the transition that absorbed it (Wollaeger et al., 2018; Bulla, 2019, e.g.,).

papers.title: Conceptual full-vehicle modeling of a modular all-wheel-drive robotic ADS test platform as a foundation for a digital twin architecture
papers.abstract: This paper presents the development of an initial full-vehicle simulation model of the PixKit modular electric test platform in IPG CarMaker. The objective is to create a physics-based and extendable model structure that can serve as a low-level foundation for future digital twin applications. The reference vehicle is a skateboard chassis combining unconventional vehicle characteristics such as four independent wheel-hub motors and rear axle steering capable of high steering angles. Since complete measurement data of the vehicle is not yet available, the model parameterization is based on a combination of manufacturer documentation, derived values and engineering assumptions. The modeling approach focuses on the system-level integration of the main vehicle subsystems rather than on a fully validated representation. The resulting model was assessed through basic driving scenarios with different steering inputs and configurations. The simulations showed stable model behavior and physically plausible interaction between the subsystems. The all-wheel-drive configuration produced symmetric wheel responses in longitudinal driving, while counter-phase rear axle steering increased the yaw response and reduced the simulated turning circle diameter compared with front axle steering only. The circular driving scenario further indicated bounded roll and slip behavior. Overall, the implemented CarMaker model provides a traceable and functional simulation basis for the PixKit vehicle. It can support future model refinement, calibration with real vehicle data and development with the goal of creating a validated digital twin architecture.

papers.intro:
Modular electric vehicle platforms with distributed drives and steer-by-wire functionality provide additional degrees of freedom for vehicle dynamics, control development and automated driving research [1]. Their simulation requires a consistent representation of interacting subsystems such as powertrain, suspension, tires, steering and vehicle body. The PixKit platform utilized in this work is a modular electric skateboard chassis with all-wheel drive, four wheel-hub motors and selectable steering modes including rear axle steering [2]. These features make the vehicle suitable for future investigations of steering strategies, vehicle dynamics and digital-twin-oriented development. The absence of a parameterized full-vehicle model of the platform available in simulation environments like IPG CarMaker was therefore the reason for this project. This paper presents the development of a first functional and extendable vehicle model of the PixKit platform in IPG CarMaker. The model is not intended as a fully validated high-fidelity representation of the real vehicle. Instead, it is designed as a physically plausible model that integrates all relevant subsystems in a traceable structure. Due to the incomplete data basis, the parameterization combines documented vehicle data, derived values and assumptions. The resulting model is evaluated through basic simulation scenarios, including straight-line acceleration, minimum turning circle comparison and steady-state circular driving. These tests are used to assess simulation stability, subsystem interaction and qualitative plausibility of the vehicle response. The main contribution of this work is the structured transfer of the PixKit vehicle architecture into an executable CarMaker model that can serve as a low-level basis for future refinement. The paper addresses the question of how the PixKit platform can be represented in IPG CarMaker as a functional and extendable full-vehicle model based on incomplete parameter data.

Modular electric vehicle platforms with distributed drives and steer-by-wire functionality provide additional degrees of freedom for vehicle dynamics, control development and automated driving research [1]. Their simulation requires a consistent representation of interacting subsystems such as powertrain, suspension, tires, steering and vehicle body. The PixKit platform utilized in this work is a modular electric skateboard chassis with all-wheel drive, four wheel-hub motors and selectable steering modes including rear axle steering [2]. These features make the vehicle suitable for future investigations of steering strategies, vehicle dynamics and digital-twin-oriented development. The absence of a parameterized full-vehicle model of the platform available in simulation environments like IPG CarMaker was therefore the reason for this project. This paper presents the development of a first functional and extendable vehicle model of the PixKit platform in IPG CarMaker. The model is not intended as a fully validated high-fidelity representation of the real vehicle. Instead, it is designed as a physically plausible model that integrates all relevant subsystems in a traceable structure. Due to the incomplete data basis, the parameterization combines documented vehicle data, derived values and assumptions. The resulting model is evaluated through basic simulation scenarios, including straight-line acceleration, minimum turning circle comparison and steady-state circular driving. These tests are used to assess simulation stability, subsystem interaction and qualitative plausibility of the vehicle response. The main contribution of this work is the structured transfer of the PixKit vehicle architecture into an executable CarMaker model that can serve as a low-level basis for future refinement. The paper addresses the question of how the PixKit platform can be represented in IPG CarMaker as a functional and extendable full-vehicle model based on incomplete parameter data.

papers.title: Render the Robot, Generate the World: One Video World Model Across Embodiments
papers.abstract: Predicting the consequences of an agent's actions requires modeling both the body's motion and the environment's response. Most video world models attempt to learn both from numerical actions, even though geometry and kinematics already specify the intended motion. We introduce Doppel, an embodiment-agnostic video world model conditioned on camera-aligned renderings of future body configurations and numerical action trajectories. By explicitly providing the intended motion, Doppel can focus on predicting object motion and interaction-driven changes in the environment. Rendered motion also provides a common visual interface across different embodiments and action spaces. To train on robot datasets without camera extrinsics, we recover camera poses and align rendered trajectories with recorded observations. We jointly train a single shared video backbone and conditioning adapter on eight datasets spanning eight robot and human embodiments, from single- and bimanual robot arms to a dexterous humanoid and human hands and bodies, using about 600 hours of video without embodiment labels. Across three robot-arm datasets, Doppel improves PSNR over action-only baselines by 1.00 dB on held-out trajectories and 1.20 dB under out-of-distribution evaluation, while predicting more consistent object motion. Training on all eight embodiments (Doppel-8) improves robot predictions over the three-robot model (Doppel-3) on four of six evaluation sets. Project page: https://doppelwm.github.io/.

papers.title: DIVO: a direct divertor configuration plasma start-up scheme aimed at tokamak fusion reactors
papers.abstract: The tokamak, one of the mainstream approaches to magnetic confinement in nuclear fusion devices, will be the first approach to reach reactor class prototyping. Plasma start-up is expected to be more challenging in large superconducting next-step tokamaks such as ITER due to the low inductive toroidal electric field and potentially long durations in limiter configuration when plasma-wall interactions lead to easier impurity contamination of the confined plasma. Such limiter start-up is the standard way of early plasma formation in the vast majority of today's experimental devices and is planned on ITER. To mitigate these issues, a novel plasma start-up scheme with divertor geometry only (DIVO start-up) was recently developed for the first time on the EAST superconducting tokamak. The key breakthrough in this work is the use of a non-inductive, electron cyclotron wave generated plasma formed in a poloidal field configuration which is a superposition of a barrel-like geometry around the centre of the vacuum vessel and a mirror-like geometry across the whole vessel cross-section. Such a non-inductive discharge avoids the drawback of low inductive electric field which is unavoidable in large superconducting devices as a consequence of the relatively low voltages which can be applied to the magnet coils. In addition to the low toroidal electric field, the DIVO start-up scheme as demonstrated on EAST significantly reduces impurity sources compared to the conventional limiter phase approach, even in cases with relatively poorly conditioned plasma-facing surfaces. The robustness of the DIVO start-up has also been verified on EAST with varying prefill gas pressure, impurity level and inductive electric field. It thus offers a potential solution to one of the main issues facing routine successful start-up on large tokamak reactors.

papers.title: Assessing Vision-Language Models for Early Prediction of Unsafe Situations in Robotics
papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) process visual information and textual instructions and, by using their ability to understand and reason about context, are well-suited for predicting robot failures before they occur. However, evidence supporting this remains limited. To address this, we present an empirical evaluation of VLMs for predicting robot failures. In particular, we experiment with Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision across three robotic case studies (HuRoN, Pal Robotics, and CrowdBot), analyzing both video and odometry data for early failure warning (i.e., before an unsafe situation occurs). Specifically, we evaluate their performance in classifying situations as safe, potentially unsafe, and unsafe, together with uncertainty quantified using various metrics, and study the relationship between uncertainty and performance. Our results showed that Qwen provides the strongest overall classification and prediction-reliability performance, while InternVL shows stronger early-warning capability in several configurations. The results further show that the effect of robot-state information and temporal history depends on the model and evaluation objective. Overall, our findings indicate that general-purpose VLMs can support early robot-safety monitoring, but the most suitable configuration depends on whether the priority is accurate assessment of safety-state, reliable confidence and uncertainty, or timely warning before unsafe events.

papers.intro:
Autonomous navigation robots are often deployed in environments with humans and other obstacles, such as offices, warehouses, and other crowded places, where they must perform their intended tasks correctly while also avoiding collisions with people and other objects. Consequently, they must be able to detect potential failures early and prevent them. Very often, the software in these robots includes functionality for object detection and failure prediction, typically using deep learning models (Alotaibi et al., 2024). However, deep learning models often perform well only on the types of data they are trained on, and their performance degrades when they encounter unseen objects (Tang et al., 2023).

Autonomous navigation robots are often deployed in environments with humans and other obstacles, such as offices, warehouses, and other crowded places, where they must perform their intended tasks correctly while also avoiding collisions with people and other objects. Consequently, they must be able to detect potential failures early and prevent them. Very often, the software in these robots includes functionality for object detection and failure prediction, typically using deep learning models (Alotaibi et al., 2024). However, deep learning models often perform well only on the types of data they are trained on, and their performance degrades when they encounter unseen objects (Tang et al., 2023).

To address the above limitation, foundation models such as Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are often advocated for their ability to generalize, enabling them to handle unseen situations (Yousaf et al., 2026). To enable robots to detect failures in advance and issue warnings about potential failures, VLMs could provide an effective solution; however, evidence supporting their use in this context remains limited. VLMs, however, have been used for various applications in robotics. For example, VLMs have been used to generate test scenarios for robotic applications (Wu et al., 2026) and to automate test oracles (Saurabh et al., 2026). In addition, VLMs and related embodied multimodal models have been explored for robotic reasoning, task planning, and control (Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023). Recent video-based VLM navigation studies have further shown that temporal visual observations can provide useful context for navigation decisions in unseen environments (Zhang et al., 2024). Nevertheless, existing studies primarily focus on task execution, navigation planning, and control, leaving the potential of VLMs to predict robot safety issues from historical observations insufficiently explored.

We provide a systematic empirical evaluation of three VLMs—Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision—for robot-safety classification across three robotic case studies. For both input types, we evaluate how the length of the visual history affects classification performance using different history settings. We go beyond classification performance by evaluating the confidence, uncertainty, and calibration of VLM predictions, providing evidence on how reliable their predictions are for safety-critical use. Finally, we evaluate VLMs as early-warning mechanisms at the event level, distinguishing actionable, too-early, too-late, and missed warnings. This connects classification performance with the practical question of whether a model can identify an unsafe situation early enough for a robot or its digital twin to take preventive action.

papers.title: A (12/11+eps)-Approximation for Nonpreemptive Throughput Maximization
papers.abstract: We study unweighted nonpreemptive throughput maximization on an arbitrary number of identical machines: each job has a processing time and a release--deadline window, and the goal is to schedule as many jobs as possible. For every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, we give a randomized $(12/11+\varepsilon)$-approximation. This improves the recent $(4/3+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Alexander Armbruster, Fabrizio Grandoni, Antoine Tinguely, and Andreas Wiese and the $(17/13+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Tong and Xu. For binary-encoded integral inputs, our algorithm runs in time $n^{O_\varepsilon(1)}\operatorname{poly}(N)$, where $N$ is the input length.

papers.intro:
A job with a release time and a deadline may have many possible execution intervals, but it contributes only once to a schedule. This distinction is central to throughput maximization. A fractional solution may place a job in several parts of the time horizon. Sampling these placements independently can produce repeated copies of that job while leaving another job absent. The resulting execution slots still have value: a spare copy can sometimes be replaced by a missing job. The difficulty is to recover this value while respecting both slot capacities and the requirement that each job count once.

An interior placement belongs to a superblock entirely contained in the job’s window. A local job is eligible in only one block. A sampling scheme partitions the blocks into small, disjoint groups. We sample a tuple from each group’s table, independently between groups. A job can appear at most once inside a group. A nonlocal job can therefore appear in both of its boundary blocks only if those blocks belong to different groups. If two jobs have strictly interleaving boundary pairs, the shorter job fits the other job’s intervening boundary slot. This creates a possible repair: a missing job can use the spare boundary slot of a duplicated job.

We address the first obstruction with a capacitated flow on crossing pairs of active jobs, whose duplication probabilities are at least a small threshold. We address the second by reserving separate fractions of each missing job’s unit capacity for interior assignments and boundary repairs. This yields a feasible fractional matching; the algorithm obtains at least its value by maximum integral matching.
