papers.title: Isometrically greedy renormings of bidemocratic unconditional bases of Banach spaces
papers.abstract: We show that if a greedy basis of a Banach space has the additional property that its dual basis is also greedy, then the space admits an equivalent norm under which the basis is isometrically greedy. This solves in the positive a question posed by Dilworth, Kutzarova, Odell, Schlumprecht and Zs\'ak in 2014. As an application, we resolve a long-standing problem explicitly posed by Albiac, Ansorena and Wallis in 2017 by proving that any subsymmetric basis of a Banach space is isometrically greedy under a suitable renorming of the ambient space.

papers.title: Analytical formulae for planet-planet or moon-moon tides
papers.abstract: Almost negligible among the solar system planets, mutual tides raised by a secondary on another secondary orbiting the same primary may gain increased importance in tightly packed systems, e.g., between the components of close-in exoplanetary systems or between the moons of gas giants. In this work, we derive an analytical formula for the planet-planet tidal potential and for the effect of mutual tides on the rotational and orbital evolution of moons or planets in a coplanar configuration. The procedure follows closely the steps of W. M. Kaula (1961), and the resulting potential and derived quantities are presented in the form of an expansion into modes of different frequencies (in the temporal domain) and spherical harmonic components (in the spatial domain). The analytical formulae are implemented into a code and compared with an independent numerical solution.

Tidal interaction is one of the major phenomena influencing the long-term orbital and thermal evolution of close-in exoplanets and planetary satellites. The expected final state of tidally evolved close-in rocky exoplanets or moons without an atmosphere is then a circular orbit and synchronous rotation [4, e.g.,].

The orbital dynamics of multiplanetary systems are also affected by the gravitational interaction between secondaries. In this context, the secondaries are typically treated as point masses and their effect on the orbits of each other is described as a third-body perturbation [24]. However, in tightly packed systems, the differences in the gravitational force acting throughout an extent (i.e., not point-mass) secondary due to another secondary might not be negligible. In such cases, where the tidal deformation is not caused by the primary, but rather by another secondary, we can speak of planet–planet or moon–moon tides.

To our knowledge, the first discussion of planet–planet tides was provided by Lingam and Loeb [19], who emphasised the astrobiological significance of this phenomenon. According to their estimates, the tidal elevation on the TRAPPIST-1 exoplanets caused by planet–planet tides should be comparable to the elevation caused on the Earth by the tidal action of the Moon. Moreover, since the TRAPPIST-1 system constitutes a resonant chain, this effect can be further enhanced during multiple conjunctions. If the surfaces of the planets are partially covered by an ocean, the complex tidal modulation caused by the conjunctions may have important consequences for abiogenesis and evolution of life [19]. Later that year, a research note dedicated to the planet–planet tides in the TRAPPIST-1 system was published by Wright [31]. Wright [31] estimated that the tidal strain and tidal heat rate produced in planet gg due to the action of planet ff may be even greater than the deformation and dissipation induced by the tidal interaction with the host star. For the other planets (except bb), the ratio between the strain due to planet–planet tides and the star–planet tides was calculated as being higher than 10%10\%; the same ratio for the tidal dissipation being above 1%1\%. Although these numbers were presented as first-order estimates, they clearly indicate that planet-planet tidal loading should be included in detailed studies of the system.

papers.title: Compositional Mapping of Martensitic and Magnetic Transitions in Ni-Fe-Ga Bulk Alloys and Microwires
papers.abstract: Despite extensive research on Ni-Fe-Ga magnetic shape-memory alloys, the compositional dependence of their martensitic and magnetic transition temperatures remains unclear. We analyze published bulk-alloy data alongside two complementary microwire series. While the pooled data show no unique dependence on e/a, elemental-concentration analysis reveals that Ni and Fe are the primary compositional controls of M_s and T_c, respectively, within 26-28 at.% Ga: M_s = 43.6 c_Ni - 2079 K and T_c = 17.4 c_Fe - 30 K. At fixed Ga, this creates a trade-off: raising M_s generally lowers T_c and vice versa, making it difficult to keep both above room temperature. Around 25 at.% Ga, bulk data exhibit considerable scatter, partly attributable to gamma-phase formation. Glass-coated microwires produced by the Taylor-Ulitovsky method, in which the gamma phase has generally not been reported, extend the accessible composition range toward lower Ga contents. The Ni(73-x)Fe(x)Ga27 (x = 18-22) series and the Ga-rich Ni50Fe21Ga29 and Ni50Fe23Ga27 microwires broadly follow the corresponding bulk trends. Remarkably, Ni50Fe25Ga25 and Ni50Fe27Ga23 microwires depart sharply from these trends, combining M_s at or above room temperature with T_c > 395 K. Their functional potential is demonstrated by approximately 10% reversible strain in Ni50Fe27Ga23 microwire during thermal cycling under constant tensile stresses up to 200 MPa.

papers.title: Optical readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors with SiPMs
papers.abstract: Scintillation light readout of MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) is used for imaging and track reconstruction applications including in optical Time Projection Chambers (TPC). Typically, high resolution CCD or CMOS imaging sensors are used and PMTs can be employed to obtain auxiliary timing information. We report on the optical readout of MPGDs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) which enables limited spatial resolution. Arrays of SiPMs were used to read out Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) and Glass Micromegas amplification stages. Center of gravity reconstruction of hit positions yields a spatial resolution of approximately 1.35 mm for signals shared across multiple SiPMs. High gain of the amplification stage as well as the SiPMs enables good signal sharing and is advantageous for position reconstruction.

papers.intro:
MicroPattern Gaseous Detectors (MPGDs) combine charge amplification in microscopic electric-field structures with fine spatial granularity, high rate capability and a low material budget. Prominent examples include Gaseous Electron Multipliers (GEMs) [14], in which electron multiplication occurs inside holes in a metal-clad insulating foil, and MicroMesh Gaseous Structures (Micromegas) [11], which employ a narrow amplification gap between a micromesh and an anode. These structures amplify the primary ionisation produced by incident radiation and provide a versatile basis for particle tracking and radiation imaging.

The recording of scintillation light emitted during electron avalanche multiplications in MPGDs has been demonstrated to achieve high resolution with state-of-the-art imaging sensors [9, 5]. In combination with fast photon detectors such as Photomultiplier Tubes (PMTs), optical readout can be used for 3D track reconstruction in Time Projection Chambers where 2D information from imaging sensors is combined with depth information from PMTs. This concept is employed for directional dark matter searches by the CYGNO [1] experiment as well as for the search for the Migdal effect [2]. Optical readout relies on a good matching of the emission spectrum of the gas with the wavelength-dependent sensitivity of the recording device. The visible light sensitivity of most imaging sensors has led to the popularity of CF4 as scintillation gas as it features a strong visible scintillation band peaked around 630 nm630\text{\,}\mathrm{nm} [10]. While CF4 scintillation is well-matched to most imaging sensors, it presents a strong constraint on the gas choice and it is also facing decreasing availability due to its classification as strong greenhouse gas [8].

Scintillation light readout offers considerable flexibility in the choice and arrangement of the sensing elements. CCD and CMOS cameras provide finely sampled two-dimensional images, while optical magnification allows the field of view and effective sampling at the amplification plane to be adjusted. The optical connection electrically separates the photosensor from the amplification electrodes and allows high granularity without a correspondingly segmented charge-collection anode. Complementary fast photodetectors can measure the arrival-time distribution of the scintillation signal, providing information on electron drift and enabling three-dimensional reconstruction in time projection chambers [3, 6]. Optical readout has been demonstrated with multiple MPGD technologies, most notably Gaseous Electron Multipliers and Micromegas. While the open geometry of GEMs and their use in multi-GEM stacks is ideally suited for optical readout by imaging sensors placed below the last GEM, Micromegas had to be implemented on a transparent substrate to allow recording of emitted scintillation light [5]. Glass Micromegas have been used for X-ray and beta imaging as well as for neutron detection with good spatial resolution [7]. Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) offer a compact approach to combining spatially resolved optical detection with fast timing. Precise timing readout of a gaseous detector has been demonstrated with a combination of PICOSEC Micromegas with SiPM readout [4]. Comprising many avalanche photodiode microcells operated in Geiger mode, SiPMs provide single-photon sensitivity, high internal gain and a fast response. Arrays of independently read out SiPMs can measure the distribution of scintillation light across the sensor plane.

papers.title: Lunar laser ranging analyses of NGLR-1 data with PEP and prospects for MPAc: towards one millimeter range precision
papers.abstract: Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has provided critical data for investigating Earth-Moon dynamics, lunar internal structure, and tests of General Relativity (GR). However, the measurement precision of historical arrays (such as those from Apollo and Lunokhod missions) is inherently limited by laser pulse broadening induced by lunar librations. To overcome this limit, next-generation single Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) of large optical diameter have been developed to eliminate pulse dispersion, enabling LLR measurements to advance from centimeter-level precision down to the millimeter scale. In this work, we present a detailed analysis of LLR observations from NGLR-1 (Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1), the first single 10cm-diameter CCR deployed on the lunar surface. Carried out using the Planetary Ephemeris Program (PEP), this study investigates individual range measurements, normal points (NPs), residuals, and observational dispersion collected by the ground stations at Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging station (APOL), Wettzell, and Grasse. The results: demonstrate the success of NGLR-1 in significantly enhancing time of flight measurement precision compared to legacy Apollo and Lunokhod retroreflector arrays; indicate similar good prospects also for ESA's MPAc laser retroreflector (MoonLIGHT with Pointing Actuators) to be launched in early 2027; pave the way for a new era of LLR observations and enhanced tests of GR, alternative gravity theories in general and improved lunar geophysics and geodesy.

papers.intro:
Since 1969, Lunar Laser Ranging (LLR) has been a vital technique to measure the distance between the Earth and the Moon by using the time of flight of laser pulses from Earth that are reflected from retroreflectors on the lunar surface. This method indeed offers crucial information about the dynamics of the Earth-Moon system, the Moon’s internal structure, lunar ephemerides, and important tests of General Relativity (GR) (Murphy et al., 2012). LLR has historically relied on the retroreflector arrays of Apollo 11, 14, and 15 and Lunokhod 1 and 2, which contributed a negligible fraction of the instrumental LLR error budget. However, over the past five decades, the ground station technology has significantly improved, reducing the measurement errors and currently the instrumental LLR error budget is dominated by the spread of the returning laser pulse originating in the large size of the arrays due to the impact of lunar librations caused by the Moon’s orbital eccentricity and inclination (Martini et al., 2012; Ciocci et al., 2017; Porcelli et al., 2021). Indeed, this effect is proportional to the dimension of the retroreflector array and it results in a broadening of the laser return pulse that intrinsically limits the precision of the Earth-Moon distance measurement. This means that the spread (i.e., the standard deviation) of the reflected pulse is a measure of the precision of the LLR observation. In this scenario, next-generation single lunar Cube Corner Retroreflectors (CCRs) with large optical diameter allow us to overcome this problem (Alley et al., 1970a; Alley et al., 1970b; Bender et al., 1973; Currie et al., 2011), as their performance is unaffected by the time spread. As a matter of fact, the pulses reflected by single large-diameter CCRs return separately and can be clearly distinguished in time and space by LLR Earth stations. As a consequence, they are capable of fully exploiting the current LLR station capabilities to reach a precision below the centimeter threshold down to the desired millimeter level, providing also higher data collection rates. Such advancement will have a significant impact, enabling more accurate ephemerides, refined tests of GR and of other theories of gravity, and improved knowledge of the properties of the deep lunar interior. The first next-generation large-diameter CCR has already landed on the Moon: it is the Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1 (NGLR-1)11 1 https://www.physics.umd.edu/nglr/. (Currie et al., 2011). NGLR-1 is a single CCR with an optical diameter of 10 cm developed by the University of Maryland in collaboration with the Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare - Laboratori di Frascati (INFN-LNF). It was deployed on the Moon on the 2nd of March 2025 in Mare Crisium by Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost lunar lander (Banks et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). Since the first day after landing, NGLR-1 has been observed by the Earth stations of Grasse in France, Wettzell in Germany, and Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging (APOL) station in the USA, formerly known as the Apache Point Observatory Lunar Laser-ranging Operation (APOLLO). These stations are collecting normal points22 2 A normal point is a compressed measurement of the round-trip time of flight between a ground station and the retroreflectors on the Moon, obtained by averaging a series of raw observations (i.e., single photons or individual range measurements) collected over a specific time interval typically lasting 5 to 15 minutes. To compress data, observatories isolate true photon returns from background noise during the time window; these valid returns are then mathematically mapped to a single central time and averaged to smooth out random timing variations. This process reduces data volume while increasing measurement precision. (NPs) from NGLR-1, and we also expect measurements by the station located in Matera, Italy. Furthermore, an upgrade of the laser and detector systems of the ground stations is planned to enhance the precision of the measurements and provide a polarization angle in agreement with the one designed for NGLR-1. Finally, other LLR stations are expected to acquire data from NGLR-1 in the future. In addition, new next-generation CCRs are expected to land on the Moon. In particular, the successors of NGLR-1 are NGLR-2 and NGLR-3 and the one developed by INFN-LNF, which is MoonLIGHT+MPAc (Moon Laser Instrumentation for General relativity/geophysics High-accuracy Tests integrated with the MoonLIGHT Pointing Actuator) (Huang et al., 2024; Muccino et al., 2025). The main objective of NGLR-1 is to significantly improve the precision of the LLR measurements. In this regard, the data obtained by the operating ground stations provide important information on the ranging dispersion and the precision of the measurements. In this framework, we here present an analysis of the NGLR-1 observations that deeply investigates the individual range measurements, NPs, residuals, and spread of the observations to NGLR-1. This study is performed with the Planetary Ephemeris Program. This work clearly shows the success of NGLR-1 in enhancing the precision of the time of flight measurement compared to the "old-generation" retroreflector arrays, paving the way to a new era of LLR observations that allow for a breakthrough in some of the tests of GR and in general gravity theories. The paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 introduces the data sets used in this analysis, Sect. 3 details the use of the Planetary Ephemeris Program, its specifics, and our methodology for dealing with the LLR data, Sect. 4 outlines the results of the analyses, and Sect. 5 describes the MoonLIGHT+MPAc payload and its expected impact on the LLR analyses performed with PEP. A summary of conclusions and future prospects is provided in Sect. 6.

Such advancement will have a significant impact, enabling more accurate ephemerides, refined tests of GR and of other theories of gravity, and improved knowledge of the properties of the deep lunar interior. The first next-generation large-diameter CCR has already landed on the Moon: it is the Next Generation Lunar Retroreflector-1 (NGLR-1)11 1 https://www.physics.umd.edu/nglr/. (Currie et al., 2011). NGLR-1 is a single CCR with an optical diameter of 10 cm developed by the University of Maryland in collaboration with the Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare - Laboratori di Frascati (INFN-LNF). It was deployed on the Moon on the 2nd of March 2025 in Mare Crisium by Firefly Aerospace’s Blue Ghost lunar lander (Banks et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026). Since the first day after landing, NGLR-1 has been observed by the Earth stations of Grasse in France, Wettzell in Germany, and Apache Point Observatory Lunar laser ranging (APOL) station in the USA, formerly known as the Apache Point Observatory Lunar Laser-ranging Operation (APOLLO). These stations are collecting normal points22 2 A normal point is a compressed measurement of the round-trip time of flight between a ground station and the retroreflectors on the Moon, obtained by averaging a series of raw observations (i.e., single photons or individual range measurements) collected over a specific time interval typically lasting 5 to 15 minutes. To compress data, observatories isolate true photon returns from background noise during the time window; these valid returns are then mathematically mapped to a single central time and averaged to smooth out random timing variations. This process reduces data volume while increasing measurement precision. (NPs) from NGLR-1, and we also expect measurements by the station located in Matera, Italy. Furthermore, an upgrade of the laser and detector systems of the ground stations is planned to enhance the precision of the measurements and provide a polarization angle in agreement with the one designed for NGLR-1. Finally, other LLR stations are expected to acquire data from NGLR-1 in the future. In addition, new next-generation CCRs are expected to land on the Moon. In particular, the successors of NGLR-1 are NGLR-2 and NGLR-3 and the one developed by INFN-LNF, which is MoonLIGHT+MPAc (Moon Laser Instrumentation for General relativity/geophysics High-accuracy Tests integrated with the MoonLIGHT Pointing Actuator) (Huang et al., 2024; Muccino et al., 2025). The main objective of NGLR-1 is to significantly improve the precision of the LLR measurements. In this regard, the data obtained by the operating ground stations provide important information on the ranging dispersion and the precision of the measurements. In this framework, we here present an analysis of the NGLR-1 observations that deeply investigates the individual range measurements, NPs, residuals, and spread of the observations to NGLR-1. This study is performed with the Planetary Ephemeris Program. This work clearly shows the success of NGLR-1 in enhancing the precision of the time of flight measurement compared to the "old-generation" retroreflector arrays, paving the way to a new era of LLR observations that allow for a breakthrough in some of the tests of GR and in general gravity theories. The paper is organized as follows: Sect. 2 introduces the data sets used in this analysis, Sect. 3 details the use of the Planetary Ephemeris Program, its specifics, and our methodology for dealing with the LLR data, Sect. 4 outlines the results of the analyses, and Sect. 5 describes the MoonLIGHT+MPAc payload and its expected impact on the LLR analyses performed with PEP. A summary of conclusions and future prospects is provided in Sect. 6.

papers.title: Matroid Connectedness and Component Decomposition: Breaking the Quadratic Barrier
papers.abstract: Deciding whether a matroid is connected and computing its connected components are two fundamental algorithmic problems in matroid theory. Since the 1970s, the best known algorithms for both problems have used $O(n^2)$ independence queries on an $n$-element ground set. Our main contribution is to break this quadratic barrier: we give a deterministic algorithm that computes all connected components of a matroid on $n$ elements with $O(n \log{n})$ independence queries. Our algorithm for component decomposition combines fundamental basis exchanges with a disjoint-set union data structure, avoiding the explicit construction of the fundamental graph. Moreover, we show that our algorithm is asymptotically optimal by giving a lower bound based on a simple information-theoretic argument: any (deterministic or bounded-error randomized) algorithm to compute connected components needs $\Omega(n \log{n})$ independence queries. Then, we turn to the query complexity of deciding whether a matroid is connected. For this problem, we present an algorithm that uses $O(nh)$ independence queries, where $h \ge 1$ bounds the size of any chain of nonempty proper cyclic flats. The algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal linear query complexity on elementary split matroids, that include all paving matroids, and on arbitrary direct sums of uniform matroids.

papers.title: A Characterization of Rings Where a Linear Transformation and Its Inverse and Transpose Have the Same Information Exchange
papers.abstract: Linear transformations are considered over finite commutative rings. It is shown that the information exchange of an invertible linear transformation and that of its inverse are equal for any ring. It is also shown that the information exchange of any linear transformation and that of its transpose are equal if and only if the ring is Frobenius. Applications are presented to the Discrete Fourier Transform, to the analysis of Vandermonde transformations, and to area-time complexity.

papers.title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
papers.abstract: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.

Kernel-based regularization has become a standard nonparametric tool for linear system identification [1, 2, 3]. A positive semidefinite kernel plays two closely related roles in this framework. Deterministically, it defines a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) and hence the geometry of the regularization problem [4, 5]. Probabilistically, the same kernel can be interpreted as the covariance of a stochastic prior on the unknown impulse response, most commonly a Gaussian process [6, 7]. This dual deterministic–probabilistic interpretation is one of the main attractions of kernel methods [8, 9, 10], but it also raises a subtle issue when structural properties of dynamical systems, such as stability, are considered.

This dual deterministic–probabilistic interpretation is one of the main attractions of kernel methods [8, 9, 10], but it also raises a subtle issue when structural properties of dynamical systems, such as stability, are considered.

For discrete-time linear systems, BIBO stability requires the impulse response to be absolutely summable. In the deterministic RKHS viewpoint, this has traditionally led to the notion of a stable kernel, requiring all elements of the associated RKHS to be stable. The corresponding theory is by now well developed and includes several characterizations and kernel-design principles specifically tailored to system identification [1, 6, 11]. From a probabilistic perspective, however, the requirement is imposed on the sample paths of the stochastic process. For Gaussian processes, almost-sure BIBO stability is more restrictive than RKHS stability and is completely determined by the covariance through the diagonal square-root summability condition identified in [12].

This distinction becomes important because Gaussianity ties covariance and sample-path behavior together. Once the mean and covariance are fixed, the Gaussian law is fixed as well, so stability cannot be imposed independently of the second-order structure. Beyond Gaussianity, this restriction disappears: distinct stochastic processes may have exactly the same covariance while possessing very different higher-order structure and sample-path properties. This opens the possibility of using the covariance to describe dependence or smoothness while enforcing stability through the full prior distribution rather than through a prescribed covariance decay. Section 3 formalizes the three notions of Gaussian stability, RKHS stability, and stability-compatibility. Section 4 establishes the necessary and sufficient characterization of stability-compatible kernels. Section 5 derives practical sufficient conditions, illustrates them through representative examples including RBF and ARMA covariance models, and develops a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. Section 6 establishes the strict hierarchy among the three notions of stability. Section 7 develops a constructive family of stable non-Gaussian priors with prescribed covariance and specializes it to the stable RBF prior. Section 8 evaluates the resulting estimator numerically and compares it with standard Gaussian kernel methods, with particular emphasis on the TC prior. Conclusions then end the paper.

papers.title: Hidden topological signatures in a van der Waals ferromagnet revealed by spin-resolved circular-dichroic photoemission
papers.abstract: Layered ferromagnets with strongly correlated electrons provide a platform for exploring the interplay among magnetism, spin-orbit coupling, and nontrivial band topology. $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$ is a correlated van der Waals ferromagnet with a transition temperature of 58 K that lies close in composition to a superconducting phase that emerges upon Ni depletion. Here, we combine spin- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, circular-dichroism measurements, and density functional theory calculations to investigate its spin-resolved electronic structure. We observe spin-polarized states crossing the Fermi level and signatures of broken time-reversal symmetry in the ferromagnetic state. Spin-resolved circular-dichroism measurements further reveal a helicity-dependent spin response consistent with a finite spin Berry curvature and suggestive of local topological character. Together, these results establish an experimental connection between ferromagnetism, spin-polarized electronic states, and topological signatures in $\mathrm{Ni}_{1/4}\mathrm{TaSe}_2$, providing a foundation for investigating how these properties may relate to the emergence of superconductivity upon Ni depletion.

papers.title: Cosmological structure formation in ultralight dark matter
papers.abstract: An important challenge in cosmology is to describe the formation of galaxies and structures, starting from small inhomogeneities in the early Universe, which later grew and formed the so- called dark matter halos. We consider the dark matter to be composed of ultralight bosons and simplify the general complex problem of halo formation by using the time-dependent variational analysis approach. This yields, for the first time, a fully analytical equation for the time-evolution of perturbations towards isolated haloes. We follow the evolution of the halo size and density during different stages of its formation, revealing the role of the background density, Universe expansion, and quantum pressure.

papers.title: A Free Lunch: Gradient Averaging Achieves Optimal Statistical Efficiency in Newton Sketch
papers.abstract: We study statistical inference for online sketched Newton methods, in which each Newton system is approximately solved by an inner randomized sketching solver. Existing work reveals a computational--statistical trade-off: the sketching solver (and its accelerated variants) reduces the per-step cost of Newton methods from $O(d^3)$ to $O(d^2)$, but the randomness introduced by sketching also inflates the limiting covariance of both the last and the averaged Newton iterates. In this work, we address this trade-off via gradient averaging. We show that simply replacing the stochastic gradient with a moving average at each step can mitigate, and in some cases eliminate, the trade-off in Newton sketch. Importantly, gradient averaging requires no additional oracle evaluations and leaves the contraction bound of the inner sketching solver unchanged. In particular, we prove that the last sketched Newton iterate with gradient averaging attains a limiting covariance no larger than that without gradient averaging, while the averaged iterate even attains the minimax optimal limiting covariance, matching that of the exact Newton method. To our knowledge, this is the first analysis showing that randomness introduced to improve computational efficiency need not compromise statistical efficiency as long as proper gradient estimates are used. The key analytical challenge is that gradient averaging destroys the crucial martingale difference structure underlying central limit theorem arguments. We overcome this challenge by analyzing the coupled two-timescale recursions governing the iterate and the gradient estimator. Numerical experiments on linear and logistic regression support our theoretical covariance comparisons.

papers.title: Prognosis Without Prediction: The Intrinsic Geometry of Survival
papers.abstract: Modeling systemic failure in high-dimensional environments is fundamentally limited by supervised algorithms that attempt to predict sparse, noisy or censored endpoints. To break this reliance on explicit outcome regression, we engineered the Self-Organizing Survival Manifolds (SOSM) framework, a deep learning architecture that decouples unsupervised representation learning from survival labels and treats time-to-event progression as an emergent geometric property. The system projects heterogeneous multi-omics arrays into a unified latent space governed by a pseudotime-weighted, curvature-minimizing graph Laplacian, organizing patient trajectories along low-dissipation geodesic flows. To validate the framework, we applied this architecture to a 184-patient clear cell renal cell carcinoma multi-omics cohort. Across a deterministic 5-fold cross-validation pipeline, SOSM achieved a mean Concordance Index of $0.768 \pm 0.068$, while out-of-fold risk stratification yielded significant survival divergence (log-rank $p < 0.001$) accompanied by a 14.7% increase in local manifold dissipation among high-risk patients. Furthermore, interrogating the network's encoder weights confirmed that the model autonomously recovered canonical metabolic and microenvironmental drivers of disease progression without supervised feature selection. By demonstrating that systemic failure can be mapped as a geometric phase transition, SOSM establishes a generalizable computational engine for prognostic modeling across biological, industrial and financial complex systems.

Historically, predictive modeling has relied heavily on supervised frameworks, extending from foundational proportional hazards models [2] to modern deep learning architectures [3, 4]. However, these approaches are notoriously susceptible to catastrophic overfitting when exposed to high-dimensional datasets [5]. Furthermore, supervised models treat survival as an external annotation to be mathematically regressed, ignoring the reality that real-world time-to-event data is frequently noisy, right-censored and subject to systemic collection biases. Conversely, unsupervised representation techniques, such as factor analysis [6] and network fusion [7], successfully address the dimensionality issue but typically discard critical temporal dynamics in favor of bulk variance.

papers.title: Statistical methods for extrapolation from one population to another: a review
papers.abstract:
Background: Extrapolation refers to statistical approaches that support inference on treatment effects in a target population using data from completed clinical trials conducted in a source population. This is particularly important when only limited data are available in the target population. Extrapolation may be based on multiple sources of information, including pharmacokinetic, pharmacodynamic, mechanistic, or clinical outcome data. This review focuses on methods that enable borrowing of information from one population to support inference in another.
  Methods: We conducted a review of statistical methodologies for extrapolation, focusing on approaches that incorporate outcome data from source populations to support inference in target populations. Methods were identified across a range of settings, including extrapolation across age groups and across different clinical indications. Literature searches were conducted using the Science Citation Index Expanded database within Web of Science and included all English-language records available up to 30 June 2025.
  Results: The review identified 218 extrapolation approaches from 159 papers, which can be broadly classified into three main categories: Bayesian, frequentist, and causal inference methods. These methods vary in their assumptions, implementation, and applicability across different extrapolation settings.
  Conclusions: This review provides a comprehensive and up-to-date overview of statistical methods for extrapolation, offering a foundation for further methodological development and applied research. It also discusses key considerations for method selection and current limitations, and highlights priorities for future research, including the development of new extrapolation methods and clinical trial designs that facilitate extrapolation.

papers.title: Numerical integration of non-local master equations for renewal shot noise with drift and state-dependent amplitude
papers.abstract: The probability density of a system driven by a drift and a renewal train of kicks with state-dependent amplitude obeys a master equation that is non-local in space, because the kick operator $\hat{p}(i\partial_x I(x))$ is of infinite order, and, for non-exponential waiting times, non-local in time, with a memory kernel containing the propagator of the drift. Its solutions contain quasi-singular components, the never-kicked mass, which collapse onto the attractors of the drift. We present an accurate numerical method for such equations. The kick operator is a push-forward along the Marcus flow; in the Lamperti variable it becomes a translation, whose exact cell-to-cell weights follow from the cumulative distribution of the kicks, without quadrature. The drift is integrated by a conservative semi-Lagrangian step exact in time. The memory is represented by a sum of exponentials whose auxiliary fields are advected by the drift, at a cost linear in the number of steps. The never-kicked mass is transported exactly. For each ingredient we quantify the errors of simpler alternatives. The method is verified against exact solutions and event-driven Monte Carlo simulations with exact flow maps, from which it is statistically indistinguishable with $10^8$ trajectories. Parameters tuned for Gaussian kicks carry over unchanged to other kick distributions, and near a zero of the coupling, where the density vanishes faster than any power, the solution follows the known asymptotic law down to densities of order $10^{-37}$, far beyond Monte Carlo reach. As an application we compare the exact equation with its local and Poissonian approximations: in the range explored, the local equation deviates by up to 8% of the density width, also for waiting times with finite mean, consistently with an error estimate predicting larger deviations for slow drifts at long times. A Fortran implementation is available.

papers.title: From Activity Recognition to Shift Detection: Variational Wi-Fi Sensing with Evidential Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Human motion perturbs wireless channels, making commodity Wi-Fi devices a practical platform for device-free activity recognition. Yet Channel State Information (CSI) also depends strongly on the person, receiver position, recording session, and surrounding environment, so a classifier can continue producing activity labels after its deployment conditions have moved away from those seen during training. We propose Wi-HAR, a multi-antenna architecture in which four Variational Auto-Encoders learn compact distributions from raw Wi-Fi 6 CSI magnitudes and a delayed-fusion classifier combines their means and log-variances. On twelve activities from a public benchmark, Wi-HAR reaches 96.6% median recognition accuracy, compared with 70.8-81.5% for independently optimized single-antenna models, showing that the antennas provide complementary views of the same activity. We then use the same latent backbone to detect deployment shifts without using shifted samples for model selection or calibration. A class-conditional uncertainty score derived from Evidential Deep Learning achieves a macro-average ROC-AUC of 0.897 across eleven datasets that change receiver position, participant, recording session, or room, and detects 82.5% of shifted samples at a realized 5.2% in-distribution rejection rate. Detection performance nevertheless varies substantially across receiver positions, showing that the same physical change does not induce a uniform uncertainty response. The compact representation also supports shallow decision-tree analysis using variables from several antennas.

We address these two requirements with Wi-HAR, a multi-antenna architecture based on Variational Auto-Encoders (VAEs) [16]. Four antenna-specific encoders independently map raw CSI magnitudes to compact Gaussian latent representations, and a delayed-fusion classifier combines their means and log-variances for activity recognition. The use of multiple antennas is central to the architecture because physically separated antennas observe different multipath channels and can therefore provide complementary views of the same activity. At the same time, the representation is deliberately compact: unlike autoencoder-based Human Activity Recognition (HAR) systems that use latent spaces with tens of neurons [23], Wi-HAR represents each antenna with only 2 to 12 distribution parameters. This compression keeps the fused representation small enough to examine directly while retaining sufficient information for activity discrimination.

papers.title: Worth Another Look:Constrained World-Model Planning for Visual Inspection
papers.abstract: Visual inspection in field robotics and environmental monitoring must localize multiple targets under strict compute and sensing caps. Exhaustive sweeps waste calls on absent classes, while myopic and search-free policies stumble over heterogeneous tariff cliffs or discard viewport edits whose value emerges only after re-querying. We formulate inspection over frozen detectors as neuro-symbolic observation planning under partial observability, decoupling a compact recurrent world model (WM) from exact symbolic feasibility and tariff rules. Receding-horizon beam search with online replanning jointly schedules class queries, crops, enhancements, and termination (stop), paired with slack-aware shadow pricing and legal fallback at larger budgets. Across eight terrestrial, optical, and sonar benchmarks, multi-step lookahead outperforms static schedules and search-free offline RL under tight budgets -- gaining up to 28.4 AP percentage points over static priority on RUOD and 15.1 on ARIS -- while dynamic pricing lifts large-budget performance on all eight domains at 11 ms planning cost. Ultimately, pairing lightweight learned dynamics with exact symbolic constraints turns frozen detectors into adaptive, budget-aware inspection agents without retraining.

papers.title: Generative AI in Software Testing: Practitioners' Perspectives on the Benefits, Challenges, Opportunities, and Risks
papers.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) increasingly supports software testing, yet empirical evidence on practitioners' perceptions remains limited. This study investigates perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks of GenAI in software testing through a questionnaire survey of 64 practitioners. Closed-ended responses were analyzed descriptively, while open-ended responses were qualitatively coded to contextualize the findings. Among the respondents, 34 were users (those with regular or experimental use of GenAI in testing) and 30 were non-users (those without prior use of GenAI in testing). Results show generally positive perceptions of GenAI for reducing effort, test generation, and debugging, alongside concerns about prompt dependence, trust, and incorrect outputs. Users were more positive about several concrete benefits while also more frequently prioritizing reliability-related risks, whereas non-users showed greater uncertainty about some technically specific challenges. Overall, the findings position GenAI as an assistive technology requiring human validation and highlight the importance of considering practitioners' experience with GenAI when interpreting perceptions of GenAI-assisted testing.

Prior work increasingly frames GenAI-assisted testing as human–AI collaboration rather than fully autonomous testing, with practitioners retaining responsibility for directing tasks and evaluating generated artifacts [6, 18]. To address this gap, we investigate the following research question: What are the perceived benefits, challenges, opportunities, and risks associated with the use of GenAI in software testing tasks? We conducted a literature-informed questionnaire survey with 64 software practitioners involved in testing and quality assurance, combining closed- and open-ended responses. The analysis examines responses separately for users and non-users to consider experience-based perceptions alongside expectations of potential use. The study provides empirical evidence on practitioner perspectives of GenAI-assisted testing and implications for human–AI collaboration, validation, and integration into software testing processes.

papers.title: The Illusion of Relief: How GenAI Redistributes Cognitive Workload in Software Organizations
papers.abstract: This study explores how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes software practitioners' cognitive work across software development activities. We analyzed questionnaire responses from 44 practitioners across nine organizations using descriptive quantitative methods and qualitative analysis of relevant open-ended responses. Practitioners reported productivity and time savings, but also effort associated with providing context, prompting, reviewing, correcting, verifying, and integrating AI-generated outputs. Human judgment and accountability remained central, with practitioners anticipating a shift from direct code production to guiding, evaluating, validating, integrating, and coordinating AI-supported work. Thus, GenAI appears to redistribute cognitive work toward oversight rather than simply eliminate it, although whether overall cognitive workload increases or decreases remains undetermined.

papers.title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
papers.abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. papers.title: STAR++: A Physical-Aware Benchmark and Framework for Astronomical Super-Resolution across Multiple Filters
papers.abstract: Astronomical super-resolution (ASR) aims to reconstruct high-resolution star fields from low-resolution telescope observations across multiple filters for astrophysical analysis. However, developing a physics-aware ASR framework faces two challenges: 1) Data view: no large-scale benchmark supports field-level ASR, especially on unseen filters. 2) Method view: Existing ASR methods often fail to preserve stellar flux across spatial resolutions. Moreover, ASR requires reconstructing high-frequency components, including accurate star locations and profiles, making it more ill-posed than natural-image SR. To tackle these problems, we introduce STAR++, a large-scale benchmark comprising approximately 1.7 million flux-consistent image pairs across 36 filters, derived from Hubble Space Telescope (HST) observations. STAR++ uses a flux-preserving data generation pipeline to ensure photometric consistency across resolutions and provides the Flux Error (FE) metric to evaluate ASR models from a physical perspective. To address method-level challenges, we propose a Flux-Invariant Super-Resolution Plus (FISR++) model that generalizes to unseen filters while accurately reconstructing flux-consistent high-resolution images. Beyond the flux-preserving modules, FISR++ introduces two novel components. Specifically, a Filter-Aware Adapter (FAA) incorporates filter metadata to adapt image representations to varying spectral and optical conditions. In addition, a Spatial Ambiguity Disentangle Loss (SADL) models spatial ambiguity as pixel-shift uncertainty, mitigating the smoothing of learned conditional mean reconstructions caused by this ambiguity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FISR++ consistently outperforms existing ASR methods in reconstruction quality and flux accuracy, while generalizing to unseen filters, highlighting its effectiveness for photometrically faithful ASR.

Higher resolution is critical to astronomical observation, as it reveals finer astrophysical structures and supports more precise scientific measurements [1, 2, 3]. Achieving higher spatial resolution traditionally relies on advances in telescopes and observing systems, often at substantial instrumental and operational cost [4, 5]. Super-resolution (SR) offers a complementary computational approach to reconstruct high-resolution images from lower-resolution observations [6, 7, 8], and has shown promise in astronomical imaging [9, 10]. However, astronomical images contain physically meaningful information, such as the flux of celestial sources. Therefore, developing a physics-aware ASR framework is essential for accurately reconstructing star fields while preserving their physical fidelity.

Physics-aware ASR requires cross-filter generalization, flux consistency (i.e., consistent stellar brightness across spatial resolutions), and accurate reconstruction of stellar structures. However, existing ASR datasets and methods still face limitations from two perspectives to achieve the aforementioned goals. 1). Data perspective: Existing ASR benchmarks cover a limited number of filters and lack systematic evaluation on unseen filters [11, 12, 13], as shown in Tab. I. Moreover, existing ASR networks primarily rely on image inputs without explicitly incorporating filter-specific physical properties such as wavelength and bandwidth, limiting their adaptability to different observation conditions. 2). Method perspective: It mainly includes two challenges of flux inconsistency and spatial ill-posedness. (i) Flux inconsistency: In the real world, telescopes under different observation resolutions have a flux consistency relation [14, 15]. Specifically, although a celestial object has different levels of distortion under low resolutions, it almost has the same total flux as in high resolutions because of the telescope imaging principle [14, 16]. However, existing datasets have significant drifts from this property because they directly use simple interpolation [17, 18], suitable for natural images but conflicts with astronomical observations. (ii) Spatial ill-posedness: Unlike natural image super-resolution, which can use surrounding context to restore large objects, ASR must recover isolated, tiny point sources like stars. Without contextual clues, a single low-resolution pixel can correspond to many possible high-resolution stellar positions and profiles, making the recovery severely ill-posed. To minimize error under this spatial ambiguity, common likelihood training simply averages all candidate positions, which flattens the peak intensity, leading to over-smoothed restoration and inaccurate source flux.

It extends STAR [19] from one filter to 36 filters spanning the 222.4–906.0 nm band. STAR++ retains the flux-consistent data generation pipeline of STAR to preserve the photometric properties of astronomical observations across resolutions. Specifically, the FAA incorporates filter metadata, allowing the model to recognize filter and adapt filter-specific knowledge to restore high resolution image across different filters. papers.title: Ordinal Hegselmann-Krause Systems
papers.abstract:
We study opinion formation in the popular Hegselmann-Krause model when agents replace the traditional averaging update by a median update or more general ordinal aggregation methods. We analyze the convergence properties of synchronous and asynchronous dynamics.
  For asynchronous dynamics, we show that every HKS with a $1$-Lipschitz ordinal aggregation function converges in worst-case time $\mathcal{O}(n^4)$. For the special case of median aggregation and for the family of $k\textsf{-large}$ aggregation functions, in which agents select the $k$-th largest opinion in their neighborhood, we obtain sharper bounds of $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$. For general ordinal aggregation, some sequence of $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ updates reaches an equilibrium from every initial state. Nevertheless, other update sequences may cycle, and uniform random activation can require exponentially many updates with overwhelming probability.
  For synchronous dynamics, we obtain a tight characterization. Ordinal aggregation functions satisfying the $1$-Lipschitz condition are shown to guarantee convergence in linear time. This result applies to many natural examples such as minimum, maximum, median, and $k\textsf{-large}$ functions. When the Lipschitz condition is violated, there exist instances in which synchronous dynamics do not converge at all.

This behavior can be interpreted in a game-theoretic sense by assuming each agent strategically chooses an opinion in order to minimize a 2-norm of the vector of distances to neighboring opinions [9]. Further, aggregation via the median has desirable properties in social choice [32, 12]. For HKS with such an ordinal aggregation of agents (which we call ordinal HKS), we examine the conditions and the time needed for the system to converge to an equilibrium. In an equilibrium, all agents are stable, i.e., the current opinion of each agent equals the aggregated opinion of their current neighborhood. Our results inform the discussion of the predictive value of these models, i.e., whether or not it is realistic to expect that a stable opinion configuration emerges from ordinal aggregation (in reasonable time). We study convergence properties of both synchronous and asynchronous dynamics. For synchronous dynamics, all agents that are not stable update their opinion simultaneously at each time step; for asynchronous dynamics, exactly one agent that is not stable is chosen at each time step to update their opinion. We stress that convergence times in the two models are measured on different scales. A synchronous step may comprise between 11 and nn simultaneous individual updates, whereas an asynchronous step comprises exactly one. Consequently, bounds on the number of synchronous and asynchronous steps should not be compared directly. To the best of our knowledge, there is no prior work on the impact of alternative aggregation functions in HKS that provides rigorous quantitative bounds on the convergence behavior of such scenarios.

papers.title: ExiST: Existence-Aware Self-Training for Semi-Supervised Multi-Organ Segmentation
papers.abstract: Semi-supervised multi-organ segmentation should learn more than a dozen organs from a handful of labeled scans, and the smallest organs occupy less than one percent of the foreground. We identify a failure mode of self-training that is specific to this regime. When a teacher misses a small organ in a scan, every voxel of that organ receives the confident pseudo-label background, and the student is trained toward the organ absence. Repeated over many scans, this loop extinguishes tail organs. In a pilot study, removing the gallbladder from the pseudo-labels reduced its Dice on AMOS from 36.5 to 1.0. We argue that a missing organ should be treated as unresolved rather than absent and propose Existence-aware Self-Training (ExiST). It builds pseudo-labels by leave-one-out consensus of independently trained networks, screens them with a quality gate on validation scans, and infers, per scan and per organ, whether the organ was found. For every unresolved organ, the background voxels of that scan receive the set-valued target, trained with a marginal cross-entropy that accepts either answer and a Dice term that skips uncertain voxels. We show that this loss never pushes a candidate organ toward absence and never favors one member of the set, which leaves the decision to labeled evidence. ExiST outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods and reaches 77.1 mean Dice on Synapse with 20% labeled scans and 75.9 on AMOS with 5% labeled scans.

papers.intro:
Multi-organ segmentation of abdominal CT and MRI underlies radiotherapy planning and surgical navigation, and voxel-level annotation of a dozen organs per scan is among the most expensive labeling tasks in medical imaging [21, 28]. Semi-supervised segmentation reduces this cost by training on a few labeled scans together with many unlabeled ones [45, 57, 9, 2], most often by self-training: a teacher, typically an exponential moving average (EMA) of the student or a co-trained sibling, predicts the unlabeled scans and the student reproduces its confident predictions [44, 56]. Multi-organ data make this regime unusually hard. The liver holds roughly half of the foreground voxels of the labeled scans of Synapse and AMOS, whereas the adrenal glands and the esophagus each hold less than one percent (Fig. 1). Pseudo-labels inherit and amplify this imbalance, and general methods such as UA-MT [57] and CPS [9] leave several tail organs at zero Dice (Tab. 1). Recent work debiases pseudo-label confidence, re-weights classes, balances heads, or routes organs to experts [47, 41, 60, 32].

All of these methods share an assumption that we argue is a real bottleneck for tail organs: background is treated as certain. When the teacher misses a small organ entirely, there is no organ pseudo-label to re-weight. The organ’s voxels are confidently labeled background, the student is pushed toward the organ’s absence, the EMA teacher inherits the weaker student, and the organ is missed in more scans. We call this loop pseudo-label extinction. It is invisible to confidence filtering because the background labels that cause it are confident. A pilot study under the DHC protocol [47] shows the effect directly. When the gallbladder was removed from the pseudo-labels while its voxels stayed confident background, the mean test Dice of the student on AMOS fell from 37.4 to 29.7 and its gallbladder Dice from 36.5 to 1.0.

If the pseudo-labels of a scan contain far less of organ kk than that anatomy normally contains, organ kk was not resolved, and the student should not be told where it is absent. We therefore replace the single background label by a set-valued target. Every accepted background voxel of such a scan may be either background or organ kk, and the student is trained with the marginal likelihood of the set. papers.title: GRAFT: Graph-Regularized Prototype Fields for Realistic Test-Time Adaptation of VLMs
papers.abstract: Unlabeled test data can improve the zero-shot classifier of a vision-language model, yet transductive and test-time adaptation methods often fall below the zero-shot baseline when only a few vocabulary classes are present in a batch or when streams are correlated. We trace this failure to a shared design: every class owns independent parameters estimated from its own samples, so absent or rare classes are left at biased text anchors or fitted to foreign samples. We propose Graph-Regularized Anchor-displacement Field Transduction (GRAFT), which models the adapted prototypes as text anchors plus a displacement field that is partially pooled over a semantic class graph through a Gaussian Markov random field prior, together with an explicit class-presence model. Inference is closed-form and gradient-free on cached features. Anchor-only shrinkage and a single global shift are the two extreme settings of the prior; absent classes are provably harmonic extensions of the present ones, and the pooling strength can be chosen by empirical Bayes. Under the realistic batch and online protocols on eleven benchmarks and four ImageNet shifts, GRAFT improves over the zero-shot model in every setting and over anchor-based transduction where few classes are present.

These methods are evaluated on batches that contain every class of the vocabulary in comparable numbers, whereas a photo album or a user session contains a handful of the classes that the vocabulary names, and streams are temporally correlated. Under such conditions transductive methods lose tens of accuracy points with respect to the zero-shot model they are meant to improve [46], and a controlled benchmark reports marginal gains, poor transfer across backbones and degraded calibration [36]. The remedy proposed in [46] and refined in [18] is a statistical anchor: each class prototype is shrunk towards its text embedding with a strength that grows with the number of test samples the class receives. Anchoring prevents collapse but treats every class in isolation: a class that receives no samples stays at its text anchor, although that anchor is displaced from the image distribution by the modality gap and by the domain of the test data [24, 35], and a class with one or two samples is adapted from those samples alone. The problem addressed here is therefore to adapt all prototypes of a large vocabulary from an unlabeled batch in which most classes are absent or rare, without collapsing on the absent ones and without discarding what the present ones reveal about them.

papers.title: Effects of Locomotion and Viewpoint Control on Immersive Robot Telepresence for Navigation and Inspection
papers.abstract: In many robot telepresence interfaces, movement and viewing are managed through handheld inputs. This can divide attention between steering, looking, and inspection. We compared joystick versus omnidirectional treadmill locomotion and joystick-based versus head-guided camera control in a within-subject 2x2 study in which 17 participants used a virtual reality headset to guide a quadruped robot through a physical maze while locating marked wall symbols and capturing them as visual evidence. Mixed-effects analyses showed that head-guided camera control was associated with faster completion, lower wall-contact cost, lower workload, and more favorable presence, usability, technology acceptance, and flow than joystick-based camera control. The strongest overall objective performance was observed in the joystick locomotion plus head-guided camera condition, whereas the omnidirectional treadmill plus head-guided camera condition emerged as the strongest experiential compromise. Exploratory camera analyses showed that head-guided camera control reduced switching, increased reliance on the pan-tilt view, and supported a more stable viewing strategy across the maze. These strategy differences were consistent with the performance advantage, especially for wall-contact duration. Targets captured remained near ceiling and simulator sickness remained low across all conditions. Overall, the results indicate that viewpoint control was the stronger differentiator in this combined navigation and inspection task, while locomotion still shaped the objective and experiential tradeoff.

Mobile robot telepresence is increasingly relevant in scenarios where people must act in spaces that are distant, hazardous, or difficult to access directly. In these settings, the operator must do more than drive a remote platform from one point to another. The operator must also inspect the environment, notice relevant details, and make decisions through mediated perception. Telepresence has developed from simple mobile video access toward richer robotic systems that support navigation, inspection, collaboration, and remote action across domains such as industry, healthcare, and hazardous field work [1, 2]. In parallel, immersive interfaces have become more prominent in robot operation, with recent reviews showing growing interest in VR based control, visualization, and interaction [3, 4]. This shift matters because immersive telepresence involves concurrent driving, inspection, and viewpoint management.

This shift matters because immersive telepresence involves concurrent driving, inspection, and viewpoint management.

In many practical situations, operators must keep making progress while searching for cues, checking objects or structures, and documenting what is found. This creates a dual task burden in which navigation competes with visual inspection for attention and control. Work on multiple resource use and task switching suggests that performance can suffer when perceptual and control demands compete for overlapping resources [5, 6]. In telepresence, this burden is often expressed through viewpoint management. The operator must decide when to keep moving, when to reorient attention, and how to coordinate robot motion with the currently available view. Prior teleoperation research shows that camera and viewpoint control can directly shape workload, visual attention, usability, and operational performance [7, 8, 9].

A body coupled interface translates body motion to robot control and head motion to viewpoint, linking movement and looking to bodily action. papers.title: Gas-induced reversible spectral tuning of bound states in the continuum in perovskite metasurfaces
papers.abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) provide a powerful route to engineering optical resonances in compact photonic structures, enabling enhanced light--matter interaction for sensing, nonlinear optics, optical modulation, and lasing. The next step towards practical BIC-based meta-optics is dynamic and reversible spectral control after fabrication. However, optical and electro-optical tuning typically produces limited refractive-index changes, thermo-optical approaches require continuous external actuation, and phase-change materials often provide discrete switching rather than continuous spectral reconfiguration. Here we demonstrate giant, fully reversible, and continuous spectral tuning of BIC resonances in halide-perovskite metasurfaces. Using nanoimprint lithography, we fabricate MAPbBr$_3$ metasurfaces, that support BIC-derived resonances in the visible spectral range. Exposure to HCl vapor initiates an anion-exchange reaction in which Cl$^-$ ions diffuse into the perovskite crystalline lattice and partially replace Br$^-$ ions, producing a monotonic increase of the electronic bandgap and blueshift of the excitonic resonance on a minute timescale. This leads to a decrease in the refractive index and tunes the BIC resonance by more than 40~nm in the visible range. Subsequent exposure to HBr vapor reverses the exchange process and restores the resonance to its initial spectral position. As a functional demonstration, we show continuous reversible spectral tuning of BIC-mediated lasing from the same metasurface. Our results establish gas-phase anion exchange as a non-destructive mechanism for continuous, reversible, and large-range post-fabrication control of perovskite metasurfaces, opening opportunities for chemically programmable lasers, adaptive meta-optics, and active nanophotonic devices.

papers.intro:
Bound states in the continuum (BICs) have become a fundamental concept in resonant photonics, enabling optical modes with strongly suppressed radiation losses in open systems [1, 2, 3]. In dielectric metasurfaces, BICs generally arise from symmetry protection or destructive interference between radiation channels and remain decoupled from the far field despite lying within the radiation continuum. When weakly perturbed, these states transform into quasi-BIC resonances that retain high quality factors (Q-factors) while becoming experimentally accessible [4, 5, 6]. This combination of strong field localization, planar geometry, and far-field addressability has made BIC-metasurfaces a versatile platform for enhanced light–matter interaction with applications in sensing, nonlinear optics, optical modulation, and lasing [7, 8, 9].

Such applications of BIC-metasurfaces as sensing [10, 11], adaptive optics [12], optical telecommunication [13], information encryption [14], and neuromorphic computing [15] can employ dynamic spectral tuning, unlocking new advanced device functionalities. However, BIC resonance frequencies are primarily determined by metasurfaces’ geometrical sizes, symmetry, and constituent materials, making them largely immutable after fabrication. In many cases, BIC-based meta-optics therefore requires tuning mechanisms that are reversible, broadband, and continuously adjustable while preserving the ultrahigh-QQ nature of the resonance. Achieving these requirements remains a major challenge in reconfigurable nanophotonics.

Achieving these requirements remains a major challenge in reconfigurable nanophotonics.

Existing approaches to tunable BIC-metasurfaces address this challenge only partially. All-optical modulation based on free-carrier generation [16, 17] or polariton nonlinearities [18, 19] can provide ultrafast response, but usually relies on relatively small refractive-index changes suitable for modulator development only. Thermo-optical tuning can yield larger changes, yet typically requires continuous external actuation and introduces constraints associated with heat dissipation, thermal stability, and device integration [17, 20, 21]. Phase-change materials provide substantial optical contrast and enable reconfigurable metasurfaces [12], but they often rely on discrete or hysteretic switching rather than continuous spectral reconfiguration. These limitations motivate alternative routes in which the resonant material itself can be modified volumetrically and reversibly.

Here we demonstrate giant, fully reversible, and continuous spectral reconfiguration of BIC resonances in MAPbBr3 metasurfaces through gas-phase anion exchange (Figure 1a-c). The BIC-derived resonances undergo a wavelength shift exceeding 40 nm across the visible spectrum upon exposure to HCl vapor, representing a post-fabrication tuning range inaccessible to conventional dielectric metasurfaces. This reconfigurability originates from volumetric halide exchange, where Cl- ions diffuse throughout the perovskite crystalline lattice and partially replace Br- ions, inducing simultaneous modification of the electronic bandgap, excitonic transition, and reducing the refractive index [24, 25]. papers.title: On metric multiplicative Diophantine approximation
papers.abstract: Gallagher's theorem (1962) gives a Khintchine-type dichotomy for the Lebesgue measure of the set of multiplicatively $\psi$-approximable points in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $n \geq 2$, for monotonic functions $\psi$. We establish this dichotomy for arbitrary functions $\psi$, proving a conjecture of Beresnevich, Haynes, and Velani (2013).

papers.title: A disproof of the van Emde Boas--Kruyswijk conjecture on the Davenport constant
papers.abstract: The Davenport constant $D(G)$ of a finite abelian group $G$ is the smallest positive integer $\ell$ such that every sequence $S$ with terms from $G$ and with length $|S| \ge \ell$ has a nontrivial zero-sum subsequence. A long-standing conjecture, first proposed by van Emde Boas and Kruyswijk in 1969, states that $D(C_n^r)=r(n-1)+1$ for all positive integers $n$ and $r$. In this paper, we disprove this conjecture by showing that $D(C_6^r)>5r+1$ for every $r\ge23$.

papers.title: A counterexample to the Harper-norm silver-mean conjecture
papers.abstract: The silver-mean conjecture formulated in Gerhold and Shalit 2022 states that the norm $E(\alpha)$ of the Harper operator attains its minimum at the silver mean $\alpha = \sqrt{2}-1$. We show that this conjecture is wrong by constructing an explicit rational point with a smaller Harper-norm value: $E(181/437)<2.591046794<E(\sqrt2-1)$. The separating decimal is an exact rational number. All acceptance checks use exact integer arithmetic with rigorously proved coefficient enclosures. No floating-point eigenvalue estimates or external witness data enter the certificate.

papers.title: Log Analysis for LLM-Based Agents: A Lifecycle-Oriented Survey
papers.abstract: Logs generated by LLM-based agents support analysis of execution behavior beyond final outputs. Existing surveys give limited attention to dependencies across the lifecycle of these records. A lifecycle-oriented review of 90 core studies published between 2024 and August 2026 covers Agent Logging, Agent Log Structuring, and Agent Log Mining. Stage-specific comparisons reveal cross-stage dependencies and limitations. Detailed logs do not necessarily provide sufficient evidence. Structural uniformity does not guarantee semantic equivalence. Analytical claims require alignment with supporting evidence, reference criteria, and validation procedures. Representative open-source tools, public datasets, and future research directions are also summarized.

The report also identifies real-time behavioral monitoring and audit trails covering complete sequences of agent actions as essential governance capabilities. Together, these operational and governance needs highlight the importance of systematically capturing and analyzing runtime execution records to understand agent behavior and support reliable deployment.

(He et al., 2021) systematically reviewed conventional software-log analysis, while recent studies have surveyed agent operations and observability (Dong et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025), LLM-agent evaluation (Yehudai et al., 2026a), evidence tracing and execution provenance (Wang et al., 2026d), and trajectory analysis for failure attribution and system enhancement (Wang et al., 2026a). These studies provide important perspectives on software logs, agent operation, evaluation, provenance, and trajectory analysis. However, they primarily organize the literature around conventional software logs or particular operational and analytical objectives rather than around the lifecycle of agent-generated execution records. papers.title: Reconstructing the mass-redshift distribution of supermassive black holes using multiband gravitational-wave observations
papers.abstract: The formation and evolution of supermassive black holes (SMBHs) remain major open questions in astrophysics. Astrophysical models of SMBHs invoke black-hole (BH) seeds formed at high redshift, which subsequently grow through gas accretion and mergers. Although observations of high-redshift quasars and active galactic nuclei constrain these scenarios, the mechanisms governing SMBH formation and growth remain uncertain. Future gravitational-wave (GW) observations across the millihertz, decihertz, and audio-frequency bands will provide a complementary and direct probe of SMBH assembly by tracing their merger history. We investigate the extent to which multiband GW observations can reconstruct the mass-redshift distribution of these mergers. We simulate populations of BH mergers predicted by different astrophysical models and identify those observable by the millihertz detector LISA, the decihertz detector LGWA, and next-generation ground-based detectors operating in the audio-frequency band. We reconstruct the mass-redshift distribution of these mergers using the nonparametric inference code FIGARO. We find that combining observations across frequency bands substantially improves the reconstruction for the light-seed models considered here, whose merger populations span broad ranges of mass and redshift. In contrast, for the heavy-seed models considered here, LISA alone recovers most of the accessible mass-redshift distribution, with little additional improvement from the multiband network.

papers.intro:
Gravitational-wave (GW) observations by LIGO [1] and Virgo [4] have opened a new window on the astrophysics of black holes (BHs). Historically, BHs have been observed mainly in two mass regimes: stellar-mass (∼10−100​M⊙\sim 10-100M_{\odot}) BHs, formed as the remnants of massive stars, and supermassive (∼106\sim 10^{6}–109​M⊙10^{9}\,M_{\odot}) BHs (SMBHs), found at the centers of most galaxies. Stellar-mass BHs were discovered as x-ray binaries in our own galaxy, while SMBHs were discovered through radio and optical observations of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and quasars, out to redshifts ∼11\sim 11 [92, 68, 50, 18, 136, 138]. Recently, pulsar timing arrays have obtained evidence of a stochastic GW background, thought to be produced by inspiralling binaries of SMBHs [5, 9]. A new class of BHs, with intermediate masses (∼102\sim 10^{2}–105​M⊙10^{5}\,M_{\odot}), is also postulated to exist. Until recently, observational evidence for these intermediate-mass BHs was scant. However, LIGO-Virgo observations suggest that some of the binary BH (BBH) mergers would have produced BHs with masses ∼100−200​M⊙\sim 100-200M_{\odot} as remnants [3, 2]. At the same time, massive BHs with masses ∼104−105​M⊙\sim 10^{4}-10^{5}M_{\odot}, which are lighter than the conventional SMBHs, are also being discovered in various galaxies [17, 55, 56, 104, 105]. The historical gap between stellar-mass and supermassive BHs appears to be shrinking.

Despite compelling evidence for the existence of SMBHs, their formation and evolution remain difficult to explain within a single framework. The prevailing picture invokes BH seeds formed at high redshift, which subsequently grow through gas accretion and mergers. Light seeds (LSs), with characteristic masses of ∼100​M⊙\sim 100\,M_{\odot}, may form from the remnants of metal-free Population III stars [82, 132, 67, 64, 123]. However, observations indicate that SMBHs with masses of ∼108​M⊙\sim 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} were already present at z∼7z\sim 7–99 [92, 68, 84, 128, 78, 59, 74, 87, 71]. Growing such objects from LSs within the available cosmic time is challenging, although recent cosmological simulations suggest that sufficiently efficient gas accretion, together with realistic feedback, may allow LSs to account for at least part of the observed high-redshift SMBH population [88, 81].
