The prevailing picture invokes BH seeds formed at high redshift, which subsequently grow through gas accretion and mergers. Light seeds (LSs), with characteristic masses of ∼100​M⊙\sim 100\,M_{\odot}, may form from the remnants of metal-free Population III stars [82, 132, 67, 64, 123]. However, observations indicate that SMBHs with masses of ∼108​M⊙\sim 10^{8}\,M_{\odot} were already present at z∼7z\sim 7–99 [92, 68, 84, 128, 78, 59, 74, 87, 71]. Growing such objects from LSs within the available cosmic time is challenging, although recent cosmological simulations suggest that sufficiently efficient gas accretion, together with realistic feedback, may allow LSs to account for at least part of the observed high-redshift SMBH population [88, 81].

An alternative possibility is the formation of heavy seeds (HSs), with characteristic masses of ∼104\sim 10^{4}–106​M⊙10^{6}\,M_{\odot}, through the rapid collapse of large gas concentrations in primordial or metal-poor protogalaxies [33, 26, 133, 119, 25]. Depending on the thermodynamic evolution of the inflow, this process may pass through a supermassive-star or quasi-star phase. Massive seeds may also arise through runaway stellar collisions and gas-assisted growth in dense nuclear clusters. Although HSs alleviate the need for prolonged rapid growth when explaining high-redshift quasars, their formation generally requires restrictive conditions, including low metallicity, rapid gas inflow, suppressed fragmentation, and efficient angular-momentum transport [26, 79, 33, 37, 76, 43, 28, 58]. More exotic possibilities include primordial BHs formed from the collapse of large primordial density perturbations. Depending on their formation epoch and mass spectrum, these objects could provide either light or heavy seeds; however, their production is not a generic prediction of standard inflationary cosmology and requires particular early-Universe conditions [34, 35].

Depending on their formation epoch and mass spectrum, these objects could provide either light or heavy seeds; however, their production is not a generic prediction of standard inflationary cosmology and requires particular early-Universe conditions [34, 35].

The processes governing the growth of SMBHs from their seeds also remain poorly understood. To account for the most massive quasars observed at high redshift, LSs generally require prolonged accretion at close to (or above) the Eddington rate, with a high duty cycle [81]. Sustaining such flows (especially at super-Eddington rates) is challenging because the radiation produced by the accreting gas can oppose further accretion and drive powerful outflows. Feedback from AGNs and supernovae (SNe) may further regulate the supply of gas to the BH and interrupt its growth. BH mergers provide an additional growth channel, but their efficiency depends on the time required for the BHs to sink toward the galactic centre, form a bound binary, and harden to separations at which GW emission drives the final inspiral. In gas-poor and approximately spherical stellar systems, this evolution may stall at parsec scales, giving rise to the final-parsec problem [24, 39, 89, 90, 47]. The observed SMBH population may contain contributions from multiple seed channels, shaped by environment-dependent accretion, feedback, and merger delays. Disentangling these contributions remains an open problem.

Recent observations with the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) are refining our understanding of SMBH formation and early growth. JWST has identified SMBHs with masses ∼107\sim 10^{7}–108​M⊙10^{8}\,M_{\odot} at redshifts z≳8z\gtrsim 8, corresponding to epochs less than ∼700\sim 700 Myr after the Big Bang [92, 68, 59, 128, 84, 54]. Several of these systems appear to host BHs that are overmassive relative to their stellar hosts when compared with the local SMBH-galaxy scaling relations. This suggests that BH growth may have preceded the assembly of their host galaxies [18, 59, 84, 128]. Initial observations seemed to favor the HS models, as earlier studies had suggested that LSs are unable to grow into such overmassive SMBHs in such a short span of cosmic time. However, recent analyses of stacked JWST/JADES spectra have revealed evidence for a substantial population of lower-mass SMBHs (∼106​M⊙\sim 10^{6}\,M_{\odot}) at 3<z<73<z<7, pointing to a more diverse early SMBH population than previously inferred [54]. Fitting a parameterized BH population model jointly to PTA and JWST constraints points to heavier seeds, prompt BH coalescences after halo mergers, and phases of super-Eddington growth lasting tens of Myr [125]. Upcoming optical, X-ray, and radio facilities, including Euclid [77, 48], the Vera C. Rubin Observatory [38, 65], the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope [121, 8], the Square Kilometre Array [42, 32], and Athena [91, 40], will further clarify these questions.

papers.title: Unique-maximum colourings of planar graphs with respect to neighbourhoods
papers.abstract: A colouring of the vertices of a graph by positive integers is a unique-maximum colouring with respect to open (resp. closed) neighbourhoods if the maximum colour appears exactly once in the open (resp. closed) neighbourhood of every vertex. Fabrici, Lu\v{z}ar, Rindo\v{s}ov\'a and Sot\'ak (Discrete Appl. Math. 324 (2023) 80-92) conjectured that four colours suffice for closed neighbourhoods in planar graphs. We prove this conjecture by colouring a suitable independent dominating set with the three largest colours. They further conjectured that six colours suffice if the colouring is also proper. We disprove this conjecture by a planar graph which needs seven colours, and we show that seven colours always suffice. For open neighbourhoods, we show that eight colours suffice, even for proper colourings, which improves the previous bound of ten. In the proper case, our graph again needs seven colours. If the colouring need not be proper and the graph has no vertices of degree 2, then six colours suffice.

Conflict-free colourings of hypergraphs were introduced by Even, Lotker, Ron and Smorodinsky [5], and conflict-free colourings of graphs with respect to neighbourhoods were studied in [1, 10]. We consider a related notion. A colouring of the vertices of a graph GG by positive integers is a unique-maximum colouring with respect to open (resp. closed) neighbourhoods if, for every vertex vv, the maximum colour appears on exactly one vertex of the open neighbourhood N⁡(v)N(v) (resp. of the closed neighbourhood N⁡[v]N[v]). We call such a colouring an iUMo-colouring (resp. an iUMc-colouring). If the colouring is also proper, we call it a pUMo-colouring (resp. a pUMc-colouring). The minimum numbers of colours in these colourings are denoted by χiUMo​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{iUMo}}(G), χiUMc​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{iUMc}}(G), χpUMo​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{pUMo}}(G) and χpUMc​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{pUMc}}(G), respectively. For the open variants, we only consider graphs without isolated vertices.

papers.title: Two results on rich-neighbour $5$-colouring of subcubic graphs
papers.abstract: A rich-neighbour edge-colouring is a proper edge-colouring in which every non-isolated edge has an adjacent edge whose neighbours have pairwise distinct colours. Petru\v{s}evski and \v{S}krekovski conjectured that every connected subcubic loopless multigraph distinct from $K_4$ admits such a colouring with five colours. We prove the conjecture for two classes: claw-free subcubic loopless multigraphs and $2$-connected subcubic outerplanar loopless multigraphs. The bound is sharp in both classes, as witnessed by the diamond $K_4-e$.

papers.title: Vanguard: Knowing When to Trust the Draft in Speculative Vision-Language Agents
papers.abstract: Vision-language agents that browse websites, operate phones and act in homes reason before every action, so every step waits for a large model, a latency and cost that stand in the way of deployment. Step-level speculation lets a small model draft each step and calls the large model only on rejected drafts, but its outcome rests on the judge, and a judge that reads only a step's text cannot tell whether the step fits the screen it acts on. We find that a few samples of a small model can contain a correct step about as often as the large model gets the step right, and not always on the same steps: checked against the screen, small drafts can be not only cheaper but better. We present Vanguard, a training-free judge that leaves the draft and target models unchanged: a general decision model, with the screenshot in view, gives each candidate step a probability of being right in one forward pass; the best candidate is kept if it clears a threshold, and otherwise the large model writes the step. On web, mobile and embodied agents, a 2B draft judged by Vanguard is at least as accurate as its 8B target and significantly more accurate on Mind2Web and EB-ALFRED, while the target writes only a minority of the steps; it completes far more closed-loop episodes, and with a 27B target from another family it is both faster and more accurate. Vanguard is the most accurate judge we compare on the agent tasks; it relies on the screenshot on web and mobile tasks, its calibrated threshold transfers to unseen websites, and across model families its gain over the target grows with the draft's pass@4 relative to the target's accuracy. Vanguard composes with token-level speculative decoding and matches trained process reward models on mathematics, turning speculation from a way to save the large model's work into one that can improve on it.

papers.title: Unbounded traces, Connes' index theorem for measured foliations, and the Godbillon-Vey invariant in KK-theory
papers.abstract: We prove that unbounded positive traces define KK-elements with real coefficients. Such traces naturally arise from invariant transverse measures on foliations (Connes, 1979) and, more generally, on Lie groupoids (Crainic--Mestre, 2019). As an application, we build a canonical KK-element with real coefficients whose associated map of K-groups is the Godbillon-Vey invariant as constructed by Connes. In the process, we show how Connes' index theorem for measured foliations can be deduced from the Connes-Skandalis longitudinal index theorem, using cyclic cohomology.

papers.title: Rough vector fields with vanishing Lie brackets
papers.abstract: We consider two vector fields $X, Y \in W^{1,p}_{loc}(\mathbb R^d) \cap \mathbf L^\infty$ with bounded divergence. If $p \geq 2$, this paper shows that $DX \,Y - DY \, X = 0$ almost everywhere if and only if their Regular Lagrangian Flows commute. If instead $1 \leq p < 2$, we present an example of two divergence free locally Sobolev vector fields in $\mathbb R^2$ with vanishing Lie brackets whose flows do not commute. In the regime $2 \leq p < \infty$ this paper also yields a quantitative commutation result not depending on the Lipschitz constant for vector fields with $[X, Y] \neq 0$, which is new even in the smooth setting.

papers.title: Hydrodynamics of robotic micro-swimmers in confinement
papers.abstract: Inspired by seminal work by E.M. Purcell, we discuss the problem of predicting and optimizing the performance of autonomous robots swimming in confinement. Our approach is based on the explicit numerical resolution of the fluid flow induced by the swimmer, and it is validated experimentally on a cm-size prototype composed of a cargo head and a rotating propulsive tail. Using hydrodynamic scaling, we predict the performance of replicas of our prototype scaled down to mm- and sub-mm-size to test the feasibility of autonomous micro-robots navigating in narrow vessels. The main result of our theoretical, computational, and experimental analysis is that, while hydrodynamics seems to place no fundamental obstruction to the vision of autonomous micro-robots navigating in narrow lumens inside the human body, it does provide useful and strict guidelines for rational design at different length scales.

papers.intro:
Low Reynolds number hydrodynamics has emerged as a fundamental tool to study life and motility at the scale of unicellular organisms, see, e.g., [61, 29, 44, 12, 42, 53, 55]; these papers have inspired a rapidly increasing number of scientists. The seminal 19511951 paper [61] by G.I. Taylor and the published version of the 1976 lecture by E.M. Purcell [53, 55] contain 6 and 11 references, respectively. The influential 2009 review [39] by Lauga and Powers contains 317317 references, and it has been quoted already thousands of times. The recent roadmap paper [33] focuses on biomedical applications and contains 1765 references. A comprehensive account of the state of the art is therefore impossible, but the interested reader can find sufficient background material in the papers quoted above, and also in recent monographs [68, 40] and in the references cited therein.

In view of the envisaged applications in the field of minimally invasive biomedical tools for diagnostics and drug delivery, the study of motion in confinement is of particular interest: motion of bacteria in narrow channels was investigated recently [14, 3, 63, 50, 48], also as a collective behavior [26, 69], and it was highlighted that, at these microscopic length scales, rotational diffusion effects might play an important role [67]. Recent interesting contributions also include [46], where the problem of motion in tubular confinement is solved for a general geometry of flexible filiform swimmers, using a simplified fluid model.

In spite of the recent and explosive literature growth, the science and engineering of the possible technological applications of concepts drawn from the swimming motility of microscopic organisms is still in its infancy. With few exceptions, including, e.g., [64, 2, 20, 49, 4] most studies have concentrated on proof of concepts for mechanisms that could potentially work at microscopic scales and on externally powered actuation (e.g., by magnetic fields, light, or ultrasounds), see, e.g., [18, 25, 51, 30, 72, 58] and the many references cited therein.

However, the quantitative analysis of the performance of autonomous robotic swimmers in confined environments and, in particular, the crucial question of predicting the swimming speed and energy budget on the basis of the geometry of the swimmer (hydrodynamic properties of body and propeller) and of the characteristics of the motor (power, speed of rotation imparted to the propeller, etc.) has seen only limited progress since the seminal work by Purcell [53, 55, 54]. In this paper, we take up this challenge by considering the important case of swimming inside a cylindrical tube, which has a broad range of potential applications: from the visionary goal of microscopic machines exploring vessels inside the human body, to the more mundane one of autonomous vehicles navigating pipe networks for their inspection, maintenance and repair.

The most basic and relevant information for a swimming device is the prediction of its velocity as a function of the speed of rotation of the propeller (or of the power of the motor driving it), given the knowledge of hull and propeller geometry. We call this the velocity prediction problem (VPP, in analogy with the acronym used for velocity prediction software used in the world of competitive sailing). Purcell discusses in [53, 55] this exact problem in the context of micro-swimming (a bacterium-inspired device made of a rigid head and a rotating helical tail) and provides the elegant solution for the case in which hydrodynamic interactions between head and tail can be neglected. In this paper, we revisit Purcell’s seminal work on its fiftieth anniversary [53] and extend it in several directions. First, we consider the problem of swimming in confinement (inside a tube) and, second, we resolve explicitly the hydrodynamic interactions between hull, propeller, and the walls of the confining tube. In addition, we assess the relevance of inertial forces by comparing the results obtained by modeling the surrounding fluid both with the Navier-Stokes and the Stokes equations.

The most basic and relevant information for a swimming device is the prediction of its velocity as a function of the speed of rotation of the propeller (or of the power of the motor driving it), given the knowledge of hull and propeller geometry. We call this the velocity prediction problem (VPP, in analogy with the acronym used for velocity prediction software used in the world of competitive sailing). Purcell discusses in [53, 55] this exact problem in the context of micro-swimming (a bacterium-inspired device made of a rigid head and a rotating helical tail) and provides the elegant solution for the case in which hydrodynamic interactions between head and tail can be neglected. In this paper, we revisit Purcell’s seminal work on its fiftieth anniversary [53] and extend it in several directions. First, we consider the problem of swimming in confinement (inside a tube) and, second, we resolve explicitly the hydrodynamic interactions between hull, propeller, and the walls of the confining tube. In addition, we assess the relevance of inertial forces by comparing the results obtained by modeling the surrounding fluid both with the Navier-Stokes and the Stokes equations.

Inertial forces are essential to resolve possible unsteadiness induced by interactions between the swimmer and its wake, as in the oscillatory, and possibly chaotic motion of a piece of paper freely falling in air under the action of gravity [22]. Such unsteady effects are common and have been studied, e.g., in the case of buoyancy driven motions of disks [19, 9, 17] and winged seeds in air [41, 43]. Even for steady swimming, inertial forces lead to directional dependence of drag on bodies that are not fore-aft symmetric and are necessary to explain our experimental observation, made on cm-scale prototypes, that inverting the sign of the angular velocity of the motor (at constant rate) does not simply cause a change of sign the swimming velocity (at constant magnitude). We show, however, that the errors caused by neglecting inertial forces at cm-scale are modest, and use this observation to argue that they should become negligible at mm- and sub-mm scale. In fact, at the cm-scale of our experimental prototype the Reynolds number can be estimated to be of order 10−110^{-1}, and inertial forces are not negligible, while at the micron-scale of the load carrying micro-organisms considered in [47], the Reynolds number can be estimated to be of order 10−510^{-5}-10−410^{-4}, and inertial forces can be neglected. In addition, we exploit the correct resolution of inertial forces in the fluid to analyze the performance of micro-swimmers powered by a rotating propulsive unit shaped as a marine propeller, and compare it with the performance obtained with a propulsive unit shaped as helical tail. The hydrodynamic interactions between hull and propeller, discussed for example in [56, 27], and the presence of surrounding walls call into question the very logic behind Purcell’s analysis and VPP because the propulsive force generated by a rotating propeller is different depending on whether the propeller is alone, it is attached to a hull, and whether there are walls nearby. The same argument applies to the drag opposing the movement of the hull. This makes the VPP a three-body interaction problem, for which each case of navigation in confinement would require resolving the full geometry of the flow (e.g., through a dedicated CFD study), at least in principle. The key observation we exploit in this paper is that confinement tames some of the errors coming from neglecting hydrodynamic interactions between hull and propeller. Indeed, at high levels of confinement, the interactions of each of these two components with the channel walls become dominant over the mutual interactions between hull and propeller. This crucial observation gives new life to Purcell’s approach, suitably modified to cope with confinement effects. In other words, it opens the way to the performance prediction and design optimization of a robotic swimmer, based on the knowledge of the individual hydrodynamic properties of each of the two components of the composite system, the propeller and the hull, considered in confinement but separate one from the other. We extend in this way Purcell’s conceptual road map for the design of robotic micro-swimmers to devices operating in confinement, and propose a tool to predict and optimize their performance. We validate experimentally our tool using a prototype with radius around 11\, cm, and then use hydrodynamic scaling to extrapolate its predictions to mm- and sub-mm sizes.

papers.title: Computing with Orientation-Dependent Vector Fields in Crystallographic Texture Analysis
papers.abstract:
We present a computational framework for representing orientation-dependent vector fields. Building on (arXiv:2608.21235), we translate the differential-geometric formulation into crystallographic notation and focus on its computational use in crystallographic texture analysis.
  In crystallographic applications, small orientation changes are commonly described by rotation vectors, spin tensors, or infinitesimal misorientations. By contrast, vector fields in harmonic computations are usually represented by components with respect to Euler-angle derivatives, following the classical formulation of generalized spherical harmonics. This representation is convenient but numerically unfavorable. We instead use rotation-vector components, extending a familiar description of individual orientation changes to orientation-dependent vector fields.
  In this representation, vector fields are described by three scalar component functions, which can be expanded into generalized spherical harmonics. We derive frequency-domain formulas for gradient, divergence, and curl, enabling their evaluation directly on harmonic coefficients. In particular, the gradient of a band-limited scalar function remains band-limited with the same bandwidth.
papers.intro:
The study of crystallographic microstructures and their deformation is largely based on the analysis of orientation-valued data. More precisely, in a polycrystalline material, each crystallite is described by its crystallographic orientation relative to a fixed specimen coordinate system. This orientation describes the change from the crystal frame, fixed to the lattice, to the specimen frame. Such a change of frame is described by a rotation, and since both frames may carry symmetries, an orientation is a rotation together with these symmetries. The set of all rotations is called the rotation group and denoted by 𝒮​𝒪​(3)\operatorname{\mathcal{SO}(3)}. For simplicity, we also refer to 𝒮​𝒪​(3)\operatorname{\mathcal{SO}(3)} as the orientation space in the following. Crystallographic texture is then described as a distribution of orientations on 𝒮​𝒪​(3)\operatorname{\mathcal{SO}(3)}. The mathematical foundations of orientations and their symmetries, their different representations, and orientation distributions have been developed in detail by Bunge [5] and Morawiec [20].

Assigning such a rotation vector to every orientation yields a vector field f→:𝒮​𝒪​(3)→ℝ3\mathaccent 382{f}\colon\operatorname{\mathcal{SO}(3)}\to{\mathbb{R}}^{3} whose three component functions are ordinary scalar orientation-dependent functions, as discussed in Section 3. Crystal and specimen symmetries act on these components differently than on scalar functions, which is the subject of Section 4. Since the components are scalar functions, they can be expanded into generalized spherical harmonics and treated by the same harmonic tools as an ODF. This leads to the harmonic vector fields of Section 5. Finally, Section 6 shows that gradient, divergence, and curl can then be computed exactly and efficiently, directly from the harmonic coefficients.

papers.title: SurgCBVR: A Multi-Domain Benchmark for Content-Based Surgical Video-to-Video Retrieval
papers.abstract: Hospitals record thousands of hours of surgical video annually, yet these archives remain difficult to search by content. Surgeons cannot readily retrieve similar operations, complications, or workflow events. Existing surgical computer vision primarily produces labels rather than retrieving relevant videos. We introduce SurgCBVR, the first benchmark for content-based video-to-video retrieval in surgery. It integrates eight public datasets across four domains-ophthalmic, laparoscopic, robotic-assisted, and colonoscopy-covering six procedure types, 679 cases, and 76,489 clips (106 hours). SurgCBVR comprises two tiers: Scene, retrieving the same operative state across cases and sites, and Workflow, retrieving and localizing phase transitions and deviations. Scene includes 74,765 clips spanning 40 classes, three temporal granularities, and three playback speeds; Workflow contains 1,724 transition clips. Fixed clip lengths and frame counts, together with phase-classifier oracle and duration-only baselines, help assess label and timing shortcuts. We evaluate six generic and surgical foundation models, two video retrieval methods, and contrastive heads trained on SurgCBVR, using within-dataset, cross-dataset, and pooled-gallery retrieval restricted to the same procedure type. Frozen representations barely outperform a timing-only baseline, transition retrieval approaches chance, and trained heads lose up to half their accuracy across datasets. These findings expose substantial limitations in current video representations and establish SurgCBVR as a benchmark for advancing surgery-aware retrieval.

papers.title: Evergreen leaves and universal lifetime laws in preferential-attachment trees
papers.abstract: We study leaf lifetimes in general preferential-attachment trees. First we characterize the existence of evergreen leaves, that is, vertices that remain leaves forever. When no evergreen leaves exist, we establish, for a broad class of attachment functions, a remarkable one-parameter universality: the normalizations and limiting laws for various characteristics of leaf lifetimes depend on the attachment function only through a single numerical parameter. In particular, we obtain a shifted Pareto limit law for individual lifetimes and a joint functional limit theorem for the lifetime and label of the longest-lasting leaf. The limiting two-dimensional process, which we call the beta-decorated Fr\'echet extremal process, admits an elegant representation in terms of the Stoev--Taqqu extremal integral and the sets of optimal choices considered by Molchanov and Strokorb. We also establish a Poisson point-process limit for rescaled leaf lifetimes and corresponding labels, a finiteness criterion for long-lasting leaves, and a functional central limit theorem for their number at the critical threshold.

Preferential-attachment models, popularized by A.-L. Barabási and R. Albert [2] and subsequently extended in various directions, have become standard tools for studying the growth of complex systems, including the World Wide Web, social networks, and citation graphs. Their mechanism reflects the well-known “rich-get-richer” principle, whereby vertices with more connections are more likely to attract new ones. Much of the literature has focused on structural and geometric properties of these networks, including asymptotic degree distributions [5, 23], maximal degrees [19], tree profiles [12, 15], as well as local and scaling limits [3, 6]. In this paper, we focus on preferential-attachment trees and study a different, inherently temporal aspect of their evolution: how long vertices remain leaves and whether some do so forever.

papers.title: Welop\=o'ai: A peculiar triple system 8 pc from the Sun
papers.abstract: Context. We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf companion to the M4 V dwarf Welopo'ai Aa (IRAS 21500+5903) during a radial-velocity search for exoplanets with SPIRou. The system is located at 8.46 pc and forms a hierarchical triple with a more distant white dwarf, which has no known analogue within 30 pc. Aims. We characterise the orbital architecture and component masses through a joint Keplerian fit of radial velocities and astrometry, derive the physical parameters of the M dwarf and both white dwarfs, and discuss the implications for common-envelope evolution and hierarchical triple dynamics. Methods. We obtained radial velocity measurements with SPIRou spread over 4.8 yr, revealing a large-amplitude signal ($\sim$16 km/s peak-to-peak) that is inconsistent with planetary companions. Follow-up speckle imaging with 'Alopeke at Gemini North and near-infrared (NIR) imaging with GNIRS confirmed a white dwarf companion at sub-arcsecond separation. Results. The system comprises an inner binary with a semi-major axis of $4.644 \pm 0.017$ au ($P \approx 9.83$ yr), consisting of the primary M4 V ($M = 0.4189^{+0.0073}_{-0.0072} M_\odot$) and a white dwarf companion ($M = 0.6180^{+0.0046}_{-0.0045} M_\odot$, $T_{\rm eff} \sim 5210 \pm 320$ K, cooling age 5.3-5.5 Gyr). This inner pair lies at a projected separation of 123.9 au ($P > 1000$ yr) from a previously known white dwarf. The dynamically determined mass of the inner white dwarf is one of only a handful of such measurements for white dwarfs within 20 pc, and the most precise, at the sub-percent (0.7%) level. Conclusions. This system is the closest known triple containing multiple white dwarfs and offers direct dynamical constraints on common-envelope evolution and hierarchical triple stability. Furthermore, a tentative near-infrared (IR) excess towards the inner white dwarf further hints at circumstellar dust.

papers.intro:
Serendipity has long played a key role in astronomy, offering insights into new phenomena, from Galileo’s unexpected observation of Jupiter’s four largest moons with his newly constructed refractor telescope in 1610 (Galilei 1610) to Herschel’s discovery of Uranus, which he first reported as a comet when examining faint stars as part of his observations on stellar parallax (Herschel 1781). More recent examples include the discovery of Boyajian’s Star (KIC 8462852) through a citizen science examination of Kepler photometry (Boyajian et al. 2016) and the detection of the interstellar object 1I/’Oumuamua (Meech et al. 2017).

More recent examples include the discovery of Boyajian’s Star (KIC 8462852) through a citizen science examination of Kepler photometry (Boyajian et al. 2016) and the detection of the interstellar object 1I/’Oumuamua (Meech et al. 2017).

Serendipity is an accepted mode of progress in observational astronomy (de Rond & Morley 2010). Surveys of large samples, whatever their primary goal, frequently yield unexpected discoveries (Norris 2017) and radial-velocity (RV) surveys for exoplanets are no exception. The discovery of the first exoplanet orbiting a main sequence star (Mayor & Queloz 1995) was unexpected: formation models placed giant planets beyond ∼\sim5 au, on orbits of a decade or longer, but the survey instead revealed a hot Jupiter on a 4.2 d4.2\text{\,}\mathrm{d} orbit, a configuration that these models had not anticipated. This discovery reshaped our understanding of planetary system architectures and demonstrated the power of high-precision RV monitoring to reveal unexpected configurations.

We report the serendipitous discovery of a white dwarf (WD) companion to an M dwarf in the solar vicinity (d∼8d\sim 8 pc), uncovered during a blind RV planet search. The system is unique among nearby examples: it is a hierarchical triple made of one M dwarf and two WDs, in which the M dwarf may have survived common-envelope evolution and it has no known analogue within 30 pc30\text{\,}\mathrm{pc}. The discovery via RV is discussed in Sect. 2, the activity of the M dwarf in Sect. 3.1, direct imaging follow-up in Sect. 3.2, Keplerian orbital fitting in Sect. 3.3, and the properties of the M dwarf and of the inner WD are presented in Sects. 3.4 and 3.5, respectively. We discuss the secular evolution of the system in Sect. 4 and present our conclusions in Sect. 5.

papers.title: Cumulant Generating Function of the Hill-Lane-Sudderth urn model
papers.abstract: We consider the Hill, Lane and Sudderth urn, in which a black or white ball is added at each step with probabilities depending on the current proportion of black balls. We solve the equation for the limiting normalized cumulant generating function when the urn function is invertible on the outer branches beyond the fixed points and the corresponding inverses are Lipschitz. The solution has a parametric representation through three quadratures of the urn function and a limit of compositions of radicals, with no derivatives or inverses of the urn function in the final formula. We prove an error bound that does not accumulate along the partition and remains valid when starting from the initial singularity. Four examples with exact solutions illustrate the two orientations of the construction, the non-affine case and the presence of zeros.

papers.intro:
The Hill, Lane and Sudderth (HLS) urn is a two-color reinforcement model: one ball is added at each step, and the probabilities of the two colors depend on the current composition [1]. The current proportion thus summarizes the past additions, while the urn function determines how this history influences the next addition. Varying this response gives a common mathematical description of growth processes arising in different settings [2, 3].

Among these processes are leaf counts in random trees [4] and elephant random walks with either one or a fixed number of draws with replacement from the past [5, 6]. Nonlinear responses arise naturally when past choices affect subsequent preferences. In technological diffusion, current market shares influence later adoptions through positive or negative feedback [7]; increasing returns and social influence can produce competing long-run outcomes [8]. When return weights are proportional to a common power of wealth, the two-agent model with wages [9] also has an autonomous urn description. Each allocation of the capital return is an urn addition, with a probability determined by the current wealth shares. Deterministic wages make accumulated wealth an affine transformation of the urn count, so its fluctuations can be studied through the same process [3].

In irreversible magnetic growth, spins are added with probabilities determined by the accumulated magnetization [10]. A nonlinear response can sustain competing magnetizations, making the distribution of growth histories relevant even when the fixed points are known. Related competition occurs between two growing neuronal extensions, or neurites [11]. Pólya urn models have also been used to describe distributions of enantiomeric excess in asymmetric autocatalysis [12]. The review [3] develops cooperative nonlinear production rules as further illustrative urn models with several possible final compositions.

Nonlinear urns also describe the accumulation of information. In broadcasting on growing recursive graphs, a new vertex samples a fixed odd number of earlier vertices, at least three, uniformly with replacement. Each sampled color is independently flipped with a probability strictly between zero and one half, and the new color is chosen by majority vote [13]. The probability of choosing a given color is therefore a polynomial of its current fraction, and the urn records the number of vertices of each color. In reinforced recommendation, the reduction to one user and two items gives an urn with power-law reinforcement [14, 3]. Related feedback rules govern which new observations are added to a stored memory, as discussed in the review. A different response arises in urns with triggering: discovering an element expands the set of available elements [15]. This mechanism leads to a rational limiting urn response for the count of distinct discoveries, such as new words in a text. The comparison of history probabilities in [3] justifies transferring the limiting free energy to this autonomous HLS description.

For random walks and polymers, the accumulated observable can also be geometric. The range counts distinct visited sites; at a fixed length it determines the number of steps returning to old sites. Conditional continuation probabilities reproduce this return-count distribution, linking urns to the Stanley polymer model [16]. The same range statistics determine survival in the Rosenstock problem with random traps, while the zero-return sector selects self-avoiding walks [3]. Attractive interactions require the additional contact statistic, as in the study of interacting self-avoiding polymers [17]. These correspondences concern the distributions of counts; applying the autonomous HLS theory requires control of the limiting urn function and of the relevant boundary regimes [3].

For continuous urn functions, the basic asymptotic picture is given by almost sure convergence of the color proportion to a fixed point [1, 18]. Which limiting behaviors are possible depends on the local shape of the response, as illustrated by convergence to points of tangency [19] and by critical behavior in nonlinear urns [20]. Together with the characterization of the exchangeable cases [21], these results describe typical outcomes and special structures of reinforced growth. The fixed points alone do not determine the exponential cost of other final compositions. Our concern is how weighting these compositions changes the balance between growth histories. This leads to the growth of exponential moments and hence to the free energy studied below.

papers.title: Blanket theory for dense networks
papers.abstract: We show how Blanket theory provides a constructive method for calculating cavity functionals in dense spin networks. Building on the description through interfaces and magnetization shells, we develop the calculation from the low-temperature fluctuations around the ground state. In this regime, dilute defects reveal the mechanism of random energy model (REM) universality for linear energies, while their sharing and renewal across layers organize the energies and Gibbs weights into a hierarchy. Because the same configurations determine the covariances of the fresh cavity fields, this construction identifies the fields and weights with an Aizenman-Sims-Starr random overlap structure. The cavity contributions can then be evaluated through recursive fractional means, yielding an explicit free-energy functional parametrized by layer magnetizations and hierarchical exponents, with coefficients determined by the interaction variances and the network normalization. Under the stated moment and normalization conditions, comparison of pressures transfers the limiting mean pressure from the Gaussian representative to networks with independent centered non-Gaussian couplings having the same variances. We illustrate the method with the deterministic Curie-Weiss model, recover the Parisi functional for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, and derive the functionals for restricted and deep Boltzmann machines, including the full replica symmetry breaking (fullRSB) limit.

papers.intro:
Blanket theory [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] describes spin networks by organizing their interactions according to a partition of the sites. Each layer contributes a core of internal couplings and an interface connecting it to the preceding layers. In dense systems, refinement makes the internal contribution negligible under the appropriate scaling conditions, leading to a thermodynamic description through interfaces and states of fixed magnetization. The purpose of the present work is to show how this description can be used to construct and calculate cavity functionals. We thus continue the development of Ref. [4] by making explicit the connection between the decomposition of the interactions and the calculation of free energy.

The constructive cavity method (CCM) uses the layer decomposition to calculate the Parisi functional for the Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) model [1]. The kernel representation makes the organization of the states and their weights explicit [2], while the description of low-temperature excitations around the ground state provides the physical justification for the construction [6]. We follow that mechanism here. Once the core contribution has been controlled, rectification on the ground state describes these excitations as a dilute gas of defects, whose number in each layer is fixed by its magnetization. Controlling the term bilinear in the defects reduces the fluctuations to linear energies and reveals the mechanism of random energy model (REM) universality [3, 7, 8]. Descendants inherit the defects and energy contributions of their ancestors, while new branches introduce new fluctuations. This organization provides the physical basis for the hierarchical description of the energies and Gibbs weights, developed first with finitely many defects and then extended to exponential populations of states.

The usefulness of this hierarchy for cavity calculations comes from its joint description of the weights and fields. Counting states with energies near the edge determines the exponents of the hierarchical masses; their Poisson representation [9] then makes averages over these masses calculable through fractional means. This gives the functional (4.16), parametrized by layer magnetizations and hierarchical exponents. The common component of the linear field remains in the terminal function and is integrated after the hierarchical averages. Averaging the cavity contributions along a growing family of networks connects this calculation to the thermodynamic pressure.

papers.title: Reconciling Models for Infinite-Layer Nickelate Superconductors: Role of Interstitial-$s$ Band or $A$-Pocket
papers.abstract: Understanding the minimal model that captures the essential physics of infinite-layer nickelate superconductors remains a central challenge. Using first-principles density-functional theory combined with dynamical mean-field theory (DFT+DMFT), we compute and compare the strongly correlated electronic structures and optical spectra of various effective models for the infinite-layer nickelate LaNiO$_2$, ranging from a $d_{x^2-y^2}$ 1-band model to a full 6-band model with all Ni-$3d$ plus an interstitial-$s$ orbital. The results demonstrate that Ni-$3d$ 5-band models overestimate the Hundness picture, whereas 6-band models, which explicitly include the interstitial-$s$ band and have an $A$-pocket, recover the characteristic Mottness physics. Importantly, the influence of the interstitial-$s$ band on the correlations of the $d_{x^2-y^2}$ band is negligible. Thus, superconductivity in infinite-layer nickelates can be reliably described within a single-band Hubbard framework, while the accurate description of inter-orbital properties such as (optical) conductivities requires the inclusion of at least the interstitial-$s$ band.

papers.title: Norm Approximation with Linear Growth of Error for Bosonic Dynamics in the Mean-Field Regime
papers.abstract: We consider the quantum many-body dynamics of a homogeneous confined Bose gas in three dimensions in the mean-field scaling regime. We study the Cauchy problem for a class of initial data describing finitely many excitations over a Bose-Einstein condensate. Using a rigorous version of Bogolyubov's theory, we prove that the many-body evolution can be approximated in Fock space norm by a quasifree evolution of the excitations with an error which grows linearly in time. In distinction from earlier results, the slow growth in time holds even though the effective equation is not dispersive.

papers.title: A Lie-Group Approach to Alfv\'enic Turbulence: The SO(3) Rotational p-model
papers.abstract: The inner heliosphere is permeated by fully developed, highly intermittent nonlinear turbulence. Conventional stochastic models synthesize these multiscale fluctuations by injecting additive noise within a flat Euclidean space. However, such approaches fundamentally violate the topological constraints of ideal magnetohydrodynamics, inadvertently breaking the kinetic incompressibility of the plasma and introducing spurious magnetic compressibility. To preserve the exact geometrical invariants of Alfv\'enic fluctuations, a novel mathematical framework is presented: the rotational p-model. By mapping a multifractal singular measure directly into the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ and integrating the associated stochastic differential equations in the Stratonovich sense on the spherical manifold $S^{2}$, the model generates highly intermittent, scale-dependent rotational dynamics. This Lie-group formulation conserves the magnetic field modulus while perfectly reproducing the fractional spectral envelopes and the non-Gaussian directional intermittency observed in space plasmas. Furthermore, by isolating purely directional reorientations, the framework provides exact analytical control over the waiting time statistics of magnetic intermittent bursts and the multifractal scaling exponents of angular deflections, offering a powerful new paradigm for the study of nonlinear turbulent phenomena.

Early attempts to build solenoidal and incompressive magnetic fluctuations were able to reduce the fluctuations’ amplitude to a few percent (Roberts, 2012), which was more recently further reduced to less than 1%1\% (Valentini et al., 2019). papers.title: Proof of the polygonal Saint-Venant inequality conjectured by P\'olya--Szeg\"o
papers.abstract: We prove the polygonal Saint--Venant inequality conjectured by P\'olya and Szeg\"o: for every $n\geq 3$, among (possibly non--convex) polygons of prescribed area with at most $n$ sides, the regular $n$-gon uniquely maximizes torsional rigidity. The proof is purely analytic and stems from the local version of the result given in our previous paper: it combines an area--angle proportional partition of a polygon, inspired by Solynin and Zalgaller, with a sharp comparison for the mixed torsional rigidity of the partition cells, and with an angular concavity property of this functional on the class of isosceles triangles.

papers.title: Discovery of HEC14: an ultra-faint stellar system in M31's outer halo at the globular cluster-dwarf galaxy boundary
papers.abstract: We present the discovery of HEC14, an ultra-faint stellar system near M31, visually identified in the Pan-Andromeda Archaeological Survey and characterised with deeper OSIRIS+@GTC imaging. HEC14's colour-magnitude diagram shows a clear red giant branch and a well-populated blue horizontal branch, indicating old (>10 Gyr), metal poor stellar populations. We find 912$^{+88}_{-80}$ kpc to be the best-fitting heliocentric distance to the satellite, consistent with M31's outer halo. With $M_{V} \sim -5.00^{+0.51}_{-0.44}$ and a half-light radius of $r_{\rm h} \sim 31^{+13}_{-9}$pc HEC14 lies in the size-luminosity gap between globular clusters and dwarf galaxies. The satellite therefore sits in the extended clusters (EC) regime, making it one of the faintest ECs discovered yet in M31. HEC14 is a new member of M31's halo EC population, whose origins remain unclear two decades after their discovery. We serendipitously find that HEC14's size and luminosity match theoretical predictions for dwarf galaxies with globular cluster-like sizes. Star formation history and/or spectroscopic studies are required to determine whether HEC14 (and possibly all ECs) is genuinely an extended globular cluster or a compact dwarf galaxy.

papers.intro:
Historically, dwarf galaxies and globular clusters (GCs) were considered two distinct classes with little debate on their definitions. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies (dSphs) were regarded as extended systems (half-light radius rh>100r_{h}>100 pc) formed in the early Universe, with prolonged star formation histories (SFHs) and high dynamical-to-stellar mass ratios owing to the presence of a dark matter (DM) halo (e.g., Aaronson 1983; Grebel 1997). GCs, on the other hand, were viewed as compact (rh∼1−10r_{h}\sim 1-10 pc) low-mass systems composed of a chemically homogeneous stellar population, with light element abundance variations unique to GCs only (see Kraft 1994 and references therein), showing no dynamical evidence for DM (e.g., Illingworth 1976; Peterson & Latham 1986). Although the two classes span similar luminosities, measuring their apparent sizes was typically sufficient to cleanly separate the two in the luminosity-size plane.

GCs, on the other hand, were viewed as compact (rh∼1−10r_{h}\sim 1-10 pc) low-mass systems composed of a chemically homogeneous stellar population, with light element abundance variations unique to GCs only (see Kraft 1994 and references therein), showing no dynamical evidence for DM (e.g., Illingworth 1976; Peterson & Latham 1986). Although the two classes span similar luminosities, measuring their apparent sizes was typically sufficient to cleanly separate the two in the luminosity-size plane.

The first challenge to these definitions came from the discovery of ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs) in the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS; Abazajian et al. 2009). These diffuse, unusually faint systems quickly filled the size gap between GCs and dSphs (e.g., Willman et al. 2005a; Willman et al. 2005b; Belokurov et al. 2006; Zucker et al. 2006) and it was not immediately clear that UFDs were galaxies until the presence of DM was spectroscopically confirmed (e.g. Simon & Geha 2007). UFDs are now known to be the least luminous, least massive (MV>M_{V}> –7.7, M∗≤105​M⊙M_{*}\leq 10^{5}M_{\odot}; see Simon 2019 for a review) and the most DM-dominated galaxies to exist (Bullock & Boylan-Kolchin 2017). UFDs constitute the relics of the earliest galaxies having formed most of their stars before the epoch of reionisation (e.g.Gnedin & Kravtsov 2006) as reflected in their short SFHs and very low metallicities ([Fe/H] ≲−2.2\lesssim-2.2; e.g., Kirby et al. 2011; Weisz et al. 2026). As the depth and sensitivity of wide-field sky surveys improved (e.g., PanSTARRS: Chambers et al. 2016; the Dark Energy Survey: DES Collaboration et al. 2016; the DESI Legacy Survey: Dey et al. 2019; DELVE: Drlica-Wagner et al. 2021; Drlica-Wagner et al. 2022; UNIONS: Gwyn et al. 2025) new discoveries of Milky Way (MW) UFDs and hyper-faint GCs rapidly populated the size-luminosity plane down to extreme luminosities of MV∼M_{V}\sim 0 (Pace 2025). Fainter than MV∼−4M_{V}\sim-4, however, UFDs are comparable in size to the most extended MW GCs (rh≲30r_{h}\lesssim 30 pc) and spectroscopy is required to segregate these systems, sometimes with fewer than 10 stars to test for a metallicity spread or DM (e.g., Cerny et al. 2026). Each new UFD or ancient GC is therefore a valuable test of the role of DM in small-scale structure formation.

We currently know of stellar systems down to MV∼−4M_{V}\sim-4 for our nearest massive neighbour, Andromeda. Wide-field surveys with 4-m class telescopes struggle to find satellites fainter than MV∼−6M_{V}\sim-6 given that, at the distance of M31 (776 kpc, Savino et al. 2022), these telescopes are typically able to resolve red giant branch (RGB) stars only. Such faint satellites usually have very few RGB stars, necessitating deeper follow up imaging for their characterisation with either 10-m class telescopes (which reach the horizontal branch, HB) or with very deep space photometry (down to the oldest main-sequence turnoff). The emergence of so-called "extended clusters" in M31 (ECs: Huxor et al. 2005; Mackey et al. 2006; Huxor et al. 2011; Tanvir et al. 2012; Mackey et al. 2013; Huxor et al. 2014), populating the gap between GCs and UFDs (15≤rh≤3515\leq r_{h}\leq 35 pc; −8≤MV≤−5-8\leq M_{V}\leq-5), provoked special interest. First, while the faintest ECs overlap with the MW’s Palomar-type GCs, no MW counterparts are known for the four brightest M31 ECs (EC1, EC2, EC3, EC411 1 We note that ECs1-4 were renamed to HEC5, HEC7, HEC4, HEC12 (Halo Extended Clusters) by Huxor et al. (2011) to reflect their location in the M31 halo.). Second, it remains to be convincingly demonstrated that all 13 ECs are indeed GCs- only the brightest ECs have been shown to be predominantly old and metal-poor, with no metallicity spread detected (down to the HB; Mackey et al. 2006). Similarly, no kinematic study has yet ruled out the presence of DM (Collins et al. 2009; Veljanoski et al. 2014).

papers.title: A curvature-corrected port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model for dissipative sloshing with contact-line hysteresis in low-gravity tanks
papers.abstract: A physics-based reduced-order model unifies curved-meniscus inertia, viscous losses and nonsmooth contact-line stick-slip in a passive port-Hamiltonian formulation for lateral sloshing in cylindrical tanks. Dirichlet-Neumann and Jacobi operators describe inertia and restoring forces, while a convex potential combines bulk, Stokes-layer and contact-line dissipation. Analytical propagation between stick-slip events supports faster-than-real-time simulation of coupled spacecraft translation and sloshing. The viscous closure agrees within 5% with a reference Stokes calculation, and the model reproduces the Henderson-Miles modal measurements and the Cocciaro hysteretic decay. Across 42 drop-tower and ground measurements, curvature correction reduces the root-mean-square frequency error from 24 to 4%. For flight and ground tests from the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE), frequency errors range from 0.9 to 7.1%, while ideal contact lines underestimate the damping ratios from the MODE fits by 38-87%. One hysteresis width, calibrated on the lowest orbital water excitation, predicts higher orbital excitations and the ground test with normalised force errors of 11-35%, against 149-208% for an ideal pinned line. It predicts 8.5% resonance softening against 7.3% measured, which the tested one-parameter damping laws miss. Uncertain wetting and remaining response discrepancies motivate damping ranges in spacecraft control analyses.

papers.intro:
Liquid propellant can represent a large fraction of spacecraft mass, and its motion couples to attitude control, docking and in-orbit refuelling [1, 2]. Guidance, navigation and control (GNC) design relies on fast, energy-consistent equivalent pendulum and mass–spring models, whose parameters follow from flat-interface theory when the Bond number 𝐵𝑜=ρ​g​R2/σ\mathit{Bo}=\rho gR^{2}/\sigma is large, with ρ\rho the liquid density, σ\sigma the surface tension, gg the axial acceleration and RR the tank radius. In orbit the Bond number of a 0.50.5\,m water tank falls from about 10410^{4} to below one. The liquid then rests beneath a curved meniscus selected by the static contact angle θc\theta_{c} [3], and the parameters require curved-interface modelling or calibration [4, 5, 6]. Flight and drop-tower campaigns, from the NASA drop-tower tests [7] and the Middeck 0-Gravity Dynamics Experiment (MODE) [8, 9] to Sloshsat-FLEVO, SPHERES-Slosh, FLUIDICS and ferrofluid experiments [10, 11, 12, 13], highlight uncertainties in contact-line modelling [14, 15]. Meniscus-dependent sloshing also couples to spacecraft pitching and flexible appendages [16]. Interface-resolving computational fluid dynamics (CFD), when validated for the relevant flow regime, can simulate spacecraft manoeuvres [11], although its computational cost can limit repeated GNC analyses and real-time applications.

Curved-interface spectra and edge constraints have established low-gravity formulations [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. In Zakharov–Craig–Sulem variables [22, 23], curvature appears in two explicit operators, the Dirichlet–Neumann (DN) map of the curved domain and the Jacobi operator of the meniscus. The conservative formulation of Cassoni [24] recovers the curved-meniscus benchmark trends of Kopachevskii [3] and separates the kinetic and capillary contributions to wetting/non-wetting asymmetry. Damping and forced response add boundary layers [25], corner and capillary layers [26, 27], and contact-line friction and hysteresis [28, 29]. Utsumi [30], Utsumi [31] added the work of the wall boundary layer and of a contact-line friction force to the low-gravity modal equation and found that friction damping grows markedly as the Bond number decreases. Port-Hamiltonian shallow-water models couple sloshing and flexible structures [32]. Viscous slip-length models with a hysteretic contact law [33] and successive modal projections for stick–slip relaxation [34] cover parts of this physics.

This work extends the conservative curved-meniscus formulation of Cassoni [24] to dissipative lateral sloshing in low-Bond cylindrical tanks, incorporating bulk and Stokes-layer losses together with nonsmooth contact-line hysteresis. The same curved-domain harmonic fields determine inertia and viscous dissipation, while a convex contact-line potential introduces linear resistance and stick–slip dynamics within a port-Hamiltonian reduced-order model. The inclusion is passive on the admissible discrete space and propagated analytically between stick–slip events. Unlike the friction-work model of Utsumi [31], it resolves stick phases and their effects on frequency, force phase and damping. One width calibrated on the lowest orbital MODE excitation predicts two higher excitations and the ground response, including softening missed by the tested linear and quadratic damping laws. A design chart supplies frequencies and slosh masses, with frequencies checked against independent drop-tower data. Pole ranges quantify contact-line sensitivity across gravity levels.

papers.title: A variational approach to an anisotropic nonlocal porous medium equation with drift
papers.abstract: We study nonlocal porous-medium equations driven by anisotropic Riesz-type repulsive interactions and an external confining potential. The pressure is determined by convolution with an interaction potential of the form $$ W(x)=|x|^{-s}\Omega\left(\frac{x}{|x|}\right), \qquad d-2<s<d, $$ where $\Omega$ is a smooth, even, and strictly positive angular profile. For quadratic confinement and $s\in(d-2,d)\cap(0,5]$, under suitable positivity assumptions on the anisotropic kernels, we prove that the unique energy minimizer is the only steady state among bounded continuous probability densities. We then establish the long-time convergence of global weak solutions to this equilibrium, both locally and globally in H\"older norms. To obtain these results, we derive uniform $L^p$, $L^\infty$, and H\"older estimates, adapting the regularity theory for fractional porous-medium equations to the anisotropic setting. We also construct global weak solutions through a minimizing-movement scheme in Wasserstein space, establish the corresponding energy-dissipation inequality, and prove a Talagrand-type transport inequality.

papers.title: Effect of scrape-off losses and current flattening on runaway electron dynamics in ARC
papers.abstract: Disruptions in high-current tokamaks, such as ARC, may result in megaampere-scale runaway electron currents. In this work, we evaluate mitigation strategies via massive material injection, accounting for the combined impact of scrape-off losses due to vertical displacement events and current profile relaxation during the thermal quench. We find that scrape-off losses alone yield only modest reductions in runaway electron currents, but combining them with current flattening creates a beneficial synergistic effect. The latter broadens the current channel outward, shifting efficient runaway electron generation closer to the plasma edge where the dynamically contracting boundary can effectively scrape off the electron beams. This interplay significantly expands the operational window for mitigation toward lower assimilated densities, theoretically reducing runaway currents to manageable levels at experimentally feasible assimilated quantities.

papers.intro:
One of the challenges in designing a viable tokamak fusion power plant is the mitigation of plasma disruptions; events where thermal and magnetic confinement are rapidly lost (Hender et al., 2007; Sweeney et al., 2020). Disruptions pose severe risks to the structural integrity of a reactor via three primary mechanisms: intense, localized heat loads on plasma-facing components during the thermal quench (TQ); large electromagnetic forces from eddy and halo currents during the current quench (CQ); and the generation of a relativistic beam of runaway electrons (REs) capable of causing damage upon wall impact (Hollmann et al., 2015).

To mitigate these hazards, baseline disruption mitigation systems (DMS) for next-step devices rely on massive material injection (MMI) to rapidly radiate away thermal energy and control the subsequent current decay. Such mitigation strategies are being extensively studied on present-day tokamaks (Commaux et al., 2011; Bakhtiari et al., 2011; Lehnen et al., 2015; Reux et al., 2015; Pautasso et al., 2015; Pautasso et al., 2017; Eidietis et al., 2017; Shiraki et al., 2016; Commaux et al., 2016; Herfindal et al., 2019; Sheikh et al., 2021; Sheikh et al., 2024; Jachmich et al., 2021). This has motivated the widespread use of reduced-dimensionality tools, such as the 1D fluid-kinetic framework DREAM (Hoppe et al., 2021).

papers.title: A GPU-Native Nested Sampling Framework for Finite-Temperature Materials Modelling with Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
papers.abstract: Modern equivariant machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have dramatically improved the accuracy of and the scales accessible to atomistic simulation, yet the thermodynamic sampling methods needed to turn those potentials into finite-temperature phase stability predictions have not kept pace computationally. We present the GPU-native, massively parallel nested sampling framework JAXRENS, implemented on top of JAX, which removes the practical bottlenecks preventing atomistic nested sampling from being combined with state-of-the-art MLIPs. The framework provides distributed multi-GPU execution, vectorised ensembles of walkers, and direct interoperability with modern force fields. We demonstrate the highly beneficial scaling of JAXRENS on hardware accelerators, and apply it to the simulation of the ZnS phase diagram based on a MACE foundation model, a procedure previously computationally inaccessible. Despite requiring in the order of 10^10 model evaluations, the final converged simulation completed within six days on four GPUs, marking an important step towards routine, first-principles-quality predictions of finite-temperature phase stability using machine-learned interatomic potentials.

Over the past several years, machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs), and in particular equivariant message-passing architectures [6, 7], have transformed atomistic simulation by delivering near first-principles accuracy at a small fraction of the cost. More recently, the field has moved towards foundation models: potentials pre-trained on vast, chemically diverse datasets that aim to describe much of the structural and chemical spaces out of the box and offer the possibility to be fine-tuned for specific systems [5, 22].

The thermodynamic sampling needed to turn state-of-the-art MLIPs into finite-temperature predictions, however, remains a computational bottleneck. Converging a single free energy requires a very large number of energy and force evaluations, and a phase diagram multiplies that cost across many temperatures, pressures, and compositions. Over the past decade, nested sampling (NS), originally introduced for Bayesian evidence computation[32], has emerged as a powerful tool for addressing this challenge [28, 3]. By directly evaluating the partition function, nested sampling can provide the free energy and other thermodynamic observables across an entire temperature range from a single run. Crucially for materials applications, it captures phase transitions without predefined order parameters or prior knowledge of the competing phases. These strengths have enabled applications ranging from pressure–temperature phase diagrams of bulk solids [3, 2, 24, 35, 13, 19] to surface phase behaviour and molecular clusters [41, 29].

The independent evolutions of the NS walkers are inherently parallel. However, existing NS implementations are difficult to combine with GPU-native workflows, modern MLIPs, distributed hardware, and large atomistic systems. Established atomistic NS codes, like pymatnest [8] and the more recent FreeBird.jl [41], are CPU-oriented and were not designed to exploit the massively parallel throughput of modern accelerators. Meanwhile, differentiable, GPU-native engines such as JAX-MD [31], and more recently torch-sim [15] and kUPS [16], have demonstrated the value of running many independent systems as batched, vectorised computations for atomistic simulations. While these efforts mainly target molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo, and structural relaxation, they signal a broader shift towards batched, accelerator-native sampling.

papers.title: Validating Concurrent Correctness Witnesses with Ghosts by Thread-Modular Abstract Interpretation
papers.abstract: Concurrent programs are notoriously difficult to write and to reason about, and even tools based on sound theoretical foundations can produce incorrect results due to implementation bugs. Correctness witnesses have been proposed as a way to increase the confidence in the verdicts of software verifiers by enabling independent validation. Recently, correctness witnesses have been extended to the concurrent setting, by introducing ghost variables to allow encoding more expressive invariants. While different approaches to producing witnesses with ghosts exist, validation techniques are still lacking; instead of leveraging the information encoded in the ghosts to guide the validation process, validators merely treat ghost instrumentation and invariants over ghost variables as additional proof obligations. We propose a novel framework for the validation of concurrent correctness witnesses that exploits the semantic information encoded in ghost variables. It combines a checking phase, which establishes the semantic content of the ghost instrumentation, with an exploitation phase making use of this information. Both phases are formulated as thread-modular abstract interpretation. In particular, we consider two different classes of ghost variables and techniques for exploiting them, one based on resource invariants and one based on phases. Phase ghosts guide the degree to which the abstract interpretation considers interleavings instead of always abstracting them coarsely. In this way, the abstract interpreter can validate witnesses containing invariants beyond the reach of unguided thread-modular analysis, while still retaining its scalability benefits. We have implemented our framework in a static analyzer and evaluate it on witnesses encoding resource invariants obtained from a state-of-the-art software verifier, as well as on hand-crafted witnesses encoding phase information.

papers.intro:
Concurrent programs are prone to subtle bugs. This has prompted the development of a wide range of automated techniques, from those that catch bugs during execution such as fuzzing or dynamic analysis, to sound approaches that can establish the absence of bugs by considering all possible executions. The latter class encompasses approaches as diverse as those based on commutativity reasoning, automata-based model checking, Petri nets, sequentialization, or abstract interpretation. While the underlying theories are elegant and simple, their implementations are often in large and complex (Cousot et al., 2009; Monat et al., 2024; Baudin et al., 2021; Beyer and Rosenfeld, 2026; Saan et al., 2024a) software systems. Thus, even tools firmly based on a sound theory have been shown to occasionally produce incorrect results (see, e.g., (Kaindlstorfer et al., 2024; Erhard et al., 2025; Klinger et al., 2019; Vishwanathan et al., 2023) for some recent work that has identified implementation bugs in mature static analyzers).

papers.title: 44 Tropen by Josef Matthias Hauer as orbits under the group of interval shifts
papers.abstract: We generate a splitting of the 924 monotonically ascending twelve tone half series H=(H_1,..,H_6) in [0,..,11]^6 in 80 orbits H^G under the additive cyclic group G=Z/12Z of transpositions (interval shifts). By classification according to cardinality and forming the union of the orbits H^G and K^G of a half series H and its complement K, we obtain exactly the 44 Tropen by Josef Matthias Hauer, completely independent of symmetry properties, however, fundamentally due to so-called wider-gleiche orbits. This was not clear in previous literature.
papers.intro:
Here, we neither touch upon the neo-Riemannian operations (NRO) [3] nor the uniform triadic transformations (UTT) [7], which provide a way for the description of the chronological harmonic evolution of a musical work of art. However, we presuppose a familiarity with the foundations of both of these theories. Both are based on the concept of triads, which we recall in section §2 concerning pitch classes and their transpositions and inversion. In section §3, we deliver an exact mathematical proof for the precise number of 4444 Tropen, which J. M. Hauer [5, 6] developed as phrases in the sense of a flexible ground material for the composition of twelve tone plays, independently of the chronological harmonic evolution. This clarifies expositions in previous literature.

papers.title: Playing the SMR Game with Existential Honesty
papers.abstract:
State machine replication protocols are usually proven secure in the honest-Byzantine setting, which requires an honest supermajority of validators. Deployed systems offer no such guarantee: validators participate for profit and may deviate from the protocol whenever doing so increases their gains. In our work, every validator is rational or Byzantine, and none is honest. Rational validators may collude with each other and with the Byzantine ones, who may also bribe them to deviate. Known impossibility results show that, without honest validators, clients that decide whether to accept a transaction based on a non-interactive certificate and without further communication cannot be kept safe. To bypass these results, we let clients relay the certificates they receive to full nodes and wait before confirming transactions. We also assume that one full node, whose identity is unknown, is honest and always online.
  Under this assumption, we build a finalization layer over any certifiable quorum-based protocol in a synchronous network. Clients run an existing freezing gadget and fetch past certificates from the honest full node, which makes the protocol \emph{always-safe}: no two honest clients confirm conflicting ledgers, for any strategy of the validators. We incentivize participation through rewards, which the adversary may use to bribe rational validators into censoring transactions. In this setting, we formalize censorship and characterize it tightly: paying only with his rewards, the adversary censors less than a $\bw$ fraction of the available fees at each height, where $\bw$ is the fraction of the quorum he signs, and every coin of censorship beyond that comes from his own funds.

State machine replication (SMR) lets a set of validators agree on a single ordered log of transactions, and it is the core of proof-of-stake blockchains that today secure hundreds of billions of dollars. Quorum-based SMR protocols such as PBFT [11], Tendermint [10], and HotStuff [36] are typically analyzed in the honest-Byzantine setting: every validator either follows the protocol or deviates arbitrarily. These protocols remain safe and live as long as fewer than a third of the validators are Byzantine, so their security rests on an honest supermajority. Clients rely on the same assumption when they accept a transaction from a quorum certificate: the quorum is guaranteed to contain honest validators that have followed the protocol.

This setting may not describe how validators behave in deployed proof-of-stake systems. Validators participate for profit: they follow the protocol when doing so pays, and may deviate when they can earn more by doing so. An adversary may offer them a bribe to deviate, or validators may collude by pooling their stake and profiting from a double-spend. Thus, the honest supermajority may fail not because validators are intrinsically malicious, but because deviating has become more profitable than following the protocol. An analysis in the honest-Byzantine setting provides no guarantees in this case. This raises the question we study: what happens to the security of a quorum-based SMR protocol when every validator is rational or Byzantine, and no validator is assumed to be honest?

Rational and Byzantine validators. BAR [3] introduced a model with Byzantine, altruistic, and rational participants, and a line of work since then has studied consensus with rational validators [4, 5, 22, 18]. These works either assume that rational validators act independently or rule out collusion between rational and Byzantine validators against clients. Abraham et al. [1, 2] introduced solution concepts that allow coalitions of rational and Byzantine players, and TRAP [25] used these concepts to solve consensus on a single value by baiting rational players into exposing a coalition. In TRAP, the single-shot setting bounds the amount that can be double-spent against clients. Multi-shot state machine replication has no such bound, as shown by CoBRA [6]. CoBRA instead considers quorum-based SMR with silent clients and shows that, without honest validators, safety is impossible even in a synchronous network. Here, a silent client is one that decides whether to confirm a transaction based only on the certificates it receives, without communicating with other parties. Such a client cannot tell whether a certificate it sees belongs to a history that conflicts with one another client has accepted.

Safety beyond the honest majority. Another line of work keeps clients safe when Byzantine validators exceed the classic thresholds, by changing what clients do. Sridhar et al. [31] show that the achievable resilience depends on the client model, whether clients are sleepy or always on, and silent or communicating, and characterize it for each combination. In flexible BFT [21, 23], clients trade liveness for safety by requiring larger quorums. Better Safe than Sorry [32] introduces the freezing gadget we build on: a client that sees two conflicting histories confirms neither, which keeps clients safe under an adversarial majority, and a recovery procedure restores progress once an honest majority returns. Sridhar et al. prove the gadget safe against any number of adversarial validators when past messages reach a client that wakes [31, Theorem 4], and note that querying online parties provides this. Our safety theorem instantiates theirs with one honest full node. In both works liveness is lost while the adversary holds the majority, and in a purely Byzantine model this cannot be avoided, since Byzantine validators can simply stop voting.

Accountability and recovery. Accountable protocols [14, 30, 13, 24] identify the validators responsible for a safety violation so that their stake can be slashed, and recoverable protocols [26, 17, 20] restore a consistent state after a violation. Both act after the violation. Punishment deters a rational validator only when the gain from an attack is smaller than the stake it risks, and in multi-shot SMR the gain from a double-spend has no natural bound.

We quantify this effect: the share of the fees that the adversary earns by signing is exactly what he can spend on censorship at every height.

[34, Theorem 1] and Lewis-Pye and Roughgarden [19, Theorem 10.1] show that a client that joins late cannot then identify the correct history without further trust. Deployed systems therefore require a recent checkpoint [7] and bound the trusting period of light clients by the unbonding period [9]. We carry this bound over to rational validators and an honest full node, and show that it is exact.

Our work lies in the middle: we keep the Byzantine validators within the resilience of the underlying protocol, while every other validator is rational and may collude with the adversary; none is honest.

papers.title: Note on parallel transport of IHS manifolds of Kummer type
papers.abstract: We give a characterization of parallel transport operators for irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds of Kummer type.
papers.intro:
The Hodge-theoretic global Torelli theorem of Huybrechts–Markman–Verbitsky is a key tool to study irreducible holomorphic symplectic (IHS) manifolds via lattice theory. Let XX and YY be two IHS manifolds which are deformation equivalent. The aforementioned theorem implies that an invertible linear map g:H2​(Y,ℤ)→H2​(X,ℤ)g\colon H^{2}(Y,\mathbb{Z)}\to H^{2}(X,\mathbb{Z}) is induced by a biholomorphic (resp. bimeromorphic) map f:X⇢Yf\colon X\dashrightarrow Y, i.e. g=f∗g=f^{*} if and only if gg preserves the weight two Hodge structures, the Kähler cones (resp. fundamental exceptional chambers), the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki (BBF) quadratic forms and if gg is a parallel transport operator. papers.title: Cox rings of Jacobian elliptic surfaces of Kodaira dimension one
papers.abstract: We study Cox rings of relatively minimal semistable Jacobian elliptic surfaces over $\mathbb P^1$ with $\chi=\chi(\mathcal O_X)\ge3$ and finite Mordell--Weil group. When the Mori cone is generated by the zero section and the reducible-fiber components, we give a finite criterion for Cox-ring generation: a numerically determined set of nef classes must admit sections nonvanishing along the zero section. The criterion supplies a minimal homogeneous generating set without assuming finite generation in advance. We prove that its nonvanishing condition holds whenever $\sum_i n_i\le2\chi+4$, where $I_{n_i}$ are the reducible fibers; hence every such surface is a Mori dream surface. Independently of this condition, we exclude ample generator degrees throughout the stated cone range. We also determine the section--fiber subring and give minimal complete-intersection presentations when all $s$ reducible fibers have type $I_2$ and $s\le2\chi+1$, including the endpoint beyond that cone range.

papers.title: Faster polynomial-space algorithms for poset problems
papers.abstract: We give a polynomial-space, deterministic, exact algorithm for counting linear extensions of partial orders over $n$ elements, with running time $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n}) \subseteq O(2.829^n)$. This improves upon the long-standing bound of $O^*(4^{n})$ attainable by standard divide and conquer (Savitch 1970, Gurevich and Shelah 1987). Our algorithm uses a similar balanced splitting approach as the classical algorithm, but applies it only to the elements outside a largest antichain. For the elements of the antichain itself we develop a formula based on inclusion-exclusion that accounts for the ways in which they can appear in a linear extension. The technique is also applicable to other problems on posets, which we illustrate by solving the well-studied jump number problem in a similar running time of $O^*((2\sqrt{2})^{n})$ and polynomial space. To our knowledge, these are the first polynomial-space algorithms with a running time below $4^n$ for both problems.
