A partially ordered set (poset) 𝒫=(X,≺)\mathcal{P}=(X,\prec) consists of a ground set XX and a binary relation ≺\prec that describes precedences between elements of XX. Posets are often used to model the intermediate state of comparison-based algorithms (such as for sorting), when some pairs have already been compared (or their ordering inferred), while the ordering of other pairs is still unknown. The relation ≺\prec is asymmetric (a≺ba\prec b implies b⊀ab\not\prec a) and transitive (a≺ba\prec b and b≺cb\prec c imply a≺ca\prec c).

papers.title: A characterization of uniformly discrete crystalline measures with unit weights
papers.abstract: We prove that every uniformly discrete set $\emptyset\ne\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ admitting a Fourier summation formula with a discrete set of frequencies $S(\Lambda)\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ arises from the Alon--Kummer--Kurasov--Vinzant construction using a Lee--Yang variety. In particular, every crystalline measure with uniformly discrete support and unit weights is a Fourier quasicrystal coming from the above construction. It also implies that every set $\Lambda\subset\mathbb{R}^d\subset\mathbb{C}^d$ as above is the common zero set in $\mathbb{C}^d$ of finitely many trigonometric polynomials, extending the one-dimensional theorem of Olevskii and Ulanovskii. As part of the proof, we generalize Meyer's notion of lighthouse measures to higher codimension and introduce lighthouse manifolds, which we characterize, up to a monomial change of coordinates, as the torus parts of Lee--Yang varieties.

papers.title: Machine-learned potentials for iron oxides at extreme conditions
papers.abstract: Reliable phase stability requires accurate relative free energies, which small force errors alone do not guarantee. We develop atomic-cluster-expansion potentials for five iron oxides from Fe$_2$O to Fe$_2$O$_3$, covering crystalline and liquid states at 140--260\,GPa and 1000--11000\,K, with electronic and ionic temperatures matched. Force-dominated training leaves systematic energy offsets between structure families of up to 41\,meV/atom that persist despite additional training data. Stronger energy weighting and weaker regularization largely remove these offsets, while converged k-point sampling prevents further composition-dependent biases. The final potentials achieve held-out energy errors of 2.0--5.5\,meV/atom and first-order free-energy errors within 3.4\,meV/atom for liquids at 5000--9000\,K. However, an untrained NiAs-type FeO phase exhibits a free-energy error of 57\,meV/atom despite a low extrapolation grade. These results show that reliable phase-diagram calculations require control of relative energy offsets and explicit free-energy validation of every competing phase.

papers.intro:
Iron oxides, FexOy, are important components of planetary materials, whose stability and physical properties influence oxygen cycling, chemical heterogeneity and transport in deep interiors. Despite their simple elemental composition, they exhibit a rich variety of stoichiometries and crystal structures under extreme conditions, accompanied by changes in coordination, spin state and electronic conductivity [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]. Establishing the resulting pressure–temperature–composition phase diagram therefore requires accurate free-energy differences across numerous crystalline and liquid phases, with consistent treatment of electronic excitations and magnetic properties[6, 7, 8, 9]. Although first-principles calculations provide the underlying energetics, the system sizes and extensive statistical sampling required for converged phase boundaries make a comprehensive exploration computationally demanding. Developing accurate machine-learned interatomic potentials is therefore essential for making such calculations tractable, enabling large-scale simulations and free-energy sampling while retaining a quantitative connection to the first-principles reference [10].

papers.title: Zero-Temperature Energetics of a First-Order Surface Phase Transition from Diffraction
papers.abstract: First-order phase transitions are governed by the balance between zero-temperature energy, thermal vibrational energy, and entropy, yet these contributions are rarely accessible experimentally. Here, we establish a diffraction-based route to determine them for the prototypical Si(111)-In atomic-wire system. From the temperature-dependent Debye-Waller attenuation of reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) intensities we extract distinct Debye temperatures for the low-temperature $(8{\times}2)$ ground state and the high-temperature $(4{\times}1)$ phase. The softer vibrational spectrum of the high-temperature phase yields the entropy gain that stabilizes this phase above the critical temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$. Evaluating the thermodynamic balance between internal energy and entropy at $T_\mathrm{c} = 125\,\mathrm{K}$ yields a zero-temperature energy difference of $\Delta E_0 = 138\,\mathrm{meV}/(8{\times}2)$, including the difference in vibrational zero-point energies of the two phases, thus providing direct access to hidden thermodynamic parameters of a first-order surface phase transition.

papers.title: Defining equations for two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties
papers.abstract: We give a complete algebraic characterization of two-block shallow ReLU pattern varieties. We show that the determinantal equations arising from rank constraints imposed by the activation patterns generate the defining ideals, thereby proving a conjecture of Alexandr-Mont\'ufar. The set-theoretic proof uses a characterization of orbit closures of matrix pencils in terms of the Kronecker canonical form.

papers.intro:
A ReLU neural network defines a piecewise linear map from inputs to outputs. Within each input region where the same hidden neurons are active, the network acts as a linear map. Since the different linear maps share the same network parameters, their coefficients satisfy algebraic relations. Describing these relations helps characterize the functions represented by a given ReLU architecture. ReLU pattern varieties were introduced in [1] to study these algebraic relations.

For a fixed collection of activation patterns, the associated pattern variety is the Zariski closure of the image of the polynomial map that sends network parameters to the corresponding linear maps. For a pair of activation patterns in a shallow network, natural rank constraints give determinantal equations that vanish on the associated pattern variety. These equations were conjectured to generate the defining ideal [1, Conjecture 26]. In this paper, we prove this conjecture for arbitrary input, hidden, and output dimensions.

Selecting a subset of activation patterns amounts to taking the Zariski closure of a coordinate projection of the full pattern variety. The defining ideal of the pattern variety for a subset of activation patterns therefore amounts to considering an elimination ideal, for which finding explicit generators is generally a difficult nonlinear algebra problem. Theorem 1 describes the generators for the defining ideal for the variety associated to any pair of activation patterns. In particular, these impose polynomial constraints on the two observed maps associated to the pair of patterns, whether or not the grouped neuron contributions can be recovered linearly from the two maps. Our result also imposes necessary compatibility constraints on every pair of patterns’ linear maps within a larger collection of patterns.

papers.title: Tropical Geometry of $G_2$
papers.abstract: We tropicalize the Grassmannian and the flag variety of the algebraic group of type $G_2$. The two tropical varieties are strictly contained in the associated Dressians. Their points are trees in the $G_2$-forest and decorated trees in the $G_2$-orchard. These form hexagons in incidence geometry. We classify all toric degenerations and their Newton-Okounkov polytopes. Mukai theory leads us to tropical canonical curves of genus 10. This article serves as a blueprint for studies of reductive groups in tropical geometry.

papers.title: Agent Verifiers in Counterfactual Analysis: A Pilot Study Benchmarking Agentic Heterogeneous Treatment Effects
papers.abstract: Agents can expand the covariate space of randomized experiments by retrieving fast-moving local context missed by slow-changing survey baseline covariates, helping characterize who benefits most from an intervention. Verifying such covariates is difficult: individual treatment effects are unobserved, retrieval leakage can pull post-treatment information into nominally pretreatment summaries, and encoder leakage can inject post-treatment pretraining knowledge into representations even after temporal filtering of inputs. Guided by a two-channel information bound separating summary provenance from encoder weights, we propose a three-layer benchmark protocol: (i) retrieval admissibility via pre-treatment date filtering; (ii) heterogeneity validation scored rank-weighted average treatment effects (RATEs); and (iii) encoder admissibility checked with chronologically vintaged encoders, future-fact probes, and weight perturbations. Across 11 datasets anchored by Uganda's Youth Opportunities Program, we compare session-isolated retrieval (sandboxed, bounded-budget agent runs per study) against a persistent workspace teammate (xAI's GrokBot) that builds one date-verified corpus per study while blinded to outcomes. The workspace teammate yields higher mean RATE ratios in 6/11 datasets for text alone and 7 for combined features, though paired tests show neither workflow universally dominates. Even on fixed retrieved text, encoder choice significantly shifts heterogeneity signal. Chronologically vintaged probes show no clear evidence of weight leakage, but single-record adapter perturbation analyses show that memorized future facts, once present, persist until injected noise degrades model output. Temporal filtering of retrieval is necessary but insufficient: verifying agent-generated covariates requires jointly examining source provenance, out-of-sample treatment-effect signal, and encoder weights.

papers.title: Flexibility for the Monge-Ampere system implies flexibility for isometric immersions into Riemannian manifolds
papers.abstract: We prove that any flexibility result for the Monge-Amp\`ere system implies the corresponding flexibility result for the isometric immersion system, with the same H\"older regularity. We treat the general isometric immersion system, in which both the source and the ambient metrics are arbitrary H\"older regular, in arbitrary dimension and codimension. Combining this implication with existing results for the Monge-Amp\`ere system, we obtain new ${C}^{1,\alpha}$ flexibility statement for isometric immersions with arbitrary source and ambient metrics. To our knowledge, these are the first such results for non-Euclidean ambient metrics.

papers.title: A Topologist's Proof of Krasnosel'skii's Bifurcation Theorem
papers.abstract: This note offers a proof of Krasnosel'skii's bifurcation theorem that bypasses the traditional machinery of nonlinear analysis: neither the Leray-Schauder degree nor the Lyapunov-Schmidt reduction is used. The argument rests only on elementary operator theory and straightforward vector-bundle topology, providing a topologist's perspective on a classical result in nonlinear functional analysis.

papers.title: OMNIS+: Semantic RAN Slicing and Quantization for Dynamic Split Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Edge computing enables resource-constrained devices to execute machine learning (ML) applications via task offloading, with radio access network (RAN) slicing playing a crucial role in provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, existing RAN slicing frameworks rely on static computing models, limiting their ability to exploit dynamic semantic data representations enabled by modern neural architectures. To address this limitation, we propose OMNIS+, a semantic RAN slicing framework for multi-cell edge computing built upon a new generation of dynamic split neural models. OMNIS+ incorporates dynamic neural compression paired with adaptive quantization for task offloading, providing a versatile decision space across communication payload and compute dimensions. We leveraged a novel ``box'' quantization scheme that markedly enhances resilience to transmission bit errors across diverse compression rates. Considering partial system observability and distinct node objectives, we formulate two interdependent optimization problems: (i)~mobile devices (MDs) maximize inference accuracy under quality-of-service (QoS) and queue-stability constraints by jointly adapting dynamic split deep neural network (DNN) branches and cell association; and (ii)~each edge server (ES) allocates bandwidth, graphics processing unit (GPU) frequency, and modulation and coding scheme (MCS) to maximize the max--min inference accuracy among associated MDs under cell capacity limits. We solve these problems using a multi-agent distributed optimization framework, where MDs act as causal contextual multi-armed bandit (MAB) agents under backlog-aware Lyapunov control, while each ES executes resource allocation via block coordinate descent (BCD). Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, OMNIS+ reduces the QoS violation probability by up to 1.75 while achieving a better accuracy--violation trade-off.

papers.intro:
The rapid proliferation of machine learning (ML)-driven applications–such as real-time video analytics, autonomous driving, and augmented reality–has introduced computationally intensive, latency-critical workloads that involve complex neural models and high-volume sensor data [2]. Resource-constrained mobile devices (MDs) often struggle to meet these stringent quality-of-service (QoS) demands. To alleviate this bottleneck, mobile edge computing (MEC) offloads computation-heavy ML tasks to edge servers (ESs), significantly reducing execution latency [3]. In this context, radio access network (RAN) slicing plays a pivotal role by flexibly provisioning joint communication and computing resources. However, conventional RAN slicing frameworks for edge computing transmit raw sensor data directly to ESs [4, 5], requiring impractically high data rates (e.g., hundreds of kilobits per frame for joint photographic experts group (JPEG) images on the common objects in context (COCO) dataset [6]). Although recent split-computing schemes [3] (Fig. 1(a)) partition deep neural networks (DNNs) and transmit intermediate feature tensors from MDs, raw tensors remain bandwidth-prohibitive; for instance, ResNet-50’s “conv3” feature map requires 3.1 MB in 32-bit floating-point (FP32) format [7]. Alternatively, semantic communication frameworks (Fig. 1(b)) compress data into compact latent representations. Specifically, [8] relies on static autoencoders that lack adaptability under fluctuating bit error rates (BERs), whereas [9] introduces an adjustable compression factor for dynamic semantic control. Nevertheless, these schemes fail to specify concrete, deployable implementations of flexible compression under realistic wireless channel corruptions.

To address these limitations, we propose OMNIS+, a novel semantic RAN slicing framework tailored for multi-cell edge computing. OMNIS+ connects semantic slicing with dynamic neural networks – specifically, multi-branch architectures that flexibly map input data into a compact latent space with adaptive quantization. Throughout this paper, neural compression refers to the neural-encoder mapping from the input to the latent space, while compression denotes the combined neural-compression and quantization process determining the uplink payload size; radio channel coding follows 5G New Radio (5G NR) modulation and coding scheme (MCS) link adaptation. papers.title: Failure of the $L^p$ Neumann problem in bi-Lipschitz images of a ball
papers.abstract: For every $n\geq 2$ we construct a bounded domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^{n+1}$, which is the image of the unit ball under a bi-Lipschitz homeomorphism of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$, and a bounded Neumann datum $g$ with zero mean such that the variational solution $u$ of the Neumann problem with datum $g$ satisfies $\mathcal N(\nabla u)\notin L^1(\partial\Omega)$. In particular, the $L^p$ Neumann problem is not solvable in $\Omega$ for any $1<p<\infty$, although $\Omega$ is a two-sided chord-arc domain whose boundary supports a weak $(1,1)$-Poincar\'e inequality, and although in this class of domains the Dirichlet and the regularity problems are solvable for some exponents. This answers in the negative a question of C. Kenig, and it also shows that, unlike the solvability of the Dirichlet problem, the solvability of the $L^p$ Neumann problem for some $p\in (1,\infty)$ is not invariant under bi-Lipschitz homeomorphisms of $\mathbb R^{n+1}$.

papers.title: Instability of layered two-phase flow in a vertical plane channel
papers.abstract: The equilibrium two-phase flows in a vertical plane channel are explored by adopting an approximate Boussinesq-like model. The class of stationary parallel flows examined in this paper features three-layer configurations in which the central core is less dense than the peripheral layers. Such flows are considered purely buoyant, induced by the density difference between the phases. The simplified scheme leads to a formulation where the parameters driving the transition to linear instability of the equilibrium flow are the Archimedes number and the dimensionless positions of the interfaces between the phases. The analysis takes into consideration symmetric and asymmetric flows, including, as special cases, also two-layer configurations with one phase close to the left-hand boundary wall and the other close to the right-hand wall. In particular, the completely antisymmetric flow, where the equilibrium velocity profile is an odd function of the transverse coordinate, shows up as the least stable configuration among those examined in this study.

papers.intro:
Buoyancy-driven exchange flow in a vertical conduit is characterised by the concurrent upward motion of a less dense fluid and the downward motion of a denser fluid. When the conduit connects closed reservoirs or when a zero net volumetric flux is otherwise enforced, the opposing volume fluxes must be equal. Such flow configurations are encountered in volcanic conduits, groundwater wells, industrial pipelines, and other confined counter-current systems. However, even within the laminar regime, the density and viscosity ratios alone do not uniquely determine the cross-sectional flow configuration: concentric and eccentric core–annular structures, side-by-side stratified layers, and temporally unsteady switching between these states may all be realised. This multiplicity of admissible configurations is central to the present study, in which the internal interface may be either centred or displaced from the mid-plane of a vertical planar channel.

Early studies of exchange in vertical tubes exposed a basic closure problem: zero net flux does not by itself determine the size or topology of the counter-current regions. Huppert and Hallworth [12] combined experiments, dimensional analysis and a steady axisymmetric Newtonian model, clarifying the balance among buoyancy, viscous stresses, and inertia. However, their core radius was selected through a maximum-flux hypothesis, and the model excluded asymmetric or fragmented states. Beckett et al. [4] observed core–annular, side-by-side, and transitional regimes over a wide range of viscosity ratios. The viscosity contrast organised the regimes but did not uniquely select them, while neither the final topology nor the measured flux systematically maximised exchange. Suckale et al. [18] addressed non-uniqueness through a steady model and transient simulations, identifying thin- and thick-core branches and showing that boundary conditions and flow history can determine the realised state. Their results weaken universal selection rules based on maximum flux or minimum dissipation, although the analytical model does not independently determine the exchange flux. Longo et al. [14] studied an axisymmetric non-Newtonian long drop rising in a vertical tube while a Newtonian liquid descended through the annulus. Under lubrication and zero-net flow assumptions, an energy balance yielded an asymptotic core radius that complied reasonably well with measured radii, velocities, and selected profiles. The approach provides a selection mechanism within a prescribed core–annular topology but not among competing topologies. Charabin and Frigaard [5] examined the reversed rheological arrangement, with a viscoplastic fluid surrounding a lighter Newtonian finger. Yield stress could stop exchange or produce helical, disconnected-finger, and slug regimes, and the energy-based radius selection of Longo et al. [14] did not produce an equilibrium in their parameter range. Collectively, these studies indicate that rheology, interface geometry, boundary conditions, and flow history all influence the observed state; no universal selection principle has emerged.

The linear stability of vertical core–annular pipe flow has been investigated using increasingly comprehensive two-fluid models. Hickox [10] examined the fully developed concentric flow of two immiscible Newtonian fluids, accounting for density and viscosity contrasts, gravity, inertia, and surface tension. A long-wave asymptotic expansion demonstrated that stratification can destabilise the axisymmetric base flow; however, this analysis was restricted to long-wavelength perturbations and to configurations with a less viscous core fluid. Chen et al. [6] subsequently removed the long-wave limitation while retaining the effects of gravity, capillarity, inertia, and an imposed pressure gradient that could assist or oppose gravity. Their computations disentangled the respective roles of capillary forces, interfacial shear, and gravitational effects and identified a stability window corresponding to nearly ideal core–annular flow, which was later corroborated by free-fall experiments. In both studies, the base flow was assumed to be perfectly concentric and the analysis was primarily concerned with axisymmetric perturbations.

Bai et al. [2] compared linear theory with vertical oil–water experiments in upward and downward flow. The theory reproduced wave celerities sufficiently well to classify regimes and relate them to bamboo and corkscrew waves, but it predicted wavelengths that were shorter than those observed and could not represent the three-dimensional corkscrew deformation. Hu and Patankar [11] therefore extended the theory to non-axisymmetric modes and showed that, for thin cores, a sinuous azimuthal disturbance can be more dangerous than the axisymmetric mode, providing a linear mechanism for corkscrew waves. These pipe-flow studies all employ a deformable interface with full kinematic and dynamic jump conditions; therefore, their instabilities are genuinely interfacial, unlike the prescribed-density approximation adopted here.

A central Newtonian layer was symmetrically bounded by a second fluid, with deformable interfaces, density and viscosity contrasts, and surface tension. The stability problem contained snake and varicose interfacial modes, as well as modes related to single-fluid Poiseuille flow. Stability depended jointly on layer ordering, thickness, and properties: density and viscosity stratification could reinforce or oppose one another, and finite-wavelength modes could remain unstable even when the long-wave limit was stable. This is the closest sharp-interface predecessor to the present geometry, but it was restricted to a centred layer with symmetric outer regions and did not impose zero net flux.

papers.title: A Well-Separated Pair Decomposition of Linear Size for Unit-Disk Graphs
papers.abstract: We prove that every connected Euclidean-weighted unit-disk graph on $n$ vertices has a $(1/\varepsilon)$-well-separated pair decomposition of size $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\varepsilon))$. This resolves an open problem posed by Gao and Zhang in 2003. We also show that this bound is tight: there are connected unit-disk graphs for which any $(1/\varepsilon)$-well-separated pair decomposition has size $\Omega(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log (1/\varepsilon))$.

papers.title: Orbital-weighted learning for transition metal complexes
papers.abstract: Frontier orbital energies are key to the description of molecular light-matter interaction and pose a challenge both for electronic structure calculations and for machine learning approaches, especially for transition metal complexes (TMC). These are highly relevant since the gap between the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) is in the range of visible light. For TMCs, gap position and magnitude are determined by the metal center, its coordination and ligand identity. Since the systems exhibit a wide range of charge and spin states, frontier orbital energies can only be predicted with machine learning models that explicitly incorporate spin and charge. In this work, we show that a semi-empirical orbital population as a weight rather than a feature can increase efficiency for both physics-based and neural-network-based atomic representations. Because orbital populations are highly sensitive to both charge and spin, they offer a general pathway to render existing geometry-based machine learning representations useful for orbital energies. On TMC datasets, our approach reduces the required training data by up to 95 %, and improves physics-based representations to almost match the accuracy of pre-trained neural network representations at 12% of the inference compute cost. This greatly reduces the data and compute requirements to accurately model frontier orbitals in TMCs

papers.intro:
The highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) together are the frontier orbitals. Both their absolute energy value as well as the difference, the so-called gap, are of fundamental interest to interactions between molecules and light, even as approximation[40, 45]. The HOMO energy is approximately the negative of the ionization potential, and as such describes approximately the amount of energy required to remove one electron from a molecule. The negative of the LUMO energy, again, is a proxy for the electron affinity, a measure of how easily a molecule would accept an electron. The orbital energies and the gap are relevant for applications such as OLEDs[1] or organic solar cells[73], but in theoretical modeling also finds use in reactivity analysis[53, 63].

papers.title: Capacity-Aware Redistribution Control for Mitigation of Cascading Failures in Networks
papers.abstract: This paper studies the control of irreversible cascading failures in networks with finite node capacities. Each node carries a nonnegative divisible quantity, referred to as load, and fails irreversibly when its load exceeds its capacity. The network dynamics are represented by topology-dependent row-stochastic matrices. When nodes fail, these matrices must be updated. However, directly deleting rows and columns corresponding to failed nodes can reduce the total load in the network. We therefore introduce a topology update that preserves unit row sums and quantifies any unserved load explicitly. We derive the resulting load-balance relation and a necessary and sufficient condition for lossless redistribution after simultaneous failures. Based on these results, we formulate a two-stage optimization problem: the first stage minimizes unserved load, and the second stage minimizes the highest capacity utilization among the surviving nodes. Simulations on grid and Barabasi-Albert networks show that, unlike the standard equal and residual-capacity redistribution approaches, the proposed method prevents secondary failures in all tested cases, with a tradeoff against served load on scale-free networks.

papers.intro:
Many networked systems, such as power, transportation, communication, and service networks, move a conserved quantity, hereafter referred to as load, among nodes with finite capacities such as substations, stations, or routers. When the load at a node exceeds its capacity, the node fails permanently, and its load is either transferred to surviving nodes or remains unserved. Redistribution may overload further nodes and trigger a cascade of failures [1, 2, 3]. Each failure also changes the network topology and thereby alters subsequent load transfers.

When the load at a node exceeds its capacity, the node fails permanently, and its load is either transferred to surviving nodes or remains unserved. Redistribution may overload further nodes and trigger a cascade of failures [1, 2, 3]. Each failure also changes the network topology and thereby alters subsequent load transfers.

Capacity-based models [1, 2] describe how overload and changes in network flows can lead to propagating failures. Decentralized redistribution using neighboring information is proposed in [4], and optimal reassignment of failed-link loads in multilayer networks is studied in [5]. Related cascade models and mitigation strategies have been studied in the complex-networks literature [6, 7, 8]. For local redistribution, equal sharing can be used. It requires no optimization, but ignores the residual capacities of surviving nodes. It also does not coordinate transfers from simultaneously failing nodes that share a receiver, i.e., a surviving neighbor.

In power networks, the method in [9] computes load-shedding schedules over successive cascades using linearized power-flow equations. For a similar application, homogeneous load reduction, optimized shedding, and a tree heuristic approach are compared in [10]. For networks with external inflows, [11] investigates distributed routing under irreversible link failures and reductions in link capacities. For continuous-time flow networks, throughput and overload properties under monotone distributed routing are derived in [12]. Generally, existing cascade models typically change load only at failures and treat each failed node separately. Moreover, the optimization-based and robust approaches in [9, 10, 11, 12] rely on power-flow models or on flow networks with external inflows, and are thus not directly applicable when a finite node load is reassigned at failures. It therefore remains unclear how load transfers between failures should adapt to node removal, and under which conditions the loads of simultaneously failing nodes can be reassigned without overloading shared receivers.

In this work, we consider a finite divisible load held at the nodes, with no continuing external inflow. Nominal transfers follow a topology-dependent row-stochastic matrix, whereas loads of failed nodes are reassigned among surviving neighbors. When nodes fail, directly deleting the corresponding rows and columns can reduce the total load before redistribution. We propose an alternative to this strategy. In this context, our contributions are as follows. First, we show that our alternative topology update preserves row stochasticity after single or simultaneous failures and derive the corresponding total-load balance. Second, when the nominal surviving-node loads have enough capacity, we give a necessary and sufficient condition for lossless redistribution after simultaneous failures and determine the minimum load that must remain unserved. Third, we formulate a two-stage linear program that first minimizes unserved load and then minimizes the highest surviving-node capacity utilization. We give a necessary and sufficient condition under which no further failures occur. Fourth, in simulations with grid and scale-free networks, we compare our approach with standard heuristics, i.e., equal and residual-capacity redistribution, after two initial failures with a common surviving neighbor occur, and redistribution requires accounting for shared receiver capacities.

First, we show that our alternative topology update preserves row stochasticity after single or simultaneous failures and derive the corresponding total-load balance. Second, when the nominal surviving-node loads have enough capacity, we give a necessary and sufficient condition for lossless redistribution after simultaneous failures and determine the minimum load that must remain unserved. Third, we formulate a two-stage linear program that first minimizes unserved load and then minimizes the highest surviving-node capacity utilization. We give a necessary and sufficient condition under which no further failures occur. Fourth, in simulations with grid and scale-free networks, we compare our approach with standard heuristics, i.e., equal and residual-capacity redistribution, after two initial failures with a common surviving neighbor occur, and redistribution requires accounting for shared receiver capacities.

papers.title: ReSynth: Constructing Synthetic Supervision for Multi-Image Understanding
papers.abstract: People often understand the world by comparing different views of it. Vision-language models (VLMs), however, receive these views as separate images and still struggle to relate them. One problem is data. Training on these tasks requires groups of images with a known relationship: the same object from different viewpoints, or the same scene before and after a change. Such examples are hard to collect at scale from existing photo collections. We introduce ReSynth, which turns single-image perception and controllable image generation into cross-image relational supervision. Localized editing produces before-and-after pairs, viewpoint generation produces multiple views of the same instance, and verified scene contents support comparisons of counts and attributes. ReSynth combines Qwen3-VL-8B's captioning, grounding, and counting capabilities with Qwen-Image-2.1's generation and editing capabilities. It verifies single-image facts such as object counts and attributes, then combines these facts to construct multi-image QA. Using GRPO on approximately 440K ReSynth questions, with no real images during training, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B improve by 17.73 and 6.10 average points on BLINK, MUIRBench, and VLM2-Bench, while single-image performance is broadly preserved on Qwen2.5-VL-7B and improves across all four evaluated benchmarks on Qwen3-VL-8B. Notably, this supervision enables the 8B perception model itself to outperform Qwen3-VL-235B on BLINK and MUIRBench.

papers.title: Read Together, Answer Apart: How Earlier Questions Help Vision-Language Models Look
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are often asked several questions about the same image in a single prompt (co-asking), yet existing evaluations report conflicting accuracy gains and hallucinations at the prompt level without tracking how individual answers change. By pairing each question's single-question and co-asked answers across 22 open-weight VLMs (1B-35B), we find that erratic net shifts reflect two opposing effects: on Densely Captioned Images (DCI), every model repairs 15.4%-29.8% of its single-question errors under co-asking, while the share of correct answers turned wrong falls from 30.8% on weaker models to 4.7% on stronger ones. Across all 14 models supporting custom attention masks, we show through attention readouts and layer-window interventions that earlier same-image questions read visual information into their question tokens in the early-to-middle layers during prefill, helping later questions concentrate image attention onto their queried targets. This visual help accumulates across the scene even across non-overlapping regions, whereas blocking earlier questions from attending to the image lowers both target localization and accuracy in all 14 models. While cross-question help is established during shared question reading, part of the co-asking damage enters later during answer decoding when the decoder attends to other question stems. We therefore introduce Read Together, Answer Apart, a training-free decoding mask that keeps shared prefill intact and isolates each answer from other stems, improving co-asking accuracy on 12 of 14 models on DCI (up to +4.71 percentage points, closing 70% of the pooled gap to asking alone) and on 10, 8, and 5 of the 14 models on WebUI, FinTabNet, and GQA (up to +11.4, +5.3, and +1.1 points).

authors.name: Chao He
authors.institution: Institute of Materials Research and Engineering

papers.title: MRASLive: An online parameter estimation toolbox for time-dependent PDEs
papers.abstract: We present MRASLive, a toolbox for online parameter identification in time-dependent partial differential equations based on a model reference adaptive system (MRAS). Building on the MRAS proposed by Kaltenbacher and Nguyen (Inverse Problems 37(5) 2021) and its first numerical realization by the authors (Applied Mathematics for Modern Challenges 8 2026), the toolbox is designed for ease of use, utilising the user's weak form specification to prepare the data, the discretized MRAS and its solvers, and to verify the assumptions of MRAS's convergence theory semi-automatically.

authors.name: Tram Thi Ngoc Nguyen
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research

papers.title: Sharp error estimates for Lagrange interpolation and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted $L_p$-spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish sharp direct and inverse approximation estimates for algebraic Lagrange interpolation polynomials and Kantorovich-type operators in weighted $L_p$ spaces on $[-1,1]$. A well-known limitation in the theory of approximation by interpolation polynomials states that for small rates of convergence $\alpha \le 1/p$, classical moduli of smoothness fail to provide matching direct and inverse estimates due to the insufficiency of integral metrics to determine pointwise values at the interpolation nodes. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce new special semi-discrete measures of smoothness based on Steklov averaging operators, which combine global $L_p$-smoothness with discrete deviations from Steklov averages at the interpolation nodes. By using these measures, we establish fully matching direct and inverse approximation theorems for Lagrange interpolation polynomials, thereby providing complete two-sided characterizations of the rate of convergence for an arbitrary rate $\alpha > 0$. As a natural application of the developed approach, we also obtain corresponding direct and inverse estimates, as well as strong converse inequalities, for Kantorovich-type operators constructed via Lagrange polynomials.

papers.title: Scalable Non-Parametric Bayesian Inference of Free Energy Landscapes and Emission Functions from Observations
papers.abstract: Free-energy landscapes govern processes from protein conformational change to climate oscillations, but are typically observed only indirectly, through observables such as FRET intensity or optical-tweezer transmittance. Neither the landscape shape, nor the emission function mapping latent state to signal, is usually known, and distinct states may produce the same signal. We therefore infer landscape and emission function jointly and non-parametrically, using the exact non-linear Bayesian filtering likelihood, to fully use the information contained in observable trajectories that are often noisy, scarce and costly to acquire. A novel parallel-in-time algorithm makes this tractable: it is up to 27 times faster than sequential filtering on one GPU, scales near-ideally across GPUs, and, given enough resources, has runtime independent of trajectory length. We demonstrate the method on a single-protein optical tweezer recording, where distinct conformations produce the same signal, and beyond biology on the El Nino-Southern Oscillation and financial market volatility.

authors.name: Eliane Briand
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences

authors.name: Helmut Grubmuller
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Multidisciplinary Sciences

papers.title: Kinetic study of Reaction-Control-Jet Interference in Rarefied Hypersonic Crossflow
papers.abstract: A 1975 wind-tunnel study at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) of a helium jet blowing from a flat plate into a Mach 11 to 12 air crossflow at three freestream densities is revisited using two- and three-dimensional Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) computations at Knudsen numbers 0.021 to 0.125. The planar slot used in two-dimensional model computations reproduces the shock topology, the sign and two-lobed structure of the interference pressure and its trend with rarefaction, and its plate-alone boundary layer is consistent with the three-dimensional one and with a similarity solution with slip and temperature jump. However, two-dimensional simulations overpredict the peak interference pressure about twelvefold at every condition and carry it farther upstream. A resolution sweep at the most rarefied condition converges the planar interference to within 1% of its extrapolated limit. Three-dimensional DSMC reproduces the measured interference pressure at all three densities, within 25% at the lobe peak and 3 mm in its position, although two- and three-dimensional simulations overpredict the plate-alone wall pressure by 50 to 75%. Continuum breakdown around the jet persists even at the lowest Knudsen number examined. Fully three-dimensional kinetic simulations are underway to extend the present validation to a comparison of jet strength and forces over wider Knudsen number ranges, and to an examination of lateral relief as a reason for the discrepancy.

papers.title: Interpersonal trust, institutional trust and trust in technology in Air Traffic Control
papers.abstract: Air traffic control (ATC), the safe, orderly and efficient management of planes through controlled airspace is a complex task. In this article, we explore the roles that different kinds of trust play in ATC. Our study provides the essential foundations for examining the conditions that need to be satisfied if Air Traffic Controllers are to establish and sustain trust relationships with technical innovations, such as agent-based systems, and so ensure their safe and dependable embedding within ATC work.

papers.title: Towards Transparent Computational Agents for Air Traffic Control: Explainability, Interpretability and Trust
papers.abstract: We report preliminary findings from an ongoing investigation into transparency techniques for computational Air Traffic Control agents. Air Traffic Controller Officers (ATCOs) observed two types of agent in simulated air traffic controlling exercises. ATCOs found the chosen transparency techniques helpful to some extent: revealing how agents were making controlling decisions was an essential foundation for trust. However, the ATCOs' trust depended on whether they could be made sense of in a live, operational context and the agents' actions where judged to be professionally competent.

papers.title: Reactive Phase Change of a Single Droplet in Turbulent Flow with Reactive Vapor-Liquid Equilibrium Using a Two-Scalar Diffusive-Interface Method
papers.abstract: Reactive phase change fluids have been shown to enhance thermodynamic performance by integrating chemical reactions with thermodynamic cycles. This study investigates the turbulent evaporation of a single droplet using Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) to model the behavior of reactive phase change fluids. Applying Reactive Vapor--Liquid Equilibrium (RVLE) thermodynamics, the study simultaneously captures the dynamics of reactive phase transitions, mass transfer, and heat transfer during the evaporation of dinitrogen tetroxide (N___O___). A second-order phase field framework is used to derive two scalar transport equations, accurately describing species behavior at equilibrium. The equilibrium is maintained by balancing concentration exchange rates across both the liquid-to-vapor and vapor-to-liquid phases. Results indicate that chemical reactivity significantly influences phase transition dynamics, altering the phase dome structure by modifying critical points and the thermodynamic saturation lines. Endothermic and exothermic behaviors are observed at the interface during the fast reversible evaporation process of N___O___(l) ___ 2NO___(v,l). Turbulence simulations further show enhanced mixing efficiency and improved gas-liquid separation, driven by chaotic flow patterns. This study elucidates the role of reactive phase change fluids in contrast to conventional non-reactive phase flows, emphasizing the influence of chemical reactions on phase transition dynamics and overall system performance..

authors.name: Silvia Lasala
authors.institution: Laboratoire Réactions et Génie des Procédés

papers.title: On the local boundedness of weak solutions to doubly nonlinear equations with variable exponents
papers.abstract: We establish local boundedness, together with quantitative estimates, for non-negative weak sub-solutions to a class of doubly nonlinear parabolic equations whose prototype is \[ (u^q)_t-\operatorname{div} \Big(|Du|^{p(x,t)-2}Du\Big)=0, \qquad p(x,t)>1,\quad q>0. \] The results are obtained under a logarithmic continuity condition on the variable exponent $p(x,t)$ and suitable relations between $q$ and the local bounds of $p(x,t)$. In certain ranges of the exponents, an additional local integrability assumption is required.

authors.name: Mariia O. Savchenko
authors.institution: National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine

authors.name: Yevhen S. Zozulia
authors.institution: Institute of Applied Mathematics and Mechanics

papers.title: Encapsulating Reactive Behaviour in Goal-based Plans for Programming BDI Agents
papers.abstract: Reactive behaviour in BDI-based models and architectures adopted in agent programming is typically specified in terms of reactive plans not bound to any specific goal. In this paper, we present and discuss an extension of the plan model used in BDI programming languages in which goal-based plans encapsulate both proactive and reactive behaviour. This brings important benefits both to the practice of agent programming and in supporting agent reasoning at runtime. The paper first introduces the model formally, abstracting away from particular programming languages. The approach is then evaluated through concrete implementations based on two existing agent programming platforms, namely Jason and ASTRA. The paper reports on experiments showing that the approach provides for elegant programming and can also be efficient.

authors.name: Rafael H. Bordini
authors.institution: Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Rio Grande do Sul

papers.title: A Comparison of Heuristic, Human-Sensitive, and Self-Play DRL Policies in Human-Agent Teaming
papers.abstract: Dynamical Perceptual-Motor Primitives (DPMPs) offer a tractable framework for generating human-like movement dynamics in artificial agents (AAs) and have been used to support coordination in human-AI teaming tasks. Traditionally, DPMP controllers rely on heuristic (rule-based) decision policies derived from human behavior to guide goal selection and action sequencing. Although effective in structured tasks, such heuristics can be difficult to generalize to more complex settings, motivating interest in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approaches for learning decision policies for human-AI interaction. A key challenge, however, is ensuring that DRL policies remain aligned with human strategies, particularly when agents are trained through self-play. To examine this issue, we compared three target-selection policies governing DPMP-based AAs in a first-person herding task: (1) a human-derived heuristic policy, (2) a self-play DRL policy (SP-DRL), and (3) a human-sensitive DRL policy (HS-DRL) trained alongside a heuristic agent. Results showed that heuristic agents most closely matched typical human-human coordination patterns, followed by HS-DRL agents, whereas SP-DRL agents deviated most. These findings highlight the importance of human-informed training when developing DRL-based teammates and suggest that simple heuristic policies may remain an effective approach for designing human-aligned AAs capable of human-AI collaboration.

papers.title: Characterization of the $b$-anisotropy for axisymmetric early-type galaxies in TNG50
papers.abstract: High-quality observations reveal that internal dynamics of axisymmetric ETGs can be more complicated than commonly adopted in modelizations based on the Jeans equations (JEs), with the identity of the radial and vertical velocity dispersions. A well known generalization is obtained by solving the JEs with the prescription of a proportionality factor $b$ between the radial and vertical velocity dispersions; in its simplest form $b$ is assumed constant, while in recent studies $b=b(z)$. We investigate the properties of the $b$ parameter and of the other kinematical decomposition parameters commonly adopted in modeling in a sample of ETGs taken from the high-resolution cosmological simulations TNG50. From a selection of highly axisymmetric and passive TNG50 (satellite and central) galaxies at equilibrium, we recovered the maps of $b(R,z)$ and of other important kinematic quantities entering the JEs. In all the selected galaxies the only significantly non-zero velocity streaming component is the azimuthal one, and the velocity dispersion tensor is cylindrically aligned. The maps of $b$ are clearly not constant, and not stratified over planes, instead they present a common structure, with the largest values values near the center, and a wedge structure at large (cylindrical) radii. A phenomenological formula for $b(R,z)$ to be used in applications is proposed. Also the other decomposition parameters are non-constant. No significant differences are found as a function of galaxy flattening and mass, while some difference is observed between satellite and central galaxies. The internal dynamics of the TNG50 galaxies present interesting regularities, worth of investigation. On the other hand, in Jeans based studies of real galaxies some simple assumptions for the choice of anisotropy and kinematical decomposition parameters do not seem appropriate. [abridged]

authors.name: L. De Deo
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Norte

papers.title: Taming the Tails of Stochastic Gradient Descent in the Interpolation Regime
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study stochastic gradient descent in the smooth interpolation regime, where the population objective shares a common minimizer with the sample losses. In contrast to prior work, which has largely focused on in-expectation analysis, we obtain high-probability convergence guarantees under the same assumptions. In the convex case, we prove a fast rate of order $\log(\beta^{-1}) \cdot n^{-1}$ after $n$ iterations, with failure probability at most $\beta$. In the strongly convex case, we derive a family of moment-based bounds of order $\beta^{-p} \cdot \exp(-\mathcal{O}(p \cdot n))$ for $p \in (0,1]$, and complement them with a matching lower bound showing that the corresponding deterioration in the exponential rate is essentially unavoidable. In both settings, our theoretical results are unified across a broad class of step-size schedules. Building on this analysis, we extend our results to a low-noise regime and to nonconvex objectives satisfying the Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition.

papers.title: Machine learning interatomic potentials and orientational defects in polymers
papers.abstract: Photopolymerization of acrylated epoxidized soybean oil (AESO) is a convenient model of a self-organizing process in a soft, bio-based material: ultraviolet light starts a free-radical chain reaction, the growing network releases heat, and the mobility of molecular groups changes on several time scales at once. We follow this process from two sides. Experimentally, the real and imaginary parts of the dielectric permittivity of an AESO:VDM (1:0.5) mixture with 3 mol% of the photoinitiator DMPA were recorded at 500-5000 Hz under an intermittent on/off illumination protocol, and the resulting time series were analysed with a sliding-window Shannon entropy and the Grassberger-Procaccia correlation integral. Both measures show that short light pulses at the start of curing trigger strongly correlated, collective relaxation, which fades as the network forms, leaving only localized reorientations active. We describe these reorientations as orientational defects and quantify their energetics with the MACE-OFF23 machine learning interatomic potential, using relaxed dihedral scans of five rotational modes ($\alpha$, $\alpha/\beta$, $\beta$, $\gamma$, $\delta$) of an AESO fragment. Compared with density functional theory (DFT) reference profiles, MACE reproduces the shape of all five profiles (Pearson $r=0.95$-$0.98$) and the hierarchy of barriers - from 2.9 eV for the constrained main-chain rotation, through 0.54-0.81 eV for the acrylate rotations, to 0.16-0.18 eV for the methyl and 0.06 eV for the hydroxyl rotation - while underestimating the barrier heights by 3-20%. A simple Arrhenius estimate shows that the acrylate rotations are the modes closest to the frequency window of the dielectric measurement.

papers.title: How random are affine maps over finite cyclic groups and generalized cyclotomic permutations over finite fields?
papers.abstract: We analyze the dynamical behavior of affine permutations over the ring $\mathbb{Z}_{p^e}$ and generalized cyclotomic permutations (GCPs) over the finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$. We use the description of their functional graphs to determine two statistical parameters: the expected number of cycles and the expected length of a cycle that contains a random element. We obtain explicit closed-form expressions for both expectations and an exact reduction from GCPs to affine permutations. We compare these parameters with the corresponding expectations for random permutations, to determine how closely the cycle statistics of each family resemble those of random permutations.

papers.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.

authors.name: Colin Christian
authors.institution: Institut de Recherche sur les Systèmes Nucléaires pour la production d'Energie bas carbone

papers.title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
papers.abstract: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

papers.title: Bound States in the Continuum as Converging Scattering Zeros in Metasurfaces: Why Accidental BICs Require Nonlocality
papers.abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) allow metasurfaces to achieve extremely high quality factors, yet it remains unclear how they emerge and how they can be described by effective material parameters. We address this question by modeling BICs through the reflection and transmission zeros of a metasurface described by effective susceptibilities. By decomposing its response into even and odd parts, and inspecting the interaction of the corresponding poles and zeros, we show that a high-Q resonance appears as a transmission zero squeezed between two reflection zeros, or vice versa. The separation between these scattering zeros is set by the linewidth of the corresponding even or odd resonance, so that a BIC corresponds to a convergence of these zeros. This simple concept explains symmetry-protected BICs and their transformation into quasi-BICs. However, it also reveals a fundamental limitation for accidental BICs: in a passive local dipolar model, the zeros cannot converge at oblique incidence unless one of the susceptibility resonances has a negative amplitude, which would make the metasurface active according to Foster's theorem. We demonstrate that this negative amplitude is in fact the signature of higher-order multipoles or lattice coupling effects that the local model cannot properly capture, which shows that accidental BICs are intrinsically nonlocal. We confirm this conclusion by simulating a silicon-ridge metasurface, whose response is reproduced and predicted by a passive, spatially dispersive model, which also describes how breaking the mirror symmetry of the metasurface turns the accidental BIC into a quasi-BIC.

papers.title: Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to evaluate the primary stability of the pedicle screw: A proof of concept
papers.abstract: The long-term success of spinal instrumentation depends on the initial stability of pedicle screws (PS), yet current intraoperative assessments rely on surgeon subjectivity. This study introduces a quantitative, non-invasive approach-the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM)-to support intraoperative decision-making. The IBAM measures screw stability using low-amplitude impacts delivered with an instrumented hammer on the surgical screwdriver after screw insertion. An IBAM indicator, defined as the average time difference between the two earliest local maxima in the force signal, was analyzed under varying stability conditions in artificial bone samples. Experimental factors included bone density ($\rho$), insertion depth ( D ), and pilot hole diameter ( $\Phi$ ). The IBAM indicator was compared with the PS pull-out force for each configuration. Although the main effects showed opposite trends for the pull-out force and the IBAM indicator, their relative magnitudes were similar ( $\rho$ $\sim$35%, D $\sim$25%, $\Phi$ $\sim$15%). The relationship between the pull-out force and the IBAM indicator followed a power-law model (adjusted R 2 =___0.85) with a negative exponent. As screw stability increased, the pull-out force rose while the IBAM indicator decreased, demonstrating complementary sensitivity to bone-implant interface changes. While results are promising, the simplified experimental design limited the ability to fully capture bone-implant interaction complexity. Future studies should aim to validate IBAM in vivo to confirm its clinical applicability..

authors.name: Eric Wagnac
authors.institution: Centre intégré universitaire de santé et de services sociaux du Nord-de-l’Île-de-Montréal

papers.title: Harvesting Expert-Parallel Bubbles for Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract:
GPUs are expensive, yet latency-critical large language model (LLM) inference leaves part of them idle. Colocation reclaims this capacity by running best-effort work, such as fine-tuning, alongside serving. Many leading LLMs now use a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture, which adds a new source of idle time. Under expert parallelism, MoE experts are spread across GPUs, and because the router sends uneven numbers of tokens to each GPU, lightly loaded GPUs wait for the most loaded one. Even after applying load balancing solutions, such bubbles still take 8--13% of prefill time.
  We present BubbleTea, the first colocation system that leverages expert-parallel bubbles for fine-tuning. Unlike existing colocation systems, which make one scheduling decision for all GPUs per forward pass, BubbleTea predicts each GPU's bubble at every layer from the router's token assignment, and fills it with short chunks of fine-tuning work that reuse the weights already loaded for serving. We also introduce compiler passes that automatically derive these chunks from the served LLM as-is, without porting each model architecture to a separate training engine.
  Our evaluation on three MoE models, served on four A100 GPUs, shows that fine-tuning throughput with BubbleTea is 1.9--6.2$\times$ faster than with LLMStation, a state-of-the-art colocation system. BubbleTea keeps p90 inference latency within 10% of serving alone in 50 of 63 workloads, compared to 44 for LLMStation. On bursty production traces, BubbleTea trains 3.3$\times$ faster than LLMStation and 14$\times$ faster than a stock trainer colocated under CUDA MPS, with p90 inference latency staying within 7% of serving alone.

papers.title: A counterexample to Molchan's orthant persistence conjecture
papers.abstract: We refute Molchan's conjecture that the persistence probability of the isotropic fractional Brownian field on $[0,R]^d$ satisfies $p_{d,H}(R)=R^{-d(1-H)+o(1)}$ as $R\to\infty$. We prove $$ \limsup_{d\to\infty}\limsup_{R\to\infty} \frac{-\log p_{d,H}(R)}{d\log R} \le 1-\frac{49}{48}H+o(H), \qquad H\downarrow 0. $$ Thus the conjecture fails for every sufficiently small fixed Hurst parameter in all sufficiently large dimensions. A finite-step Gaussian interpolation inequality on the exact positive sphere is proved in an appendix.

papers.title: The Optimal Competitive Ratio for Subadditive Online Combinatorial Auctions is Less Than 1/2
papers.abstract: We construct a four-buyer online combinatorial auction with independent subadditive valuations and a fixed, known arrival order in which every online rule earns strictly less than $1/2$ of the expected offline optimum. A common partition, revealed at the third arrival, gives the first three buyers one unit of welfare per item. If the rule uses three distinct partitions, either an item allocated early contributes zero or the fourth buyer's expected value for the remaining bundle is one less than its size. We compute the optimal online and offline welfare exactly and show that a $1/2$ guarantee always holds with at most three buyers.

papers.title: Minimal norm of regular vectors in the root lattice of a crystallographic root system
papers.abstract: For a crystallographic root system $\Phi$ with Weyl group $W$ and root lattice $L = \mathbb{Z}\Phi$, we determine the minimum norm of a vector of $L$ having trivial stabilizer in $W$, and we prove that the vectors attaining it form a single orbit of $W$. Although this is a minimization of a quadratic function over the lattice points of a cone, the minimizer in the dominant chamber is always unique: it is $\rho + \lambda$, where $\rho$ is the Weyl vector and $\lambda$ is $0$ or the minuscule weight in the class of $\rho$ modulo $L$. In particular, the optimal vector is the Weyl vector exactly when the Weyl vector lies in $L$. We give explicit formulas for the families $A_n$, $B_n$, $C_n$ and $D_n$, with elementary proofs, and the values for the exceptional types $E_6$, $E_7$, $E_8$, $F_4$ and $G_2$. Finally, we explain the coincidences between the minimal norms by the folding of Dynkin diagrams.

papers.title: Local-global compatibility with $p$-adic Langlands program for completed (co)homology of $\mathrm{GL}_2$ over CM fields
papers.abstract: For each place $v \mid p$ such that $F_v \simeq \mathbf{Q}_p$, we establish a compatibility with $p$-adic Langlands program for completed homology with integral coefficients for $\mathrm{GL}_2$ over CM fields $F$ with $[F:\mathbf{Q}]>2$, after localization with respect to a non-Eisenstein decomposed generic maximal ideal of a Hecke algebra.

papers.title: Mid-Infrared Integrated Acousto-Optic Phase Modulation on GaAs/AlGaAs
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a mid-infrared (7.5-10 um) integrated acousto-optic phase modulator operating at 460MHz based on a GaAs/AlGaAs heterostructure. The combination of broad mid-infrared transparency and piezoelectric properties of GaAs based structures allows monolithic integration of all the device functions (electro-acoustic transduction and acousto-optic interaction) on a single material platform. Addressing the challenge presented by comparable mid-infrared and acoustic wavelengths, simultaneous propagation and confinement of surface acoustic waves and guided light is achieved using a deep-etched sub-wavelength grating. We develop a comprehensive and quantitative simulation framework to design the modulator devices, characterize their acoustic properties in a heterodyne vibrometer and perform a full, quantitative analysis of the device performance by inserting them in an integrated Mach-Zehnder interferometer. Remarkable agreement with simulations validates the proposed design flow, and opens the way to improved integrated acousto-optic devices operating in the longer end of the mid-infrared.

papers.title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.

papers.title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.

papers.title: Sixth and twelfth moments of Dirichlet $L$-functions in prime power moduli
papers.abstract: For a fixed odd prime $p$ and $q=p^n$, we establish power-saving bounds for the sixth and twelfth moments of central values of primitive Dirichlet $L$-functions, with exponents $5/4-3/332$ and $2-51/261961$, respectively. More generally, our methods yield a power saving over the classical interpolation bound for every moment of order $4<j\le12$. Our approach begins with short second moments over character cosets and preserves the dependence on the character parameter. An exact linearization of the $p$-adic stationary phases reduces the critical large-value range to exponential sums with perturbed square-root phases over prime-power rings. We establish a large-value estimate for these sums by combining congruence-spacing bounds, higher congruence energies, and an average of quadratic Gauss sums over the dual frequency. For the remaining high-value range, we develop an incomplete-correlation estimate using $p$-adic exponent pairs.

papers.title: Probing the Turbulent Magnetised Interstellar Medium of the Small Magellanic Cloud through Depolarisation with POSSUM Observations
papers.abstract: The interstellar medium (ISM) of the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) provides a unique laboratory for studying magnetised gas in a low-metallicity, tidally disturbed environment. We investigate this magnetised turbulent medium using broad-band polarimetric data from the Australian Square Kilometre Array Pathfinder (ASKAP)'s Polarisation Sky Survey of the Universe's Magnetism (POSSUM), leveraging a high-density Rotation Measure (RM) grid comprising 951 RMs ($\sim24$ RMs per square degree) to probe the magneto-ionic structure of the SMC. We statistically compare the number densities of polarised and non-polarised non-thermal background sources on a per-square-degree basis, revealing spatially coherent depolarisation signatures that correlate with enhanced plane-of-sky RM fluctuations. This is consistent with a turbulent cascade from large-scale structures. Analysed through RM synthesis and Stokes $QU$-fitting, we attribute the depolarisation to a turbulent magneto-ionic medium within the telescope's beam ($\lesssim6~\mathrm{pc}$). Faraday complexity is detected in $\sim$24% of the RM sources; however, no coherent spatial structure is observed in the complexity distribution, and we attribute this primarily to internal source structure or an extended halo surrounding the SMC rather than to its main body. Furthermore, as previously identified in the Large Magellanic Cloud, depolarisation in the SMC increases with emission measure; however, the underlying Faraday dispersion is $\sim$6 times weaker. With the thermal electron density smooth on the scales of the field fluctuations, this depolarisation is likely driven by magnetic field fluctuations.

papers.title: Inapproximability of Euclidean Steiner Tree
papers.abstract:
We consider the Euclidean Steiner Tree problem of connecting $n$ given points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ by a shortest network allowing the addition of Steiner points anywhere in the space. Arora [FOCS'96/'97, J. ACM'98] gave a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) for Euclidean Steiner Tree and TSP in every fixed dimension, and Trevisan [STOC'97, SICOMP'00] proved that Euclidean TSP is APX-hard in $O(\log n)$ dimensions. They left open whether Euclidean Steiner Tree admits a PTAS in high dimension. Our first contribution settles this thirty-year-old question by proving APX-hardness in $O(\log n)$ dimensions. Assuming that not all problems in NP can be solved in subexponential time (NP $\not\subseteq $SUBEXP), we also rule out a PTAS for Euclidean Steiner Tree in $O(\log\log n)$ dimensions. This dimension bound is tight up to a factor of $O(\log\log\log n)$, since Arora's scheme is a PTAS in up to $\log\log n/\log\log\log n$ dimensions.
  In fixed dimension, Kisfaludi-Bak, Nederlof, and W\k{e}grzycki [FOCS'21, J. ACM'25] obtained approximation schemes running in time $2^{O_d(\varepsilon^{-(d-1)})}n\log n$ and proved matching Gap-ETH lower bounds for Euclidean TSP and Rectilinear Steiner Tree, but left a corresponding lower bound for Euclidean Steiner Tree as an open question. Our second contribution answers this question with a nearly tight lower bound on the dependence on accuracy for Euclidean Steiner Tree. However, given the recent claimed refutations of ETH and hence Gap-ETH by OpenAI and Anthropic, we use the weaker assumption that 3SAT has no truly subexponential-time algorithm, that is, no $2^{n^\gamma}$-time algorithm on formulas of size $n$ for any constant $\gamma<1$ (a hypothesis one might call weak ETH). Under this assumption, we prove that no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm runs in time $2^{O(\varepsilon^{-\gamma(d-1)})} poly(n)$ for any such $\gamma$.

papers.title: A $10^5\,M_\odot$ Black Hole in the Bulgeless Spiral Galaxy IC 342: First Stellar-Dynamical $M_{\rm BH}$ Measurement with Keck/OSIRIS LGS-AO
papers.abstract: We present the first direct stellar-dynamical measurement of an intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) in IC 342, a nearby nearly face-on ($i\approx31^\circ$) bulgeless spiral at $D=3.45\pm0.13$ Mpc, using near-infrared integral-field spectroscopy with Keck/OSIRIS LGS-AO. The heavy foreground extinction ($A_{\mathrm{F814W}}\approx0.74$ mag) renders the nucleus inaccessible to optical spectroscopy, making $K$-band observations at $\sim$2.3 $\mu$m the only viable path to high-resolution nuclear kinematics. Two-dimensional stellar kinematics extracted from the CO bandheads via pPXF at $0.062''$ resolution reveal a central velocity dispersion rising from $\sim$42 km s$^{-1}$ at $r\gtrsim0.2''$ to a peak of $\sim$49 km s$^{-1}$, providing kinematic evidence for a central dark mass within the nuclear star cluster (NSC; $M_\mathrm{NSC}\approx1.17\times10^7~M_\odot$). Modeling these kinematics with an ensemble of four JAM models, spanning cylindrical and spherical velocity-ellipsoid alignments and two PSF representations, combined with an MGE mass model constructed from a three-S\'ersic plus exponential-disk decomposition of archival HST/WFC3 F814W imaging and incorporating a physically motivated stellar mass-to-light ratio gradient, driven by the young central NSC population, yields $M_\mathrm{BH}=(1.95\pm0.61)\times10^5~M_\odot$. Accounting for this stellar population gradient is essential for the detection: standard constant-$M/L$ models systematically overestimate the central stellar mass, hiding the BH signature and yielding only an upper limit. The stellar orbits are near-isotropic ($\beta\approx0$), typical of fast-rotating late-type spirals. This measurement places IC 342 among the rare bulgeless spirals with a direct dynamical $M_{\rm BH}$ at the IMBH mass scale, where both the NSC and BH are directly characterized, providing a new anchor for compact massive object co-evolution models.

papers.title: Large entropy implies H\"older regularity on large sets
papers.abstract: Let $F$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of $\mathbb{P}^k(\mathbb C)$ of algebraic degree $d\ge2$, with $k\ge1$. We prove that every ergodic $F$-invariant probability measure $\mu$ of entropy strictly greater than $(k-1)\log d$ admits compact sets of $\mu$-measure arbitrarily close to one on which the restrictions of $\mu$ have H\"older continuous super-potentials. Consequently, $\mu$ gives zero mass to every Borel pluripolar set.
