papers.title: PULSAR-V: I/O-Aware Post-Update Attestation for RISC-V
papers.abstract: Post-update attestation proves that a device installed the intended firmware, not that the image stayed protected until the report was signed. In a multi-master SoC, a master outside the attested processor can corrupt update-critical memory. In contrast, the firmware identity, lifecycle state, and the CPU's protection evidence remain byte-identical to a healthy device's. We present PULSAR-V, a post-update attestation architecture which binds the authenticated update commit to the effective permissions and immutability of both gates (PMP/EPMP on the CPU, the I/O policy mediating DMA), sampled at the commit and at attestation, the I/O gate latching its own commit-time state in hardware. In a RISC-V SoC prototyped on a ZCU102 FPGA (CV32E40S core with 16 PMP regions, IOPMP-style unit, AXI write guard), a 256-byte write from the board's Arm DMA engine bypasses PMP and corrupts the committed image: every conventional claim stays true, and PULSAR-V rejects the device on its I/O-policy evidence alone. It also rejects an intact device whose policy left the image writable, a verdict no integrity check can reach. The gate and its commit latch cost 436 LUTs, 4.6% of the SoC, and evidence collection takes 43.1k cycles independent of image size, 41x less than re-hashing 16 KiB.

papers.title: RAID: Representation Autoencoder for Intrinsic Decomposition
papers.abstract: Single-image intrinsic decomposition is an inherently ill-posed problem, requiring the disentanglement of strongly coupled appearance factors from a single RGB observation. Recent methods address this ambiguity with diffusion priors, at the cost of large, iterative, and often stochastic models. We show that accurate decomposition does not require a large generative model. Our key idea is to decouple reconstruction from decomposition on top of a strong pretrained representation. First, an $X \rightarrow X$ teacher learns to reconstruct each intrinsic map from DINOv3 features using a shared decoder, without paired RGB-to-intrinsic supervision. Then, a DINOv3-based student predicts the corresponding teacher representations from RGB through lightweight, modality-specific projections, enabling training on partially annotated datasets and predicting all intrinsics in a single forward pass. \textbf{RAID}, predicts intrinsic properties in the structured latent space, enabling a compact 165M-parameter model, 100x faster than diffusion-based methods. Despite its compact size, it achieves competitive or superior decomposition quality, with improved robustness to input resolution. Additionally, our learned projections yield interpretable, modality-specific feature spaces.

papers.title: Modelling population distribution across cities on spatial networks using the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems
papers.abstract: We investigate the urban population distribution of the Italian region of Sardinia through the kinetic theory of multi-agent systems on spatial networks, interpreting cities both as agents and vertices of a graph, and representing interurban links as edges. We consider various emigration rules to model the interactions between agents, obtaining two main results: the bimodal lognormal fit of the total population distribution among cities and the Pareto fit of the tail. Overall, our model provides results consistent with the actual distribution derived from ISTAT data of Sardinia; furthermore, the bimodal lognormal fit generally follows the distribution tail more accurately than the Pareto one, although the two coincide in the first half.

papers.title: F$^3$: What Makes Good Experience in World-Action Models?
papers.abstract: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. Form compresses successful and failed rollouts alike into short, verified operation records; Fit teaches the policy to read a record and to predict when it helps; Fusion injects the record's images, text and actions into the policy as a prefix and an action prior. Trained once on only 200 examples and deployed with a growing experience library, the model achieves state-of-the-art results on MolmoSpaces and RoboLab without any training on RoboLab: over native Cosmos 3 Nano, it raises success by 12.0 pp and 10.8 pp, reduces steps to success by 12.2% and 11.3%, and cuts regressions by 57%.

papers.title: Proof-Relevant Interpolation for Circular Proofs in Linear Logic
papers.abstract: First introduced for proving Craig's interpolation theorem, Maehara's method provides a constructive, proof-theoretic procedure for extracting interpolants in sequent calculus proofs. Building on this method, Saurin developed a ``proof-relevant'' interpolation theorem for first-order linear logic, in the sense that the interpolated proof is obtained by cut-introduction steps that can be reversed via cut-elimination. In this work, we extend Saurin's proof-relevant interpolation to linear logic proofs with cuts as well as to circular proofs in linear logic with fixed-points. We specifically show how Maehara's method can be extended in a proof-relevant way to work on non-cut-free and non-well-founded (but regular) proof objects, and guarantee that the interpolation procedure preserves strong validity. We also study conditions under which one can interpolate system L terms that are not necessarily in normal form.

papers.title: On least energy solutions for a critical nonlinear Schr\"odinger system with $K$-wise interaction: the competitive case
papers.abstract: We study least energy fully non-trivial solutions of a nonlinear Schr\"odinger system with Sobolev critical nonlinearities and repulsive interaction involving all the components at the same time. Under the scalar Brezis-Nirenberg assumptions on the linear coefficients, we prove existence of least energy fully non-trivial solutions on smooth bounded domains for every negative coupling in dimensions \(N=5,6\). For \(N=3,4\), due to the lack of $L^2$-integrability of the Aubin-Talenti bubbles, the same conclusion holds under additional sufficient assumptions, and in particular we provide an explicit condition on the domain and coefficients. We also investigate the strong competition limit, and characterize fully non-trivial limiting profiles as minimizers of a partially segregated variational problem. A preliminary study of independent interest concerns the whole-space problem. For general admissible \(K\), we determine the component-wise Nehari infimum and prove that it is not attained, even in the radial class. Finally, when the linear coefficients coincide, we establish a sharp criterion for the existence of positive synchronized solutions in terms of the strength of the competition.

papers.title: Learning the Dynamics of Deformable Linear Objects Through Coupled Oscillators for Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
papers.abstract: Many learning-based approaches for deformable linear objects (DLOs) rely on simplified deformation models that neglect dynamic effects and the mechanical response of the objects, limiting their applicability to lightweight, compliant objects and slow motions. Inspired by recent advances in learning physically structured dynamics with coupled oscillator networks (CONs), we propose $\Phi$-CON for learning force-driven DLO dynamics. The model combines a floating-base coupled oscillator network (FBCON), whose latent potential energy depends only on the DLO's shape, with a learned affine diffeomorphism $\Phi$ between observed positions along the DLO and latent coordinates. Its shape dynamics are stable by construction, and its Lagrangian structure yields explicit expressions for kinetic and potential energy. We exploit this structure to design a model-based proportional-derivative (PD) controller that compensates for the learned potential forces, thereby establishing closed-loop stability guarantees and ensuring convergence. We evaluate the approach on four simulated DLOs and a real bimanual robot setup. In simulation, $\Phi$-CON achieves prediction accuracy comparable to neural ordinary differential equation (NODE) models and Lagrangian neural networks (LNNs), with $97.2\%$ and $90.2\%$ fewer parameters, respectively. Relative to a model-free PD baseline, the proposed controller reduces mean endpoint regulation error by $97.5$-$99.7\%$ in simulation and achieves a mean per-target reduction of $27.9\%$ across both endpoints in real-world experiments, demonstrating the importance of explicitly accounting for the mechanical response of stiff and heavy objects.

papers.title: Wegner model in high dimension: singular continuous spectrum from U(1) symmetry breaking and AAT self-consistency
papers.abstract: We analyze the energy-spectral decomposition of the Wegner one-orbital model in high lattice dimension using ideas from field theory and statistical mechanics. Most notably, we identify a local spectral measure of singular continuous type for the disordered model at the Anderson transition. The key mechanism that leads to a singular continuous spectrum is a novel scenario of spontaneous symmetry breaking, intimately connected to the non-compactness of the global symmetry group of the field theory. While that symmetry breaks down to a compact subgroup in the metallic phase, it spontaneously breaks down to a nilpotent subgroup at criticality. We describe the symmetry-breaking extremal states approximately, by applying the self-consistent theory of localization due to Abou-Chacra, Anderson, and Thouless. The thrust of our work is to provide a field-theoretical foundation for disorder phenomena associated with singular continuous spectra.

papers.title: RSIBench-Infra: Can Agents Optimize Their Own Training and Inference Infrastructure at Production Scale?
papers.abstract: Improving the efficiency of training and inference infrastructure is a practical component of recursive self-improvement. Existing benchmarks for agent-driven optimization largely focus on individual software layers such as kernel, leaving unclear whether agents can deliver end-to-end performance gains under production workloads. We introduce RSIBench-Infra, a benchmark of 20 training and inference tasks spanning diverse model families and modalities, with deployments of up to 32 accelerators on NVIDIA GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Agents start from runnable baselines derived from official recipes and can modify the software stack across engine, kernel, and instruction levels. An OCI image-layer submission protocol captures these changes for reproducible deployment, while independent evaluation measures end-to-end performance under task-specific quality constraints. Across all task results, 66.2% exceed $1.10\times$ validated speedup. These results demonstrate that current agents can improve production-scale training and inference performance, but identifying effective optimization strategies and consistently translating local improvements into end-to-end gains remain challenging.

papers.title: Benchmarking LLM abilities on postdoc-level natural science problems
papers.abstract: Scientific problems have no answer key, so evaluating an agent means deciding what counts as a better solution before any agent is run. Existing benchmarks either match a symbolic answer against a key or, where they require executable work, score it by unit tests, by a rubric, or by position on a competition leaderboard. None of these is the criterion by which a field decides that one published method beats another. STEMBench adopts that criterion directly. Each of its twelve research problems in high-energy physics, astrophysics and neuroscience is scored by its own field's figure of merit, and each comes with two measured anchors: a submission that uses no domain knowledge, and an expert reference reproducing a published method, both obtained by running code shipped with the benchmark. The interval between them states how much of a problem is crossed by scientific insight rather than by engineering. Across eight frontier models, task-level wins and domain-level leadership dissociate: a model that wins five of the twelve tasks leads no domain mean. In the high-effort cross-model comparison, at least one model's mean score exceeds the expert anchor on seven of twelve tasks. The remaining five span uncertainty estimation, latent and causal inference, and cross-site clinical classification. Numerical scores and official-submission validity capture different aspects of performance and are reported separately. We release the tasks, graders, anchors and harness.

papers.title: Finite-temperature effects on the single-particle Green's function of a mobile impurity in a Luttinger liquid
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of a quadratically-dispersing quantum impurity interacting through a contact density-density term with a one-dimensional (1D) superfluid described by Luttinger liquid theory. By means of a field-theoretical approach based on the linked-cluster expansion, we quantitatively address the effects of a finite temperature of the 1D bath on the momentum-space single-particle Green's function. Through a careful identification of the resonant phonon-impurity scattering processes, we obtain asymptotic large-time estimates for the thermally-induced exponential damping of the zero-temperature signal both in the $\textit{quasiparticle}$ regime, dominated by the presence of a finite lifetime for the host impurity, and in the $\textit{infrared-dominated}$ regime, where the impurity causes a Anderson's orthogonality catastrophe of the 1D bath. In both cases, we identify a temperature-induced coherence time that sets the characteristic timescale of the exponentially-decaying finite-temperature correction to the amplitude of the zero-temperature single-particle Green's function. Moreover, we draw connections between the aforesaid thermal timescale and the microscopic parameters of the Lieb-Liniger model, which admits an effective Luttinger-liquid description, highlighting the dependence of the inverse coherence time on the intra-bath interactions across the different dynamical regimes of the impurity.

papers.title: Effect of a role model-based show on the STEM aspirations of primary school students
papers.abstract: A STEM outreach show called 'Who wants to be a Superhero' went into primary schools across England and Wales, delivered by professional science communicators. The show was structured around four female STEM role models and two male STEM role models as part of a wider narrative about scientists and engineers being real-life superheroes. The show was found to increase both boys' and girls' aspirations for a STEM career, with a bigger effect seen in the girls. The intervention also increased positive attitudes, and decreased negative attitudes, towards scientists measured through word association given by the audiences pre- and post-show. There was a larger reduction in negative stereotypes from the girls after the show, especially in the 'nerdy' and 'crazy' stereotypes. The show saw an increase in both boys' and girls' perceptions of the 'helpful' nature of science and engineering. It was also found that some students may not want to do a STEM job because of the perceived dangerous nature of the job.

authors.name: Sophie Bartlett
authors.institution: Wales Institute of Social and Economic Research, Data and Methods

papers.title: Breaking the Myth of Four-Tier Stacked Transistors for Logic: an Investigation from Process to Device and Block-Level PPA
papers.abstract: For the first time, this work evaluated whether 4-tier stacked transistors can translate the straightforward density gains into realistic chip-level scaling benefits. A practical dual-sided 4-tier transistor-stacking CFFET (Flipped CFET-to-CFET) process was proposed, on which a DTCO framework spanning standard-cell design, local interconnects, RO analysis, and physical implementation was built under 2A node design rules. The CFFET was also benchmarked with its 2-tier transistor-stacking counterparts FFET. Among CFFET configurations, the best-performing Symmetric Power still lags FFET by 11.2% in RO frequency due to the complex MOL parasitics. At the block level, CFFET reduces the Ibex RISC-V core area by only 12.8% (far below the 40% nominal cell-height reduction), while running 10.9% slower at iso-power. We further introduced a novel Tetris-like cell stitching to minimize the area overhead, which allows non-rectangular cell design and recovers 7.4% area in a 1-bit ALU design. An optimized NanoStack CFFET was finally proposed, inspired by previous work. This work indicates that straightforward vertical 4-tier stacking proves insufficient to guarantee enough PPA benefits, though the resulting design insights may guide future advanced architectures.

papers.title: Analysis of the (1+1)-EA-ES-Bilevel on Mixed Discrete-Continuous Optimization Problems with Interactions
papers.abstract: Mixed discrete-continuous optimization problems can pose challenges -- especially for previous integrated approaches -- when interactions cause beneficial discrete changes to be rejected before sufficient continuous adjustment. We introduce ProximityOneMax as a simple benchmark with pairwise discrete-continuous interactions. On this function, we prove an exponential lower bound on the expected time for the (1+1)-EA-ES-Integrated to reach the target accuracy when initialized near a continuous optimum for a suboptimal discrete configuration with a sufficiently small step size. Experiments show frequent entries into such states from random initialization. We introduce the (1+1)-EA-ES-Bilevel, which uses an upper-level (1+1)-EA to optimize discrete variables and a lower-level (1+1)-ES to optimize continuous variables for each fixed discrete offspring before selection. For several interaction benchmarks and sufficiently small target values $\epsilon > 0$ that require an optimal discrete configuration, using fixed continuous initialization and a suitable fixed budget per lower-level call, we prove that the expected number of fitness evaluations to reach objective value at most $\epsilon$ is $\Theta(n_d \cdot \log n_d \cdot n_c \cdot \log(R/\sqrt{\epsilon}))$, where $n_d$ is the number of discrete variables, $n_c$ is the number of continuous variables, and $R$ bounds the distances from the fixed continuous starting point to all relevant continuous optima for fixed discrete configurations.

papers.title: Extreme value statistics for majorisation partial orders
papers.abstract: We study extreme-value phenomena for random samples in partially ordered sets through their meets and joins, the order-theoretic analogues of minima and maxima. In this paper we consider the probability simplex equipped with either UT-majorisation or majorisation, with samples drawn uniformly from the corresponding simplex. We analyse these extrema both at fixed dimension and as the dimension grows, identifying almost-sure collapse to the bottom or top elements and critical scalings with nondegenerate limiting laws.

authors.name: Giovanni Gramegna
authors.institution: Istituto Nazionale di Fisica Nucleare, Sezione di Bari

papers.title: Benchmarking Reasoning Reliability,Prior_Evidence Contrast,and Spectral Discrimination in Remote-Sensing Geological Image Interpretation
papers.abstract: Reliable lithology interpretation requires accurate geological recognition and reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Although Multimodal Large Language Models show promise in remote sensing, their reliability in geological interpretation remains unclear. We introduce HyGeoBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 10,000 questions based on hyperspectral imagery across three dimensions: reasoning reliability, prior_evidence contrast, and spectral discrimination. It covers ten task types, with both multiple-choice and open-ended response formats. Integrating hyperspectral satellite imagery with geological annotations and verified evidence, HyGeoBench examines reasoning errors, conflicts between geological priors and visual evidence, and cross-band inconsistencies. Evaluations reveal limitations in fine-grained recognition and evidence-grounded interpretation. To address these challenges, we propose HyGeoAgent, a tool-augmented framework integrating region observation, text knowledge retrieval, same-band image retrieval, and native PCA analysis through adaptive tool use. Experiments demonstrate consistent improvements over the corresponding base models, improving geological image interpretation across diagnostic dimensions.

papers.title: Moment approximations in optimal transport: geometric estimates and a semiclassical limit
papers.abstract: We study finite moment approximations of linear optimization problems over measures. Under suitable assumptions, we establish the existence of discrete minimizers with a controlled number of support points, duality and $\Gamma$-convergence as the moment approximation is refined. This framework accommodates several transport problems, in which marginal constraints are replaced by finitely many moment constraints. For moment functions localized at scale $r_n$, we prove an estimate controlling $W_\infty$ by $W_p$ up to an additive error of order $r_n$, which also applies to discrete measures. For repulsive costs, we show that minimizers remain separated from the diagonal, uniformly in the number of moments, and we derive consequences for dual potentials. Finally, under a moment-correction assumption, we prove that the fermionic minimum energies converge in the semiclassical limit to the moment-constrained Coulomb transport value for a fixed family of moment functions.

authors.name: Luca Nenna
authors.institution: École nationale des ponts et chaussées

papers.title: Orbital parameters for 50 million stars observed by Gaia and spectroscopic surveys
papers.abstract: Together with ground-based spectroscopic stellar surveys, the Gaia mission has changed Galactic archaeology over the past decade. Nevertheless, attempts to combine these datasets remain scarce, even though precise orbital parameters for as many stars as possible are crucial to unraveling the Galaxy's formation and evolutionary history. This work aims to construct the largest homogeneous catalog of stellar orbital parameters ever compiled to date, using the most up-to-date data from nine large-scale spectroscopic stellar surveys (Gaia RVS DR3, APOGEE DR19, BOSS DR19, LAMOST DR11, Gaia-ESO DR5, GALAH DR4, RAVE DR6, SEGUE DR12, DESI DR1), combined with Gaia DR3 astrometric data and employing an orbital integration tool for orbital modeling. Our catalog includes orbital parameters, such as orbital distances, eccentricity, inclination, energy, angular momentum, and actions, for 52,423,233 stellar sources from Bailer-Jones distances, and 40,355,569 stellar sources from recomputed StarHorse distances, of which 41,100,866 and 30,777,133 are unique objects, respectively. We also included probabilities of belonging to specific Galactic components based on kinematic classification and chemical-abundance classification. Using this catalog, we recover the known kinematic substructures of the Galactic disk while extending their mapping to Galactocentric distances of $\sim17$ kpc, demonstrating the potential of the combined dataset for studies of Galactic dynamics and evolution. We expect that this catalog will benefit a broad range of research areas, from stellar astrophysics to Galactic archaeology.

authors.name: Helio J. Rocha Pinto
authors.institution: Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro

authors.name: Eder Martioli
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: The balance of evidence indicates a slowing AMOC
papers.abstract: The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a critical component of the climate system. Climate models have long predicted a slowing of the AMOC due to anthropogenic forcing, with a risk of passing tipping points in the future. The question of whether the AMOC is already weakening is still somewhat controversial. Continuous monitoring is only available for the past two decades, a period too short to tease apart contributions of natural variability and climate change. Reconstructions of AMOC strength going back further in time have different limitations which are debated in the literature. Here we compile and discuss this heterogeneous body of evidence, focusing on latitudes south of 45{\deg}N where northward and southward flow are separated vertically. We conclude that the balance of multiple lines of evidence strongly supports a past and ongoing AMOC slowing in response to global warming, although some uncertainty remains regarding its magnitude and timing.

authors.name: Levke Caesar
authors.institution: Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research

papers.title: ORGANIC3D: Grounding 3D CT Vision Language Models in Organ Level Image Text Coupling
papers.abstract: Vision language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance in 3D computed tomography (CT) classification, but high accuracy does not reflect whether their predictions rely on the correct anatomical evidence. We introduce ORGANIC3D, a framework for evaluating and improving organ level image text alignment through controlled anatomical interventions. Our benchmark assesses 12 vision encoder checkpoints and 7 generative VLMs using matched patient comparisons, organ erasure, lesion replacement, and laterality perturbations, revealing substantial alignment failures even among top performing models. To learn organ level image text correspondence, ORGANIC3D aligns each finding sentence with the anatomy aware image features and trains on edited scans to anchor this alignment in the organ's image evidence. We further extend this framework to generative VLMs, promoting evidence dependent question answering and report generation. Trained exclusively on public data, ORGANIC3D achieves SOTA classification AUROC on CTRATE, Merlin, and the heldout RADChestCT dataset and reaches 77% laterality accuracy, compared with at most 66% for prior models. Its generative VLM matches or exceeds all evaluated publicly released VLMs on visual question answering, achieves the highest report accuracy, and retracts 96 to 99% of target organ findings after organ removal, versus a maximum of 69% for other models. Together, these results establish ORGANIC3D as a framework for testing whether 3D CT vision language models ground their predictions in anatomical evidence and for improving organ level alignment alongside predictive accuracy.

authors.name: Zelong Liu
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

authors.name: Alexander Dimitrakakis
authors.institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai

authors.name: Jiahua Lu
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Sun-like stars show lowered X-ray activity together with over-rotation at beyond-solar ages
papers.abstract: In recent years, substructure in the age-rotation relationship of cool, sun-like stars has been identified, showing deviations from the historical Skumanich law. Since magnetic activity is expected to be the physical root cause of the stellar spin-down, namely via the magnetic braking process mediated through stellar winds, changes in spin-down should correspond to unusual activity behaviour. We selected a sample of old sun-like stars in the solar neighborhood with asteroseismic age estimates and measured rotation periods, and present an analysis of their magnetic activity using deep X-ray observations from XMM-Newton. We observe that sample stars less massive than the Sun (late-G and early-K) agree well with the established rotation-activity relationship, while early-G and late-F stars with masses above solar tend to be unusually X-ray dim for their rotation period. The latter stars rotate faster than same-colour stars in the solar-age open cluster M67, despite being older than M67. Those stars are characterized by either low metallicity ([Fe/H]$\approx -0.2$ dex compared to solar) or by a mix of low coronal temperatures ($< 1.5$ million K) and very low X-ray surface fluxes ($\lesssim 10^4$ erg s$^{-1}$ cm$^{-2}$). We conclude that there is sufficient dynamo activity for coronal emission in the sample stars, since we successfully detect the majority of them in our X-ray observations. We argue that stars with extremely low coronal temperature and/or low X-ray flux through the stellar surface may produce an inefficient spin-down through hampered angular momentum shedding. If this is indeed the cause for their over-rotation, the onset age of this effect would need to be at an age of approximately 3~Gyr. However, this behaviour is at odds with studies of stars in the open cluster M67 with a cluster age of $\sim4$ Gyr, which do not show a faster-rotating population of sun-like stars.

authors.name: M. M. Jardine
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Infinite-dimensional invariant tori for the perturbed modified KdV equation
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider the perturbed modified KdV equation $u_t=-u_{xxx}+6u^2u_x+\partial_x(u^5)$ on the circle, without external parameters. We prove that it admits plenty of almost periodic solutions.

authors.name: Yuchen Wu
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Counting $6$-Cliques in $O(n^{5.97})$ time and $O(\log n)$ space
papers.abstract: We present an algorithm that, given read-only access to the adjacency matrix of an $n$-vertex graph $G$, computes the number of $6$-cliques in $G$ using $O(n^{5.97})$ time and $O(\log n)$ space. We achieve this by exploiting a decomposition of an equality indicator function underlying, among others, the refutations of the Exponential Time Hypothesis by OpenAI and Anthropic, and of the $k$-Clique Conjecture by Vassilevska Williams and Zamir [arXiv, 2026]. Via known reductions, this implies an $O(1.994^n)$ time and polynomial space algorithm for Max Cut on $n$-vertex graphs.

papers.title: Powerful Radio Jets and Galaxy Assembly Align at Cosmic Noon
papers.abstract: Powerful radio galaxies at cosmic noon ($1<z<2$) offer a unique laboratory for investigating jet-driven supermassive black hole (SMBH) feedback on their host galaxies and surrounding environments. Unlike broad-lined quasars, radio galaxies lack a dominant nuclear point source in the rest-frame optical--UV, enabling direct constraints on host-galaxy structure and its relation to the radio jet. We analyze Hubble Space Telescope (HST) WFC3/IR (rest-frame optical) and WFC3/UVIS (rest-frame UV) imaging of the $z>1$ 3CR radio galaxies. Beyond confirming the classical rest-frame UV alignment effect, we find that the radio jets preferentially align with the major axes of the smooth rest-frame optical hosts, extending the alignment to the older stellar component. The projected axes of candidate mergers in eight systems preferentially follow the radio axes. This multiscale coherence suggests a common projected axis linking the radio source to host assembly, perhaps established by repeated mergers or anisotropic infall. We test scattered quasar light and jet-triggered star formation as origins of the UV emission along this axis. The much shallower-than-expected radial decline in UV surface brightness disfavors simple scattering as the dominant population-wide origin, while ionized-gas masses further disfavor electron scattering. The required dust masses are small relative to global reservoirs, so dust scattering remains feasible in individual regions. Comparing stellar-population ages and jet-propagation times, we identify seven UV-emitting regions as strong candidates for recently initiated jet-triggered star formation. Together, these alignments reveal an assembly-linked direction along which jets may shock or compress material and hidden-quasar radiation may illuminate it.

papers.title: Fuzzy Dark Matter as a diffractive barrier: Wave-optics Signatures of Ultralight Fields on Lensed Gravitational Waves
papers.abstract: Gravitational waves (GWs) propagate through the universe from sources at high redshift, experiencing the gravitational fields of the intervening matter distribution. Halos composed of ultralight dark matter (ULDM) contain strong density fluctuations, reflecting the interference pattern in the field distribution of the ultralight bosons. In the wave-optics regime, ULDM fluctuations act as a diffractive grating, imprinting frequency-dependent modulations of GWs, in addition to magnification and other gravitational lensing effects. Since lensing depends on the projected surface density, we derive its approximate probability distribution and show how it departs from a Gaussian distribution depending on the halo profile and coherence length. We then quantify how the GW diffraction signatures produced by the granules depend on macroimage magnification and parity. The ULDM interference network imprints stochastic diffraction fluctuations at the $O(1)\%$ level on GWs moderately lensed by the host when the Fresnel scale is comparable to the granule coherence length $r_F(f)\sim\ell_c$. These fluctuations can be enhanced to $\gtrsim10\%$ when the host macroimage forms near the critical curve or for Type II macroimages. For massive black hole binaries observed by LISA, the diffraction signature can be detectable around the ULDM particle mass $m_\phi\sim10^{-21}$ eV, providing either a smoking-gun signature of ULDM or new constraints on $m_\phi$.

authors.name: Miguel Zumalacarregui
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics

papers.title: Tell Me How Sure You Are: Communicating Uncertainty in Auxiliary Evidence to Foundation Models
papers.abstract:
In many queries, the context information provided to generative foundation models, such as LLMs and VLMs, is inherently uncertain, including its representations of the physical world. While conventional prompting discards the associated uncertainty, this paper, for the first time in the literature, systematically demonstrates that communicating such uncertainty in context provides useful additional cues for downstream decisions and yields improvements across a wide range of settings.
  We formulate the decision-making problem as a zero-shot foundation model-assisted image classification task supported by auxiliary text-based characteristics. We choose this due to the availability of well-defined auxiliary properties, associated uncertainty, and unambiguous task correctness. Using five downstream foundation models across three datasets, we extensively evaluate uncertainty arising from both humans and learned models when observing or predicting auxiliary evidence. Across all settings, we find that communicating uncertainty substantially improves downstream LLM classification performance: macro-F1 improves up to $26.18$ percentage points compared to when the uncertainty information is not communicated.
  We further observe how the foundation models process such uncertainty information and find that auxiliary uncertainty contains predictive information about the correctness of downstream decisions. Together, these results establish uncertainty as useful contextual information and motivate more systematic consideration of uncertainty communication in future foundation-model inference pipelines.

authors.name: Abhirup Ghosh
authors.institution: Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics

papers.title: Simpler Tiny Recursive Models
papers.abstract: Small models that execute deep looped computational graphs have shown great experimental results on puzzle-like problems like Sudoku, finding shortest paths through mazes, etc. The most well-known one is TRM (tiny recursive model), a simplification of HRM (hierarchical reasoning model). However, the underlying recursion is complicated and involves a high-level and a low-level state, a nested loop recursion, and the network calls with different input and output signatures depending on where we are in the loops. These mechanisms are needed to avoid memorization and overfitting. We propose STRM, a simplified design with a single state and a uniform update. STRM does not sacrifice generalization, improves training speed and final performance. Our key architectural choices that allow our simpler recursion to work are exponential moving updates on the states with varying rates that are jittered during training and readout of the solution on slow-updating channels only. We test STRM on Sudoku-Extreme, PPBench and Maze-Hard with the same data, parameters and compute as TRM: we improve over TRM by $3.8$ points on Sudoku-Extreme and $8.4$ points on PPBench and match it on Maze-Hard. On ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2, STRM improves over the published TRM results by $5.4$ and $0.5$ points. We will release our code upon acceptance of the paper.

papers.title: Recent developments in stochastic systems with singular dynamics -- a brief survey --
papers.abstract: Diffusions with singular drifts appear naturally in the study of certain classes of interesting particle systems. Due to the singularities involved in the equations describing them, studying their dynamics is both interesting and challenging as they fall outside of the usual regularity assumptions on the vector fields in the literature. One needs to introduce and study them with different methods, with the use of symmetric polynomials being a particularly promising approach. In this expository work, we give an overview of some models and methods, and we further explore their interactions with the areas of Multiple Loewner chains (in particular, multiple Schramm-Loewner Evolutions), the new links with Random Matrices, and the novel area of Machine Learning for Singular Dynamics.

authors.name: Jacek Małecki
authors.institution: Wrocław University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Vlad Margarint
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Charlotte

papers.title: The Comprehension Gap in LLM-Assisted Software Development: An Experiment
papers.abstract: When LLM tools are pushed beyond their capabilities for software development tasks, developers must be able to step in. However, the comprehension that developers acquire during development might be negatively impacted due to excessive code generation. This could create a cognitive debt that needs to be resolved before tasks can be solved efficiently again. We explore how well developers understand code they generated by prompting in comparison to self-written and unseen code and how they reflect on their comprehension. We conduct a crossover experiment and interviews with 35 participants consisting of students, academic personnel, and software developers. After completing two programming tasks with or without LLM chat usage, respectively, participants are tasked with finding introduced mutations in the produced and additional unseen code. We use insights from interviews and screen recordings to supplement our results. Regarding the experiment, 36% of participants report a better understanding of self-written code compared to their generated code. On average, participants solved the comprehension task 20% faster for self-written code than for generated code and found 11% more mutations. Participants needed significantly less time to solve programming tasks when working with the LLM. However, participants with high reliance on the LLM chat and low task engagement showed significantly decreased comprehension. Our qualitative results show great variability in individual perspectives on comprehension differences and strategies to mitigate issues. Strategies for dealing with comprehension differences range from accepting comprehension differences to adapting their LLM interactions or avoiding the tools altogether. Our results warrant further investigation into cognitive debt in larger systems and developer practices to mitigate issues.

authors.name: Jil Klunder
authors.institution: University of Applied Sciences FHDW Hannover

papers.title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.

papers.title: First Implementation and Characterization of a Fiber Amplifier in a Gravitational Wave Detector
papers.abstract: Gravitational-wave detectors rely on large-scale interferometers operating at exquisite sensitivities, where the laser source plays a central and critical role. The sensitivity of these instruments is directly influenced by the power level and noise properties of the injected light. Fiber amplifiers are a promising technology that are currently considered for the next generation of detectors because of their potential in laser power scaling and their superior output beam quality. In the context of the Virgo gravitational wave detector, we report the first implementation of a fiber amplifier into Virgo's injection system as a high-power laser source. We demonstrate a 130 W output beam that fulfills the requirements in terms of frequency noise, power noise, and beam-pointing noise. Additionally, we also show the performance of the stabilization loops that enable the commissioning of the Virgo detector. With more than 17,000 hours of operation, this work represents the longest continuous characterization and operation of a high-power and single-frequency fiber amplifier developed for gravitational-wave detection.

papers.title: Cross-Vehicle Transferability of Lateral Velocity Estimation on Production Vehicles through Input Selection and Data Augmentation
papers.abstract: Lateral velocity is safety-critical for vehicle-dynamics control but cannot be measured with production sensors. Model-based estimators such as Kalman filters are established, whereas data-driven estimators are more accurate within the training regime but suspected to lose accuracy beyond it. Their transfer to a structurally different vehicle has rarely been tested. We record real-world test drives of three series-production vehicles, train a neural-network estimator on production CAN signals of a compact car, and evaluate it zero-shot on an SUV and a van against a GNSS-aided inertial reference. On the unseen vehicles, the network's error exceeds that on the training vehicle by an order of magnitude, a gap not quantified on production vehicles before. A systematic comparison of input sets from ten production CAN signals identifies a five-signal set that transfers most robustly. To narrow this gap, we introduce three physically motivated augmentations of training data. Two improve generalization, namely exploiting the vehicle's left-right symmetry and emulating accelerometer bias. Combined, they reduce the error on the validation maneuvers of the SUV and van by 13% and 15%. Contrary to common expectation, on the SUV the data-driven estimator trained with both augmentations matches a model-based estimator tuned on the same training data.

papers.title: TableControl: Gesture Interaction Through Surface Vibrations
papers.abstract: Integrating gesture sensing into furniture offers a way to interact with digital applications and physical devices through familiar surfaces. We present TableControl, an interactive demonstration of continuous surface-vibration-based gesture recognition with the complete processing pipeline running on a microcontroller. Using four concealed piezoelectric sensors, the system combines signal acquisition and preprocessing with neural event detection and gesture classification. The resulting labels for knock, swipe-up, and swipe-down gestures are transmitted to a host computer without streaming the underlying sensor signals. Visitors explore two example applications through hands-on interaction: an endless runner game and a physical table lamp with on/off and brightness control. A dashboard displays recognized gestures, class probabilities, and processing times.

papers.title: Perceived Effectiveness of Social Debt Mitigation Measures: A Preliminary Vignette-Based Survey
papers.abstract: Software engineering is a socio-technical discipline in which unresolved social and organizational problems accumulate as social debt, gradually eroding collaboration and project health. The literature offers a solid vocabulary for these problems but says little about which countermeasures practitioners consider effective. We address this gap with a vignette-based survey: six social debt problem dimensions (Organizational Silo, Newcomer Isolation, Communication Breakdown, Knowledge Bottleneck, Cultural and Geographical Distance, Psychological Safety Deficit) were presented as realistic team scenarios, and 23 IT professionals and advanced students rated 41 literature-derived mitigation measures. Rankings were analyzed with paired t-tests and a hierarchical Bayesian model that accounts for the within-subject design and yields, for each measure, the probability of being the best option in its scenario. Only for Communication Breakdown is the answer unambiguous: consolidating communication into a single primary channel is almost certainly preferred (P(best)=0.91). For the other five dimensions, the model identifies favorites with moderate evidence (P(best) between 0.38 and 0.58), such as structured knowledge transfer and blameless retrospectives. Across scenarios, structural measures that change how information, decisions, and knowledge are organized were rated higher than role-based or attitudinal measures (by 0.3 to 0.4 scale points), although not in every scenario. Given the small convenience sample, the results are exploratory, but they offer software engineering managers an evidence-graded starting point for selecting mitigation measures.

papers.title: Training for sustainable scientific software in the AI era: from code production to scientific stewardship
papers.abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) systems are changing how researchers interact with scientific software. Their effects on productivity vary across tasks and users, but they can weaken the connection between producing a successful computational artifact and retaining scientific command over the consequential choices and evidence on which it depends. For high-energy physics, this shifts part of the training challenge from code production toward scientific stewardship: researchers must be able to validate, explain, reproduce, maintain, and justify software and workflows partly generated or modified by AI. We argue that AI-aware software training should therefore combine dedicated instruction on AI systems with the integration of AI into established software and analysis training. Testing, provenance, reproducibility, resource judgment, and scientific validation should be exercised in AI-assisted workflows, with competence judged by the evidence supporting a result rather than by code generation alone. We frame this as a problem of sustainable scientific software: AI-assisted workflows should remain trustworthy and maintainable, use computational resources responsibly, and avoid making core competence unnecessarily dependent on privileged access to particular tools or infrastructure.

papers.title: Depth Hierarchies for Symmetric Algebraic Circuits
papers.abstract: Algebraic complexity studies the cost of computing families of polynomials by algebraic circuits, with the central goal of proving super-polynomial circuit lower bounds and separations between different models of algebraic computation. Since such lower bounds remain elusive for general circuits, a common strategy is to focus on restricted models. A recent line of work (ICALP 2020, ITCS & STOC 2026) introduces and studies symmetry as a syntactic circuit restriction, showing exponential symmetric lower bounds for the permanent, as well as separations between symmetric analogues of algebraic formulas ($\mathsf{VF}$), skew circuits ($\mathsf{VS}$), and circuits ($\mathsf{VP}$). We investigate the role of depth as a complexity parameter in symmetric circuits. For every fixed $\Delta \geq 1$, we exhibit a family of polynomials computable by symmetric circuits of polynomial size and depth $2\Delta +3$, but requiring size $n^{\Omega(\log n)}$ at depth $\Delta$. We also define symmetric versions of the bounded-depth algebraic complexity classes $\mathsf{VAC}^k$, for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$, that we call $\mathsf{symVAC}^k$, and establish two strict hierarchies: Firstly, a hierarchy within $\mathsf{symVAC}^0$, and secondly, a hierarchy of the form $\mathsf{symVAC}^k \subsetneq \mathsf{symVAC}^{k+1}$ for all $k$. The latter shows that symmetric circuits of depth $(\log n)^{k+1}$ are strictly more powerful than depth-$(\log n)^k$ circuits. Moreover, we place the bounded-depth classes within the landscape of symmetric algebraic complexity developed by Dwivedi, Pago and Seppelt (STOC 2026). We complement this picture by introducing $\mathsf{symVNP}$, a symmetric analogue of $\mathsf{VNP}$, and establishing $\mathsf{symVNP}$-completeness of the permanent under symmetric projections.

papers.title: List packing for graphs with small arboricity
papers.abstract: We prove that every graph $G$ whose edge set is the union of $r$ forests has list packing number at most $2^r$. This means that for all $k\ge 2^r$ and every list-assignment $L$ with lists of size $k$, the graph $G$ admits $k$ disjoint proper $L$-colourings. While for large $r$ this bound is far from optimal, for $r\in\{1,2\}$ it is sharp. As a direct corollary of the case $r=2$, we obtain that every triangle-free planar graph has list packing number at most $4$, thus improving upon a result of Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Masa\v{r}\'ik, Mus\'ilek and Pangr\'ac and providing the optimal answer to a question of Dvo\v{r}\'ak, Postle and Norin on (weighted) $\epsilon$-flexibility of such graphs. As a corollary of the case $r=3$, we obtain a short alternative proof that every $K_5$-minor-free (and hence every planar) graph has list-packing number at most $8$, matching the state of the art. All results above also hold for the stronger notion of correspondence packing.

papers.title: Compactifying the $G_2'$-Hitchin component via almost-complex curves
papers.abstract: By studying limits of induced metrics of equivariant almost-complex curves in the pseudosphere $\mathbb{S}^{2,4}$, we compactify the $G_{2}'$-Hitchin component.

papers.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
papers.abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

authors.name: Bastien Le Guellec
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Vertical Structure-Based Composites for Analyzing Atmospheric Front Environments
papers.abstract: In many mid-latitude regions, a substantial fraction of extreme precipitation events occur in the vicinity of atmospheric fronts. To understand the processes that lead to such extreme precipitation, it is important to study the environment of the front. In this paper, we introduce a new method for computing vertical composites of frontal environments. Existing approaches construct such composites relative to front lines that represent the front at a single pressure level. However, fronts are vertically tilted and can exhibit substantial geometric variability, both within an individual front and between distinct events. Therefore, at levels away from the reference front line, the alignment of front environments based on a single front line commonly blurs the signals in the analyzed atmospheric variables. Our method accounts for the vertical structure of the front by computing composites relative to the actual front position at all height levels. We showcase the method using ERA5 reanalysis data for 50 cold fronts over Europe and apply it to thermodynamic and kinematic fields. Compared with conventional line-based composites, the new approach yields signals that are sharper and spatially more coherent. It also provides a visualization in which front-relative distances can be interpreted directly throughout the vertical column. Our method offers a general framework to study atmospheric processes in frontal environments and can be applied to different types and definitions of fronts.

papers.title: Mean Curvature Minimizing Foliations Of A Vector Field
papers.abstract: Streamline patterns are ubiquitous in nature. Prominent examples include white matter fibre tracts in the mammalian brain and arrangements of elongated cells, such as cardiomyocytes in the heart wall. It has been posited that such organisations foliate into locally smooth surfaces to optimise function. However, the recovery of these foliations from a single vector field aligned with the local orientation of the underlying sheets remains an open problem. We address this challenge by introducing a mathematical model of a sheet and developing an algorithm for sheet inference, from measurements of the oriented structures. Given an input vector field, our model estimates a second vector field that is orthonormal to it, while also requiring the Lie bracket of the two to vanish. To balance sheet likelihood against low surface area, we also reduce the mean curvature of the recovered local surface. We compute the first variation of an associated energy and provide a numerical method which admits an efficient, parallel implementation for sheet estimation. We demonstrate our approach on both synthetic and biological examples, motivated by applications to medical imaging. These include white matter fibre tracts from a brain atlas and confocal microscopy images of cleared heart wall tissue. For the latter we are able to reconstruct sheets aligned with local cardiomyocyte directions at unprecedented (micrometre) scale.

papers.title: ZERITH V2.5: From Predictive Power to Policy Learnability
papers.abstract:
When humans learn to manipulate an unfamiliar object, they may already be able to anticipate how its state will change while still being unable to control it skillfully. This gap between prediction and control motivates us to study how the priors acquired by video generation models can be used effectively by an action policy. We present ZERITH V2.5, a video-action model (VAM) in which the action policy reads intermediate features of a video generation model, and use it to study, under fixed demonstrations and a fixed total number of updates, what kind of predictive training improves subsequent action learning.
  We find that the way video predictive training is supervised affects subsequent action learning. In our experiments, adapting at many noise levels yields a large gain, while adapting only at the noise level used at deployment yields none. Weight-transfer experiments further show that the gain stays with the adapted weights when they remain in the video generation model and disappears when they are used only to initialize the action policy. Initial loss and gradient measurements at the start of joint training indicate that target-domain predictive training gives the video model a better starting state, making subsequent joint learning of prediction and action easier. Under matched data and training budgets, predictive adaptation improves control. We evaluate the complete policy on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, Meta-World MT50, and real-robot tasks.

authors.name: Alvin
authors.institution: University of Pembangunan Nasional Veteran Jawa Timur

authors.name: Yizhe Li
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

papers.title: Optimal universal sets for submodular functions
papers.abstract:
We resolve the question of deterministic non-adaptive algorithms for nonnegative submodular maximization: We prove that for every $n \geq 2$ and $\epsilon \in (0,\frac{1}{4})$, there is a polynomial-size family ${F}_{n,\epsilon}$, $|{F}_{n,\epsilon}| = n^{O(1/\epsilon^2 \log (1/\epsilon))}$, such that for every nonnegative submodular function $f:2^{[n]} \to {\bf R}$, $\max_{S \in {F}_{n,\epsilon}} f(S) \geq (1/4 - \epsilon) \max_{S \subseteq [n]} f(S)$. It is also easy to show that a factor better than $1/4$ cannot be achieved by any fixed polynomial-size family.
  A related result that we prove is that there is a distribution ${D}_{n,\epsilon}$ supported on polynomially many subsets of $[n]$ such that $(1 - \epsilon) {\bf E}_{R \sim {U}_n}[f(R)] \leq {\bf E}_{R \sim {D}_{n,\epsilon}}[f(R)] \leq {\bf E}_{R \sim {U}_n}[f(R)]$, where ${U}_n$ is the uniform distribution on $2^{[n]}$, and $f$ is any nonnegative submodular function. This is interesting in light of the fact that uniform convergence does not hold for submodular functions: Sampling polynomially many sets from ${U}_n$ and taking the empirical mean does not converge to the true expectation uniformly for all submodular functions.
  The construction of ${F}_{n,\epsilon}$ and ${D}_{n,\epsilon}$ is based on a new semidefinite extension of submodular functions: We show that the Goemans-Williamson rounding technique for a near-orthogonal arrangement of vectors gives a value close to the uniform expectation, and this rounding can be derandomized, since near-orthogonal vectors can be constructed in logarithmic dimension.

papers.title: Asteroseismology of AI Velorum: a prototype of high-amplitude delta Scuti stars
papers.abstract:
AI Velorum is exceptional among high-amplitude \delta Scuti (HADS) stars because of its multimode pulsations. Despite being an excellent target for asteroseismology, this prototype star has not been studied in detail.
  We determine the stellar parameters, age, and evolutionary stage of AI Vel, constrain envelope convection and convective core overshooting, and test three opacity data sets: OPAL, OP, and OPLIB.
  We analysed TESS photometry, ground-based Str\"omgren photometry, and HARPS spectroscopy. Modes were identified using photometric and spectroscopic methods, and empirical values of the non-adiabatic f-parameter were derived for both radial modes. Seismic modelling was performed within a Bayesian framework supported by Monte Carlo simulations.
  We confirm the radial nature of the two dominant modes and identify one non-radial mode as most likely an axisymmetric dipole or quadrupole mode. Within the explored parameter space, only OPAL models reproduce the observed position of AI Vel in the HR diagram, whereas OP and OPLIB models are too cool and underluminous. All seismic models favour inefficient envelope convection (mixing-length parameter alpha_{mlt}\lesssim 0.5). Including the non-radial mode substantially reduces the formal posterior uncertainties, but the ambiguity in its identification introduces additional model-dependent uncertainties. AI Vel is an evolved, slowly rotating star in the hydrogen shell-burning phase.
  Our results demonstrate the diagnostic power of combining pulsation frequencies with empirical f-parameters. The preference for OPAL opacities is consistent with results for several other HADS and SX Phoenicis stars but does not imply a general superiority of OPAL opacities.

papers.title: Curvature Gradients Turn Shear into Superflow in Supersolids
papers.abstract: Supersolids on curved surfaces are becoming experimentally accessible. We develop a Galilean-covariant effective field theory of supersolids on curved surfaces and show that gradients of Gaussian curvature couple lattice shear to compression with a strength fixed by the shear modulus and the curvature gradient. As a result, shear drives superflow. On spheroids this yields geometric selection rules and multiplet splittings; near mode crossings, weak deformations produce hybrids in which superfluid and lattice carry comparable kinetic energy, and shear becomes visible as a density response.

authors.name: Piotr Surowka

papers.title: Structure and Thermal Conductivity of Epoxy-Graphene Oxide Composites from 4.5 to 300 K
papers.abstract: The microscopic mechanisms of heat transport in structurally disordered polymer-carbon composites remain incompletely understood, particularly over the broad temperature range extending from cryogenic to ambient conditions. Here, we investigate the relationship between structural organization and thermal transport in epoxy-graphene oxide (GO) composites with nominal GO contents of 0.25-10 wt.% relative to the resin (0.21-6.1 wt.% of the total composite mass). X-ray diffraction reveals predominantly amorphous scattering without a detectable GO(001) reflection, suggesting substantial suppression of ordered GO stacking within the cured epoxy matrix. Raman spectroscopy confirms the increasing contribution of the carbon phase while revealing no pronounced changes in the characteristic vibrational bands of the epoxy network. Thermal-conductivity measurements (4.5-300 K) demonstrate that GO incorporation modifies the temperature dependence of heat transport rather than producing a simple conductivity enhancement. The experimental data are described by a phenomenological multichannel model comprising a temperature-independent plateau term and two or three effective Arrhenius-type contributions characterized by distinct temperature scales ranging from a few to several hundred kelvin. The low-temperature conductivity plateau observed at lower GO concentrations is no longer resolved in GO-6 and GO-10, indicating a qualitative change in the temperature dependence of heat transport. These results establish a correlation between structural organization and the redistribution of effective thermal-transport contributions in epoxy-GO composites, providing an experimental basis for further microscopic interpretation within the framework of unified vibrational thermal-transport theory.

papers.title: On a Secretary Problem with Two Equal-Sized Pools of Candidates
papers.abstract: This paper presents the solution of a secretary type problem where the decision maker observes a sequence of offers of two types. There are N objects of both types and these objects appear to the decision maker in random order. Objects can only be compared when they are of the same type. The objects of a given type that have already appeared can be ranked according to a complete order. Objects of different types are not comparable. On the appearance of an object, the decision maker must decide whether to accept that object (and thus stop searching) or irrevocably reject it (and thus continue searching). The goal of the decision maker is to accept an object that is the best of its type. The authors present the general form of the optimal policy and the asymptotical solution. The authors give a strong result describing whether an object of relative rank one should be accepted when the same number of objects of both types have been seen.

papers.title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.

authors.name: Yijia Ma
authors.institution: Chongqing University of Arts and Sciences

papers.title: 21Codec: Decoder-side Speaker Control for Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: We propose 21Codec, a streaming codec model with reduced recoverable speaker information from the token stream and decoder-side speaker control. Existing codec models infer speaker identity from token stream. Making them streamable is not sufficiently robust to speaker drift, because each chunk re-infers the identity from the local chunk context alone. Our adversarial speaker classifier and NANSY-style formant-shift data augmentation pushes the model to rely on the provided speaker embedding while reducing the recoverable speaker information from the token stream. We show that 21Codec can control speaker identity through the conditioning vector, and that the speaker identity is maintained across chunks during streaming. With the ability to control speaker identity even in mid-stream, 21Codec is a promising candidate for streaming TTS systems for better controllability of speaker identity.

papers.title: Location Matters: Layer-wise Prompt Conditioning for Voice--Style Disentanglement in Text-to-Speech
papers.abstract: Independent control of voice and emotional style characteristics of speech is a long-standing problem in text-to-speech (TTS) systems. We investigate how the conditioning location of voice and style prompts across TTS decoder layers affects the trade-off between preservation and expressiveness for voice identity and emotional style. We introduce a layer-dependent gated fusion mechanism and systematically study which layers should be influenced by which prompt type. Our findings show an asymmetric relationship. Voice benefits from early conditioning for identity preservation, while style benefits from early conditioning for expressiveness. Our findings provide practical guidance that helps neural network architects make an appropriate trade-off for the architecture of TTS systems according to their use cases.

papers.title: Coverage Governs Accuracy: When to Expand the Lexicon and When to Fall Back in Low-Resource Manchu OCR
papers.abstract: Character-level OCR for low-resource Manchu often produces near-miss spelling errors. Lexicon-constrained decoding can correct such errors with lexical knowledge, but a fixed dictionary cannot cover the many unseen word forms produced by agglutinative word formation. We study whether morphological expansion alleviates this limitation, and how the expansion size and confidence fallback affect recognition. We segment the training transcriptions with a dictionary-based stem list, extract roots and suffix chains from them, generate about 510k candidates, select the expansion size through frequency ranking on the validation set, and decompose accuracy under hard lexicon constraints into the product of coverage and in-lexicon precision. Across three CRNN training seeds, adding 250k candidates to a base dictionary of about 29k words raises the type accuracy on unseen combinations of seen roots from 63.6% to 86.3%, and overall token accuracy from 82.4% to 84.2%. Adding all candidates lowers overall token accuracy to 81.5%, showing that the coverage gain comes with a loss of in-lexicon precision. A further comparison shows that the base dictionary with confidence fallback performs best overall among the CRNN systems tested, reaching 76.1% type and 85.5% token accuracy and outperforming the expanded lexicon both with and without fallback. A Transformer recognizer shows similar trends. These results indicate that morphological expansion relieves the constraint of a fixed dictionary, but a larger lexicon does not guarantee better recognition; in the present low-resource Manchu OCR setting, a selective combination of reliable lexical constraints and open recognition is more effective.

papers.title: Object Pose: The Link between Weak Perspective, Paraperspective, and Full Perspective
papers.abstract: Recently, DeMenthon and Davis [4,5] proposed a method for determining the pose of a 3-D object with respect to a camera from 3-D to 2-D point correspondences. The method consists of iteratively improving the pose computed with a weak perspective camera model to converge, at the limit, to a pose estimation computed with a perspective camera model. In this paper we give an algebraic derivation of DeMenthon and Davis' method and we show that it belongs to a larger class of methods where the perspective camera model is approximated either at zero order (weak perspective) or first order (paraperspective). We describe in detail an iterative paraperspective pose computation method for both non coplanar and coplanar object points. We analyse the convergence of these methods and we conclude that the iterative paraperspective method (proposed in this paper) has better convergence properties than the iterative weak perspective method. We introduce a simple way of taking into account the orthogonality constraint associated with the rotation matrix. We analyse the sensitivity to camera calibration errors and we define the optimal experimental setup with respect to imprecise camera calibration. We compare the results obtained with this method and with a non-linear optimization method.

papers.title: SoU-RHS: Bayesian Structured Sparsity for Compact Architecture Recovery in CNNs
papers.abstract: Highly parameterized convolutional neural networks often achieve strong predictive performance, but their memory, computation, and deployment costs motivate the search for methods that recover compact architectures from large reference models. We propose SoU-RHS, a Bayesian structured-sparsity procedure that augments Regularized Horseshoe Shrinkage (RHS) with the so-called Sources of Uncertainty Sparse Global-Local mechanism (SoU-SGL). The resulting model sharpens the separation between active and inactive filters, providing an effective mechanism for architecture recovery. A key property of SoU-RHS is stability: across different overparameterized starting widths and under a reasonable range of pruning thresholds, it recovers compact architectures with similar total size and layer-wise allocation. This supports the interpretation that the procedure is identifying a compact structure adapted to the data, rather than merely compressing each initial model separately. Across standard image-classification benchmarks, SoU-RHS recovers substantially smaller architectures than deterministic structured-sparsity baselines, while maintaining competitive accuracy, achieving lower negative log-likelihood in every evaluated configuration and generally lower expected calibration error.

authors.name: Julyan Arbel

papers.title: Stability analysis of stochastic differential equations with the Koopman operator
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the stability of stochastic systems through the lens of the Koopman operator framework. In particular, we establish the connection between the convergence properties of the Koopman semigroup and specific stability properties of the underlying stochastic system. Moreover, we demonstrate that specific Koopman eigenfunctions capture stochastic attractivity properties and we illustrate these results with two numerical examples. This work mirrors existing Koopman operator-based stability results for deterministic systems and extends them to the stochastic framework.

papers.title: Quadratically Regularized Medians in Metric and Wasserstein Spaces
papers.abstract: In this paper, we introduce a new class of robust aggregators in Wasserstein spaces. After proving that all the commonly used Wasserstein barycenters are manipulable by one single corrupted input through a novel first-order optimality condition, we generalize both to the metric setting and to fractional exponents the concept of Lipschitz resilience introduced recently by Allouah, Guerraoui, Hoang and Villemaud. We proceed to show that adding a quadratic regularization to Wasserstein medians defined either in terms of the $W_1$-metric or linearized $W_2$-metric are resilient in that sense, by leveraging fine convexity estimates along generalized geodesics and flat interpolations. We finally show that iteratively solving the latter problem amounts to performing a Majorization-Minimization approximation of $W_2$-medians.

authors.name: Benoit Bonnet-Weill
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: GALA: Gallery-Level Alignment for Real-Life Vision Decoding from EEG
papers.abstract: Neural decoding of visual experience from electroencephalography (EEG) has achieved strong performance in intra-subject settings, but current methods fail to generalize across individuals: on the standard 200-way benchmark THINGS-EEG-2, top-1 accuracy drops from above 80% within subjects to about 32% for an unseen subject. Adapting a pre-trained encoder to new subjects and sessions typically requires labeled data, a bottleneck whose collection time severely limits practical device deployment. In a practical Brain-Computer Interface (BCI), however, the possible outcomes are known in advance and form a gallery of candidates, and the unlabeled EEG of the user accumulates as soon as the device is used. We propose a new setting, incremental transductive calibration, in which the decoder is calibrated regularly on all the unlabeled EEG received so far and on the known gallery, without any labels. This setting is closer to the conditions of a deployed BCI than the zero-shot and batch evaluations in current use. We evaluate it with a protocol in which queries arrive one at a time, with unknown and possibly unequal frequencies, and each query is decoded before it is used for calibration. In this setting, we introduce GALA : GAllery-Level Alignment, a label-free calibration method which registers the unlabeled EEG embeddings onto the gallery through shrinkage whitening, hubness correction and a Sinkhorn--Procrustes alignment with query frequencies estimated from the buffer, updated after every query. On THINGS-EEG-2, with a gallery of 200 images, it raises the top-1 accuracy on a new subject from 28% to 67% over 53 minutes of use. Across 60 evaluation settings that vary the gallery size, the query frequencies and the number of repetitions averaged per query, GALA is the most accurate label-free method in every setting, 6.6 points above the best competing method on average at the end of the stream.

papers.title: Approximation Algorithms for Product Query Optimization
papers.abstract: We study database query optimization for Cartesian products. This problem is equivalent to finding an optimal plan for multiplying non-negative integers. We call this problem multiplication ordering. We show that the problem has an FPTAS when the cost of a plan is the sum of all intermediate products; both in the case when the overall final product is counted and when it is not. We show that using the optimal solution to the well-known product partition problem does not always lead to an optimal plan, but we establish connections between the product partition and multiplication ordering problems. Finally, we prove that multiplication ordering is in PTIME (resp. \NP-complete) when integers are powers of a same base where the exponents are written in unary (resp. in binary).
