authors.institution: Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research At MIT

papers.title: On the Validity of Fisher Randomization Tests under the Weak Null
papers.abstract: Consider the problem of testing the Neyman weak null of no sample average treatment effect $H_{0N}:\tau = 0$ in randomized experiments with binary outcomes. Although the Fisher Randomization Test (FRT) is typically justified under Fisher's sharp null of no individual treatment effect, we show that it is finite-sample-valid for the weak null $H_{0N}$ in three common combinations of study design and test statistic: 1) balanced completely randomized experiments with the difference-in-means test statistic, 2) matched pairs experiments with the same test statistic, and 3) balanced Bernoulli randomized experiments with the centered Horvitz-Thompson test statistic. As an immediate corollary, Fisher's exact test in a balanced completely randomized experiment is valid under the weak null, and so is McNemar's test in a matched pairs experiment. Similar results hold for the one-sided null $H_0:\tau \leq 0$. Beyond balanced designs, we show that twice the one-sided FRT $p$-value with the same test statistics is valid under $H_{0N}$. In simulation experiments, the FRTs compare favorably to other exact procedures.

papers.title: Design and Modeling of Graded Base III-Nitride HBTs for High-Frequency Applications
papers.abstract: This work analyzes the high-frequency performance constraints of AlGaN/GaN heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs) and proposes a novel band-engineered graded base N-polar AlGaN/GaN HBT and evaluates the RF performances. Unlike conventional p-GaN base designs, we propose a graded base in the N-polar orientation which offers polarization-induced hole accumulation with quasi-electric field-assisted minority carrier transport. The proposed design simultaneously mitigates the longstanding current crowding, Webster effect, and conventional base resistance limitations. Using well-calibrated two-dimensional TCAD simulations, the proposed compositionally graded base HBT projects peak f_T/f_{max} of 190/200 GHz with a power density (V_{br}I_{max}/8 > 20 W/mm), offering a promising pathway toward simultaneous high-frequency and high-power GaN millimeter-wave electronics.

papers.title: Application of Pretrained Universal Machine Learning Force-Fields for Phase Transitions Prediction in ZrO2
papers.abstract: Pretrained universal machine-learning force fields can reduce the cost of finite-temperature molecular dynamics relative to density functional theory. However, most benchmarks test only static properties and do not assess whether these models reproduce the correct phase-transition sequence. Here, we benchmark ten open-source universal machine-learning force fields for zirconia (ZrO$_2$) using phonon dispersion calculations and variable-cell isothermal-isobaric molecular dynamics. Zirconia is a useful test because it has three thermodynamically stable crystalline phases prior to melting, following the sequence monoclinic-tetragonal-cubic. Four models reproduce this sequence: 7net-l3i5, MatterSim-v1.0.0-1M, MACE-mpa, and MACE-D3. Models with orthorhombic-tetragonal energy errors above about 10 meV/atom (7net-0, CHGNet, and MACE) instead produce an orthorhombic intermediate and predict monoclinic-orthorhombic-tetragonal-cubic-liquid upon heating. ORB-based models fail to sustain stable variable-cell dynamics because their phonon frequencies are compressed by 30-60% relative to the density functional theory reference. Across all ten models, two ground-state diagnostics predict finite-temperature behavior. Relative polymorph energetics should agree with the matched density functional theory reference within about 6 meV/atom, and the phonon spectrum should not show systematic softening. These diagnostics are practical screening metrics for assessing pretrained force fields for phase-transition predictions.

papers.title: ChainIT Transaction Truth: Stablecoins, Web3 Wallets, and Multi-Rail Commerce. A Zero-Trust Control Plane for Verified Identity, Organizational Authority, Runtime Compliance, Secure Wallet Execution, and Immutable Settlement Evidence
papers.abstract: Stablecoins can move value continuously across programmable networks, and Web3 wallets can authorize those transfers with cryptographic signatures, but neither capability, standing alone, establishes a complete commercial transaction. A blockchain may prove that a transaction satisfied protocol rules, and a wallet may prove that sufficient signing authority existed; neither proves who initiated the transaction, for which legal entity, under what current authority, against which current compliance evidence, on what exact instruction, or with what settlement and accounting outcome. We describe the ChainIT Transaction Truth Architecture, a zero-trust control, execution, and evidence architecture that places verified individual and organizational identity, the organizational authority record and authority policy of the ChainIT Authority Protocol, transaction-specific runtime compliance decisions, exact-digest approval, atomic capacity reservation, and a single-use Execution Authorization Credential in front of wallet execution, and that records settlement, reconciliation, and lifecycle evidence after the transaction. The architecture separates five boundaries: control of a key is not identity, identity is not organizational authority, authority is not compliance, compliance is not execution authority, and network confirmation is not complete commercial settlement. We describe wallet and custody profiles, including a multi-party computation (MPC) profile in which custody security is kept independent of business authority, stablecoin and Web3 evidence domains, layered finality, the U.S. stablecoin regulatory context as of September 2026, and a phased deployment in which pilot success requires that the control invariants hold under attack and failure.

papers.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
papers.abstract: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.

authors.name: Syamantak Kumar
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Equivariant Modeling with Polynomial Features via Minimal Homogeneous Generators
papers.abstract: We present a general framework for modeling and learning equivariant functions between finite dimensional semisimple real group representations, unifying constructions developed across many application areas. Our model is a linear combination of equivariant polynomial features whose coefficients are arbitrary learnable functions of invariant polynomial features. We take as features minimal homogeneous generators for the invariant algebra and the covariant module over the invariant algebra, up to prescribed degrees. We provide a Python package that automatically computes these features and fits the resulting models to training data. The algorithm for feature computation requires explicit isotypic decompositions of the input and output representations, along with explicit Clebsch-Gordan decompositions of the tensor product of irreducible representations, and achieves speedups over alternative methods in computational algebra. Numerical experiments in scientific modeling demonstrate the full learning pipeline and yield accurate predictors with few trainable parameters, using the model both for end-to-end prediction and within layers of larger architectures.

authors.name: Joe Kileel
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Are AGN Required? Updated Photoionization Models for Rest-UV Line Diagnostics in Reionization-era Galaxies
papers.abstract: Rest-frame ultraviolet (UV) emission lines in galaxies provide important probes of the ionizing radiation, chemical abundances, and interstellar medium conditions. Here, we consider UV emission-line diagnostics for galaxies with the observed physical properties of young, metal-poor stellar populations in the epoch of reionization. We study eight $z \sim 7$--$9$ galaxies using deep JWST/NIRSpec G140M and G395M spectroscopy from the Carbon-3 plus Oxygen survey. We measure rest-frame UV and optical emission lines, $\mathrm{C\,IV}$ $\lambda\lambda1548,1551$, $\mathrm{He\,II}$ $\lambda1640$, $\mathrm{O\,III]}$ $\lambda1666$, $\mathrm{C\,III]}$ $\lambda\lambda1907,1909$, $\mathrm{[O\,II]}$ $\lambda\lambda3727,3730$, H$\gamma$, $\mathrm{[O\,III]}$ $\lambda4364$, H$\beta$, and $\mathrm{[O\,III]}$ $\lambda\lambda4960,5008$. The galaxies have low oxygen abundances, $12+\log(\mathrm{O/H})=7.50$-$7.90$, low C/O ratios, $\mathrm{C/O}=0.10$-$0.32$, and high electron densities, $n_e(\mathrm{C\,III]})=(1.9-4.9)\times10^4\,\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$. We compute Cloudy photoionization models using BPASS and BC03 stellar populations to test how lower C/O and higher gas density affect the UV diagnostics. We find that reducing C/O and increasing the gas density shift the star-forming grids into regions conventionally classified as composite or AGN-like. We therefore conclude that positions within these regions alone do not establish the presence of an AGN in the galaxies studied here. However, some lines remain enigmatic, including strong $\mathrm{He\,II}$, which is not reproduced by the updated models. These results highlight the need for UV diagnostic boundaries that account for the abundance patterns and gas conditions of galaxies during the epoch of reionization.

authors.name: Anthony J. Taylor
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

authors.name: Steven L. Finkelstein
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
papers.abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

papers.title: Phase-Controlled Time-Dependent Modal Analysis of Vortex-Gust Interaction with a Cylinder Wake
papers.abstract: A vortex gust interacting with the periodic wake of a circular cylinder at $Re=100$ is studied using time-dependent dynamic mode decomposition with phase control (tDMDpc). To examine the phase dependence of the wake and lift responses, the same vortex gust is imposed at $64$ shedding phases. For these phase-controlled responses, proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) with time-independent spatial modes characterizes departures from the periodic wake, whereas tDMDpc resolves evolving structures and the frequency and growth rate of the fundamental mode. In this decomposition, the approaching gust is mainly captured by the zero-frequency mode. During the encounter, however, gust-related structures develop in the fundamental mode and persist near the cylinder as the gust convects downstream. The fundamental-mode coefficient magnitude is nearly uniform across phases at arrival but becomes phase dependent afterward. Consistent with this phase dependence, the near-wake vorticity amplitude of the fundamental conjugate pair decreases at $\alpha=\pi/2$ and increases at $\alpha=3\pi/2$ relative to the respective pre-encounter values, matching the inward and outward departures of the POD trajectories. To connect these structures to the cylinder lift, modal pressure and viscous stresses are integrated over the cylinder surface. The zero-frequency contribution carries most of the lift variation at arrival, whereas the fundamental conjugate pair dominates later oscillations. Phase averaging cannot separate these contributions because the fundamental oscillations no longer cancel across phases after the encounter. Their separation reveals that opposing contributions can yield nearly zero total lift despite an appreciable fundamental contribution. As the wake recovers, the lift amplitude approaches its undisturbed value, but a phase shift persists.

papers.title: Bias-Only Training Dynamics in ReLU Networks
papers.abstract: Neural networks with randomly initialized, fixed weights and trainable biases are universal approximators, yet the dynamics of bias-only training remain largely unexplored. We study these dynamics in one-hidden-layer ReLU networks through activation codes, the binary patterns of active neurons that partition the input space into convex polyhedral regions. We show that the gradients with respect to the biases depend on each input only through its activation code, and hence the training dynamics can be characterized with these codes. In particular, as long as the activation codes remain fixed, training reduces to a linear least-squares problem with the codes as features. Training can then be understood as a sequence of least-squares problems, with transitions occurring when neurons change their activation states. We show that the fraction of switching neurons vanishes as the network widens, and the training dynamics approach those of linear least squares on the initial activation codes in the infinite-width limit. Our experiments support these theoretical findings, showing that while activation switches can noticeably affect training in narrower networks, their relative frequency and the associated changes in the dynamics diminish as the width increases.

papers.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
papers.abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

papers.title: Restoring Power Fairly: Equitable Resource Allocation in Post-Disaster Grid Recovery
papers.abstract: Post-disaster power restoration requires allocating limited repair and power resources across affected communities, creating a fundamental tension between restoring service efficiently and providing equitable access to electricity. We develop an optimization framework incorporating horizontal fairness, which promotes comparable service across affected communities, and vertical fairness, which accounts for differences in community vulnerability. The framework integrates repair-crew scheduling with an approximation of power-system operations, including distributed generation and solar-plus-storage resources. It supports vulnerability-aware prioritization while protecting specified fractions of bus-level service under a horizontal-fairness reference plan and limiting the increase in restoration cost. Structural results characterize when the two fairness benchmarks can be attained simultaneously in an aggregate allocation model and provide a sufficient condition under which improving vertical fairness requires changing discrete decisions in the full restoration model. Using the IEEE 33-bus test system, we show that equitable restoration operates through two interconnected mechanisms: reconnecting isolated areas and allocating limited power within connected areas. In the tested setting, selected vulnerability-aware solutions attain both fairness benchmarks at a lower cost than their horizontal-fairness reference plan. The results also show that stronger emphasis on horizontal fairness can yield lower efficiency losses than intermediate fairness settings, with an identical-demand comparison illustrating the role of demand heterogeneity. The framework helps decision makers identify the operational sources of service disparities and evaluate how repair priorities, power allocation, and allowable cost increases affect the opportunities to reduce them.

papers.title: Structure-Preserving PHS RBF-FD Methods for Schrodinger Equations
papers.abstract: We develop and analyze a structure-preserving polyharmonic-spline radial-basis-function finite-difference (PHS RBF-FD) method for the two-dimensional Schr\"odinger equation with homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. The method combines a 29-point complete-shell stencil with odd boundary reflection to construct a symmetric discrete Laplacian. Unlike conventional nearest-neighbor RBF-FD discretizations, whose independently selected stencils do not generally preserve global symmetry, the proposed construction admits an exact discrete sine eigenbasis. We derive a Fourier-symbol representation and establish a sufficient criterion for strict negative definiteness, verified for the \(r^7+\mathbb P_4\) and \(r^{11}+\mathbb P_5\) formulations using validated coefficient calculations. The resulting symmetric spatial operator preserves discrete mass and energy under exact semidiscrete evolution, while fully discrete conservation depends on the time integrator. Numerical experiments examine kernel selection, dispersion, convergence, symmetry defects, and computational cost. Comparisons with conventional RBF-FD and fourth-order finite differences include exact Fourier modes and a variable-potential Schr\"odinger problem with an independently refined spectral reference. The \(r^{11}+\mathbb P_5\) formulation provides favorable accuracy in the tested problems while maintaining the desired spatial structure. The analysis establishes a connection between boundary treatment, global operator symmetry, and structure preservation in localized PHS discretizations.

papers.title: Reflections on Thiele, Schur, and Continued Fractions
papers.abstract: We survey several classical continued-fraction constructions from a common point of view centered on linear-fractional transformations, interpolation, and the recurrence relations they generate. Beginning with Thiele's interpolation algorithm, we trace how similar mechanisms reappear in the Schur algorithm, Wall's continued fractions, and multipoint Nevanlinna--Pick interpolation. Particular attention is paid to the emergence of $R_{II}$-type continued fractions, which arise naturally as even parts of Thiele continued fractions, and to the associated pencils of tridiagonal matrices. A detour through Euler's continued-fraction formula illustrates how rational Nevanlinna functions lead naturally to finite $R_{II}$-pencils, while the Schur algorithm is related to Wall pencils and, through a different reorganization, to CMV matrices. We also discuss a modified Schur transformation that removes an interpolation condition at a pair of symmetric points, which leads to a linear pencil of two Hermitian tridiagonal matrices. Finally, we indicate how periodically occurring interpolation nodes at infinity convert $R_{II}$-pencils into ordinary banded matrices, suggesting a connection with GMP matrices.

papers.title: Buoyancy-induced transitions in mixed convective flow past a heated square cylinder
papers.abstract: The effect of aiding buoyancy on flow past a square cylinder has previously been shown to suppress vortex shedding above a critical Richardson number (Ri), transitioning from unsteady to steady flow. Building on this, the present study uses two-dimensional direct numerical simulations (DNS) of vertically upward flow past a heated square cylinder to examine two buoyancy-induced transitions for a range of Ri and Reynolds number (Re). The secondary flow induced by buoyant force enhances positive entrainment in the momentum-deficit region aft of the cylinder, thereby suppressing vortex shedding. At higher Ri, this buoyant flow continues to gain downstream momentum, leading to a far-field plume-like instability. Extended domain simulations show that the far-field transition depends on the downstream distance available for buoyancy-driven disturbances to grow. Increasing Re delays near-field suppression but advances far-field instability. A local-flow analysis shows that a Reynolds number based on local mean velocity and plume width substantially improves the collapse of the far-field instability onset, while the corresponding plume-based Strouhal number also exhibits an approximate collapse across the investigated cases. Correlations for drag, surface-averaged Nusselt number, and far-field frequency are proposed using a mixed-convective velocity scale. Linear stability analysis (LSA) about the two-dimensional base flow captures both transitions as Hopf bifurcations and accurately predicts the dominant frequencies and finite-domain transition thresholds observed in DNS. The corresponding eigenmodes reveal localized oscillatory structures that shift downstream with increasing Ri. These results demonstrate the dual role of buoyancy in stabilizing the near wake while destabilizing the far field.

papers.title: Ultimate3D: Teaching Multimodal LLMs 3D Camera-Object Relations by Large-Scale Visual Instruction Data
papers.abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) struggle with accurately capturing camera-object relations, especially for object orientation, camera viewpoint, and camera shots. This stems from the fact that existing MLLMs are trained on images with limited diverse camera-object relations and corresponding textual descriptions. To address this, we propose a synthetic generation pipeline to create large-scale 3D visual instruction datasets. Our framework takes 3D assets as input and uses rendering and diffusion-based image generation models to create photorealistic images preserving precise camera-object relations. Additionally, large language models (LLMs) are used to generate text prompts for guiding visual instruction tuning and controlling image generation. We create Ultimate3D, a large-scale 3D-grounded 2D visual instruction dataset. Ultimate3D consists of 240K VQAs with precise camera-object annotations, and corresponding benchmark. MLLMs fine-tuned on our proposed dataset outperform commercial models by a large margin, achieving an average accuracy improvement of 29.7% on camera-object relation recognition tasks. Our code, dataset, and benchmark will contribute to broad MLLM applications.

authors.name: Liu He
authors.institution: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

authors.name: Min Sun
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Mineral Processing

papers.title: Gaia's promise to detect compact-object binaries II: Predictions for dormant neutron star binaries in DR4 and beyond
papers.abstract: With the fourth data release (DR4) from Gaia imminent, we predict neutron star (NS) binaries with luminous companions (LCs) expected to be detectable in DR4 and the final data release (DR5). We create realistic synthetic populations of NS--LC binaries in the Milky Way using COSMIC, assuming (a) observationally motivated initial distributions of binary properties, (b) metallicity and location dependent star formation history of the MW adopted from the FIRE-2 galaxy m12i, and (c) all relevant binary interaction physics, with the rapid and delayed supernova prescriptions. We estimate the detectable NS--LC population using an approximate Gaia\ selection function based on projected orbital size of the LC as well as gaiamock, which emulates Gaia's multi-epoch astrometry and orbit-fitting pipeline- both after taking into account extinction and reddening. Across supernova models and statistical fluctuations, the former (gaiamock) pipeline predicts $\sim14$--$29$ ($\sim1$--$8$), $4500$--$4700$ ($100$--$110$), and $4800$--$5000$ ($300$--$380$) detectable NS--LC binaries in DR3, DR4, and DR5, respectively. While the orbital-size based pipeline brackets the DR3 yield of NS--LC candidates, the gaiamock prediction falls short, suggesting uncertainties in the modeled binary evolution or contributions from other formation channels. DR4 is expected to directly shed light on the the relative importance of detectable NS--LC binaries from isolated binary evolution vis a vis other channels such as dynamical formation. Interestingly, our models suggest that future releases will also include $22^{+7}_{-5}\ (13^{+5}_{-4})$ and $124^{+14}_{-15}\ (53^{+10}_{-6})$ gaiamock-detectable pulsar--MS binaries in DR4 and DR5, respectively, for the rapid (delayed) model, which are prime targets for radio follow-up.

papers.title: Extremal Projectors and the Virasoro Algebra
papers.abstract: Extremal projectors are universal operators projecting onto the highest weight space in a representation. Their existence and uniqueness (as formal series) are known for a broad range of Lie superalgebras and quantum groups. We consider a class of Lie superalgebras that contains reductive finite-dimensional Lie algebras as well as the Virasoro algebra. We prove the existence and uniqueness of an extremal projector for this class. The existence proof is given in terms of a recursive algorithm which can be used to compute the coefficients. To illustrate the method, we compute the terms for the Virasoro extremal projector up to order 6. Furthermore, we formulate a conjecture for the denominators of the truncated extremal projector of the Virasoro algebra. We provide symbolic computational evidence up to order 6 and prove a weaker version of the conjecture.

papers.title: NEXONN: Advancing the NEXOTRANS Exoplanet Atmospheric Retrieval Framework with Transformer-Based Neural Posterior Estimation for JWST Transmission Spectroscopy of WASP-39b
papers.abstract: The James Webb Space Telescope is delivering unprecedented constraints on exoplanet atmospheres, but computationally intensive Bayesian retrievals challenge the transition from individual planets to population-level studies of planetary formation and evolution. We introduce NEXONN, a transformer-conditioned normalizing-flow framework within NEXOTRANS that enables rapid atmospheric posterior estimation with uncertainty quantification. Incorporating PandExo-based JWST noise, we benchmark NEXONN against PyMultiNest using simulated spectra and JWST observations of WASP-39 b (0.6-12 microns). For simulated MIRI/LRS data, eight posteriors achieve a mean overlap of 80.32%. Retrievals of combined NIRISS, NIRSpec, and MIRI observations yield consistent atmospheric properties. For the full dataset, NEXONN infers C/O = 0.82 (+0.01/-0.02) and [M/H] = 1.13 (+0.04/-0.04), compared with PyMultiNest values of 0.80 (+0.03/-0.01) and 1.19 (+0.05/-0.03). Divergence metrics, Wasserstein distances, posterior overlaps, and coverage tests assess posterior fidelity and uncertainty calibration, revealing parameter-dependent differences. Once trained, NEXONN performs posterior inference within seconds, enabling scalable population studies of exoplanet atmospheric composition, formation, and evolution.

papers.title: Graded version of local-global principle for Steinberg and Chevalley groups
papers.abstract: In this article, an analog of a graded version of Quillen-Suslin's local-global principle was established for Steinberg groups $St(\Phi,-)$ and Chevalley groups $G(\Phi,-)$ over a reduced irreducible root system $\Phi$.

papers.title: Confidence-Based Materials Data Quality Assessment via Domain Knowledge and Graph-Structured Learning
papers.abstract: The rapid development of materials machine learning relies on large-scale, heterogeneous datasets, yet model reliability is often compromised by imperfect data from diverse experiments, simulations, and database integration. Real-world materials databases may contain measurement errors, failed calculations, missing or duplicate records, and hidden violations of physicochemical constraints. Such problems are difficult to identify because corrupted samples may remain statistically plausible rather than appearing as explicit outliers. In this paper, we propose a confidence-based materials data quality assessment framework that integrates domain knowledge with graph-structured learning. Data quality is formulated as a continuous confidence estimation problem rather than a binary anomaly identification task, enabling sample-level assessment and historical-reference-based batch comparison. A nine-dimensional feature-quality prior and duplicate-aware sample initialization are calibrated using materials domain rules and statistical evidence. Confidence is further refined through sample-feature bipartite graph propagation and weakly supervised graph attention, while a Memory-GAT module provides historical reference scoring. Experiments on 23 ODDS benchmark datasets show that the generic module achieves an average AUC-ROC of 0.866. In five repeated mixed-contamination experiments on mp\_20, rule calibration improves HistGradientBoostingRegressor test $R^2$ from $0.538\pm0.008$ to $0.616\pm0.014$. Graph refinement increases average precision from $0.943\pm0.004$ to 0.953\pm0.004$, while the rule-calibrated configuration has the highest mean test $R^2$ among the evaluated screening configurations. Five repeated MACE subset experiments further show an increase in $R^2$ from $0.590\pm0.053$ to $0.880\pm0.027$ after rule-based screening.

authors.name: Ji Zhang
authors.institution: National Institute for Communicable Disease Control and Prevention

papers.title: Variable Length Diffuse Everything: Arbitrary Length Generative Modeling on Arbitrary State Spaces
papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow-based generative models have achieved remarkable results across diverse applications, but most assume data of fixed-dimension/length. Meanwhile, real-world problems such as layout generation often involve variable-length, multimodal data, such as continuous bounding box coordinates paired with discrete types. Existing methods typically address variable length by padding data to a fixed size or by introducing specialized objectives to model lengths explicitly, adding complexity and limiting generality. We propose Variable Length Diffuse Everything (VL-DE), a simple and general framework for variable-length multimodal generation on arbitrary state spaces. Instead of padding, VL-DE handles variable length through an insertion-based mechanism grounded in a principled theoretical framework, yielding a tractable training objective. In addition, by utilizing the fact that VL-DE is based on a generator with an additive form, we develop a higher-order sampler by appropriately handling the time dependence. Extensive experiments on layout and molecule generation demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

authors.name: Kevin Rojas
authors.institution: Universidad Católica de Santiago de Guayaquil

authors.name: Felix X. -F. Ye
authors.institution: University at Albany, State University of New York

papers.title: Expressiveness and Convertibility of Rule-Based Access Control Policies
papers.abstract: Rule-based access control models such as attribute-based access control support flexible policies based on rules with conditional expressions. The design choices in those models such as what is allowed in the conditional expressions or supporting deny rules may impact the range of the policies that are expressible. In this paper, we propose a systematic approach to investigate the semantics and compare the expressiveness of various rule-based access control models that can be built based on different design choices of rule structure and rule composition. Furthermore, we investigate the problem of convertibility of a policy from one rule-based model to another. This question is critical for policy migration to ensure that a given policy instance in a source model is expressible in a target model. Some of our major results in this paper include well-formedness properties for policy semantics, expressiveness hierarchy of models, and computational complexity of policy convertibility, all having important implications on the design and application of rule-based access control policy models.

authors.name: Amir Masoumzadeh
authors.institution: University at Albany, State University of New York

authors.name: Paliath Narendran
authors.institution: University at Albany, State University of New York

papers.title: Same Model, Different People: Numerical Execution Contracts and the Reproducibility of Fairness Audits
papers.abstract: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, but the arithmetic that evaluates it is part of that function. This study holds the model, records, threshold and audit code fixed and varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers. Tier 1 changes only how products and sums are computed, with the serialized weights byte-identical, and is the causal test of arithmetic. Tier 2 runs reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16 compute, FP8 and 8-bit weights), which can also round weights and change engines and kernels, so its effects belong to the configuration. It audits three tabular model families and two open-weight language models (4B and 24B parameters) on four public tasks, including hospital readmission, on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. Tier 1 changed decisions near the threshold, and which ones depended on the GPU and its software stack, but no verdict under the prespecified, unweighted tests. Tier 2 configurations changed more decisions and some diagnostic verdicts, but no four-fifths verdict. Serving the 24B model with vLLM FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its strict FP32 reference failed: its demographic-parity and equalized-odds gaps fell from 0.0567 and 0.0515 to 0.0417 and 0.0394, against a diagnostic tolerance of 0.05. At the reference's selection count FP8 failed demographic parity, and no reading gave its equalized-odds change a paired interval excluding zero. The declared audit depends on the configuration; FP8 is not shown to be fairer. At the frozen thresholds, every pass-fail verdict a configuration changed had a sampling interval containing its criterion. It proposes an audit stability protocol in which the auditor declares contracts, groups, weights and tests before scoring and records each verdict's range over them apart from its sampling uncertainty.

papers.title: Diffusion Models are Provably Efficient Priors for Sparse Recovery
papers.abstract: Diffusion models have transformed generative modeling through their ability to capture and generate samples from complex data distributions. This success has spurred substantial interest in using pretrained diffusion models as expressive priors for highly ill-posed inverse problems in imaging and sensing. Despite strong empirical performance, theoretical understanding of this approach remains limited: existing guarantees are often asymptotic or entail prohibitive computational costs in the worst case. In this paper, we address this gap by studying sparse recovery from a small number of linear measurements, a classical problem in compressed sensing. We show that, given an accurate diffusion model capturing a sparsity-promoting Bernoulli-Gaussian prior, a likelihood-guided annealed Langevin sampler provably recovers the sparse signal in polynomial time with near-optimal sample complexity for a broad family of random and deterministic sensing matrices. When the signal is indeed drawn from the postulated prior, we further establish total variation guarantees for posterior sampling after a final denoising step. These results lay a theoretical foundation for statistically and computationally efficient inverse solvers with diffusion priors.

papers.title: An Empirical Study of Visual Artifacts in Pull Request Descriptions
papers.abstract: Reviewers rely on pull request (PR) descriptions to understand what a change does, yet some changes, such as UI updates or runtime behavior, are hard to convey in text alone. PR authors attach visual artifacts to fill this gap, but how often they do so, what they show, and whether they change how a PR is reviewed remain unknown. We present a large-scale study of visual artifacts in GitHub PR descriptions. From 6,505,113 closed PRs in 5,012 repositories, we built VisPR, a dataset of 2,473,892 English, human-authored PRs from 647 repos where visual artifacts are an established practice. Of these, 329,185 (13.3%) are visual PRs, i.e., their descriptions contain at least one visual artifact (479,974 in total). By manually labeling a sample of 1,113 visual artifacts from 891 merged visual PRs, we derived two taxonomies: 11 content types capturing what developers show and six purposes capturing why they include visual artifacts. The dominant content type is Interaction & State, which shows how the interface responds to user actions. its share rises from 37.0% of images to 63.5% of GIFs and 79.7% of videos, whereas about a quarter of images (23.4%) show text such as logs, code, or error messages . Compared with 1,782 merged non-visual PRs matched on repository, PR type, and change size, visual PRs receive 43% more review comments and 17% more reviewers, and take 72% longer from first response to merge, time to merge and churn-normalized review efficiency do not differ significantly. LLM-assisted classification of 10,031 review comments in two groups shows that review centers on code in both, but comments on visual PRs address how the UI looks or behaves twice as often (6.4% vs.3.3%), and visual-output fixes after review are about four times as common (4.7% vs. 1.2% of PRs). Visual artifacts are thus associated with closer scrutiny of what users see, not with an overall faster review.

authors.name: Yuan Tian
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology Beijing

papers.title: Einstein Constants and Smooth Topology, Revisited
papers.abstract: In 1997, Catanese and the first author showed that, for every $m\geq 2$, there exists a smooth closed $4m$-manifold that admits both a $\lambda > 0$ Einstein metric and a $\lambda < 0$ Einstein metric; thus, the sign of the Einstein constant $\lambda$ is not always determined by the differential topology of the host compact manifold. This result was later improved by R\u{a}sdeaconu and \c{S}uvaina (2009), who showed that there are in fact at least $\binom{m + 3}{3}$ topologically distinct such examples in each dimension $4m$, $m\geq 2$. In this note, we further improve these earlier results by showing that infinitely many topologically distinct examples of this phenomenon actually occur in dimension $4m$, for each $m\geq 2$.

authors.name: Mingyang Li
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: A structure-based model of the bacterial chemosensory array reveals how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes sensory responses
papers.abstract: We introduce a structure-based Ising model of the bacterial chemosensory array to investigate how the scaffolding protein CheW tunes signaling responses. The model couples the activity states of core signaling units and of CheW subunits within hexameric rings on a lattice with the structure observed in cryoEM experiments. Recent experiments show that increasing CheW participation in hexameric rings raises response cooperativity in non-adapting cells and sensitivity in adaptation-proficient cells. Our lattice model quantitatively reproduces both effects, while mean-field theory shows that CheW increases the effective coupling between core units, sharpening the response in both cell types. The statistics of CheW placement (complete hexameric rings versus random distribution) substantially alter how responses vary with CheW abundance. Moreover, different coupling strengths can yield the same static response yet markedly different activity fluctuations and dynamics. CheW abundance further controls a crossover from relaxational to oscillatory fluctuations, whose location depends on the spatial distribution of CheW. These dynamical signatures, including oscillations predicted near native CheW levels, are testable by single-cell dynamics measurements. Combined with CheW titration and our modeling results, these measurements can probe the array's assembly dynamics and allosteric couplings. Beyond the chemosensory array, our approach can generalize to other large protein complexes, providing a framework to study the functional role of scaffolding proteins and allosteric interfaces in signal processing.

authors.name: David Hathcock
authors.institution: IBM Research - Thomas J. Watson Research Center

papers.title: AGAMOTTO: An AI-Enabled Framework for Time-Critical Tactical Course-of-Action Evaluation and Generation
papers.abstract: Current command and control (C2) platforms lack integrated simulation capabilities that would allow commanders to dynamically explore courses of action (COAs) during live operations. This paper presents ongoing research and contributions to the development of AGAMOTTO (Advanced Guidance and Analytics for Military Operations, Tactical Threats, and Outcomes) as part of the overarching NGC2 program, which advances the Army's efforts to modernize C2 systems, such as the Tactical Assault Kit (TAK). The paper outlines the current design, preliminary findings, and the remaining research tasks, with an emphasis on how the completed work will support tactical decision-making in future time-constrained environments. While the full system is still under development, initial development and results demonstrate the feasibility of AGAMOTTO. Early experiments highlight both the potential benefits and practical constraints of deploying AI-enabled tools in operational settings, and introduce lessons learned and a viable training strategy to make AI-generated COAs feasible in tactical scenarios.

papers.title: The Value Semantics Layer: Enabling Machine-Understandable Databases for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.

papers.title: From geometric curvature to effective backgrounds: a dictionary for Dirac fermions in one, two and three spatial dimensions
papers.abstract: Dirac equation on curved backgrounds can be rewritten as a flat-space equation in which geometry appears as a tensorial Fermi velocity together with a set of background fields. We derive this correspondence from a single Clifford-algebra identity and follow it through one, two, and three spatial dimensions. Once the spin connection is written in terms of Ricci rotation coefficients, only two contractions can occur. The trace produces a term with the index structure of a vector potential in every dimensionality; it enters with an imaginary factor i and is precisely the term that keeps the operator Hermitian when the Fermi velocity depends on position. The totally antisymmetric contraction produces an object that depends on the number of indices available to the Levi-Civita symbol: a trace on a line, a pseudoscalar mass on a surface, and an axial vector potential in a volume. Neither contraction is invariant under local rotations of the frame, and we give the transformation laws. On a surface, the curl of the trace term can always be removed by a frame rotation, while its divergence is proportional to the Gaussian curvature. We apply the correspondence to a Gaussian bump, where the local density of states at the center falls below its flat value and obeys a closed form at low energy; to a wire, where a nonuniform lapse binds states inside the gap and a nonuniform velocity cannot; to stationary frames on a surface, where a circulating drag shifts the Dirac mass locally with either sign; and to twisted and rotating frames in a volume, where the axial term takes the form of a chiral chemical potential produced by the frame alone, or separates Weyl nodes in a rotating sample. We separate the geometric contribution from the lattice pseudogauge field that dominates the response of strained samples

authors.name: Alfredo Raya
authors.institution: Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolás de Hidalgo

papers.title: Linking Dynamical Time Scales and Experimental Design to Parameter Identifiability from Time-Series Observations
papers.abstract: Parameter estimation in chaotic models often relies on prescribed summary statistics, whose ability to constrain parameters may be difficult to establish in advance. Different parameters influence different features and time scales of the dynamics, so the record length and sampling interval needed to constrain them may differ. We choose to learn a representation directly from the trajectory and use it as our summary statistic. The recurrent encoder that produces this representation is trained jointly with a conditional normalizing flow for amortized posterior estimation. We use the Lorenz-63 and two-scale Lorenz-96 systems to investigate how inference depends on the observed variables, record length and sampling interval, and compare our results with the state-of-the-art Calibrate--Emulate--Sample method. In Lorenz-96, learned summaries of a 2 model-time-unit (MTU) record achieve estimation skill comparable to prescribed second-moment statistics from substantially longer records for several parameters. Fast-process parameters remain weakly constrained by slow-variable records across the tested 2 to 100 MTU windows, while adding fast-field averages improves their recovery from 2 MTU. Coarser sampling weakens inference from fast-field observations, but longer coverage can partly compensate. Once trained for a given observation setting, the estimator we develop returns posteriors for compatible records without further model integration. These proof-of-concept results illustrate how data-driven learning of summaries can be used to inform the design of observations in dynamical systems.

papers.title: Degree-three Euclidean spanning trees within a factor of 1.514 of the minimum
papers.abstract: For every finite point set $X$ in a Euclidean space of arbitrary dimension, we prove that there is a spanning tree of maximum degree three and total length at most $(757/500)\MST(X)=1.514\MST(X)$, where $\MST(X)$ denotes the unrestricted minimum spanning-tree length. More strongly, for any root and any finite list of other points, there is a Hamiltonian path starting at the root whose length is at most $1.514$ times the sum of the root-to-point distances. The proof follows the rooted-path and variable-block framework used in earlier work, and applies Young's weighted-distance inequality to explicit rational mixtures of paths. Eight ordered radius regions cover the normalized domain. Their local estimates require only 29 vertex comparisons, all certified by rational arithmetic. The cover uses the three thresholds $1/4$, $3/8$, and $1/2$; its largest block has nine vertices. We give complete proofs of the normalization transfer, the global induction, and the terminal cases with zero or one actual tail point. We also give a fixed-dimensional cross-polytope lower bound, present Zbarsky's orthogonal simplex-cluster construction in explicit coordinates, and compare their finite-dimension bounds. The base cases complete the upper-bound argument before the lower-bound constructions are presented.

papers.title: ReLoco: Unified Humanoid Locomotion and Fall Recovery via Behavior-Conditioned Motion Priors
papers.abstract: Humanoid robots must recover from falls and resume commanded motion to sustain locomotion. Learning these behaviors in one policy requires supervision that accommodates both upright movement and ground-contact recovery. We present ReLoco, a framework that uses behavior-conditioned adversarial motion priors to learn locomotion, get-up from arbitrary fallen postures, and command resumption within one proprioceptive policy. During training, robot posture selects the expert pool and conditions a shared discriminator with two behavior-specific outputs. Task rewards and shared regularization support command tracking and recovery, while temporary assistance facilitates exploration. A simulation-based refinement stage supplies robot-executed motion references for this supervision. Ablations examine conditional supervision, output separation, and reference quality under matched settings. At a common training iteration, the full policy achieves $96.80\%$ independent get-up success and $96.96\%$ push-recovery success, including command resumption. Its torso planar velocity root-mean-square error is $0.1266$~m/s, $14.7\%$ lower than the conditional single-output variant, with similar joint-angle discrepancy measured by dynamic time warping. Deployment on the 64.5-kg Tiangong~3.0 humanoid demonstrates walking, running, get-up, and locomotion resumption after falls using one proprioceptive actor, without controller switching or on-robot policy fine-tuning.

authors.name: Lequn Fu
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Xiao Li
authors.institution: Southwest University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Freeforward4d: Annotation-free feed-forward 4d reconstruction of driving scenes
papers.abstract: Feed-forward 4D reconstruction enables efficient creation of renderable driving scenes for autonomous driving simulation. However, most existing methods rely heavily on dataset-provided cameras, LiDAR depth, or 3D box annotations, limiting their applicability to unannotated driving videos. Pretrained visual models can predict cameras, depth, and object tracks from RGB alone, but their geometry is mutually inconsistent: multi-view predictions come in short windows with independent scales and frames, while monocular depth is metric only per image. Our key insight is that, once reconciled into a single metric frame, these priors can replace dataset annotations for feed-forward 4D reconstruction. We present \textbf{FreeForward4D}, which calibrates overlapping prediction windows against monocular metric depth and registers them into one frame across time. On this geometry, 2D tracks are associated across cameras in 3D, and objects move through hierarchical motion that combines a shared object velocity with local Gaussian corrections, so that both training and inference use only RGB videos. On Waymo, FreeForward4D achieves 27.66 dB PSNR and 0.836 SSIM while recovering metric-scale cameras and depth without scale alignment. It surpasses STORM, SLARM-F, UFO, DGGT, and StreetForward, which rely on dataset annotations, in full-image PSNR and attains the best RGB fidelity on 8-second windows. RGB-only fine-tuning further adapts the framework to nuScenes and Argoverse 2. Code will be released.

authors.institution: Weifang University of Science and Technology

authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: A Dynamic Model and Stability Analysis of a Grid-Interactive Data Center
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of data centers is creating new interactions between computational workload and power-system dynamics, with potentially significant implications for grid stability. We develop a four-dimensional nonlinear dynamical model of a data center campus interconnected with the bulk power system through a modified Single Machine Infinite Bus system. The model couples generator swing dynamics with a fluid-limit model of computational workload backlog and a grid-interactive data center power controller that incorporates both frequency feedback and computational backpressure. This formulation captures the coupled evolution of generator frequency, rotor angle, computational workload, and data center power consumption, providing a framework for studying the stability implications of flexible data center operation.

authors.name: Xinyang Zhou
authors.institution: Xi'an University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Total Positivity Properties of American Options
papers.abstract: Call option prices, viewed as functions of strike and time-to-expiration, are totally positive of order 2 (TP2) if the ratio of the price of a higher-strike call to a lower-strike call increases with time-to-expiration. A corresponding property applies to put option prices. Prior work has developed conditions for these properties to hold for European options; here we establish these properties for American options. The key condition we require is that log returns on the underlying asset have a log-concave density. Gaussian densities provide an important special case. Within our framework, we show that total positivity properties hold more broadly for American than European options. Empirically, we find that violations of TP2 properties are infrequent, typically small, and reverse quickly. Trades that bet against violations achieve high hit rates. Violations are more frequent among European than American options, a pattern that is qualitatively consistent with our theoretical results.

papers.title: Do Thinking VLMs Need to Keep Looking at Long Videos? Write It Down, Then Look Away
papers.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) reason about long videos over hundreds to thousands of tokens. Every decoding step re-reads the key-value (KV) cache of the entire video. Must the model keep looking while it reasons? In LookAway, the model first writes timestamped notes on what the question needs and then puts the video away. Once the notes close, the inference engine hides the video's KV cache for the rest of the response. Across both hybrid and pure-attention VLMs, dependence on the video is concentrated early in the response. On Qwen3.6-27B, writing notes preserves accuracy better than free reasoning at the same withdrawal step. Replacing them with another video's notes harms accuracy, whereas keeping the video visible alongside the model's own notes adds no significant benefit. Without additional training, LookAway nearly matches full-video thinking accuracy at 0.12-0.13 times its modeled decode cost. To shorten this initial look, we fine-tune the model on its own correct LookAway responses. Reinforcement learning then rewards correct answers while penalizing KV reads. The trained model puts the video away after a median of 66-68 tokens. Across three held-out benchmarks, it writes more tokens than an identically trained full-video model yet reads only 27-35% as many KV positions at matched accuracy.

authors.name: Chengqian Ma
authors.institution: Institute of Population and Labor Economics

authors.name: Jun Liu
authors.institution: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: Match Rate Is Not Match Quality
papers.abstract:
Third-party identity-resolution vendors commonly emphasize match rate, the share of submitted records they can link to identifiers for advertising activation, as their core metric of quality. Yet a high match rate does not necessarily mean that those matched identifiers belong to the submitted records (i.e., the intended targets). In this paper we explore match quality as an alternative metric to match rate, utilizing a unique data set to evaluate match quality. We are able to compare two demographics, age and gender, from a submitted record (voter files) to the same demographics in self-reported surveys matched to mobile advertising identifiers linked together by two leading identity-resolution vendors. The data and matching was from 2019-20.
  There is substantial ambiguity in match quality of the returned records. First, both vendors' activation files contain multiple device identifiers per match. Second, match quality among audited pairs (Vendor A) and for explicitly labeled individual-level matches (Vendor B) is only 21.8% and 23.6%, respectively. Utilizing a mixture model that assumes that correct links always agree on these two demographics and incorrect links agree 10% of the time, these rates imply conditional identity-level precisions of approximately 15% and 13%, respectively.
  This paper utilizes identity-resolution products that are several years old, but the question we address remains fundamental: match rate alone cannot establish whether advertisers are reaching the people they intended. Evaluating identity resolution requires independent evidence of match quality alongside match rate.

authors.name: David M. Rothschild
authors.institution: Microsoft Research New York City (United States)

papers.title: Biologically-Inspired Spike Encoding and Optimization for Spiking Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer theoretical energy-efficiency advantages over conventional deep networks, but realizing these advantages on vision tasks requires sparse spike representations that naive rate-coding methods fail to provide. We combine biologically motivated spike-encoding schemes with two training improvements: Rouser adaptive-threshold surrogate gradients and Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature (K-FAC) second-order optimization. The spike encoding schemes experimented with are rate coding, latency coding, DVS-style delta modulation, and Difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) filtering. Experiments on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST demonstrate that biologically inspired encoders yield the largest accuracy gains in capacity-constrained regimes and serve as an effective parameter-efficiency lever. DoG and delta modulation encoders produce significantly sparser spike trains than rate coding. K-FAC yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements over Adam-trained baselines, and Rouser's learnable per-neuron thresholds improve Fashion-MNIST accuracy from 87.37% to 88.13% by enabling homeostatic firing-rate regulation. Biologically grounded pre-processing methods can help close the accuracy gap between SNNs and non-spiking baselines without increasing model size.

papers.title: Neural Circuit Architectural Priors for Rat Locomotion
papers.abstract: Animals generate behavior through continuous interactions between their neural circuits, bodies, and environment. Embodied simulations study these interactions by testing neural circuit models in biologically realistic settings. Recent efforts have simulated diverse animals, and emerging work on biologically grounded neural architectures has begun to integrate circuit connectivity and single-unit dynamics from experimental data into artificial neural networks, introducing stronger inductive biases and closer mechanistic alignment with biology. How can we develop embodied simulations that enable the study of increasingly complex bodies and neural circuits? In this work, we address the challenge through coordinated advances in the simulated body, neural architecture, and training infrastructure. We introduce Rat v2, an efficient and flexible biomechanical body for simulating rat behavior. To control this body, we develop Rat NCAP, a biologically grounded neural architecture for locomotion based on mammalian spinal circuits that incorporates cell-type-specific connectivity and a novel flexor-extensor neuromechanical interface. To optimize circuit parameters, we develop GPU-accelerated simulation and training infrastructure. The model learns to locomote at different speeds and transition between gaits without imitation learning, producing locomotion statistics, kinematics, and cell-type-specific neural activity consistent with experimental data. Analyses reveal that the neuromechanical interface substantially affects trainability and gait quality, and in silico cell-type ablations reproduce known gait phenotypes and predict gait changes under graded perturbations. Together, these findings support the view that embodied simulations at an intermediate level of abstraction can simultaneously reproduce complex behavior and yield mechanistic insights into the neural circuits that generate it.

papers.title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
papers.abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.

papers.title: Formalizing local gauge freedom via bi-equivariant groupoid algebras
papers.abstract: Gauge degrees of freedom appear in many different contexts. Here, we describe their emergence in the context of architected metamaterials built from self-coupling blocks with internal symmetries. Quantifying the dynamics requires choices of local frames and the many available options constitute the local gauge degrees of freedom of the problem. In the absence of internal symmetries, the dynamical matrices generating the dynamics are all built from the left regular representation of a groupoid C*-algebra canonically associated to the architecture. If the resonators display internal symmetries, we show that the mentioned groupoid C*-algebra accepts a natural 2-action by the group of internal symmetries and that the local gauge freedom can be encoded in a bi-equivariant sub-groupoid algebra generated from the mentioned 2-action. The latter is shown to be the smallest C*-algebra containing all dynamical matrices that can be engineered in a laboratory, for a given architecture and discrete group of internal symmetries.

papers.title: Quantitative Modeling of Action-Potential-Driven Sodium Dynamics in Neurons: From Sodium Influx to Sodium MRI
papers.abstract: Neuronal action potentials are accompanied by the influx of extracellular sodium ions (Na+) into axons through voltage-gated sodium channels. Repetitive neuronal firing can lead to activity-dependent increases in intracellular sodium concentration, which are subsequently reversed primarily through the Na+/K+-ATPase. Quantifying these dynamic changes provides a biophysical foundation for investigating neuronal activity using sodium (23Na) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). This mini-review examines the relationships among firing frequency, action-potential-driven sodium influx, and intracellular sodium accumulation, to establish a quantitative framework linking neuronal activity to sodium MRI. The potential sensitivity and limitation of conventional and compartment-sensitive sodium MRI for detecting activity-dependent sodium changes are also discussed. Keywords: Sodium MRI; neuronal firing; action potential; sodium influx; intracellular sodium concentration.

papers.title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

papers.title: Functorial height and Orlov's rationality conjecture
papers.abstract: An exceptional collection in the derived category of a smooth projective variety may fail to generate the whole category, and this failure cannot be detected by K-theory or by Hochschild homology. Kuznetsov's height detects it through Hochschild cohomology, that is, through natural transformations from the identity functor to its shifts. We replace the identity functor by an arbitrary endofunctor $F$ and define the height of a collection with coefficient $F$. It controls, in a range of degrees, the restriction of natural transformations $\mathrm{id}\to F$ to the orthogonal complement of the collection, and it is computed from the collection by a finite complex. For collections of line bundles on surfaces whose Hom divisors have nonnegative canonical degree, the tensor product with a skyscraper sheaf has height exactly two, and the projections of skyscraper sheaves form a two-dimensional family of point-like objects in the orthogonal complement. We apply these tools to Orlov's rationality conjecture. A smooth projective complex surface is rational if its derived category has a full exceptional collection in which all members except possibly one are line bundles, or one that consists of at most three completely orthogonal blocks of arbitrary objects; we also obtain rationality in several cases with four blocks or with a hereditary component. If $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of the form $(M_i\boxtimes\mathcal O(a_i))$, then the $M_i$ with relative degrees of a fixed parity form a full exceptional collection on $S$; consequently $S$ is rational whenever $S\times\mathbb P^1$ has a full exceptional collection of line bundles. Finally, we show that the general case of the conjecture for surfaces is equivalent to the surjectivity and injectivity of two maps in Hochschild cohomology.

papers.title: Kernel Design in Particle Mesh Ewald Methods: Splitting, Interpolation, and Upsampling
papers.abstract: For more than thirty years, particle mesh Ewald (PME) methods have dominated the computation of electrostatic interactions in molecular dynamics. A PME method uses a splitting kernel to divide the interaction into a local part, summed within a cutoff, and a smooth part, computed on a grid with a spreading and interpolation (SI) kernel. The established methods use Ewald's Gaussian split with B-spline SI kernels, and the recent Ewald summation with prolates accelerates them severalfold by using a prolate spheroidal wave function (PSWF) for both kernels. Neither choice meets two needs of molecular dynamics: a smooth energy, which long simulations need in order to conserve it, and a low-order SI kernel that stays accurate on coarse grids and gains accuracy as the grid is refined. We present a framework for designing both kernels to meet these needs. For inverse powers from the Coulomb to the dispersion interaction, our splits make the local part smooth at the cutoff to any order while keeping the Fourier concentration of the smooth part close to optimal. We show that with analytic differentiation, the force error of a continuous SI kernel of fixed shape vanishes under grid refinement only if every particle, wherever it lies, gives the grid its exact charge and dipole moment. Our SI kernel for the Coulomb interaction ensures this by construction and is twice continuously differentiable. Compared with the B-spline of the same order, it needs fewer grid points by a factor of up to nearly five; on coarse grids, it mostly needs a lower order than the PSWF kernel. In simulations of liquid water over 100 million time steps, the new kernels reduce the energy drift of both the established and the PSWF kernels by about three orders of magnitude, with a smaller force error than either. Existing PME codes can adopt them by replacing only the two kernels and the Fourier multiplier.

authors.name: Libin Lu
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Nonradial threshold scattering for the planar cubic--quintic NLS
papers.abstract:
We study the planar cubic--quintic nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation \[
  i\partial_tu+\Delta u=-|u|^2u+|u|^4u,
  \qquad (t,x)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^2, \] with initial data $u_0\in H^1_x(\mathbb R^2)$. We prove scattering in both time directions when the mass of \(u_0\) equals the mass of the ground state for the focusing cubic equation. This resolves the nonradial threshold scattering problem posed by Murphy [\emph{Comm.\ Partial Differential Equations} \textbf{46} (2021), 2213--2234]. Together with the known subthreshold scattering theory and the existence of standing waves at every larger mass, this identifies the sharp mass range in which every $H^1$ solution scatters. The proof combines localized interaction Morawetz estimates with propagation estimates on moving halfspaces to control exterior kinetic energy.

papers.title: RoughCut-Bench: A Benchmark for Automatic Video Rough-Cut with Large Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: Video rough-cut is a core stage in media production workflows, organizing raw media materials into an initial video cut. Despite recent advances in large vision-language models (LVLMs) for video-related tasks, automatic rough-cut remains underexplored, without a comprehensive benchmark for evaluation or mature workflows for producing executable cut plans. To address the evaluation gap, we introduce RoughCut-Bench, which covers two practical settings: (1) a visually driven setting over video cases, covering highlight detection and selection, source-video ordering, and adherence to user requirements when provided; and (2) a speech-driven setting over automatic speech recognition (ASR) transcripts, covering filler removal, expression deduplication, and low-value content trimming. Across these settings, the benchmark contains 101 visually driven cases, including 831 raw videos with 1,476 highlight annotations. It also includes 84 speech-driven cases, each consisting of an ASR transcript with annotated cleanup spans. The evaluation compares cut plans with these annotations in both settings and additionally uses a human-aligned agentic evaluator to assess rendered-cut quality in the visual setting. To apply LVLMs to automatic rough-cut, we further propose agentic workflows that guide them to produce structured cut plans from input materials. Experiments show that current LVLMs remain limited in producing expert-aligned cut plans. Our benchmark, code, and prompts are released at https://whalesong-zrs.github.io/RoughCut-Bench-Project-Page.

authors.name: Ruisi Zhao
authors.institution: Huazhong University of Science and Technology

authors.name: You Li
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

authors.name: Zhen Yang
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Retained Encrypted Search with Certified Split Joins
papers.abstract: Retaining encrypted search across data edits and worker replacement requires separating computational validity from current release authority. We give exact Hamming search with at most one authorized decryption and decoding attempt per query preparation. Under authenticated prescribed execution, exclusive nonrollback owner state, an ideal public seed-expansion interface and a stated observation model, we reduce bounded adaptive privacy to ordinary ring learning with errors (Ring-LWE). Expanded second components depend only on public masks and fixed maps, independently of queries and the fresh database key. This compiler invariant permits a retained split join against a smaller-modulus encrypted database. A simultaneous bound on the completed circuit covers a finite honest reservation family, including adaptive queries and slot selection, with explicit statistical correctness and privacy losses. In three post-calibration local CPU comparisons on 32,768 vectors of 512 bits, the 60-bit-join construction takes a median 9.825 s for an end-to-end two-query workload, versus 12.159 s for the optimized full-source-modulus baseline. These times include setup, transfers, preparation and private completion. They are local implementation results, not deployment or concrete-security claims.

papers.title: Stable admissible neural classes and convergent physics-informed neural networks
papers.abstract: Residual-based methods, including physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), physics-informed Kolmogorov--Arnold networks, and some physics-informed neural operator architectures, approximate PDE solutions by minimizing a discrete least-squares loss formed from the PDE and boundary residuals over a prescribed trial class. This structure is shared by classical least-squares Kansa collocation, whose kernel trial spaces admit an established convergence theory. For neural trial classes, approximation power alone does not ensure that discrete residuals control the continuous solution error.
