papers.title: Temporal Fair Division: Simultaneous Guarantees for Goods and Chores
papers.abstract: We study temporal fair division of indivisible items in both the goods and chores settings, with $n \ge 2$ agents and nonnegative additive values or costs. Items arrive one at a time and must be assigned immediately and irrevocably. The arrival order and all agents' values or costs are known in advance, and the cumulative allocation must satisfy the fairness requirements after each arrival. For goods, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact temporal proportionality up to one item (TPROP1), a $1/n$ approximation to temporal maximin share (TMMS), and a $1/(n-1)$ approximation to temporal envy-freeness up to one item (TEF1). The TMMS factor is optimal. For chores, we give a polynomial-time algorithm that simultaneously achieves exact TPROP1 and a $2-1/n$ approximation to TMMS. Classical scheduling lower bounds based on fixed sequences carry over to chores TMMS, establishing the optimality of this factor for $n=2,3$. For every $n \ge 2$, we further show that $2-1/n$ is the optimal TMMS factor subject to exact TPROP1. For every fixed $n \ge 3$ and every finite $\beta \ge 1$, we construct an instance of chores admitting no $\beta$-TEF1 allocation.

papers.title: ReflectScene:MLLM-Guided Closed-Loop Diffusion for 3D Indoor Scene Generation
papers.abstract: Text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation requires layouts satisfying geometric, functional, and semantic constraints. However, existing diffusion methods rely primarily on static textual conditions, limiting their ability to assess evolving scenes and translate semantic discrepancies into executable object-level corrections. MLLM-based post-hoc refinement provides semantic feedback but remains decoupled from denoising, potentially disrupting scene coherence.We propose ReflectScene, an MLLM-guided closed-loop diffusion framework. First, we introduce Hierarchical Prior-Grounded Scene Understanding that aligns structured layouts with multi-view visual evidence, to interpret object-specific context and scene global semantics via a frozen multi-modal large language model (MLLM). Second, we propose MLLM-Guided Semantic Reward Evaluation to distill MLLM's diagnoses and assessments on possible candidate corrections into a lightweight Reward Predictor, enabling correction decision making with reduced computation burden. Finally, Decision-Conditioned Trajectory-Consistent Diffusion is proposed to integrate selected corrections through transient conditioning and persistent clean-estimate projection, correcting object layout in the generated scene while preserving non-target arrangements throughout denoising.Experiments on 3D-FRONT demonstrate improved functional consistency and semantic alignment while maintaining competitive generation quality and diversity.

authors.name: Jiawei Shen
authors.institution: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology

papers.title: Beyond Additive Composition: Interventional Modeling of State-Dependent Cross-Degradation Responses for Composite Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Composite image restoration aims to recover images corrupted by multiple coexisting degradations. Existing methods predominantly decompose composite corruptions into individual factors, relying on these isolated priors to guide restoration. However, coexisting degradations are inherently interdependent: the manifestation of one degradation dynamically shifts with the states of others, inducing non-additive interactions that factor-wise paradigms fail to capture. To bridge this gap, we formulate state-dependent cross-degradation responses and propose PROBE, an interventional framework that explicitly models how coexisting degradations influence one another. Specifically, we first construct unified degradation axes by aligning visual and textual degraded-clean offsets. Along these axes, a calibrated coordinate head estimates current degradation states, while bidirectional feature perturbations are injected to probe cross-coordinate responses under the current states. Contrasting these responses with corresponding intensity-matched single-degradation references quantifies intrinsic non-additive deviations, allowing the resulting response descriptors and state coordinates to jointly guide restoration. For comprehensive evaluation, we introduce SCD-15, a new benchmark covering all 15 nonempty combinations of four degradation factors at three severity levels. Experiments demonstrate that PROBE achieves state-of-the-art performance on the CDD-11, AWMM-100K, and SCD-15 composite restoration datasets using a compact model with modest GPU memory requirements.

papers.title: TOMAS: Topology-Aware Operation Modeling and Adaptive Staging for Egocentric Hand Forecasting
papers.abstract: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.

authors.name: Yuxuan Wu
authors.institution: Kunming University of Science and Technology

authors.name: Yanzi Miao
authors.institution: China University of Mining and Technology

authors.name: Hesheng Wang
authors.institution: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: Psychometrics-Inspired Coreset Selection for Image Quality Assessment
papers.abstract: Collecting large-scale subjective annotations remains a critical bottleneck in training accurate image quality assessment (IQA) models. Coreset selection reduces this burden by selecting representative images before annotation. However, diversity in a visual feature space does not necessarily reflect diversity in perceptual quality, raising a fundamental question about which quality-related factors the representation should encode. We propose GRAM, a quality-aware representation learning framework inspired by the graded response model (GRM) from psychometrics. GRM describes how an individual's latent ability determines the probabilities of reaching successive assessment grades, with response sensitivity and grade thresholds governing this relationship. In this paper, we find that this principle naturally aligns with perceptual quality assessment, where the impact of image degradation depends on image content and distortion characteristics. Building on this connection, GRAM models quality judgments through three complementary factors: latent quality, content-dependent response sensitivity, and distortion-dependent grade thresholds. These factors jointly determine the probabilities of attaining different quality grades and the resulting expected quality score. The learned parameters provide a structured quality-aware representation that complements general visual features for coreset selection. Experiments on nine datasets demonstrate improvements across different selection strategies, downstream IQA models, and annotation budgets. The code will be made publicly available.

authors.name: Xuelin Shen
authors.institution: Guangdong Laboratory of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Economy (Shenzhen)

authors.name: Baoliang Chen
authors.institution: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Fuse to Recognize the Unseen: Class-Relative Infrared-Visible Fusion for Open-Vocabulary Semantic Segmentation
papers.abstract: Visible-infrared image fusion leverages complementary thermal cues to enhance visual perception, particularly under challenging illumination. However, such perceptual complementarity does not readily translate into semantic gains in open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVSS), where CLIP-based models are predominantly pretrained on RGB imagery. Directly introducing IR information may instead disrupt RGB-language alignment, turning promising thermal cues into semantic interference that undermines unseen-class recognition. Our pixel-level RGB-IR semantic analysis reveals that class-relevant thermal cues can correct certain RGB misclassifications while preserving reliable RGB predictions, motivating RGB-anchored, class-relative thermal cue selection. Based on this insight, we propose EmergeFuse, an infrared-visible fusion framework for OVSS that selectively converts complementary thermal evidence into unseen-class semantic corrections. Specifically, class-relative cue selection evaluates RGB-IR semantic responses and calibrated thermal evidence relative to RGB predictions, generating class-relative correction requests through competitive selection. Text-contrast image rectification then translates these selected requests into semantic rectification directions through text contrasts, guiding evidence-gated feature updates to realize complementary thermal evidence for unseen-class recognition. Experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate gains of up to 4.755% in unseen-class mIoU and 15.730% in strict complementary conversion rate over existing fusion methods, while maintaining competitive fusion quality.

authors.name: Zehao Gao
authors.institution: Ministry of Industry and Information Technology

papers.title: Uneven gains in protein-RNA affinity and mutation-effect prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate matched affinities determine mutation effects, but gains in aggregate affinity prediction may transfer unevenly to average effects, ordering and local accuracy. We evaluated eleven method families using method-specific matched populations. Controlled CoPRA reduced absolute-affinity mean absolute error from 1.2898 to 1.1431 pKd. Across 220 mutation pairs from 20 families, it generated stronger responses and improved mean-effect accuracy, with uncertain ranking gains and no decrease in mean centered local error. In an independent external test (24 quantitative pairs from three source-matched families), absolute and ordinary mutation-effect errors fell in all three families. Mean centered local error fell from 0.4198 to 0.3761 pKd, with improvements in two families and higher error in one. Error decomposition localized gains in landscape means. PRA-Pred feature tracing, fixed-weight M2-PRNet input controls and matched supervision interventions identified specific restrictions on mutation response. These results establish the need to evaluate average effects, ordering and quantitative local variation jointly.

papers.title: xTBloom: GPU Batching for High-Throughput GFN-xTB Calculations
papers.abstract: Conformational searches and multiwindow free-energy sampling require large numbers of GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations across molecular conformations and sampling windows. Processing each system separately on a GPU makes it difficult to amortize memory management, host-device data transfer, and kernel-launch overhead. Here, we present xTBloom, a GPU batching library for GFN-xTB energy and force evaluations. xTBloom sorts evaluation queues by atomic orbital (AO) count before forming batches, accommodates size differences through a native ragged layout, maintains independent self-consistent charge (SCC) and failure states for each system, and selects execution paths according to data residency. We focus the quantitative evaluation on GFN2-xTB through cross-program comparisons on QM9 and OMol25, CPU-CUDA comparisons, finite-difference force checks, and controlled failure tests. On a near-size OMol25 workload, GPU execution achieved a 2.9-fold speedup over xTBloom's single-core CPU backend. A companion LAMMPS plugin integrates cross-window batching with periodic quantum mechanical/molecular mechanical (QM/MM) simulation. In a short synchronized test with 48 windows on one GPU, the complete coupled workflow achieved an aggregate speedup of approximately 14 over sequential execution of the same windows. These results demonstrate the throughput benefits of batched GFN-xTB evaluation for repeated electronic-structure calculations and multiwindow sampling.

authors.name: Qiangqiang Gu
authors.institution: University of Science and Technology of China

papers.title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
papers.abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

authors.name: Tianyu Gao
authors.institution: Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences & Peking Union Medical College

papers.title: PrismRestore: A Compact Restoration Toolbox for Agentic Image Restoration
papers.abstract: Agentic image restoration composes operations to handle mixed degradations, yet its toolbox often requires storing multiple restoration networks. We propose PrismRestore, which constructs a compact bank of callable restoration actions from a single frozen all-in-one model. Our approach builds on task-dependent yet overlapping channel responses in the shared model. An offline task-prior search uses activation and gradient statistics to group channels with similar response profiles, then searches task-specific modulation coefficients over non-representative channels while leaving representative channels unmodulated. The resulting prior bank enables explicit action selection and composition without additional restoration backbones or task-specific adapter modules. A state-conditioned policy learns to compose these actions using Group Relative Policy Optimization. Its objective separately normalizes fidelity and perceptual feedback within groups of trajectories sampled for the same input, and combines terminal evaluation with return-to-go derived from stepwise quality changes. Experiments on synthetic composite-degradation and real-world multi-task benchmarks show improvements over the evaluated all-in-one baselines and restoration quality competitive with multi-model agents. PrismRestore achieves these results with a single restoration backbone and faster inference than the evaluated agentic baselines.

authors.name: Yiang Chen
authors.institution: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology

papers.title: JITAtlas: Checking Lifetime and Protection Obligations in Compiler Rewrites
papers.abstract: Compiler rewrites can preserve returned values while violating object lifetime or ownership. Such failures arise when a rewrite changes when an object remains live, whether a borrowed pointer stays supported, or what ownership reaches the caller. We present JITAtlas, a source-level checker that reconstructs reference and target computations from optimizer code and checks valid uses, continuous borrow support, and caller-visible ownership. On a 58-input benchmark constructed and labeled independently of JITAtlas output, JITAtlas detects all 29 defects and reports none of 29 safe inputs; PyRefcon detects 20 defects and CpyChecker 18. Across three CPython snapshots, JITAtlas extracts 3,332 rewrite alternatives, retains 801 under recovered receiving contexts, and reports 194 violations. Manual review confirms 92 reports, giving 47.42% precision. End-to-end analysis takes 35.56-42.31 s per snapshot. JITAtlas further identifies 15 new bugs across five failure classes, each with a reproducible proof of concept.

papers.title: Thinking Fast, Anywhere: One System-1 for the Decision Points of Any Agent Workflow
papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents incur substantial cost and latency by invoking a large model (System-2) at every step, even when many intermediate actions choose among a small set of known candidates. Existing dual-system agents offload such decisions to a lightweight System-1 model, but rely on workflow-specific hooks authored per environment. We present AnyS1, a framework that turns human-authored procedural skills, whose instructions naturally specify where choices arise and which options apply, into a shared, domain-general source of decision points. Offline, AnyS1 mines grounded enumerable decisions across over 1,000 public skills, gathers execution-grounded trajectory states inside isolated containers to construct Any-DP, and trains a single calibrated 4B pointer System-1 with label smoothing. At run time, compiled workflows resolve routine decisions in one forward pass and fall back to System-2 when confidence falls below a calibrated threshold. Across three unseen benchmarks and distinct System-2 model families, AnyS1 preserves task reliability while cutting episode cost by 75-91% and model-call time by 63-92% relative to an uncompiled System-2 agent, and maintains performance under zero-shot threshold transfer.

papers.title: Benchmarking Traditional and Learning-Based Reference-Free Compressors for Long-Read Sequencing Data
papers.abstract: Long-read sequencing technologies generate large volumes of data, creating substantial storage and transmission demands. Although reference-based compressors can achieve high compression, their reliance on an appropriate reference genome limits their use. We present LRCBench, a benchmark and survey of reference-free lossless compressors for long-read sequencing data. We review traditional and learning-based general-purpose and sequencing-specific methods, then evaluate 35 compressors on 16 real-world datasets from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio platforms. We compare compression ratio, storage savings, runtime, peak memory use, and robustness across datasets. Learning-based compressors are evaluated on six MinION datasets because of their high computational costs. CoLoRd achieves the best overall compression ratios in our experiments, while other methods offer trade-offs in speed, memory use, and robustness. We also examine multithreaded speedup and discuss future directions in parallel acceleration, privacy protection, adaptive parameter tuning, and hardware-algorithm co-design.

authors.institution: Southern University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Keep the Image in Mind: A Visual Board for Multimodal Agents
papers.abstract: Multi-step visual reasoning suffers when early visual misinterpretations persist as incorrect premises in subsequent reasoning. We argue that how visual evidence is represented during reasoning matters as much as how much of it is gathered. Rather than appending observations and inferences to an ever-growing dialogue, we introduce a Visual Board-centered harness that separates visual observations, uncertain interpretations, and derived reasoning within a structured, capacity-bounded, and revisable workspace. This separation makes each premise explicit and auditable, so that conflicts between what is seen and what is derived become detectable even by a text-only critic and can trigger targeted reinspection of the original image. Without task-specific training, our harness consistently outperforms standalone models across 4B, 8B, Qwen3-VL-Flash, and 32B configurations on Euclid30K, SolidGeo, and ChartQA bar charts, with gains of up to 11.68, 18.42, and 24.82 percentage points, respectively. Under identical tools, critic, and interaction limits, the structured Board outperforms shared free-form notes by 6.67 to 13.00 points and no-Board retries by 7.35 to 18.80 points while using 7.9\% to 38.2\% fewer tokens. Supervised fine-tuning on harness trajectories further improves direct answering and critic-free tool use, with positive transfer to chart reasoning.

papers.title: Ego2X: Contact-aware Transfer from Egocentric Human Data to Any Robot
papers.abstract: Embodied models depend on real interaction data, yet collecting it on physical robots is slow and labor-intensive. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines retarget first-person view human videos to robot data via transferring hand and arm motion. They judge fidelity mainly by visual appearance. However, trajectories often fail in terms of physics: fingers hover beside objects, and grippers close on empty space. We argue that how the object moves and the contacts that drive the motion count. Thus, we present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers. Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact on the object by its surface anchor, as well as relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state. Throughout the pipeline, CORE corrects hand-object drift via object-relative constraints, steers inverse kinematics toward contacts the robot must realize, and preserves held objects during arm erasure and robot compositing. On HOT3D, contact-driven correction reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7%, while on EgoDex, contact-driven retargeting realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts, surpassing the official HuRo pipeline (27.9%). In RoboTwin 2.0, post-training X-VLA on Ego2X episodes alone, without simulator demonstrations, raises task success rate from 40.5% zero-shot to 67.0% across 200 paired scenes. We will publicly release our conversion pipeline and CORE-annotated dataset for dexterous hands and parallel grippers.

papers.title: Erased but Recoverable: On the Fragility of Concept Erasure Under Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Existing concept erasure methods for text-to-image diffusion models primarily focus on suppressing target concepts while preserving non-target generation quality. However, in practical applications, open-source diffusion models are often further adapted through DreamBooth, LoRA, or Custom Diffusion. Such adaptations can reshape internal representations, thereby weakening or even reversing the erasure effects achieved by existing methods. We identify erasure persistence as a key yet underexplored dimension of concept erasure and analyze how downstream fine-tuning reshapes internal representations. Our analysis reveals that fine-tuning of the original model does not uniformly modify the model, but preserves certain high-contribution structures, particularly attention heads with stable output subspaces and response magnitudes. We also observe that, after downstream fine-tuning of concept-erased models, these heads' output representations more readily realign with their pretrained counterparts. Motivated by this observation, we propose Stable-Head-Aware Concept Erasure (SHACE), which improves erasure persistence by preserving stable attention structures during concept erasure. SHACE identifies stability-critical attention heads through Attention-Head Stability Profiling and keeps their corresponding parameter blocks unchanged during erasure via Stable-Head Gradient Preservation. Extensive experiments show that SHACE improves resistance to concept recovery across diverse fine-tuning settings while maintaining strong suppression and non-target generation quality.

papers.title: Look Closer, Look Back, or Wait for Agentic Streaming Video Understanding
papers.abstract: Streaming video models must answer questions about a live video under strict memory and latency limits. Feeding only the latest few frames keeps present perception sharp, whereas adding past frames dilutes attention on the current scene and triggers hallucinations. Recent cascade methods retrieve past frames when uncertain, but they still fail when current frames are blurry or when decisive future clues have not appeared yet. We introduce ActiveForager, a streaming video agent that maintains a clean short working window and gathers extra evidence only on demand. For each query, the agent either answers directly, zooms into high-resolution recent frames, recalls past events from memory, or waits for upcoming frames. When recalling history, a shared-weight sub-agent verifies candidate clips in isolation and returns a compact evidence summary. A stream-decoupled attention mask then keeps historical evidence from interfering with present visual tokens. We train this policy using counterfactual information gain, which rewards a tool call only when the gathered evidence makes the true answer more likely and prevents tool collapse across all actions. Across Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B on OVO-Bench, ActiveForager improves real-time perception, historical recall, and proactive response at once, lifting overall accuracy on Qwen3-VL-8B from 47.6% to 65.9%. It also doubles zero-shot accuracy on the multi-hop Video-Holmes benchmark while adding minimal visual tokens per query.

authors.name: Jun Liu
authors.institution: Ministry of Education of the People's Republic of China

papers.title: The Asymptotic Capacity of the Grabbag Channel With and Without Feedback
papers.abstract: The grabbag channel models communication through a randomly mixed store. At each use, an input ball of one of $K$ colors is inserted into a bag containing $M$ balls, and one of the resulting $M+1$ balls is selected uniformly, observed, and removed. We show that, when $2\leq K\leq M+1$, both the capacity without feedback and the capacity with noiseless strictly causal output feedback are at most $9.77(K/(M+1))^{2/3}$, and that, when moreover $M+1\geq2^{22}$, both are at least an absolute constant times $(K/(M+1))^{2/3}$. Hence, both capacities are of order $(K/M)^{2/3}$, and of order $M^{-2/3}$ for every fixed $K$. The converse is a single bound on the information that a feedback code conveys in $n$ uses, valid for every initial state. For each initial state, it bounds the information in each output by the change of a potential of the posterior law of the state given the earlier outputs, defined through noisy cube roots of the color counts. A budget on the true state bounds the total cost of the uses in which the inserted color is rare. The lower bound uses a statistic of two output histograms whose expectation does not depend on the unknown initial composition, an outer code, and words with prescribed compositions. We also show that the channel is indecomposable and relate its capacities to the finite-state-channel information formulas.

authors.name: Yuta Sakai
authors.institution: National Institute for Land and Infrastructure Management

papers.title: Laplace Bayesian transport maps for generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields
papers.abstract: Transport maps provide a powerful framework for the generative modeling of complex, non-Gaussian spatial fields, such as those encountered in climate science. By mapping a complicated target distribution to a standard Gaussian reference distribution, they can serve as efficient stochastic surrogates. However, current Bayesian transport maps, which are modeled using autoregressive Gaussian processes, typically rely on empirical Bayes estimates that ignore hyperparameter uncertainty. Here, we contrast this point-estimate approach with a fully Bayesian model that provides posterior uncertainty quantification in transport map hyperparameters. To avoid the high cost of Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), we also propose a Laplace approximation to the hyperparameter posteriors, which can be computed at negligible additional computational cost relative to empirical Bayes. We provide numerical evidence and a real-data climate application demonstrating that these Laplace approximations can accurately capture most posterior summaries at a fraction of the cost of MCMC, while maintaining good predictive properties. Thus, our approach offers a scalable, uncertainty-aware framework for the generative modeling of non-Gaussian climate fields.

papers.title: GaussLearner: 3D Gaussian Primitives as Self-Regulating Continual Learners
papers.abstract: Continual learning of 3D Gaussian fields aims to maintain faithful reconstructions of the evolving world. However, directly fine-tuning an existing Gaussian field on new observations can cause catastrophic forgetting of previously reconstructed content. To address this challenge, existing methods employ selective local optimization, replay, or parameter regularization, yet still struggle to balance adaptation to scene changes with preservation of still-valid content. Our key insight is to view 3D Gaussian primitives themselves as self-regulating continual learners. Based on this insight, we introduce GaussLearner, which equips each Gaussian with a closed continual-learning loop connecting observation, self-regulation, and adaptation at the primitive level. At each novel state, GaussLearner first attributes pixel-wise inconsistencies in current observations to their contributing Gaussians. Each Gaussian then self-regulates through a learning weight that balances current observations against cross-state reliability. This weight governs both Gaussian parameter adaptation and optimizer memory refresh. As current inconsistencies are resolved, the adaptation outcome renews each Gaussian's reliability for future states. The resulting field is a globally coupled population of locally self-regulating learners. Across scenes from CL-Splats, WAT, and our CL-3D dataset, GaussLearner improves average PSNR by 3.41 dB over the strongest baseline. On CL-3D, it achieves the best reconstruction quality on both changed and unchanged views.

authors.name: Haonan Zhou
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory Fluid Power and Mechatronic Systems

authors.name: Gaoang Wang
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Asking but Missing: Decision Coverage in Natural-Language Data Querying
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to translate natural language questions about structured data into executable programs. A fundamental challenge is recognizing when a question admits multiple computational interpretations and identifying the decisions needed to resolve them. We investigate whether language models recognize these unresolved decisions before generating code, or silently adopt assumptions that may lead to incorrect results. We refer to the latter behavior as Underspecified Decision Completion (UDC). To distinguish different causes of UDC, we introduce Grounded Code Generation (GCG), a diagnostic protocol that separates the identification of unresolved decisions, their resolution using evidence, and their translation into executable code. By examining each stage separately, we can determine where the decisions responsible for incorrect results were first missed or mishandled. We evaluate this framework on BIRD-Pandas with twelve models. The results show that answering clarification questions consistently improves execution accuracy, yet substantial errors remain. Our findings suggest that the main difficulty lies not in answering clarification questions, but in recognizing which questions need to be asked in the first place.

papers.title: Scalable Iterative Multi-Agent Path Finding under Turn Constraints
papers.abstract: Large-scale multi-mobile-robot systems require fast and reliable path planning under realistic motion constraints. Multi-Agent Path Finding with turn actions (MAPF$_T$) explicitly models orientation changes and turn-induced delays, but these constraints increase the computational burden of search-based methods. Priority-inheritance-based planning offers a highly scalable alternative, yet directly extending it to MAPF$_T$ is nontrivial because turn actions break the immediate node-vacation assumption underlying conventional priority inheritance. To address this challenge, this paper proposes PIBT$^*_T$, an efficient iterative solver for MAPF$_T$. PIBT$^*_T$ advances scalable multi-agent coordination by preserving the lightweight single-timestep planning mechanism of Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), while introducing dedicated mechanisms to handle turn-induced dependencies, local deadlocks, livelock, and inefficient repeated pushing. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks show that PIBT$^*_T$ achieves high success rates and strong scalability, solving instances with up to 1000 agents within seconds. For realistic engineering environments, Action Dependency Graph (ADG)-based execution simulation and a flexible manufacturing system case study show that turn-aware planning better reflects robot execution and reduces actual makespan compared with classical MAPF planning. Experiments with TurtleBot4 robots further validate the practical feasibility of the proposed method.

papers.title: Pair Siegel-Veech constants for branched covers of tori and Veech surfaces
papers.abstract: For a locus $\mathcal{E}$ of branched covers of tori satisfying a monodromy assumption, we show there exists an explicit constant $c_A(\mathcal{E})$ so that the number of pairs of saddle connections on surfaces in $\mathcal{E}$ of length at most $R$ and cross product at most $A$ grows like $c_A(\mathcal{E})R^2$ for every Diophantine surface in $\mathcal{E}$; this constant is moreover piecewise linear in $A$. In particular, this covers the case of billiards on rectangles with a barrier. Similar pointwise results are shown for Veech surfaces. The proof uses work of Margulis-Mohammadi on the quantitative inhomogeneous Oppenheim conjecture.

papers.title: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference
papers.abstract: Causal inference seeks to learn how outcomes change under alternative interventions, but network interactions complicate this task. Under network interference, outcomes depend on both own treatment and neighbors' treatments, making causal effects functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single treatment contrasts. Existing methods primarily target prespecified causal contrasts or their estimation precision, leaving global response-function recovery largely unexplored. We study sequential experimentation under a limited experimental budget, with the goal of recovering the full exposure-dependent population-average response function. To this end, we propose FANCI (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference). For function learning, treatment-specific Gaussian processes flexibly model nonlinear conditional response surfaces. For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.

papers.title: On the asymmetry polynomial of Schubert varieties
papers.abstract:
Let $W$ be a finite Weyl group with length function $\ell$ and longest element $w_0$. For $w\in W$, let $P_w(q)$ be the Poincar\'e polynomial of the Schubert variety $X_w$. We introduce its asymmetry polynomial $D_w(q):=q^{\ell(w)}P_w(q^{-1})-P_w(q)$.
  Let $n\geq4$ and $W=S_n$ or $W(B_n)$. For $w\in W$ whose Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomial $P_{\mathrm{id},w}(q)$ satisfies $P_{\mathrm{id},w}(1)=2$, we prove the sharp bound $[q^k]D_w(q)\leq[q^{k-1}]P_{w_0}(q)$ for $1\leq k<\ell(w)/2$.
  For every $n\geq3$ and $1\leq h\leq2n-4$, we construct an element $b=b_h^n\in W(B_n)$ with $P_{\mathrm{id},b}(q)=1+q^h$, and determine the asymmetry polynomial $D_b(q)$ and all Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials $P_{x,b}(q)$ for $x\leq b$.

papers.title: The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter of the ePIC detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
papers.abstract: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) is a next-generation facility expected to address fundamental open questions in nuclear physics, including the structure and dynamics of gluons in nucleons and nuclei. The Barrel Imaging Calorimeter (BIC) is the electromagnetic calorimeter of the ePIC detector, designed to meet the stringent performance requirements of the EIC, providing precise measurements and particle identification of scattered electrons, photons, and neutral mesons. The BIC is a high-granularity sampling calorimeter based on lead absorbers interleaved with scintillating fibers, complemented by pixelated imaging layers based on the AstroPix monolithic active pixel sensor. This hybrid design enables both accurate energy and position measurements, as well as three-dimensional shower reconstruction, making it a key component for realizing the full physics potential of the EIC. The BIC has successfully completed its Preliminary Design Review last year and is currently progressing toward the Final Design Review. In this talk, I will present an overview of the BIC concept and focus on its current status and performance results from bench tests, system integration studies, and recent beam tests.

authors.name: for the ePIC Barrel Imaging Calorimeter

papers.title: Construction of Ternary Minimal Linear Codes with Dimension $n+r$ Via Index Codes and The Access Structures of Their Dual Codes
papers.abstract: Recently, minimal linear codes have been extensively studied due to their applications in secret sharing schemes, secure two-party computations, and so on. Constructing minimal linear codes violating the Ashikhmin-Barg condition and then determining their weight distributions have been interesting in coding theory and cryptography. In this paper, we present a general construction of ternary linear codes of dimension $n+r$, where $n$ and $r$ are positive integers, and derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the resulting codes to be minimal. We first specialize the construction using index codes arising from spreads, with three classes of index codes satisfying the minimality condition, we obtain the parameters and weight enumerators of the corresponding minimal codes, and determine the access structures type of the secret-sharing schemes based on their dual codes. By the index codes from Krawtchouk polynomials, we then give a second specialization of the construction, with a class of index codes satisfying the minimality condition, we obtain the parameters of the resulting minimal codes, and determine the access-structure type of the secret-sharing scheme based on each dual code. Several constructed families of minimal codes violate the Ashikhmin-Barg condition.

papers.title: WAM-Policy: World Action Models with On-Policy Distillation for Quadrupedal Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Arm-free quadrupeds can perform loco-manipulation, walking on three legs while manipulating with a front leg, yet no existing policy for it follows language instructions. World action models (WAMs) have emerged as effective language-conditioned manipulation policies, but are pretrained for robot arms and sample slowly. WAM-Policy turns one WAM into a quadrupedal loco-manipulation policy via two stages. The first, Cross-Morphology Policy Adaptation and Acceleration, adapts the arm-centric WAM to quadrupeds and distills the transferred policy into a student with one video and two action steps by on-policy self-distillation (OPSD). This student, however, is bounded by its teacher, which only imitates demonstrations. The second stage, Task-Specific Improvement and Merging, therefore tunes the teacher by reinforcement learning (RL) and merges the slow specialists into one few-step student by multi-teacher on-policy distillation (M-OPD). On QLM-Bench, ten simulated tasks with 1,000 demonstrations synthesized without teleoperation, the transferred policy reaches 77.0%, and the OPSD student keeps 76.7% while sampling 14 times faster. Task-specific RL and M-OPD lift it to 85.0%. We also deploy the OPSD student on a real Unitree Go2 Air. WAM-Policy thus achieves a stronger quadrupedal policy at a fraction of the inference cost.

authors.name: Yue Yang
authors.institution: Beijing Institute of Nanoenergy and Nanosystems

papers.title: Interference-Aware Tone Selection for Bluetooth Channel Sounding
papers.abstract: Bluetooth Channel Sounding enables distance estimation using phase measurements across multiple frequencies. However, coexistence with Wi-Fi and other 2.4 GHz radios can fragment the available frequency band, making reliable ranging difficult when only a limited number of tones can be selected. Drawing on sparse antenna-array theory, we show that interference avoidance alone is insufficient: the spacing of selected tones can introduce repeated peaks in the ranging response, leading to estimation errors. We propose a lightweight, interference-aware tone-selection method that jointly considers frequency occupancy, tone spacing, and frequency span. Our method constructs a 15-tone map using a three-step rule without ranging measurements, ground-truth distance, or online candidate-map search. We evaluate the method using simulations of 900 indoor environments, a public Bluetooth Channel Sounding dataset, and measurements from commercial Nordic nRF54L15 hardware. Compared with random interference avoiding baseline, our proposed method improves ranging success percentage by 39 points under mixed interference, 29 points on the public dataset, and 82 points in hardware experiments. These results demonstrate the importance of tone selection for practical Bluetooth Channel Sounding.

authors.name: Taewoo Kim
authors.institution: The Catholic University of Korea Incheon St. Mary's Hospital

papers.title: ShadowTransfer: A Geographic Transfer Benchmark for Overhead Shadow Detection
papers.abstract: Overhead aerial imagery feeds dense-prediction pipelines that are routinely trained in one geographic region and deployed in another, yet no benchmark measures how shadow detection models transfer across regions. Existing overhead shadow datasets either lack a geographic transfer protocol or rely on automatically generated labels. We introduce ShadowTransfer, a benchmark of 4,500 human-verified shadow masks across three U.S. cities at two native resolutions, paired with a leave-one-city-out evaluation protocol. Under vanilla training, holding out the test city costs 3.5 to 7.8 mIoU across four architectures, the gap remains significant when the training set grows from 225 to 900 images, and six of eight adaptation methods degrade more than vanilla training on average. We propose a three-probe framework that diagnoses where and how the transfer breaks: the failure operates in feature space, beyond the reach of pixel-histogram matching, shows up as a confidence collapse on shadow pixels while background confidence stays intact, and is recoverable by retraining different architectural components depending on the model: encoder for some, decoder for others. These findings replicate on INRIA building footprints, suggesting they describe geographic transfer beyond shadows. Guided by the diagnosis, we build Spectral Information Bottleneck (SIB), a plug-in module with one component per finding. Across the 9 (architecture, held-out city) cells, SIB has the smallest mean gap to the within-city upper bound of the ten methods we evaluate (6.42 mIoU), level with FDA. The benchmark, LOCO protocol, code, and trained models are released to support reproducible evaluation of geographic transfer in overhead dense prediction.

papers.title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
papers.abstract: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

papers.title: Geography of Klein bottle Luttinger surgery
papers.abstract: We propose and study a modification of Auroux's uniqueness question on Luttinger surgery by replacing Lagrangian tori with Klein bottles. In Kodaira dimension $-\infty$, we introduce two simple graphs whose connected components give bounds and, in several cases, exact counts of Klein bottle Luttinger equivalence classes. In Kodaira dimension zero, we provide examples of numerical invariants supporting infinitely many equivalence classes and prove a homological non-triviality theorem for Lagrangian Klein bottles in all symplectic Calabi--Yau surfaces with positive Euler characteristic. In positive Kodaira dimensions, we construct examples in which Klein bottle Luttinger surgery changes the symplectic Kodaira dimension.

papers.title: Control-Aware Separating Hyperplanes for Control Barrier Functions in Planar Navigation
papers.abstract: Separating hyperplanes are widely used in Control Barrier Function (CBF)-based collision avoidance, yet their orientations strongly govern control intervention-the deviation of the applied control from the robot's nominal command. Existing methods typically select hyperplane orientations from geometry alone. Jointly optimizing orientations and control yields a continuous, non-convex problem in which local nonlinear solvers suffer from initialization sensitivity, local minima, and unpredictable latency, while discretized orientation grids scale exponentially with obstacle count. For planar navigation of a polygonal robot among polygonal obstacles, we present a solver-free, control-aware separating hyperplane selection method that directly computes a global optimum of this joint problem at each step whenever it is feasible. Exploiting the geometry of Minkowski difference polygons, we reduce this continuous non-convex optimization to evaluating a polynomial-size set of candidate control interventions via closed-form algebraic checks, selecting the feasible candidate of minimum norm. Across 250 simulated navigation scenarios, our method reduces cumulative intervention cost by 3.6% at the median and 27.3% at the 90th percentile compared to a local nonlinear solver, and completion time by 0.6% and 5.6%, respectively. In scalability benchmarks, it achieves a 6.1x per-step speedup at 16 simultaneous obstacles.

papers.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. In a 20-person deception study, interrogators choose our system over the author's own friends in 7 of 10 rounds, and the author over our system in 13 of 20; neither rate is distinguishable from chance at this sample size. We consider design improvements, applications of personal AI agents, and implications for identity and privacy.

papers.title: The Ceresa Cycle on $X_0^+(p)$
papers.abstract: We consider the curve $X_0^+(p)$ with prime $p$, which is the quotient of the modular curve $X_0(p)$ by the Fricke involution. We describe how one can explicitly calculate the shadow of a Hecke operator on $X_0^+(p)$, which is a rational divisor on $X_0^+(p)$ whose nonvanishing is an obstruction to the Ceresa cycle of $X_0^+(p)$ being torsion in the Chow group of the Jacobian of $X_0^+(p)$. We also provide an implementation of this procedure in PARI/GP and SageMath and use this on all primes below 5000.

papers.title: Stability of Parallel Transport Convolution under Riemannian Metric Perturbations
papers.abstract: Geometric convolutions on Riemannian manifolds depend on the geometry of the underlying domain, making stability under metric perturbations a fundamental question in geometric deep learning. This paper studies this question for parallel transport convolution through methods from differential geometry and analysis. On a fixed compact manifold, we establish that, for a continuous input signal and a continuous reference kernel supported in a sufficiently small normal neighborhood, the convolution output depends continuously in $L^2$ on the Riemannian metric in the $C^2$-topology, under the specified localization and transport-path conventions. The analysis develops perturbation estimates for geodesics, parallel transport, Jacobi fields, and exponential maps, and uses these estimates to compare the transported kernels. A central difficulty is the cut locus, which obstructs uniform comparison of the transport construction over the entire manifold. We address this difficulty by combining uniform estimates away from the cut locus with integral bounds on neighborhoods of arbitrarily small volume, while also controlling the change in the Riemannian volume measure. The resulting qualitative stability theorem connects perturbation theory for Riemannian geometric constructions with the analysis of spatial convolution operators in geometric deep learning.

authors.name: Andrew Stump
authors.institution: Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources

papers.title: Panini- Feasible Grammar For Robot Designs
papers.abstract: Symbolic methods make robot designs interpretable but often overlook continuous geometry; learned methods handle geometry but offer less transparent structure. We introduce a typed production grammar that uses case-role relations, parameter inheritance, and specificity-based rule arbitration to generate both manipulation skills and robot morphologies. A geometric realization map translates grammar composition into transformations in SE(3), behaving as a monoid homomorphism when inheritance is inactive and exhibiting a measurable defect when inheritance is enabled. The grammar provides a compact representation, and its arbitration decisions can be recovered from geometric containment (agreement 0.905 +/- 0.062 across 10 seeds, versus 0.611 +/- 0.090 for a Euclidean control). We also introduce PANINI, a cross-entropy search method over grammar-based morphology representations. Across 30 methods and 24 seeds, PANINI achieves the best mean rank but is not statistically distinguishable from strong generic optimizers. Its main demonstrated advantage is therefore structural rather than optimization performance: grammar-generated designs are legal by construction, and coordinated limb placement produces 95% jointly feasible edits, compared with 55% for range-constrained resampling and none for flat parameterization in 6,000 draws. These results show how typed grammars can make robot generation more interpretable and geometrically coordinated, without implying that every feasible design will locomote or that grammar-based search universally outperforms generic optimizers.

papers.title: JEPA as a Transferable Optimizer: Learning and Understanding Black-Box Optimization from Reward-Agnostic Pretraining
papers.abstract: Black-box optimization evaluates candidates through simulations, rollouts, or experiments, often without gradients. Learned optimizers are usually judged by whether they outperform existing methods. We ask a complementary question: what information does a learned optimizer use from its search history? We introduce JEPA-PS (JEPA Policy Search), based on a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture. It is pretrained on random rollouts using parameter vectors and scalar returns. Its latent-prediction objective predicts the next point in an optimization trajectory rather than its reward or gradient, allowing us to examine what was tried and how well it performed. At test time, JEPA-PS reads a short evaluation history and proposes a candidate in one forward pass, without task descriptions, reward shaping, or test-time gradients. We evaluate it on 15 control environments against 12 optimizers, including evolutionary methods, Bayesian optimization, CMA-ES, and an LLM optimizer. JEPA-PS is competitive with tuned classical baselines and outperforms the LLM optimizer by more than 2x on Swimmer at 71x lower per-step cost. It also transfers zero-shot to environments excluded from pretraining. Null-model comparisons and decoder-training ablations indicate that its latent representation carries information beyond simple history statistics; every trained decoder variant performs worse than the default frozen representation. Our main finding is that the history JEPA-PS uses depends on the task. On smooth landscapes it uses the full trajectory, whereas on rugged landscapes the best-seen point carries nearly all the signal. This memory requirement has a weak positive correlation with fitness-distance correlation (FDC; r=0.112, n=7), while an independent reward-ordering sensitivity probe does not corroborate the relationship (r=-0.024, n=7). Code: https://github.com/mdebnath22/jepa-props.

papers.title: Kernel Ridge Attention: Nonlinear Memory with Selective Forgetting
papers.abstract: Kernel Ridge Attention (KRA) is a recurrent sequence mixer that combines learned nonlinear features with covariance-guided memory updates. It stores associations through recursive ridge regression, using correlations among past keys to determine how new observations modify memory. A content-dependent Ornstein--Uhlenbeck transition controls retention and restores uncertainty for future writes. This construction admits an exact temporal-kernel interpretation and maintains an inference state whose size is independent of context length. Associative block maps and explicit adjoints support parallel training while preserving the recursive update. In controlled language-modeling experiments, KRA improves prediction quality over attention and recurrent baselines, strengthens natural associative recall over the evaluated recurrent models, and achieves practical distributed training throughput. These properties provide a principled foundation for nonlinear, adaptive sequence memory.

authors.name: Haowei Chen
authors.institution: Tianjin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Comparing Lower and Upper Spectral Gaps of Nonnegative Symmetric Matrices
papers.abstract:
We establish sharp estimates comparing the lower and upper spectral gaps of nonnegative symmetric matrices. Combining these comparisons with a multiplicity argument in the spirit of Li and Liu, we improve and extend earlier spectral gap comparison bounds of Saha and Li and Liu, which provide quantitative refinements of an observation of Breuillard, Green, Guralnick and Tao relating combinatorial expansion to two-sided spectral expansion. Our graph estimates hold for nonbipartite even-walk-regular graphs, which covers the classes of graphs, including vertex-transitive graphs, (twisted) Cayley graphs, and (twisted) Cayley sum graphs, investigated in previous work.
  Under an additional eigenmap assumption, we also establish quantitative two-sided comparisons between the lower and upper spectral gaps. In particular, these comparisons apply to walk-regular graphs.

papers.title: Fibrations and nilpotent collapsing structure
papers.abstract:
We construct fiber bundles, singular fibrations, and nilpotent collapsing structures for Riemannian manifolds with lower Ricci curvature bounds under additional geometric assumptions.
  For every $n$ and $D>0$, there exists $\epsilon(n,D)>0$ such that a closed Riemannian $n$-manifold $M$ satisfying \[ \operatorname{diam}(M)\le D,\qquad \operatorname{sec}_M\ge-1,\qquad \operatorname{Ric}_M\ge-\epsilon(n,D) \] admits a finite cover of degree at most $C(n)$ that is a smooth fiber bundle over a nilmanifold. The fibers have finite fundamental group, and the base dimension equals the Hirsch rank of $\pi_1(M)$. If $\pi_1(M)$ is torsion-free, then $M$ itself fibers smoothly over an infranilmanifold with simply connected fibers.
  We next consider a Gromov--Hausdorff convergent sequence $M_i\to X$ of closed Riemannian $n$-manifolds with uniformly bounded diameter, $\operatorname{Ric}_{M_i}\ge -(n-1)$, and the $(\rho,\delta)$ local rewinding Reifenberg condition, where $\rho>0$ is fixed and $\delta$ is sufficiently small. For all sufficiently large $i$, we construct singular fibrations $\bar{F}_i:M_i\to X$ that are $\epsilon_i$-Gromov--Hausdorff approximations, with $\epsilon_i\to0$, and whose fibers are homeomorphic to infranilmanifolds. Under the same local hypotheses, complete, possibly noncompact manifolds admit nilpotent collapsing structures on their $\epsilon(n,\rho)$-collapsed regions.

papers.title: Choosing Supervised Post-Processing for Frozen Person Detectors: Information, Object Changes, and Complete Cost
papers.abstract: A frozen detector computes hypotheses that can support better final outputs through supervised post-processing. Choosing a readout requires knowing which available information improves detection and what its processing costs. We compare candidate scores, class distributions, geometry, native-set summaries and adapted neighborhood meta classification under common candidate, supervision and operating-point conditions. On 320 held-out CrowdHuman images, adding native-set context to a 97-dimensional readout yields 275 more matches and 96 more unmatched predictions. On a separate 319-image cohort, Full100 matches 6004 objects,versus 5848 for source-selected raw WBF and 6002 for a MetaDetect-style adaptation. Its gain over raw contains 300 added and 144 lost discoveries. After execution-equivalent optimization, Full100 and the meta-statistics readout both take approximately 95 ms per complete warm request on a fixed 64-image workload. Source-frozen transfer gives positive point results on 223 MOT17Det frames from seven sequences, while the main MIAP result shows no improvement. The study supports using sufficiently informative output readouts while retaining optimized meta classification as a competitive option. It also shows why feature dimension and net detection gain alone are unreliable guides to adoption.

papers.title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

papers.title: Old Matches, New Frames: Schedule-Gated Stereo Memory from Human Vision to Machine Matching
papers.abstract: Human vision and video stereo networks both reuse disparity evidence across time, yet a refresh of the input can invalidate a match formed milliseconds earlier. What tells a system whether an old match still counts? We answer this from limited human data in three steps. First, nine temporal mechanisms share a frozen binocular-energy front end and an equal-capacity readout, so held-out behavior isolates the temporal selection rule: on 240 conditions from 10 observers, down-weighting aged evidence that has lost binocular support lowers subject RMSE from 12.6% to 10.3% and reproduces a period-dependent reversed-depth illusion, across all 59 readings of the unpublished protocol and 8 front-end perturbations. Second, four propositions establish what such data can identify: gating is identified at the level of the refresh schedule, and candidate binding is invisible to standard stimuli but exposed by a single-eye geometry flip that separates the readouts by up to 7.1%. Third, the identified rule becomes a two-field stereo memory that separates sample validity from hypothesis support. It removes a 50 ms recovery lag after geometry flips, and its regime analysis explains why plain integration stays preferable on MPI-Sintel, where 71.1% of pixels change appearance but not disparity.

papers.title: Choosing What to Observe: Budget-Paired Counterfactual Audits for Credible Evaluation of Visual Agents
papers.abstract: Visual agents that read dense documents must ration a finite observation budget across candidate regions, yet answer accuracy conflates where an agent looks, how it adapts to the reads that remain, and how it an?swers once observation stops. We introduce budget-paired counterfactual audits, an evaluation protocol that holds public evidence and region bindings fixed while perturbing only the remaining budget or de?clared task parameters, and credits every acquired history with exact continuation values. The resulting accounting decomposes lost expected accuracy into stepwise acquisition loss and terminal decision loss, separating planning from fixed-role heuristics. papers.title: Possible origins of the two {\gamma}-ray components C0 and C1 in IC 443
papers.abstract: Recent LHAASO observations of IC~443 reveal that its high-energy $\gamma$-ray emission can be decomposed into two components with clearly distinct spatial morphologies and spectral properties, namely the compact component C0 and component C1 with an angular extent of 0.67$^\circ$. We aim to explain the $\gamma$-ray emission mechanisms responsible for the two components in IC~443 and to further investigate their respective possible astrophysical counterparts. We model components C0 and C1 independently using two different physical scenarios. For component C0, we adopt an SNR-MC hadronic model that accounts for finite source-size effects to describe the escape and diffusion of high-energy particles and their $\gamma$-ray production via pp interactions with the surrounding molecular clouds. For component C1 , we employ a spatially dependent multi-zone leptonic transport model and describe the evolution of high-energy electrons under the combined action of advection, diffusion, and energy losses using a Fokker--Planck-type equation. The model reproduces the SEDs of components C0 and C1 well. Component C0 exhibits a pronounced $\pi^0$-decay feature, and the maximum energy of its escaping particles reaches the PeV scale. The $\gamma$-ray emission from component C1 can be explained by inverse Compton scattering. Its diffusion coefficient is approximately two orders of magnitude lower than that in the surrounding interstellar medium, and no significant synchrotron counterpart is detected. The $\gamma$-ray emission from IC~443 involves the combined action of multiple physical mechanisms. Component C0 may be a potential PeVatron candidate, whereas component C1 may correspond to a potential TeV halo candidate.

papers.title: TinyARM-X: A Series of Open-Source, Configurable, and Transparent Torque-Controlled Desktop-Scale Robotic Manipulators
papers.abstract: Visuomotor policies have demonstrated that imprecise low-cost robots can autonomously complete complex manipulation tasks. However, most inexpensive manipulators rely on compact and rigidly position-controlled servos for actuation, which complicate simulation, operation, and safety. This work introduces TinyARM-X, a framework for easily manufacturable, configurable, and torque-controllable low-cost (<350 USD) serial manipulators. By using a single hardware/software architecture, a <7 Degree of Freedom (DoF) TinyARM can be manually reconfigured to an operational >3 DoF robot within 10 min. Actuator modeling and dynamic compensation enable torque-controlled applications like mixed-reality impedance control teleoperation and simulator force feedback rendering. Experiments include mechanical benchmarking and real-world force-aware telemanipulation. The TinyARM-7 has a payload of 33.5 g, a max speed of 0.77 m/s, and a reach of 210 mm. Moreover, with dynamic compensation, the robot has a backdrive-breakaway force of 1.4 N and a backdrive-running force of 0.7 N. Additionally, Cartesian-Impedance Control (CIC) attains a translational stiffness of >15 N/m. Lastly, the TinyARM-X stack is open-sourced to disseminate accessible desktop-scale torque-controlled robotic manipulation to the community.

papers.title: DexAttention: Distributed Sparse Attention through Rapid Online Planning and Persistent GPU Execution
papers.abstract: Sparse attention reduces computation, but distributed execution may still transfer unnecessary data and incur substantial per-operation overhead. Mask-aware assignment and scheduling can reduce these costs, but replanning for dynamic masks must be cheaper than the execution time it saves. We present DexAttention, a distributed sparse attention system that co-designs fast online planning with persistent execution. Its assigner uses GPU-accelerated, topology-aware clustering to balance computational load and reduce communication. A lightweight greedy scheduler orders coarse communication and computation operations, while a persistent kernel on each GPU enforces fine-grained dependencies and dispatches ready tasks. This division keeps detailed synchronization out of planning while enabling overlap without repeated attention launches. The framework supports static and dynamic per-head masks across multiple attention compute kernels. On a four-node, 16-GPU cluster, DexAttention achieves a $1.39\times$ geometric-mean end-to-end training speedup over the fastest applicable baseline across 11 configurations. For dynamic video attention, it achieves $2.11$--$2.37\times$ speedups over Ring Attention including planning.

papers.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
papers.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.
