Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models are widely adopted in modern VLMs for compute-efficient scalability, yet their multi-expert architecture poses deployment challenges due to substantial memory demands. Mixed-precision quantization is an effective compression technique that reduces bit-widths while adapting to the heterogeneous hardware budgets of edge devices, particularly well-suited for MoE due to its inherent structural sparsity, which causes imbalanced importance among experts. While prior work has applied quantization for efficient MoE inference at the edge, we point out that in MoE-based VLMs, the modality-specific characteristics of visual and text tokens further impact expert quantization. To address this issue, we present MoMoVL, a modality-aware adaptive compression framework for MoE-based VLMs that brings vision-language inference within reach of on-device resource budgets. Motivated by our empirical findings on modality-induced disparities across experts, MoMoVL jointly exploits the per-expert activation profile and per-modality quantization sensitivity to guide bit-width assignment. Experimental results show that MoMoVL improves the accuracy-compression trade-off relative to state-of-the-art mixed-precision baselines and reduces memory footprint by up to 15.44% with a modest drop in accuracy over its uniform-precision baseline. Our code and data are publicly available at https://github.com/sco-edge/MoMoVL.

papers.title: Machine-learned acceleration of earthquake sequence simulations
papers.abstract: Earthquake sequence simulations involve slow interseismic processes and rapid dynamic ruptures. During interseismic periods, a numerical solver can take large time steps efficiently. During seismic periods, in contrast, the solver must drastically reduce the time step, and elastodynamic wave-mediated memory effects become significant; long-term simulations are therefore computationally expensive. We investigate the use of neural operators to accelerate earthquake sequence simulations. We train a Fourier neural operator (FNO) on data from high-fidelity, fully dynamic simulations to learn a jump map that advances the system state from before a seismic rupture to after it. We propose a hybrid modeling framework in which a conventional quasi-dynamic solver simulates the slow interseismic evolution, and the trained FNO replaces the solver during the computationally intensive seismic periods with wave-mediated inertial effects. The hybrid model reproduces key long-term statistics of fully dynamic simulations, including distributions of event magnitudes and recurrence times. Furthermore, it provides a much better approximation to the fully dynamic simulations than the commonly used quasi-dynamic approximation at a reduced computational expense.

papers.title: A higher-order smoothness indicator as refinement criterion for Newtonian and relativistic MHD simulations
papers.abstract: Adaptive mesh refinement is a widely adopted strategy for grid-based numerical simulation codes to mitigate the high computational cost of multi-length scale problems. A robust and reliable mesh refinement criterion with minimal requirement for problem-specific tuning is critical for efficient and accurate simulations. Motivated by the oscillation indicators used in the spectral methods literature, we develop a new mesh refinement criterion employing a 5-point stencil for multi-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics simulations, essentially extending the conventional 3-point L\"ohner scheme. We implement the criterion in the astrophysical fluid dynamics code AthenaK and test it across a variety of benchmark problems in Newtonian, special relativistic, and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, demonstrating its robustness and versatility.

papers.title: What Do Learned 3D Models Add to Localization from Posed References?
papers.abstract: Localizing a query from a few posed reference images avoids building a 3D point map. We ask what the camera predictions of learned 3D models add to geometric estimation from the same references, and where failures arise. Across eight learned models and variants and five test sets, we compare reference budgets, swap pose components, and intervene on the references a model sees. At fine pose-error thresholds, geometric estimation with one additional reference is significantly more accurate than every model on two references on Cambridge and NAVER B1 and never significantly worse, alone or as a fallback behind a shared acceptance gate; with the same three references, the more accurate approach depends on the scene. The gain from the learned translation magnitude depends on reference selection: it improves seven of the eight models on 12-Scenes with the spread-out pairs we select, but none of the five we test with the two top-ranked retrieved references. Where retrieval also returns references from other locations, at NAVER Gangnam Station, models fail at different stages. A robust alignment brings Pi3X and MapAnything within 3.3 pp of adding references as needed. In controlled tests, aligning on the nearby references largely restores VGGT, Pi3X and MapAnything but not Depth Anything 3, and pose-conditioned Pi3X recovers only if the far poses are masked and left out of its input-pose normalization.

papers.title: Split-and-Learn: Decoupled Learning for Reactive Transport in Heterogeneous Marine Sediments
papers.abstract: Reactive transport in heterogeneous marine sediments couples flow and multicomponent transport with nonlinear chemistry and evolving porosity and permeability, and its simulation over thousands of years is computationally expensive, especially when uncertain heterogeneity requires many simulations. We develop Split-and-Learn, a framework that keeps the sequential operator-splitting scheme of the full-order model and replaces each stage by a data-driven surrogate with its own structure. Transport is learned on a local data-driven multiscale space, either as a compressed reduced solution map (global inverse atoms) or as coarse-block pieces of the forward operator assembled into a Galerkin or least-squares Petrov-Galerkin system (local atoms). Chemistry is learned through bounded reaction extents with stoichiometric reconstruction, which preserves reaction invariants and nonnegativity. Flow uses learned interface traces and a reduced mixed multiscale solve that enforces coarse-block mass balance. We prove the stability of the split scheme with the evolving medium and bound the error of the learned solver by the accumulated one-step errors of its stages. Numerical experiments in two- and three-dimensional heterogeneous sediment domains show the accuracy and computational cost of the individual and combined learned stages against the full order split solver.

papers.title: TOGBench: Benchmarking and Improving Tiny-Object Generation Fidelity in Aerial Imagery
papers.abstract: Advances in deep generative models now enable the synthesis of realistic imagery. However, aerial imagery is dominated by tiny objects, such as vehicles, ships, and aircraft, which occupy only a few pixels owing to the overhead, wide-area nature of aerial imaging. Existing generative models struggle substantially more with tiny objects than with larger ones. This limitation has been overlooked, as prior work on generative evaluation emphasizes prompt following or human preference rather than whether small objects are rendered faithfully. To address this gap, we introduce TOGBench, a quantitative, object-level benchmark for evaluating tiny-object generation fidelity in aerial imagery. We further propose two simple train-/inference-time techniques that improve the ability of layout-to-image generators to render small objects, raising their performance on TOGBench.

authors.name: Chanhwi Jeong
authors.institution: Gwangju Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Constructive Trend to Equilibrium for Low-regularity Boltzmann and BGK equations
papers.abstract: We study the long-time behavior of global mild solutions to the cutoff Boltzmann and BGK equations on $\T^3$ under a Gaussian lower bound and a polynomially weighted $L^\infty$ upper bound. The main step is a finite-time estimate which uses free transport to control the entropy of the local Maxwellian by microscopic entropy and dissipation, without assuming Sobolev regularity. For Boltzmann, Villani's entropy-production inequality and a comparison of collision kernels give polynomial decay when the velocity weight has order $m>7$. For a sufficiently large weight, the large-amplitude theory then gives exponential decay in the weighted norm and in relative entropy. For BGK, the microscopic inequality is linear, so entropy decays exponentially from the finite-time estimate. Finally, we establish a density criterion for large-data BGK dynamics in the polynomially weighted $L^\infty$ class of Perthame and Pulvirenti. For weight order $m>10$, a uniform upper bound on the local density guarantees uniform-in-time weighted bounds and exponential convergence to equilibrium in both relative entropy and the weighted $L^\infty$ norm.

papers.title: ProxySearch: Decoupled Inference-Time Scaling for Diffusion Models via Asymmetric Noise-Rank Transfer
papers.abstract: Noise search at inference time improves text-to-image diffusion but requires many multi-step teacher rollouts per query. Distilled few-step models are now routinely released, yet their potential as proxies inside noise search is uncharacterized. We measure proxy-teacher rank agreement across three distillation regimes and three backbones (DiT, MMDiT, UNet) and find a sharp asymmetry. On our main pool, closed-form image statistics transfer from the proxy to the teacher (Spearman $\rho$ up to 0.80), while learned semantic scorers do not ($\rho \le$ 0.12). Paired null controls trace this rank to the first denoising step for coarse statistics and to distillation for finer ones. We use the asymmetry for noise search under a joint constraint: a semantic reward specifies content, and a numeric target specifies image statistics. In PROXYSEARCH, the proxy filters candidates by statistical match in 1 step, and the teacher returns the survivor with the highest semantic reward. No weight trades one objective against the other. On FLUX-1024, PROXYSEARCH tightens the statistical target by 21-23% at the same number of teacher trajectories, with no detected loss on the optimized reward.

papers.title: Physical Layer Security for Digital Semantic Communication: A Bit-Level Perspective
papers.abstract: Digital semantic communication requires reliable recovery of task-relevant information at a legitimate receiver while limiting source reconstruction by an eavesdropper. Uniform bit protection, however, does not account for the heterogeneous reliability and secrecy requirements of semantic bits. This paper proposes a bit-level physical layer security (PLS) framework that learns these requirements and incorporates them into physical-layer resource allocation. We first introduce a wiretap semantic feature channel whose two-stage training learns per-bit target bit-flip probabilities for the legitimate receiver (Bob) and the eavesdropper (Eve). These targets characterize the reliability requirements at Bob and the secrecy protection requirements against Eve. Based on the learned targets, we formulate a joint power and artificial-noise (AN) allocation problem for a multiple-input single-output wiretap channel under a worst-case angular-separation model. For a given target profile, the optimal information-AN power split admits a closed-form solution, and the per-bit power allocation is obtained by water-filling. We further develop a leakage-aware selection method among multiple learned-target profiles and extend the design to multiple-input multiple-output channels. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves a better trade-off between preserving reconstruction quality at Bob and degrading that at Eve than uniform power allocation and the evaluated learning-based secure semantic communication schemes.

authors.name: Yo-Seb Jeon
authors.institution: Pohang University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Agreement Is Not Accuracy: LiDAR Elevation Errors Hidden in LiDAR-Camera Extrinsics
papers.abstract: LiDAR and cameras provide complementary measurements for 3D vision, yet agreement between their observations does not establish the accuracy of either sensor's internal geometry. We show that systematic LiDAR elevation biases can be absorbed into the estimated extrinsics. Using synchronized LiDAR intensities and camera-estimated checkerboard poses, we jointly estimate a sensor-specific elevation correction shared across recordings and extrinsics for each recording. Ray-plane intersections locate the checker pattern without using reported ranges, preventing range errors from directly moving the lookup. Under matched intensity and correction models, this lookup gives smaller camera-consistency residuals than measured-point lookup. Across six identically designed rigs using the same sensor models, recording-excluded corrections reduce the mean translation-reference distance from 7.57 to 3.04 mm. On separate structures, they reduce inter-plane angle errors against references from independent dense camera scans and improve image-edge alignment. Rolling the rigs shifts the plane pairs exhibiting the largest angular improvements, as predicted for an elevation-only correction. Within the ray-plane model, calibration-target projections and loop-consistency residuals change little despite these geometric improvements. These findings show why agreement after extrinsic calibration need not establish correct internal LiDAR geometry. Synchronized observations of a familiar checkerboard provide a practical route to estimating and testing elevation corrections without a dedicated large calibration field. We plan to release code and data for reproducing the main results.

authors.name: Yeon Kun Lee
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

authors.name: Dongseok Yang
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

authors.name: Deok-Kyeong Jang
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

authors.name: Choongho Chung
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Grading Executable Legal Rules Against Independent Records: Transitional Provisions and Korean SME Status
papers.abstract: Laws are increasingly turned into programs that decide cases, such as whether a firm was a small or medium enterprise (SME) on a given date, and large language models (LLMs) now write them. The programs are usually graded against answers written by someone who read the same law, so a program can score well by sharing the grader's reading rather than by getting the law right. LexTemporis grades them instead against records of what actually happened: 10,901 firm-years of SME status disclosed by Korean listed companies, with every version of the governing rules. An appendix adds comparison cases from US income tax and German hospital minimum volumes. The date changes outcomes mainly through provisions outside the main statutory text: one transitional provision raises agreement with the disclosures from 83-86% to 89-90%. The disclosures also test the author's reading of a contested provision, favouring it in 130 of 189 firm-years where readings diverge. Four LLMs wrote the rules, given different selections of the law. A pre-registered comparison finds no condition better across all four models. In exploratory analyses, supplying the right provisions looks better graded against the author's reading than against the records: the advantage shrinks for three models (for one, to between a quarter and three-fifths of its size), and per firm-year it is several times larger where the author's reading is wrong, partly by construction, since there reproducing that reading more faithfully must lose. Grading legal programs against the grader's own reading can overstate how well they work.

papers.title: Inherited Adapter Experts for Replay-Free Domain-Incremental Learning
papers.abstract: Replay-free domain-incremental learning trains a model on the same classes in successive domains without keeping earlier images. Per-domain learners freeze a pre-trained ViT and train an additional expert for each new domain: the small set of parameters and the classification head learned on that domain. Test images carry no domain label, so a router selects one expert for each image. Recent work trains this router. However, a training-free Mahalanobis router costs the analyzed learners under 2.7 points of final accuracy relative to always selecting each image's own-domain expert. The experts, not this router, limit accuracy. Our learner, Lamarck, therefore uses this router and strengthens the experts. Its adapters, small trainable layers that correct every image token after each deep ViT block, add 4.4 points of final accuracy on the deepfake benchmark CDDB-Hard. In addition, each expert is initialized from its predecessor at no extra cost: the domains share their classes, so an image misrouted to a later expert loses less. Against twelve frozen-backbone baselines under one protocol, Lamarck is first on CDDB-Hard by 5.2 points, second on DomainNet and OfficeHome, and highest in mean accuracy.

papers.title: Moment-Fourier approach to parallel closures and transport for a toroidally confined multi-ion plasma
papers.abstract: We develop a multi-ion closure framework for tokamak plasmas by solving the drift-kinetic equation using the moment-Fourier method. The model extends our previous single-ion formulation to plasmas containing multiple ion species and consistently incorporates inter-species collisional effects in the moment system. As a representative case, we consider a deuterium-carbon plasma, assuming a common zeroth-order ion temperature on each flux surface while allowing the electron temperature to differ. The first-order fluid moments, namely density, temperature, and parallel flow velocity, are computed for electrons, deuterium ions, and carbon ions. The framework enables a direct comparison of the first-order parallel flow velocities of deuterium and carbon ions, thereby providing a quantitative basis for interpreting charge-exchange spectroscopy measurements and for systematic multi-ion neoclassical transport studies.

papers.title: Structure-Preserving Neural Approximation of Convex, Semiconvex, and Quasiconvex Functions
papers.abstract: Input convex neural networks provide a natural way to enforce convexity globally through architectural constraints. We study how this structure-preserving approximation framework extends to semiconvex, quasiconvex, and convex transformable functions. For $C^{1,1}$ convex functions on compact convex domains, we establish the sharp $W^{1,p}$ minimax rate $m^{-1/d}$ under max-affine approximation with $m$ affine pieces, and show that every max-affine function admits an exact bounded-width ICNN representation with complexity linear in $m$. The same $W^{1,p}$ approximation rate extends to semiconvex functions through quadratic lifting and to convex transformable functions through monotone composition. For general Lipschitz quasiconvex functions, we develop a quantitative finite-probe approximation theory based on monotone responses to affine projections and obtain a structure-preserving IqCNN with an $L^\infty$ approximation guarantee. We further show that these approximation results extend to ReLU-transferable smooth activations, including Softplus and ELU. Numerical experiments on PDE-based approximation problems compare the proposed architectures with parameter-matched MLPs and validation-tuned shape penalties, demonstrating global structural validity without penalty tuning while maintaining competitive approximation accuracy. Overall, the results identify recoverable convex latent structure as the key mechanism enabling gradient-level structure-preserving approximation beyond convexity.

authors.name: Yeoneung Kim
authors.institution: Seoul National University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Teaching VLMs What to Say, Not How to Reason: Rethinking Counterfactual Reasoning in Autonomous Driving
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have been shown to suffer from shortcut learning and causal confusion, limiting their ability to generalize robustly under distribution shift. To mitigate these limitations, recent works based on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have explored incorporating linguistic reasoning capabilities into driving decision-making, reporting improvements in driving performance. In particular, counterfactual (CF) reasoning has been proposed to enable self-reflective, high-level causal understanding. However, it remains unclear whether the language-based reasoning mitigates shortcut learning or merely shifts it from visual representations to linguistic patterns, creating an illusion of causal understanding. Moreover, existing approaches often conflate intervention-based reasoning with CF reasoning, leaving the effects of genuine CF reasoning unexplored. In this work, we examine what CF reasoning actually induces in VLM-based autonomous driving and observe that it shifts the action distribution toward more conservative behaviors while increasing uncertainty in reasoning and decision-making. This effect persists under reinforcement fine-tuning, suggesting that it is not merely a transient artifact. Furthermore, visual attention analysis shows that CF reasoning does not alter visual grounding, while causal intervention experiments reveal that masking causally relevant and non-causal factors in accident scenarios results in comparable decision change rates. Overall, these results suggest that CF reasoning does not induce genuine causal reasoning grounded in visual evidence. Instead, it acts as a linguistic shortcut that reshapes the action distribution, teaching models what to say but not how to reason, highlighting a gap between language-based reasoning and causal understanding in autonomous driving.

papers.title: Cosmetic crossings and the knot complement problem
papers.abstract: We prove the cosmetic crossing conjecture, Problem 1.58 in Kirby's list, and the generalized cosmetic crossing conjecture for every knot whose branched double cover is an L-space; in particular, both hold for all alternating and all quasi-alternating knots. We also prove the oriented knot complement conjecture, Problem 1.81(D), for all closed 3-manifolds with finite fundamental group, in particular for all lens spaces: in such a manifold, every knot whose exterior is irreducible and not a solid torus is determined by its complement. Both results rest on a monotonicity theorem for Heegaard Floer correction terms: if a knot in a rational homology sphere has an isotropic, nonzero homology class, then the sum of all correction terms strictly increases along its surgeries with coefficients -1/j relative to the rational longitude, so no nontrivial surgery yields the original oriented manifold. We also show that every purely cosmetic band surgery on a knot with an L-space branched double cover is weakly nugatory, which answers a question of Rogers for these knots.

papers.title: Real Fr{\o}yshov invariants and lattice homology
papers.abstract: For a class of almost rational plumbing 4-manifolds equipped with smooth involutions, we give a description of the Real Fr{\o}yshov invariants of their boundaries in terms of lattice homology. Our approach uses the $S^1$-stable equivalence between Seiberg-Witten Floer spectra and lattice spectra constructed by Dai-Sasahira-Stoffregen, and the $\operatorname{O}(2)$-equivariant versions of these spectra developed by Kang-Park-Taniguchi. As applications, we derive a formula for these invariants for every $\operatorname{spin}^c$ structure on the double branched covers of even torus knots $T_{2p,q}$, and determine the smooth nonorientable $4$-genus of an infinite family of torus knots $T_{4,q}$.

papers.title: Smooth structures on polyhedral products of disks and spheres
papers.abstract: We prove that every polyhedral product of disks and their boundary spheres that is a topological manifold admits a stably parallelizable smooth structure. We also show that if a moment-angle complex or a real moment-angle complex admits a smooth structure for which the coordinate action is smooth, then the link of every face of the underlying simplicial complex is a simplicial sphere, and every such smooth structure is stably parallelizable.

authors.name: Suyoung Choi
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Finding four vertices of a square of area $n$ in a grid by geometric construction
papers.abstract: In this study, we consider geometric construction in an infinite square grid. Our purpose is to find efficient methods for constructing a square of area $n\in\mathbb{N}$ based on arithmetic properties of the sum of squares. As a consequence, for each $n\in\mathbb{N}$, we derive the optimal number of construction steps required to determine the four vertices of the square. Furthermore, we classify all positive integers into three classes according to these optimal numbers.

authors.name: Dohyeok Kim
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Variational Estimates for the Hardy--Littlewood Maximal Operator on Finite Graphs
papers.abstract: We study edge variation for the centered Hardy--Littlewood maximal operator on finite connected graphs. We determine the optimal uniform coefficient controlling the oscillation of the maximal function by the edge variation of the original function and derive two-sided estimates for the variational constant of an individual graph. These estimates involve point-mass tests, the diameter, and the number of edges. On star graphs, we determine the sharp constant for exponents greater than one and characterize all nonconstant real-valued extremizers for every exponent.

papers.title: Variational Estimates for the Fractional Maximal Operator on Finite Graphs
papers.abstract: We study edge variation estimates for the centered fractional maximal operator on finite connected graphs. For $0<\alpha<1$, we determine the optimal coefficient in the uniform estimate of the oscillation of the maximal function by the edge $p$-variation of the original function. We also obtain two-sided variation bounds involving the number of vertices and the diameter. On complete graphs, we prove that the sharp $(p,q)$ constant is $(1-n^{\alpha-1})(n-1)^{1/q-1/p}$ for all $0<p\leq q\leq\infty$. On star graphs with $n\geq4$, we determine the sharp infinite-exponent constant and show that the sharp constant for $p=2$ equals $1-n^{\alpha-1}$ if and only if $n^{\alpha-1}\geq1/2$. Combining this with the known estimate for $p=1$, we also obtain sharp mixed estimates. Extremizers and counterexamples are given.

papers.title: Rigidity for the quadratic Riemann curvature functional in dimensions greater than four
papers.abstract: We investigate rigidity properties of critical metrics for the quadratic Riemann curvature functional on Riemannian manifolds of dimension greater than four. This functional is the integral of the squared norm of the Riemann curvature tensor. On noncompact manifolds, criticality is understood with respect to compactly supported variations, without assuming finite total curvature energy. We prove that every complete noncompact critical metric with finite curvature energy is either flat or has strictly negative scalar curvature everywhere. We further show that every complete critical metric with concircular scalar curvature is flat. Here concircularity means that the Hessian of the scalar curvature is pointwise proportional to the metric. Consequently, every complete weakly Einstein critical metric with divergence-free Cotton tensor is flat. The latter two flatness results require neither noncompactness nor finite curvature energy. Finally, we construct a complete nonflat critical metric in dimension five with vanishing Cotton tensor, showing that the concircularity and weakly Einstein assumptions are essential in the respective flatness results.

papers.title: Superspecial curves of genus two over prime fields: Frobenius types and rational (2,2)-kernels
papers.abstract: Superspecial curves of genus two over a prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$, and the rational $(2,2)$-isogenies between their Jacobians, are the vertices and edges of the graph on which genus-two isogeny-based cryptography is built. Let $C$ be such a curve, with Jacobian $J$ and Frobenius endomorphism $\pi$. We show that $\pi^2 = p\,\alpha_*$ for a unique automorphism $\alpha$ of $C$ over $\mathbb{F}_p$ whose action on the Weierstrass points is the square of that of Frobenius. For $p \ge 7$ this gives the list of Frobenius types of the Weierstrass points: eight types, each with its Weil polynomial, a congruence condition on $p$, and its number 15, 3, 3, 7, 1, 1, 3 or 1 of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational $(2,2)$-kernels; when all Weierstrass points are rational, the 2-Tate pairing on $J[2]$ is determined by $p \bmod 8$. We then prove closed formulas, in terms of class numbers of imaginary quadratic orders and of $\zeta_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt p)}(-1)$, for the mass of the curves of each type and for the mass of the rational kernels whose quotient is a product of elliptic curves. For $\pi^2 = \pm p$ the total masses are due to Ibukiyama and to Xue and Yu; our proofs use the 2-adic Tate modules, the symmetry of the Richelot correspondence and Eichler's mass formula, and, for the other curves, modules over orders of a quartic CM field. The kernels are counted through gluings of supersingular elliptic curves. As a consequence, the proportion of rational kernels with decomposed quotient is of order $p^{-1/2}(1+L(1,\chi))$, where $\chi$ is the quadratic character of $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{-p})$. All formulas agree with an exact enumeration for the 37 primes $7 \le p \le 173$. Finally we describe the graph of $\mathbb{F}_p$-rational Richelot isogenies, which is far from connected in the range computed, and discuss what these results say about its use in isogeny-based cryptography.

papers.title: A Hardware-Aware Comprehensive Study of Edge Vision Deployment with A Unified Hardware-Model-Runtime Mapping Framework
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of deep learning has driven the deployment of computer vision directly on resource-constrained edge devices. However, the extreme heterogeneity of edge hardware architectures poses major challenges in selecting and designing suitable vision models. This survey bridges the gap between edge hardware constraints, model architectures, and deployment software toolchains. We establish a comprehensive taxonomy classifying edge hardware into three distinct tiers: mid-range devices (GPUs and dedicated NPUs or TPUs), dedicated embedded MPU or SoC processors, and microcontrollers (MCUs). We aggregate and analyze multi-source benchmark results for image classification and object detection across the computing spectrum, spanning from tens of watts down to milliwatt-scale bare-metal MCUs. Based on these empirical findings, we propose a two-tiered hardware-to-model mapping framework that provides concrete model selection matrices across performance priorities (Speed, Balanced, Accuracy) and actionable architectural design principles (peak SRAM budgeting, resolution-first scaling, and algorithm-compiler co-design). Finally, we highlight critical deployment challenges including toolchain fragmentation, operator incompatibility, and Vision Transformer feasibility, and outline promising future research directions in on-device adaptation and sustainable Edge AI.

authors.name: Le Duc An
authors.institution: Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology

authors.name: Le Duc Thanh
authors.institution: Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City

authors.name: Vo Hoai Viet
authors.institution: Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City

papers.title: Towards Deep Learning-Based Linear Assignment Problem Solvers for Multi-Object Tracking
papers.abstract: This paper proposes and evaluates deep learning (DL)-based linear assignment problem (LAP) solvers as a replacement for the classical Hungarian algorithm in multi-object tracking (MOT) systems. Three representative neural models are studied, namely a convolutional network (CNN), a graph neural network (GNN), and the graph-based linear assignment network (GLAN). A cost-matrix embedding is introduced so that a single model operates on cost matrices of any size, as required in MOT where the number of objects varies over time, without training a separate model for each input shape. Extensive simulations show that the embedding improves the accuracy of the neural solvers (i.e., CNN and GNN), while GLAN attains the best accuracy among them. These solvers are then integrated into a generalized labeled multi-Bernoulli (GLMB) tracker and evaluated on the WILDTRACK dataset, where GLAN yields tracking accuracy close to the Hungarian reference and comparable to recent DL-based trackers.

authors.name: Tran Thi Thuy Quynh
authors.institution: VNU University of Engineering and Technology

papers.title: Regularity and stabilization of integral closures of powers of homogeneous ideals
papers.abstract: In this paper, we establish explicit polynomial bounds for the regularity defect and the stabilization index of integral closures of powers of arbitrary homogeneous ideals over fields of any characteristic. Specifically, let $I \subseteq K[x_{1}, \dots, x_{n}]$ be a nonzero proper homogeneous ideal generated in degrees at most $d$. We prove that $\reg \overline{I^{s}} \le \rho(I)s + d^{(n-1)2^{n}}$ for every $s \ge 1$, where $\rho(I) \le d$ denotes the eventual slope of $\reg \overline{I^{s}}$. Furthermore, the stabilization bound is polynomial in $d$ for a fixed number of variables $n$. In characteristic zero, an upper bound for the first Hilbert coefficient yields a significantly sharper exponent. Our approach relies on exact equigenerated reductions, free lattice constructions within normalized Rees algebras, monic Frobenius presentations, and Tor-module regularity controls, complemented by generic source hyperplanes that reduce the stabilization behavior to the eventual nonvanishing of graded components.

papers.title: Geometry-bridge flow matching for blind rigid-motion correction in head cone-beam CT
papers.abstract: Rigid motion of a patient head during head cone-beam CT (CBCT) scan can degrade image quality and complicate recovery of accurate anatomical structures from the measured projections. We present a 3D flow-matching prior approach that learns the image changes induced by motion. Its geometry-bridge connects motion-corrupted and motion-free Feldkamp-Davis-Kress (FDK) reconstructed images of the same source volume through progressively reduced simulated motion. The forward projector's geometry derivative supplies analytic velocity targets along this path. A plug-and-play loop encompasses the learned image updates together with spline-based pose estimation, conjugate-gradient data consistency, and image total-variation regularization. Both the refined image volume and the FDK reconstructed image volume at the estimated poses are evaluated. On simulated 360-view scans from 30 held-out CQ500 patients with nominal per-component motion amplitudes within 10 mm / 10 degrees, the framework achieved state-of-the-art image reconstruction quality and motion accuracy in comparison with other methos such as learned autofocus and diffusion-based joint reconstruction. Mean peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) reached 37.1 dB and mean detector-plane reprojection error (RPE) was 0.27 mm. With matched endpoints at the inference settings, the geometry bridge improved PSNR by 1.6 dB and reduced RPE by 33% relative to image-linear training. With 50 prior updates and coarse-to-fine motion estimation, total processing time averaged 9.1 minutes per patient on an RTX A6000.

authors.name: Seungryong Cho
authors.institution: Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology

papers.title: Inferring Neural Activity Changes under Recording Uncertainty with Transformers and Variational Inference
papers.abstract: A difference in recorded firing rate across days may reflect a change in neuronal activity, missed spikes or recording a different neuron. We present a statistical approach that combines neuron tracking with Bayesian estimates of stationary mean recorded firing rates. Bounds under assumed differences in spike detection connect recorded rates to biological rate changes. We assess recording loss and uncertainty in rate changes in simulations, and count-model fit in recordings. We also compare two transformer estimators with Gaussian and flow variational inference under a shared temporal negative-binomial model. Flow variational inference agrees most closely with reference posteriors, while predictive performance varies across mice. Rate-change intervals contain true simulated changes less often than intended. In UnitMatch recordings from five mice, some inferred changes remain supported when spike detection is allowed to differ between days; others depend on equal detection. These interpretations require a correct neuron match. The approach identifies which inferred rate changes remain supported under specified recording assumptions and where uncertainty limits interpretation.

papers.title: Learning Martial Arts Motion Skills for Animating Opponents in VR Sparring Games
papers.abstract: Animating virtual opponents is an important yet challenging task in game development. In martial arts games, opponent motions must not only be physically plausible but also exhibit appropriate technique, timing, transitions, and target-directed intent. Traditional game animations often rely on handcrafted clips, state machine transitions, and procedural adjustments, which can be labor-intensive and may limit the behavioral diversity of non-player characters. This paper presents a martial arts motion skills learning framework for character animation in virtual sparring games. Inspired by Tang Soo Do, we collected a martial arts motion capture dataset containing isolated attacking and defending techniques, technique combinations and transitions, and contextual sparring variations. We first pretrained a reusable repertoire of martial arts motion skills from the captured data using reinforcement learning (RL) with adversarial style rewards, and then adapted these skills with task-specific rewards for target-directed striking and threat-aware evasion. We evaluated the motions generated by the learned policy through a user study, in which participants assessed their physical plausibility, smoothness, and martial arts form. To demonstrate their applicability to interactive gameplay, we developed a VR sparring prototype for Meta Quest headsets. The prototype combines policy-generated motion clips with lightweight state-based control to support interactive opponent behavior. Together, these findings support the feasibility of using a learned martial arts skill repertoire as a motion foundation for animating opponents in VR sparring games.

authors.name: Pavan Turaga
authors.institution: The University of Texas at Austin

papers.title: Optimal Control of RKHS Diffeomorphic Flows for Classification and Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: We develop a unified optimal-control framework that solves supervised classification and likelihood-based density estimation with a single diffeomorphic flow whose velocity lives in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS); the two tasks share all structure except the objective. Variable projection eliminates the terminal model (a classifier, or a Gaussian-mixture (GMM) reference), leaving a reduced control problem whose gradient comes from an analytic discrete adjoint. The RKHS parameterization makes the flow's divergence exact and deterministic at the cost of one kernel matrix-vector product, avoiding the stochastic trace estimators and potential-flow restrictions of existing continuous normalizing flows. Because the objective and gradient are deterministic, matrix-free reduced Gauss-Newton (GN) and related second-order solvers are practical for both tasks, which we benchmark against a range of first- and second-order optimizers; the learned map is a diffeomorphism with explicitly controlled regularity. In experiments from dimension 2 to 256, the reduced GN solvers use the fewest iterations of any optimizer tested and, together with joint L-BFGS, the least work; a multiscale kernel improves the density fit, and a trainable GMM reference reduces the deformation needed for multimodal transport at comparable likelihood while lowering the likelihood on real data. The full-model solve is quadratic in the particle count and sub-linear in dimension; a control-point reduction makes the particle-count scaling linear at near-lossless accuracy.

papers.title: Laguerre-MPPI
papers.abstract: Model Predictive Path Integral control (MPPI) is a sampling-based control method that handles nonlinear dynamics and non-convex costs without gradient information. Since MPPI samples the entire input sequence, longer prediction horizons lead to a higher-dimensional sampling space, potentially degrading control performance. This paper proposes Laguerre-MPPI, which parameterizes the control input sequence using discrete-time Laguerre basis functions and samples the basis coefficients. The resulting search dimension is independent of the prediction horizon. Hence, a longer prediction horizon does not require more samples to maintain the sampling density. For linear systems with quadratic costs, we derive a closed-loop stability condition in the infinite-sample limit. Under finite sampling, we provide a closed-form expression for the limit of the ratio of the effective sample size to the number of samples. We also show that the upper bound of this limit for Laguerre-MPPI is no lower than that for conventional MPPI. Numerical experiments demonstrate smoother inputs in obstacle avoidance and maintained performance over long horizons. Moreover, they verify the lower bound on the number of samples given by the finite-sample analysis.

papers.title: Asymmetric Optical Image Watermarking
papers.abstract: Watermark detectors held by a provider cannot be checked by third parties, and a party that can detect a mark can usually also forge it. We study a two-layer image watermark in which the Fourier transform at the core of the pipeline is performed by a coherent optical 4F unit. Layer 1 carries an Ed25519 signature bound to the image content in Fourier magnitudes, so anyone with the public key verifies offline. Layer 2 is a key-defined carrier written by a secret phase hologram and read by a matched-filter correlator. The optics is a scalar-diffraction simulation with finite modulator bits, pixel aperture, pupil, defocus, misalignment, and sensor noise. No hardware is built. All criteria were fixed in a hashed specification before any optical result. The simulated optical signer reproduces the digital pipeline (field error 1.7e-15, bit agreement 99.997%), verifies at least 99.5% of 877 images under each of 8 post-sensor settings, one unattacked, and accepts none of 40,670 unmarked images. The optical carrier is key-selective: the matched key detects it on 99.8% of the unattacked images, and detection falls to 0% under a scale error of 1% and to 0% under a mask shift of 1 bin. Security rests on the signature and the content binding, for which we separate what is provable from what is measured.

papers.title: A Complete Classification of the One-Dimensional Nonlocal Eigenvalue Problem
papers.abstract: We give a complete classification of the spectral stability of the following one-dimensional nonlocal eigenvalue problem (NLEP) $$ \partial_x^2\phi-\phi+pw^{p-1}\phi-\gamma(p-1)\frac{\int_{\mathbb{R}}w^{r-1}\phi dx}{\int_{\mathbb{R}}w^r dx}w^p=\lambda\phi, $$ where $w$ is the unique positive even solution of $w''-w+w^p=0$ decaying at infinity, $p,r>1$, and $\gamma\in\mathbb{C}$ with $\Re\gamma\ge0$. This type of NLEP appears frequently in pattern formation in reaction-diffusion systems. We show that on the even subspace, strict spectral stability holds exactly for $\Re\gamma>1$ when $r=(p+3)/2$. In the $\gamma$-plane, when $r>(p+3)/2$, two conjugate boundary arcs open to the left from $\gamma=1$, and the strictly stable region lies to their right. When $r<(p+3)/2$, the arcs open to the right, and the strictly stable region lies between them. Their common endpoint is $\gamma=1$ when $r\ge(p-1)/2$ and $\gamma=\gamma_H>1$ when $1<r<(p-1)/2$. In each case, the two arcs approach a common vertical asymptote. As an application, for real $\gamma\ge0$, the condition for strict spectral stability is $\gamma>1$ when $r\ge(p-1)/2$ and $\gamma>\gamma_H$ when $1<r<(p-1)/2$, where $\gamma_H>1$ is the value at which a conjugate pair of eigenvalues crosses the imaginary axis. The key ingredient in determining how the number of eigenvalues in the open right half-plane changes at imaginary-axis crossings is a cumulative estimate for the mixed-sign spectral weights that arise for certain $p$ and $r$ with $1<p<3$ and $1<r<2$.

papers.title: Volume growth and gap Theorem for manifolds with non-negative complex sectional curvature
papers.abstract: The combined work of Liu, Ni, and Ni-Tam established that a complete K\"ahler manifold with positive bisectional curvature has Euclidean volume growth if and only if its curvature decays quadratically on average. In this work, we use the approximation scheme developed by Cabezas-Rivas and Wilking to establish the Riemannian analogue under the assumption of nonnegative complex sectional curvature. As an application, we prove an optimal gap theorem for manifolds with nonnegative complex sectional curvature. These results generalize the authors' earlier work.

papers.title: Learning through Discernment: when a small language model learns from user feedback on the job, and when it decays
papers.abstract: Small language models on devices could keep improving by learning, overnight, from their own daily work. Without a true outcome, however, something must decide which attempts are worth learning from, and both the model's own judgment and the user's reaction can be wrong. We study a small model (Qwen3 0.6B and 1.7B) with a LoRA adapter, fine-tuned each night on the attempts a judge accepts, over 127 lives of up to a year on WebShop and $\tau^2$-bench. We compare the true outcome, the user's stated verdict and the model's own judgment with a separate, frozen "feedback sense" that reads the user's reaction, built in three versions. Judging itself, the model improved and then decayed, over a year and whatever its adapter. A sense that took polite give-ups for success collapsed 3 of 5 lives; one built for discernment, which first asks whether the user gave a clear verdict, kept 4 of 5 near the oracle for two weeks, then faded on clean but scarce lessons, to the level of self-judging by day 60. When the user cannot see the outcome ($\tau^2$-bench), the sense read reactions correctly, yet 80% of its lessons were failures the customer had thanked. Across 97 lives, the share of failed attempts among the lessons predicted the outcome (Spearman $\rho$ = -0.81). In our experiments, learning from users held up only where the judge kept failures out and the user could see the outcome; lopsided lessons may also narrow the model.

papers.title: Weight Space Programming for Vision Language Model Repair
papers.abstract: In weight-space programming, a language model edits a network's weights directly, without gradients. We ask what a successful repair of this kind relies on. We plant faults in the weights of two vision-language models, SmolVLM-256M and LFM2-VL-450M, and check each edit made by a coding agent against the original weights. Without being told where to look, the agent finds rescaled rows in the projector and noise in the vision encoder of both models, infers the unknown scale factors, restores most or all of the rescaled weights to their exact original values, and returns accuracy to near its original level; programs that it writes from such weights repair unseen checkpoints of the same model without feedback. These repairs depend on a trace of how the faults were computed. The original weights have 16-bit precision, and faults computed in 32-bit arithmetic leave low bits that only the damaged weights carry. Rounding those bits away leaves each model's answers to our test questions unchanged, and the agent, unaided, then restores no weight exactly: on SmolVLM it no longer finds the damage, and in a single session on LFM2-VL its only gain comes from rescaling answer-token embeddings, which changes how often the model answers yes. Marking the damaged weights again in their low bits brings the edits back to them. Rounded weights still hold statistical evidence of the rescaling, in the distribution of stored values and in row norms, and one sentence in the prompt that names such a statistic directs the agent's edits to the damaged rows on both models. Swapped rows or columns, which leave the set of stored values unchanged, are not found unaided on either model within our session budgets. We recommend that studies of weight repair report the number format of the weights and include a rounded control.

papers.title: Large Single Crystal Growth and Transport Properties of KCd$_4$As$_3$ and RbCd$_4$As$_3$
papers.abstract: Large-size KCd$_4$As$_3$ and RbCd$_4$As$_3$ single crystals were grown using the flux method. Appropriate flux for growing single crystals was determined to be Cd$_2$As, resulting in the increase in their size to be a centimeter for KCd$_4$As$_3$. The KCd$_4$As$_3$ and RbCd$_4$As$_3$ crystals exhibited metal-like temperature dependences of their electrical resistivities with negative Seebeck coefficients, characterizing them as n-type thermoelectric materials.

papers.title: Second-Order Steady-State Approximation of Heterogeneous Mean-Field Models
papers.abstract: Mean-field models provide tractable approximations for large stochastic systems, but second-order steady-state results are largely limited to homogeneous or fixed-dimensional population processes. This paper develops a second-order steady-state approximation for fully heterogeneous mean-field models. Conditioning on the realized agent parameters, we study fixed-dimensional weighted occupancies even though the dimension of the full heterogeneous mean-field system grows linearly with the number of agents $M$. We first establish an $O(M^{-1})$ bound on the mean-field approximation error for stationary expectations of twice continuously differentiable functions of these occupancies. We then characterize the leading term in this error in terms of the stationary mean bias and covariance of the weighted occupancies. A Lyapunov equation for the linearized dynamics yields an approximation to the stationary covariance of the unscaled weighted occupancy with error $O(M^{-3/2})$. Its solution, together with the drift derivatives at equilibrium, also gives an explicit $1/M$ correction to the mean-field prediction of the stationary mean. The corrected mean has error $o(M^{-1})$, which improves to $O(M^{-3/2})$ under a stronger bound on the drift remainder. The resulting covariance and mean-refinement equations have the same structure as the finite-time heterogeneous refined mean-field equations, but our results directly provide steady-state guarantees for weighted occupancies rather than marginal state probabilities of individual agents. The results are illustrated through a heterogeneous power-of-two load-balancing model with buffer size two.

authors.name: Lei Ying
authors.institution: State Key Laboratory of Luminescent Materials and Devices

papers.title: FormalFixer: Intent-Aligned Automated Hardware Repair via Joint Refinement of Specifications, Assertions, and RTL Implementations
papers.abstract:
Functional errors in hardware designs can compromise correctness and security, and must be fixed before tape-out. Formal property verification (FPV) provides strong guarantees by proving or refuting assertions, but a failed assertion is not always evidence of an RTL defect: the failure may also come from a buggy assertion or from a specification that is semantically correct but too ambiguous or incomplete for direct formalization. This creates a practical repair problem that existing RTL-centric methods do not directly address: the repair loop must align specification intent, verification intent, and RTL behavior before deciding which artifact to change.
  \textsc{FormalFixer} addresses this problem with a multi-stage, intent-aligned repair workflow for Verilog designs with assertions. It preserves the original specification as authoritative ground truth and appends confidence-filtered refinements to clarify implicit constraints. \textsc{FormalFixer} uses both intent mismatch and verifier-generated counterexample cone graphs to guide iterative RTL patching. This workflow explicitly checks specification--assertion--RTL correspondence. Results support intent alignment for FPV-based hardware repair.

papers.title: Critical spectral weights on triangulated disk
papers.abstract: We solve the common-positive-weight support problem at the local spectral threshold 1/2 for relative triangulated disks with interior degrees at most five and an empty or connected degree-five core. We characterize feasibility by a finite decomposition into three elementary pieces and a condition on the original boundary marking. The proof passes from spectral equality to a positive conjugate rectangle, then uses geometric reductions to obtain a serial presentation. The empty-face inequality holds for some common positive weights exactly when such a presentation has only old join endpoints. Whenever this condition holds, our construction yields weights with a positive definite empty-face matrix. Positive Schur responses establish sufficiency, and a uniform face-counting obstruction proves necessity. This gives a finite combinatorial criterion for critical spectral feasibility together with a constructive choice of common weights.

papers.title: Phase factors and optimal seminorms for polynomial averages of commuting transformations
papers.abstract:
For invertible commuting measure-preserving transformations $T_1, \ldots, T_\ell$ on a standard probability space, we study polynomial averages along both integers and primes. We provide a rank-based criterion ensuring that, even when the polynomials are linearly dependent, finite-order phase factors are characteristic factors. For polynomials with integer coefficients and zero constant terms, it suffices that the dimension of the space spanned (over $\mathbb{Q}$) by any nonempty subfamily of $k$ polynomials exceeds $k/2$. These phase factors are generated by polynomial phases associated with positive integer powers of the individual transformations and may be strictly smaller than the corresponding Host-Kra factors of the same order. The required order depends only on the number of polynomials and their maximum degree. A four-term example involving a totally ergodic Heisenberg nilsystem shows that this criterion may fail if the equality $k/2$ is permitted.
  For a family of three polynomials, this criterion is equivalent to the condition that the polynomials are pairwise linearly independent. Consequently, it applies to the family $t, t^2, t^2+t$, where the third polynomial is the sum of the first two. For this specific family, we prove that the optimal orders for the phase factors and the Host-Kra factors are $4, 2, 2$, respectively--a result that holds for both integers and primes. The corresponding optimal seminorms are $U^5(T_1)$, $U^3(T_2)$, and $U^3(T_3)$, which provides an answer to a question posed by Kuca.

papers.title: On cyclic codes generated by cyclotomic polynomials
papers.abstract: Let $n$ be a composite positive integer coprime to $\operatorname{char}(\mathbb{F}_q)$ and let $t = \operatorname{lpf}(n)$ be the least prime factor of $n$. In this paper we study the cyclic codes $\mathcal{C}_{n,t} = \langle Q_n(X)Q_t(X)\rangle$ and $\mathcal{C}_{n,t,1} = \langle Q_n(X)Q_t(X)Q_1(X)\rangle$ over $\mathbb{F}_q$, where $Q_d(X)$ denotes the $d$-th cyclotomic polynomial. These codes extend the families $\mathcal{C}_n = \langle Q_n(X)\rangle$ and $\mathcal{C}_{n,1} = \langle Q_n(X)Q_1(X)\rangle$ recently studied by Bhagat and Sarma. We determine the exact minimum distances of $\mathcal{C}_{n,t}$ and $\mathcal{C}_{n,t,1}$, showing that $d(\mathcal{C}_{n,t,1}) = 2t$ and that $d(\mathcal{C}_{n,t})$ equals $t$ if $t^2 \nmid n$, and $2t$ if $t^2 \mid n$. For the dual codes, we establish $d(\mathcal{C}_{n,t}^\perp) = 2^{\omega(n)}$, handling the case $\omega(n) \le 2$ via the Hartmann--Tzeng bound, and the case $\omega(n) \ge 3$ via a direct-sum decomposition $\mathcal{C}_{n,t}^\perp = \mathcal{C}_n^\perp \oplus \mathcal{V}_t$ and the tensor-product structure of $\mathcal{C}_n^\perp$ over its prime-power components. As applications, we show that all four code families are linear complementary dual (LCD) and locally recoverable (LRC), and we determine their locality parameters, identifying several infinite families that are $r$-optimal or $d$-optimal with respect to the Singleton-type bound for LRC codes.

papers.title: Anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test by $e$-spacings
papers.abstract: To perform an anytime-valid goodness-of-fit test, we propose spacing-based \(e\)-processes that control the type-I error rate under arbitrary stopping rules. Based on the maximum spacing of order statistics, we construct spacing-based \(e\)-processes for nonparametrically testing distribution. The resulting procedures are simple and computationally efficient, and are power-consistent. We call them $e$-spacing tests. This approach is especially powerful in detecting localized discrepancy between the data-generating density and the null density. Under mild conditions, the logarithm of the proposed \(e\)-process is asymptotically equivalent to that of the oracle-optimal \(e\)-process. We further generalize the construction from maximal spacing to maximum spacing set in the form of the \(1/k\) fraction of the largest \(m\)th order spacings, as a measure of the lower-level set of density. It boosts power under more global discrepancy from the null. Furthermore, we propose a greedy predictable scheme, via argmax or softmax rules, to combine multiple $e$-spacing testing strategies. We prove that it optimally tunes the $e$-spacing test. The proposed approach is readily generalizable to multivariate testing via a coordinate-wise Rosenblatt-transform. Simulation studies demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably relative to the considered anytime-valid competitors as well as various types of multiple test-adjusted Kolmogorov--Smirnov tests.

papers.title: Mapping the Design Space of Feature Sampling for Optical Flow
papers.abstract: The computation of correlation features is crucial for optical flow estimation. Existing methods (e.g., RAFT) perform fixed-radius lookups on a cost volume, yielding a set of correlation features for each position; alternatively, WAFT performs single-point feature indexing, yielding one correlation feature vector per position. None of them designs a suitable correlation feature sampling scheme for each position according to regional characteristics. Our insight is that not every position requires the same sampling scheme. Applying an identical sampling scheme to every position is either redundant or insufficient and ignores the specific characteristics of the corresponding region. This paper rethinks the design of feature sampling and investigates the following question: should the support of feature sampling---i.e., the extent and directions over which evidence is aggregated---be learned separately for each query position? To study this question, we propose SAGE (Sampling with Anisotropic Gaussian Expectation). This method replaces single-point sampling with a per-pixel anisotropic Gaussian expectation on a fixed candidate grid centered on the current optical flow estimate. A positive-definite precision matrix controls the scale, anisotropy, and orientation of the sampling support, with single-point sampling included as its limiting case. Consequently, the sampling support becomes an explicit and analyzable design variable and provides a principled way to analyze how directional feature aggregation affects correspondence learning. Extensive experiments show that SAGE, while adding only 1.5% multiply-accumulate operations (MACs), effectively improves zero-shot cross-dataset generalization. When trained only on FlyingChairs and FlyingThings, SAGE reduces the end-point error (EPE) by 24.2% and 16.4% on Sintel clean and final, and reduces KITTI F1-epe and F1-all by 7.2% and 11.6%.

papers.title: When Exact Inference Changes Code Selection: A Decision-Theoretic Analysis of B4
papers.abstract: When generated programs are ranked using generated tests, a more exact posterior computation need not improve the selected program. We characterize this distinction in the published B4 code--test model. Identical execution signatures reduce exact candidate marginalization to N summands and nonempty joint maximum a posteriori (MAP) inference to two weights per group. A prior--budget condition guarantees that B4's whole-group rule already attains MAP; a sharp finite correction bound certifies when candidate marginals must select the same group. All 2,421 default-setting comparisons on 807 development matrices select the same candidates. A prospectively specified validation on 1,345 execution snapshots from a separate public archive also finds no changes in 4,035 default-setting comparisons. Across 80 literature-derived priors, this new archive yields 85 changed top sets in 107,600 comparisons; only six coincide with failure of whole-group MAP. Under finite-test proxy labels, four changes increase and five decrease expected success. These descriptive changes span seven snapshots; per-prior mean differences range from -0.074 to +0.045 percentage points. The results do not recommend a tuned prior or a new performance method. Exact enumeration and independent high-precision checks support the formulas and decision diagnostics. A supplementary fixed-test analysis separates asymptotic failure from observational ambiguity. The contribution is a model-specific account of when an inference intervention can change a software-testing decision, and when its effect must be sought in the priors or evidence instead.

papers.title: Approximating Anisotropic Solar Radiation Pressure
papers.abstract: Solar radiation pressure (SRP) significantly influences satellite dynamics in high-altitude orbits, depending not only on the satellite's trajectory and attitude but also on its surface optical characteristics. Metallic surfaces, such as solar cells with periodic metal bars, exhibit anisotropic reflection that produces an anisotropic SRP. The difficulty in dealing with anisotropic SRP arises because anisotropic SRP does not have a general analytical solution, and accurate computation therefore requires numerical integration. An analytical formulation of anisotropic SRP is useful for stability analysis and controller design for satellites that exploit SRP. To this end, this paper derives an analytical approximation method to calculate the anisotropic SRP modeled with the Ashikhmin-Shirley model. The anisotropy is approximated using multiple spherical Gaussians. Because the product of spherical Gaussians is also a spherical Gaussian, anisotropic reflection can be expressed in an analytically tractable form. The approximation accuracy of the anisotropic SRP is numerically verified for two cases: weak anisotropy and strong anisotropy.

papers.title: Boundary limits of the Bergman kernel and metric on generally decoupled domains of infinite type
papers.abstract: In this paper, we compute the precise nontangential boundary limits of the Bergman kernel on the diagonal and its related invariants on generally decoupled domains in $\mathbb{C}^{n+1}$ ($n\ge1$) at a boundary point of infinite type. Our results extend recent work by Jaiswal for exponentially flat domains.

papers.title: Meaning Reaches Object Choice but Not Completion: Where Is a VLA Vulnerable to Landmark Synonyms?
papers.abstract: VLA policies are fragile to rewording. Success rates alone cannot say whether a policy fails to choose the object or to complete the task, nor where in the policy to intervene. We study the released GR00T N1.7 on two LIBERO-Spatial tasks differing only in the landmark word telling which of two bowls to take. Synonyms absent from the training instructions send the policy to the bowl they name, unlike made-up words, yet complete 67.6% of one task's closed-loop episodes, against the original word's 100%. Before the connector between the vision-language model and the action generator, replacing only the landmark tokens' vectors with the other landmark's (pasting) sends nearly every episode to the other bowl. After the connector, pasting at the landmark, the remaining instruction, or the image tokens alone rarely moves the choice, but any two do. Hiding the landmark tokens from the action generator after the connector still lowers completion for the synonyms that fall short. Finetuning on diversified landmark words repairs that one task's completion for synonyms absent from finetuning; finetuning on the original instructions does not. Training only the connector on the diversified words suffices, as does copying the connector of a policy fully finetuned on them into one finetuned on the original instructions. An open-loop score on starting frames misses that weights outside the connector also carry part of the repair. For now, on this evidence, robustness to rewording should be judged in closed loop, with actions executed, intervening on both sides of the connector, scoring choice and completion separately.

papers.title: Chemotactic aggregation as cue-mediated adaptation toward Nash equilibrium in a spatial patterning game
papers.abstract: Chemotactic cells generate their own chemical gradients to form spatial patterns that support collective functions ranging from cooperative metabolism to immunity. Despite progress in understanding the optimality of chemotaxis in imposed chemical gradients, it remains unclear how close decentralized cell populations can come to maximizing the population-wide benefit of spatial organization through individual movement and local modulation of chemical gradients. We employ mean field game theory to characterize efficient spatial patterns achievable by decentralized populations as Nash equilibria: each agent optimizes its positioning given the spatial density of the other cells, whereas the population density is determined by the positioning of all individuals. We derive coupled dynamics of population movement and cue modulation that drive adaptation toward these equilibria and verify its structural correspondence to established phenomenological models of chemotactic pattern formation. We apply our framework to self-organized aggregation and numerically demonstrate that the dynamics can form multiple equilibrium patterns, some of which are comparable to the population-level optimum under moderate incentives to aggregate. We also show that the relative timescales of cue modulation and movement influence pattern selection and population-level efficiency: slower cue modulation can yield more coherent and efficient equilibrium patterns. Our framework thus highlights fundamental limits on collective optimization in decentralized cell populations, and suggests a functional role for timescales in self-organized coordination through environmental feedback.

papers.title: Kinetic theory of dry granular particles under simple shear: steady flows and relaxation dynamics
papers.abstract: We develop a kinetic theory for dry granular particles under simple shear flow using the Enskog approximation combined with Grad's moment method for moderately dense granular gases with the volume fraction $\varphi\le 0.5$. The collisional moments and stresses are expressed in terms of generalized hypergeometric functions, retaining all orders in the dimensionless shear-rate parameter within the adopted Grad closure. Within this framework, we derive a complete set of equations governing the kinetic stress and the collisional contribution to the stress tensor. The steady-state solutions reproduce the shear viscosity over a broad parameter range and improve the predictions of the kinetic temperature relative to the anisotropic Gaussian theory at the parameter values examined. Temperature still shows appreciable deviations under strongly inelastic conditions. Additionally, the theory captures the overall trends of the normal stress differences, while their quantitative accuracy depends on density and restitution coefficient. We further examine relaxation following an instantaneous reduction in $\varphi$ from $0.35$ to $0.20$ at a restitution coefficient of $0.90$. The theory reproduces the temperature and viscosity relaxation for this protocol.

papers.title: How Well Do Generalist CT Foundation Models Differentiate Liver Tumors?
papers.abstract: Generalist CT foundation models detect many findings with high performance, but their ability to differentiate detected lesions remains largely unevaluated. This retrospective study evaluated two generalist models, RADAR and Merlin, for differentiating liver tumors using a public single-institution multiphase CT dataset (517 cases: hepatocellular carcinoma, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, breast and colorectal cancer liver metastases, and hemangioma). The models were evaluated in a zero-shot setting using their existing outputs and with linear probing, in which only a linear classifier was trained on frozen image features (stratified fivefold cross-validation repeated five times). In the zero-shot setting, RADAR achieved an accuracy of 54.4% (95% CI: 49.9, 58.8) and a $\kappa$ of 0.37 for four-class differentiation at the portal venous phase and predicted 31% (129 of 421) of malignant tumors as hemangioma. With linear probing of four-phase features, its accuracy improved to 79.9% (95% CI: 76.6, 83.4) with a $\kappa$ of 0.72, and 1% (five of 421) of malignant tumors were predicted as hemangioma; Merlin achieved an accuracy of 60.9% (95% CI: 56.9, 65.0). Generalist CT foundation models showed limited zero-shot ability to differentiate liver tumors, which improved substantially with linear probing alone.

papers.title: Charged Schr\"odinger blocks in $1+1$ dimensions from the quartic Casimir and endpoint equations
papers.abstract: We construct charge-two Schr\"odinger conformal blocks in one spatial dimension, independently of any dynamical realization. We consider ordered vacuum four-point functions of fundamental fields of dimension $1/2$, with homogeneous Schr\"odinger equations at the earliest and latest insertions and interactions allowed in the intermediate two-particle interval. For reduced blocks analytic in signed spatial coordinates and even under simultaneous spatial inversion, two functions of the time cross-ratio determine the full spatial dependence: the collinear value and a rescaled mixed spatial derivative. An exact Kummer lift, built from confluent hypergeometric functions, gives this reconstruction. An operator identity reduces the quartic Casimir equation, modulo the endpoint equations, to an equivalent coupled system for this pair. At generic exchanged dimension, OPE conditions select a unique block up to normalization for each primary parity. We obtain collinear ${}_4F_3$ functions and sums of Kummer products, including the shadow branches. The blocks depend on the relative sign of the signed coordinates, distinguishing piecewise linear worldlines with an inflection from those with monotone segment velocities. In the Calogero model, we recover the previously derived bosonic four-point function and obtain its fermionic counterpart, with an independent integral check. At the diffusion-limited fixed point of $A+B\to\emptyset$, two blocks of opposite primary parity give the same collinear unlike-species response. Nonnegativity for all positions and ordered times selects the even family, thereby establishing that the response summed over species contains the even shadow pair with dimensions $\Delta=1,2$. The nonnegativity argument demonstrates a concrete constraint for a Schr\"odinger bootstrap beyond collinear data.

authors.name: Hirohiko Shimada
authors.institution: National Institute of Technology, Tsuyama College

papers.title: Interface Weyl electrons in the kagome-bilayers
papers.abstract: What makes a topological character prominent is whether its characteristic electronic states are located near the Fermi energy. While the kagome-metals possess unique topological characteristics owing to their distinctive electronic band structures, i.e. flat and Dirac bands, the control of Fermi energy to accentuate these characteristics has scarcely been studied in these materials. Here, we propose a new concept for activating the topological characteristics of Weyl electrons specifically near the interface of kagome-bilayers, namely interface Weyl electrons. The kagome-bilayers prepared by a sputtering technique surprisingly exhibit atomically abrupt interfaces thanks to the suppression of interdiffusion for maintaining the crystal symmetry of the hexagonal-type D0$_{19}$ and cubic-type L1$_{2}$ structures. Much higher electrical conductivity of the kagome-bilayers compared to single-layer films indicates the emergent contribution of a highly conductive electronic state at the interfaces. The enhanced electrical conductivity and the exceptionally large anomalous Hall conductivity about 2000 $\Omega$$^{-1}$cm$^{-1}$ in the intrinsic mechanism indicates that the emergent interface electronic states comprise Weyl nodes in the D0$_{19}$ structure identified in our theoretical band calculations, triggered by nontrivial charge transfer. These results demonstrate that topological transport can be engineered at the interface of intermetallic compounds, leading further design principles towards development of device functionality.

authors.institution: Institute for Materials Research, Tohoku University
