papers.title: Explainable and CPU-Efficient Brain Tumor Classification from MRI Using Two-Phase EfficientNetB3 Fine-Tuning
papers.abstract: Brain tumors are among the most lethal neurological disorders, with over 308,000 new diagnoses annually worldwide. Accurate classification of tumor type from Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) scans is critical for treatment planning; however, manual radiological interpretation is time-consuming and prone to inter-observer variability. This paper proposes an automated deep learning pipeline for four-class brain MRI classification (glioma, meningioma, no tumor, and pituitary tumor) using EfficientNetB3 transfer learning with a custom classification head. A two-phase training strategy is adopted: Phase 1 trains the head with a frozen backbone (best validation accuracy: 92.77%), and Phase 2 selectively fine-tunes the top 37 layers at a 100x reduced learning rate (best validation accuracy: 94.91%). On an independent balanced test set of 1,600 MRI images, the system achieves 90.62% overall accuracy and a macro-average AUC of 0.9854. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) is integrated for class-discriminative visual explainability. The proposed system simultaneously addresses three dimensions absent in prior work: high accuracy, CPU-only computational efficiency, and clinical interpretability.

papers.title: Passivity Control for Synchronous Machine Systems using Battery, Field Current and Governor Actuation
papers.abstract: The passivity of synchronous machines enables power system stability to be established from local conditions. A recent state-feedback design enforces robust passivity using battery actuation at the machine terminal bus. This paper extends that design to a model that includes the field winding and the dynamics of a steam turbine and its governor. The extended model provides two additional actuator signals: the exciter input and the governor input. The nonlinear terms in the model depend on speed and field current deviations, and are represented as bounded uncertainties. Robust positive real conditions are derived in terms of a single algebraic Riccati equation. From its solution, a state-feedback controller is designed in closed form. Numerical results show that, unlike the design with battery actuation alone, the proposed controller leads to passivity at all loading levels when the damping is low.

papers.title: Subsequent Dust-Fading Events of the Wolf-Rayet Star WR 59: A Continuous Visual Record
papers.abstract: This paper presents long-term visual and space-based monitoring of the WC9d Wolf-Rayet star WR 59 from 2017 to 2026, documenting a profound physical transition from a stable baseline to an ongoing phase of continuous dust production. Visual observations using a 22-inch telescope initially established a four-year quiescent baseline at magnitude 13.9. Following the historic May 2021 discovery fade to magnitude 15.2, long-term nightly visual monitoring documented an accelerating sequence of twelve distinct fading episodes over subsequent years, characterised by progressively shorter inter-fade recovery intervals. Due to severe pixel crowding and flux contamination from a close 11.7 V companion star 11 arcseconds away, automated large-pixel survey pipelines remain completely blind to these high-amplitude fading events. Direct comparisons with NASA's TESS satellite photometry during quiet phases show that targeted visual magnitude estimates measure systemic baseline micro-variations with professional accuracy while bridging space mission coverage gaps. High-density observation blocks during the minimum floor reveal a highly dynamic, rapid, minute-by-minute bimodal oscillation and sub-minute flickering between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2. At the time of writing, the system remains locked in an unprecedented deep minimum, varying between magnitudes 15.0 and 15.2 for a sustained period exceeding 102 consecutive days. Intensive visual monitoring is ongoing to record the eventual egress recovery profile.

papers.title: A Dual-SOM Learner Model of Instructional Efficiency within Cognitive Load Theory
papers.abstract: This paper presents a novel methodological framework, integrating a dual self-organising map (SOM) neural network architecture with Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), for assessing instructional efficiency within learning environments. By representing curriculum content as a directed acyclic graph of topic dependencies, the proposed model captures collective learning behaviour across two core dimensions: academic performance and subjective/introspective mental effort. During SOM training, representative data sets of successful learner trajectories are compressed into two topologically ordered, identically structured neural networks: PSOM (performance space) and ESOM (mental effort space). By pairing these behavioural maps, the model serves as a decision-support tool that enables instructors to simultaneously pinpoint structural instructional design defects, such as hidden topic prerequisites, and evaluate collective cognitive load profiles. The implementation and performance of the PSOM component (and, by extension, its symmetrical twin, ESOM) is linked to an earlier modelling study employing a SOM with identical structure and encoding semantics situated in the same domain (i.e., a learning environment). This paper combines the study of behavioural phenomena with theoretical work on human cognitive architecture via SOM neurocomputational cognitive behavioural modelling.

papers.title: Response-Relevant Information Is Not Sufficient for Neural Training-State Equivalence
papers.abstract: Response-relevant information is not sufficient evidence that two neural networks are in the same training state. We define training-state equivalence operationally: two checkpoints are equivalent, relative to an intervention family and horizon, if they respond alike when training is perturbed and continues. On fresh runs of a one-layer transformer learning modular addition, response to a weight-decay pulse is highly reproducible relative to between-checkpoint differences (rho_state = 0.934 at 500 steps), establishing the target as measurable. Fifteen descriptors of weight spectra, representation geometry and optimiser geometry carry within-run response-relevant information beyond weight norm and loss on a development dataset, predicting held-out response deviation across seed blocks. But their apparent 16.1% advantage at matching checkpoints by future response does not separate from a conditional placebo preserving each descriptor's fitted dependence on the conventional observables, and a calibrated positive control makes simple insensitivity an unlikely explanation. Information a decoder can extract need not be organised in the pairwise geometry that similarity judgments require.
papers.intro:
Similarity between neural networks asks whether two networks are alike now. A different question is whether they are alike in what they will do next. Two checkpoints on two training runs can agree on loss, on weight norm and on the geometry of their representations, and still be at different points in whatever process determines how training proceeds from there.

That distinction turns on a requirement that is easy to state and easy to conflate with a weaker one. Predicting an attribute from a representation needs a decoder: some function of the representation must recover the attribute. Deciding that two examples are equivalent with respect to that attribute needs something else — the pairwise geometry of the representation must order examples by it. A representation can satisfy the first requirement and fail the second, because the distances that decide which examples are near each other may be dominated by directions carrying nothing about the attribute. This paper is a concrete instance of that gap, in a setting where the attribute is a network’s future behaviour.

Weight-space measures ask whether two parameter vectors are equivalent under the symmetries of the architecture; function- and representation-space measures ask whether two networks compute or encode the same thing. None is a claim about future behaviour, and one line of work argues explicitly that behavioural comparisons cannot substitute for them, being evaluated on whatever slice of input space is at hand (Nissen Gonzalez et al., 2026). A separate literature perturbs networks and reads structure from the response, but uses response to characterise a single network or training trajectory rather than to test whether two independently trained networks are interchangeable.

We take the second question directly, and treat similarity of future intervention response as an operational criterion for training-state equivalence: relative to a class of interventions and a horizon, two checkpoints provide stronger evidence of sharing a state when their reproducible responses are more similar. This is a criterion for evidence, not a formal equivalence relation, and it inherits an operational scope — it says nothing about interventions or horizons at which it was not measured. Training state is not defined here as intervention response itself; reproducible response is used as one operational observable of state. If two checkpoints are claimed to occupy the same state relative to a specified intervention family and horizon, materially different future responses are evidence against that claim, and agreement under one intervention is local evidence, not a universal equivalence relation. Its first requirement is empirical. If the same checkpoint, perturbed identically twice, responds differently by as much as two different checkpoints do, then there is nothing here to identify.

papers.title: Exploring Parkinson's Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Techniques
papers.abstract: In recent years, machine learning (ML) techniques have emerged as promising tools for accurate and timely diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD) which is an incurable neurodegenerative disorder. This study explores the integration of ML algorithms and PD diagnosis, highlighting their potential applications in various aspects of the disease. ML methods such as support vector machines, decision trees, multilayer perceptron, k-nearest neighbours, logistic regression and random forest (with and without particle swarm optimisation) were applied on a PD dataset obtained from Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust containing data from 58 people. In terms of accuracy, the Decision Tree and Logistic Regression performed the best with scores of 72-76% while multilayer perceptron was least effective. All the models were remarkable in classifying positive PD cases with sensitivity scores going up to 97.56%, with SVM classifier at the pinnacle. However, ability to classify healthy controls from PD cases was insignificant throughout the board. Although, all the employed models delivered reasonable results in categorising PD patients in the presented dataset; access to more data, further study and advancement of these ML approaches could lead to enhanced diagnostic outcomes, supplementing to an improved understanding of Parkinson's disease.

papers.title: Octahedrally and Icosahedrally Symmetric Solutions of the N-Vortex Problem on the Sphere
papers.abstract: We investigate the octahedrally and icosahedrally symmetric solutions of the N-vortex problem on the sphere, for N = 24 and N = 60 respectively, in the case of equal vorticities. Exploiting the symmetries arising from rotations and permutations of the vortices, the problem is reduced to the analysis of a one-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian system on the sphere. The original contributions of this article concern the analysis of this reduced system yielding in particular a classification of the equilibrium and collision configurations with the prescribed symmetries. The computational complexity of the analysis is overcome by exploiting the associated discrete symmetries through the invariant theory of reflection groups and Palais' principle of symmetric criticality, and, in some cases, by resorting to numerical approximations.

papers.intro:
The problem of NN-point vortices moving on a sphere is by now a classical topic in fluid dynamics. The foundations were laid by the work of Gromeka [6] in 1885 and by Zermelo’s dissertation [18] in 1902. Later, in 1977, Bogomolov [1] derived the equations of motion. A comprehensive introduction to the subject (reflecting developments up to the 2000s) is presented in Newton’s book [12] and in the references therein. A non-exhaustive list of modern references includes [15, 8, 10, 2, 9, 3, 11, 13, 4].

In this article, we study families of octahedrally and icosahedrally symmetric solutions of the NN-vortex problem on the sphere, in the case of equal vorticities, for N=24N=24 and N=60N=60. The analysis of these families was proposed in the “Future Work” section of [5]. These two values of NN are dictated by the symmetry: a symmetric configuration is the orbit of a single vortex under a finite rotation group K<S​O​(3)K<SO(3), hence consists of |K|\lvert K\rvert vortices, and we take KK to be the chiral octahedral group 𝕆\mathbb{O} (|𝕆|=24\lvert\mathbb{O}\rvert=24) and the chiral icosahedral group 𝕀\mathbb{I} (|𝕀|=60\lvert\mathbb{I}\rvert=60), identified with appropriate representations in S​O​(3)SO(3). Such solutions are characterised by the property that the motion of the entire system can be recovered from the motion of a single vortex through the action of 𝕆\mathbb{O} and 𝕀\mathbb{I}, respectively. In particular, our analysis focuses on the classification of equilibrium and collision configurations with these symmetries.

papers.title: Affine extensions and central compression for product-one-free sequences
papers.abstract: Let $H_s=H_{27}\times C_3^s$, where $H_{27}$ is the nonabelian group of order $27$ and exponent three. We study the elements which can be adjoined to a product-one-free sequence $L$ of length $2s+5$. Let $Q$ be its central subsequence and let $h$ be the dimension of the subgroup generated by $Q$. If $2h-|Q|\le1$, all admissible individual extensions lie in one affine hyperplane of the full additive group coordinates, avoiding the identity. The proof combines coefficient identities with finite, explicitly verified configurations and a transfer valid in every dimension. We also prove an exact central compression theorem: a central zero-sum-free block of length $2h-1$ can be replaced by one term after quotienting by an $(h-1)$-dimensional central subgroup, with a forward implication for product-one-freeness and admissible extensions. For the extraspecial group $E_2$ of order $3^5$ and exponent three, a finite stress obstruction and central compression yield a further uniform restriction: in any product-one-free sequence of length $2r+11$ over $E_2\times C_3^r$, the central subsequence is nonempty and has length at most $2h-2$, where $h$ is its full central rank.

papers.title: Optimal Development Path: An Empirical Evaluation of Tiered Dependency-Aware Sequencing
papers.abstract: The Optimal Development Path (ODP) in D-POAF orders Feature Blocks in a Wave Candidate by choosing the eligible block with the lowest effort-and-risk-to-value ratio (ERS/BVS), while respecting declared prerequisites. We evaluate native ODP (L0) against four dependency-aware strategies: unlock count (L1), unlocked value (L2), multi-hop potential (L3), and one-step rollout (L4), alongside local search, Sidney decomposition, and an exact reference. On held-out synthetic graphs with about one prerequisite per block, L0 attains 0.978 of the surrogate optimum at 12 blocks, versus 0.993 for L2 and 0.994 for L4. At 100 blocks, L0 attains 0.942 and L2 0.983. In contrast, 373 historical Jira sprints from 21 open-source projects in TAWOS, used as scheduling proxies rather than D-POAF Waves, contain sparse recorded dependencies. On these instances, L0 attains 0.998 of the surrogate optimum and is exactly optimal in 69% of sprints. Unlock bonuses calibrated on synthetic graphs do not deliver significant average gains on these sprint-derived instances and can worsen the surrogate. L4 never worsens the declared surrogate relative to L0, but this guarantee does not extend to operational outcomes. Retrospective calendar replays using recorded Jira durations show that surrogate improvements do not reliably improve value-weighted completion. The findings support keeping L0 as the default and presenting rollout and exact references as auditable alternatives. Dependency-valid sequences expose prerequisite readiness, but their effects on interruptions, rework, costs, and delivery times remain unmeasured.
papers.intro:
Prioritizing software work is not only a matter of assigning scores to requirements. Teams must decide which needs merit limited resources, what can be developed in the presence of prerequisites, and how to revise an ordering when the available evidence changes. Value-based software engineering and cost-value analysis established business value and development cost as explicit decision criteria [1, 2]. Subsequent research proposed numerous approaches to requirements prioritization, yet empirical support and applicability vary across settings. A review of 102 studies reported that many proposed techniques had not been evaluated in real-life contexts [3]. More recent reviews document both the range of task-ranking methods and continuing concerns about scale and practical evaluation [4, 5]. An industrial study further found that the criteria influencing prioritization decisions change as requirements move through development [6]. These findings argue against treating any one scoring rule as a universally appropriate development order.

A review of 102 studies reported that many proposed techniques had not been evaluated in real-life contexts [3]. More recent reviews document both the range of task-ranking methods and continuing concerns about scale and practical evaluation [4, 5]. An industrial study further found that the criteria influencing prioritization decisions change as requirements move through development [6]. These findings argue against treating any one scoring rule as a universally appropriate development order.

Two decisions are often discussed together but must be separated analytically. The Next Release Problem addresses selection: which requirements should enter a release under resource and dependency constraints [7, 8]. Once a set has been selected, sequencing asks in which precedence-valid order its constituent items should be considered. Industry-inspired ratios such as Weighted Shortest Job First (WSJF) offer interpretable priorities based on delay cost and size [9, 10], but a ratio alone does not establish an optimal order under general precedence relations. The distinction also matters for evaluation. A ranking may perform well on a score-based criterion without improving completion dates or value realized after release.

The distinction also matters for evaluation. A ranking may perform well on a score-based criterion without improving completion dates or value realized after release.

Operations research provides more demanding comparators than simple priority scores. Smith’s rule characterizes the optimum of total weighted completion time when there are no precedence constraints [11]. General precedence-constrained sequencing is considerably harder [12], and Sidney’s decomposition, followed by later decomposition and approximation work, makes explicit how groups of dependent jobs can alter an otherwise appealing local decision [13, 14, 15]. Rollout methods offer a different route: evaluate a proposed next action through a complete heuristic continuation, under conditions that can guarantee improvement on the declared objective [16]. These results are relevant to software planning, but their classical processing times and weights do not automatically represent organizational risk, elapsed calendar time, or observed business value.

D-POAF supplies the concrete decision context studied here. A Wave is a unit of verifiable progress and a governance container spanning Instruct & Scope, Shape & Align, Execute & Evolve, and Learn & Adapt, with defined scope, delegation limits and proof obligations (PoD, PoV and PoR) [17, 18]. Within a Wave, a candidate set of Feature Blocks and their declared prerequisites is evaluated through a versioned Matrix snapshot. The native Optimal Development Path (ODP) then orders currently eligible blocks by the stored effort-and-risk-to-value ratio, subject to dependency closure and deterministic tie-breaking [19]. This rule is transparent but greedy: it cannot explicitly credit a lower-ranked prerequisite for high-value blocks it unlocks later. Our companion study reported a measurable gap from a specified score-based optimum on synthetic graphs [20]. That result motivates further comparison, not an assumption that a more elaborate algorithm will improve delivery.

TAWOS provides sprint issue sets, effort proxies, links and status records suitable for reconstructing precedence graphs [21, 22]. A Scrum sprint is a timeboxed event, not a D-POAF Wave or a substitute for Wave governance and evidence obligations [23]. In this paper, sprint-derived issues are therefore proxy scheduling items, their reported priorities and story points are proxy inputs, and the evaluation tests the transfer of sequencing behaviour to observed graph structures. Neither those records nor retrospective calendar replays establish that a D-POAF Wave was governed, that a Feature Block’s business value was delivered, or that production costs fell.

We retain native ODP as Level 0 and compare four anticipation strategies with established scheduling baselines. The contributions are: 1. A formal statement of the Wave-pinned ODP implementation contract (closure, eligibility, distance, PVS tie-break, names, stored rounding) and a measurement of its tie-break and rounding effects. 2. A transparent family of unlock-based priorities (L1–L3) and a one-step rollout (L4) whose non-worsening property follows from rollout theory. 3. An exact reference for instances whose Sidney modules fit within a dynamic-programming limit, validated against brute-force dynamic programming on small instances. 4. A synthetic benchmark harmonized with the companion article, with strength parameters selected on training seeds and evaluated on held-out seeds, and exact optima up to 100 blocks. 5. An evaluation on 373 historical Jira sprints from 21 open-source projects, transformed into scheduling proxies rather than treated as D-POAF Waves, with exact optima, retrospective calendar replays and recorded issue-resolution orders. 6. A governed adoption design, in which alternatives are shown as read-only comparisons with their surrogate and calendar evidence, plus a distinct acceptance case from the Blackridge Atlas private beta. This case examines a configured Wave graph, not operational cost or value outcomes.

papers.title: Gram's law for moving targets of the Riemann zeta-function
papers.abstract: We study the solutions of $\zeta(s)=f(s)$ for targets $f$ that grow with $|s|$, and Gram's law for them: the statement that each shifted Gram interval contains exactly one solution. The deviation from Gram's law is an integer phase-slip counter, equal up to rounding to $-\frac{1}{2}S(t;x_c)$, where $S(t;x)=\pi^{-1}\arg\zeta(x+it)$ and $x_c\approx 1/2+\log|f(it)|/\log t$ is a balance abscissa determined by the target. If $|f|\asymp t^{\kappa}$ with $\kappa>\kappa_1=0.5339\ldots$, where $\sum_p\arcsin(p^{-1/2-\kappa_1})=\pi$, and $\arg f$ converges, then every sufficiently high shifted Gram interval contains exactly one solution, which is simple; this localises the fixed points of $\zeta$. The threshold is sharp: for $f=c(-s)^{\kappa}$ with $1/2<\kappa<\kappa_1$, Gram's law fails in $\asymp T$ intervals up to height $T$, and for $0<\kappa\le 1/2$ it fails infinitely often but with density zero. In both ranges the counter has an explicit limiting distribution. For targets growing more slowly than any power, such as $\log(-s)$, the solutions lie on average $(1+o(1))\log|f(iT)|/\log T$ to the left of the critical line. If $\log|f(iT)|/\sqrt{\log\log T}\to\infty$, the proportion of solutions to the right of the line tends to $0$, whereas for fixed targets Selberg conjectured a quarter, and the counting error at the shifted Gram points is asymptotically Gaussian with variance $(8\pi^2)^{-1}\log(\log T/\log|f(iT)|)+O(1)$. For $\log(-s)$ the solutions follow neither $\theta(T)/\pi$ nor the zeros of $\zeta$. All results are unconditional; numerical computations for $\log(-s)$ illustrate how slowly they take effect.

They are as numerous as the zeros, and almost all of them cluster around the critical line [13]. On RH he showed, in unpublished work, that about half of them lie to the left at distance of order log⁡log⁡T/log⁡T\sqrt{\log\log T}/\log T (see [23, 12]).

papers.title: Record Sufficiency: What a Decision Record Must Preserve When an Unsettled Claim Becomes an Operative Status
papers.abstract: Organisations keep evidence, logs and approvals, but often not the step by which an unsettled claim became an operative status, such as an accepted label or a released image, so later readers cannot tell what the status was allowed to mean. We call a decision record sufficient if it is true and a reader who has only the record and the items it cites can explain the status, bound it, re-derive it and challenge it. From these four uses we argue for ten questions a record must answer, map them onto the author's earlier JSON Schema for decision records (DRK v0.1), and define four mechanical checks. We separate conformance, which the checks decide; adequacy, whether the answers are specific enough to use, which needs a reader; fidelity, which no check on the record decides; and merits, which sufficiency does not require. On 164 single-defect variants of three synthetic records, schema validation, the only check DRK v0.1 implements, rejects every variant with a deleted required property and none of the others, and it accepts a record whose claim, rule, scope, limits and challenge route are empty. These are properties of the schema shown on defects we seeded, not estimates of performance on real records. A false record passes every check. The statement-of-reasons schema of the EU Digital Services Act Transparency Database answers 4 of the questions in full, 2 in part and 4 not at all: why the matter was unsettled, what the status depends on, whether it can be re-derived, and how to challenge it. In 25 real statements from 25 platforms, drawn by a seeded rule and coded by a language model and checked by the author, free text addressed any of those four in only 2, and in 18 (24 under a stricter reading adopted during coding) no free text said why the item fell under the rule. No deployment or legal claim is made.
papers.intro:
A dataset item receives an accepted label. An image is released for a campaign. A change in a clinical-trial registry is flagged as material. In each case somebody asserted that a thing should have a status, the matter was not obvious, and a person, a body or a rule settled it. Organisations usually keep the inputs to such decisions (votes, licences, registry versions, logs) and the outcome. They less often keep the step in between: which rule was applied, by whom, to which material, and with what limits. When that step is missing, a later reader cannot tell what the status was allowed to mean, and status words are read too broadly. “Accepted” is read as “true”, “released” as “cleared for any use”, “material” as “misconduct”.

This paper is about the record of that step. A claim is an assertion that something should have a status. A disposition is the status that a competent authority or rule assigns in response.11 1 “Disposition” is used in its legal sense, the outcome by which a matter is disposed of. In records management the same word means the retention, transfer or destruction of records [25]. That sense is not intended. We call a claim unsettled when neither inspection of the object nor the mechanical application of an agreed rule decides it: people disagree, the evidence is incomplete or conflicting, which rule governs or how it applies is a matter of judgment, or the answer depends on a condition that may change. A decision record is the record of one disposition of one unsettled claim.

We ask what such a record must contain, and how much of that can be checked. The answer we propose is record sufficiency: a decision record is sufficient when a reader who has only the record, and the items it cites, can explain why the status was assigned, bound what the status may be relied on for, re-derive the decision, and challenge it; and when what the record says about the decision is true. The term borrows from administrative law, where review is confined to the grounds that were given when the decision was taken [43, 45].

Three bodies of work come close. Reviewability asks what an organisation must keep so that automated decisions can be reviewed, and leaves record formats to future work [11]. Article 17 of the EU Digital Services Act prescribes a statement of reasons for one kind of decision, the restriction of content or accounts by a hosting provider [19]. Work on AI agents published during 2026 proposes schemas for reasoning records and conditions under which claims about agents can be checked against records [7, 49, 6]. Design-rationale notations and architecture decision records keep the issues, options and arguments behind a decision [31, 32, 38], but not the authority, rule, scope, limits and route of challenge that an institutional status needs. None of these states, for an individual disposition in general, what the record must answer and why, and none measures how much of that a schema validator can see. Several of them draw a line between what a record can and cannot establish, and we build on that line.

The paper makes five contributions. 1. A definition of record sufficiency, and ten questions a decision record must answer, argued for from the four uses the record serves (Section 3). 2. A separation of conformance, adequacy, fidelity and merits, which applies to decision records a distinction that law draws for reasons and that recent work draws for agent logs. Only conformance can be decided by generic mechanical checks; adequacy needs a reader, and fidelity needs something outside the record. Sufficiency requires adequacy and fidelity, and not merits (Section 3.3). 3. Four executable checks of conformance over the Disposition Record Kernel (DRK) v0.1, a JSON Schema with domain profiles that the author wrote earlier and onto which the ten questions are mapped (Section 4). 4. An evaluation on synthetic records: a mutation study that illustrates what each check detects, the emptiest record the schema accepts, and two constructed records that mark the limit of every generic check (Section 7). 5. A test of the ten questions on a format designed independently of them: the statement-of-reasons schema of the Digital Services Act Transparency Database, and 25 real statements drawn from the database by a seeded rule (Sections 7.5 and 7.6).

The only real records examined are 25 published statements of reasons, coded once, by a language model whose grades the author checked; there was no independent human coder. The individual fields are not new; Section 2 identifies where each already appears. What the paper adds is the argument from use, the separation, and the measurements.

papers.title: Antidirected paths on five vertices in 5-chromatic digraphs
papers.abstract: We prove that every 5-chromatic digraph containing no copy of the regular tournament on five vertices contains both antidirected paths on five vertices. This answers a question posed by El Sahili in 2004. The proof uses an edge bound for 5-critical graphs to constrain the out-degrees in a counterexample and obtain a contradiction by constructing a proper 4-colouring.
papers.intro:
An oriented path is an orientation of a path; its order is its number of vertices and its length is its number of arcs. A block is a maximal directed subpath, and P⁡(k1,…,kt)P(k_{1},\dots,k_{t}) denotes the oriented path with tt blocks of lengths k1,…,ktk_{1},\dots,k_{t}, starting with a forward block. An antidirected path is an oriented path in which every block has length 11. On five vertices there are two such paths up to isomorphism P⁡(1,1,1,1)P(1,1,1,1) and its converse. A digraph HH is nn-universal if every nn-chromatic digraph contains HH. The Gallai–Hasse–Roy–Vitaver theorem [13, 15, 20, 22] states that the directed path of order nn is nn-universal. Tournaments of order nn are nn-chromatic, and the problem has been completely solved for them. After the work of Grünbaum [14], Rosenfeld [19] and Thomason [21], Havet and Thomassé [16] proved Rosenfeld’s conjecture: every tournament of order n≥8n\geq 8 contains every oriented path of order nn. papers.title: Formal Adequacy Index (based on Polish-language material)
papers.abstract: Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.
papers.intro:
The way in which an text is formulated is linked to the communicative situation in which it is produced. The choice of linguistic means may depend, amongst other things, on the purpose of communication, the genre of the text, the relationship between the speaker and the listener, and the norms prevailing in a given environment. One aspect of this variation is linguistic formality. Although its level can be described on the basis of the text’s characteristics, assessing the appropriateness of the style used requires taking into account the expectations arising from the communicative context. Consequently, a text with a specific level of formality may be appropriate in one situation, whilst in another it may be perceived as too formal or too informal.

The distinction between the formality of a text and the adequacy of its level to a given communicative situation provides the starting point for proposing a distinct measurement approach. In this article, formality adequacy is understood as the degree to which the observed level of formality of a text matches the level expected in a given communicative context. This approach assumes that an assessment of appropriateness requires consideration of two elements: the linguistic properties of the text under analysis and the characteristics of the communicative situation, which shape expectations regarding how that text should be formulated.

papers.title: A System 1 Decision Model for Medical Multiple-Choice Questions Built on Frozen Language Models
papers.abstract: A System 1 model answers a multiple-choice question in a single pass. A frozen language model turns the question and each option into vectors, two small, trained heads place them in a shared space, and the closest option wins. The design has been shown on agent decisions, but we are not aware of a study of how far it goes on exam questions that need medical knowledge, where the right option is often no more similar to the question than the wrong ones. We rebuilt the recipe from scratch for MedMCQA and trained only two projection heads and one temperature on top of frozen Qwen3.5-0.8B, Granite-4.2-3B and Qwen3-8B, using a contrastive loss with in-batch and hard negatives and a mask for repeated answers. With plain last-token vectors, both small encoders answer about one question in three correctly (33.1% and 33.0% on 3,842 held-out questions, where chance is 25.0%). Writing each text inside a one-word-summary prompt and lowering the learning rate of the heads raised this to 41.7% and 42.5% for the two small encoders and to 46.0% +-0.2 (three seeds) for Qwen3-8B. Shuffling the questions against the options returns accuracy to chance, so the heads do use the question. Flan-PaLM and Med-PaLM 2 report 57.6% and 72.3% on MedMCQA under a different protocol, so ours is a cheap, fast baseline and not a competitive system. We also say what our evidence cannot show: validation gains were about 1.7 to 2 times the test gains, and we could not separate the effect of reading several encoder layers from the other changes.

papers.title: Analysis of the Second-Harmonic Generation Process in Nonlinear Metasurfaces Based on Multiple Quantum Wells: The Approach of Nonlinear Current Density, and The Development of Boundary Conditions
papers.abstract:
Using plasmonic metasurfaces integrated with nonlinear materials, such as multiple quantum wells (MQWs), has been an excellent solution to enhance nonlinear light-matter interactions. In this approach, a plasmonic resonator enhances the intensity of the fundamental harmonic within the MQWs region, increasing the strength of the intersubband transitions inside the MQWs. As a result, the efficiency of second harmonic generation (SHG) increases significantly. In this paper, we present a new approach to analyze the SHG process in nonlinear metasurfaces based on MQWs. In this approach, first, we formulate the nonlinear current density within the MQW region, which serves as the radiation source of the second harmonic wave. Notably, the saturation effect in MQWs, that limits the nonlinear response, is accounted for. Second, we address the development of boundary conditions for the second harmonic (SH) field in periodic structures, which ultimately leads us to define periodic boundary conditions for the SH field. Third, we combine these elements into a semi-analytical framework and validate it against previously reported experimental data. Finally, an efficient MQWs structure and plasmonic metasurface are designed for the fundamental wavelength of 8 $\mu$m. After implementing the proposed algorithm, we observe that the designed nonlinear metasurface achieves a significant conversion efficiency of 0.02% under the incident intensity of 23.5 kW/cm$^2$.
  KEYWORDS: Second harmonic generation, metasurface, multiple quantum wells, nonlinear current density, periodic boundary conditions

papers.title: MoE-Context: Show the Model Only What It Needs
papers.abstract: AI agents read their whole history at every step. People do not work like that: we keep what the moment needs and hold the rest as a rough note we can recall. MoE-Context applies this to language models. The context is split into blocks. Before each step a fast yes or no pass decides which blocks the step needs; the rest stay as one-line notes that can be brought back, and nothing is deleted. In the version we build, one model makes this decision and then answers, over a single key-value cache where hidden blocks are masked rather than removed. On a laptop with Qwen3-1.7B and a synthetic lookup task, showing only the needed block raises accuracy from 93 to 119 of 120, and a masked block is as hidden as a deleted one. The model's own picking is the weak part. A supervised linear probe written into spare output rows lifts its accuracy from 80 to 110 of 120, but simple keyword search picks perfectly on this task, and the probe does not transfer to a second task. We report these results openly, along with two cheap usage patterns that block switching enables: undoing a failed attempt and running subagents without a new context.
papers.intro:
You do not load your whole life into your head before making tea. You hold what the task needs; older things stay as a faint memory, and with a little effort the detail comes back. An agent today does the opposite: every message, every reply and every file it has read sits in its context at every step.

MoE-Context treats the context like memory (Figure 1). The context is a set of blocks: a message, a reply, a tool call with its result, a file read. Before each step a fast decide pass asks of every block: is this needed for the next step? Needed blocks are shown in full. The rest are shown as a one-line note, such as “read login.py, 300 lines”. If the model misses something it recalls the block; nothing is deleted. Some blocks, like instructions, are pinned.

papers.title: An asymptotic ball algebra with countably determined spectra and a nonseparable character space
papers.abstract: Let $X=\partial\mathbb B_2\subset\mathbb C^2$ and let $\mathcal R$ be the restrictions to $X$ of functions in the ball algebra $A(\overline{\mathbb B_2})$. The unital uniform Banach algebra \[ \mathcal A=\{(f_n)\in\ell^\infty(\mathbb N,C(X)):\mathrm{dist}_{C(X)}(f_n,\mathcal R)\longrightarrow0\} \] is inverse-closed in $\ell^\infty(\mathbb N,C(X))$. Consequently one countable family of evaluation characters generates the spectrum of every element of $\mathcal A$. Nevertheless $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ contains continuum many pairwise disjoint nonempty open subsets and is therefore nonseparable. This gives a negative answer to a problem posed by Ohrysko, Wojciechowski and Graham.

papers.title: A limit theorem for deviation of ergodic integrals on a class of flows on the two-torus
papers.abstract: We study the fluctuations of ergodic integrals for locally Hamiltonian flows on the two-torus with a single non-degenerate saddle (Arnol'd flows). We sample a flow from a suitably random family, together with a base point $p$ chosen uniformly at random on that flow's domain. For a smooth observable $f$, we show that the centered Birkhoff integral $\int_{0}^t f(\phi_s p)\,ds-t\bar f$, where $\bar f$ is the spatial mean of $f$, normalized by $(\log t)^2$, converges in distribution to the product of two independent random variables. Using special representation of locally Hamiltonian flows, we reduce the problem to studying ergodic sums of functions with logarithmic singularities over circle rotations. Then, we prove a Cauchy limit theorem for such ergodic sums, which is a result of independent interest.

papers.title: Clover-35B-A3B-Preview Technical Report
papers.abstract: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. On internal agent workloads, it reaches a reported generation speed of 680 tokens/s using one NVIDIA GB300 GPU at BF16 precision and batch size one. We organize the evaluation around model quality, drafting and verification costs, and deployment under constrained memory. We also describe a decision-model variant that generates answers to related questions in one denoising pass. On an internal set of 500 groups, joint prediction raises question accuracy from 90.37% to 93.88% and all-correct group accuracy from 65.4% to 77.0%.
papers.intro:
Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a different route to language generation: reconstructing sequences through iterative denoising, with multiple tokens predicted in parallel. This formulation connects flexible generation order with the prospect of efficient inference. Progress in diffusion formulations, model scaling, and decoding has brought DLMs from specialized text-generation settings to increasingly capable general-purpose models. The next step is to translate these advances into strong performance and practical efficiency across demanding applications.

papers.abstract: Given a simplicial set $X$, let $\operatorname{B}({X})$ denote its poset of nondegenerate simplices. We define a natural stratification $\left\vert{X}\right\vert\rightarrow\operatorname{B}({X})$. When $X$ is locally finite, we prove that this stratification is conical. papers.title: A simplicial model for manifold calculus through the configuration category
papers.abstract:
Let $M$ be a closed $d$-dimensional smooth manifold and $X:\Delta^{op}\rightarrow\operatorname{Fin}$ a finite simplicial set whose geometric realization is homeomorphic to $M$. Given the $\infty$-category $\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}_{/M}$ of disks embedded in $M$ and the path components functor $\pi_0:\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}_{/M}\rightarrow\operatorname{Fin}$, we construct a cofinal functor $\Gamma_X:\Delta^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}_{/M}$ such that $X=\pi_0\circ\Gamma_X$.
  This result provides an alternative construction of a simplicial model developed by Boavida de Brito, Lambrechts, Pryor and Songhafouo Tsopm\'en\'e to compute the space-valued presheaf $\operatorname{Emb}(-,M):\mathcal{D}\mathrm{isk}^{op}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}$. We also extend the result to manifolds with a $G$-structure and discuss applications to manifold calculus, factorization homology, and a possible generalization to manifolds with boundary.

papers.title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
papers.abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.
papers.intro:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has made programmatic checks a central training signal for reasoning models [19, 13], and agents are now asked to do science: they are expected to choose informative experiments, take the results into account and commit to a conclusion. For such agents an environment is only useful if its reward measures that skill. The answer must be checked exactly against something the agent cannot look up, the conditions for success must be stated, no policy that skips the reasoning may score well, and the levels must stay hard as models improve.

For such agents an environment is only useful if its reward measures that skill. The answer must be checked exactly against something the agent cannot look up, the conditions for success must be stated, no policy that skips the reasoning may score well, and the levels must stay hard as models improve.

Existing discovery environments cover a wide range of science and have shown how far agents are from autonomous discovery (Table 1). To our knowledge, none of them admits a level only after showing that scripted policies which skip the reasoning stay below a fixed success rate on it, and none shows the agent the complete rule it is judged by: tolerances, partial credit and judge rubrics stay inside the evaluator. Most end each episode with a single answer, and, to our knowledge, none chains several irrevocably committed answers on one hidden system, with later stages depending on earlier ones, so none tests whether an agent can carry its own conclusions through a campaign. And on the easiest levels, frontier models can already approach the ceiling: on NewtonBench, reasoning models reach 70–100% symbolic accuracy in the easiest setting, while in the hardest only two of them exceed 6% [50].

To fill this gap we introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environment families with 178 calibrated difficulty levels (Section 3). Each family hides a truth, publishes its full scoring rule in every observation and verifies a committed answer exactly or within a published tolerance. The families range from classic puzzles that isolate experimental reasoning, such as group testing and the counterfeit-coin problem, to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry. Each level is admitted by a calibration gate: on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle must succeed on at least 0.75 of them, while the strongest plausible non-deductive policy may succeed on at most 0.25 and every gated shortcut on at most 0.35; we call a level that passes the gate calibrated. The gate’s measurements also show what each family tests: with the oracle interpreting the readings, a fixed sequence of every allowed experiment solves 0.98–1.00 of core mechanism-discrimination development instances, where the difficulty lies in the analysis, but only 0.02–0.28 of rule-induction ones, where the experiments must be chosen (Table 15). The 92 levels of the core tier span all 27 families. The 86 rungs of the frontier tier extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder single questions (H1–H3) and with long-horizon campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system (L1–L3). Evaluation instances come from a key that is never distributed, and a hosted service plays them.

Openhagen Worlds was built first as a training ground for smaller models. Its core tier is sized so that models of a few billion parameters find first successes and a learning signal, with the aim of shaping them into specialised scientific reasoners for narrow domains, where a small model trained for one kind of experiment can be cheaper and more reliable than a general one. That a frontier model approaches saturation on this tier is therefore expected: the pilot model solves all 45 of its core instances, and Flash solves 0.93 of the core episodes it finishes, though 0.37 of its episodes end without a legal action because its turns are cut at the per-call token limit. The frontier tier applies the same construction to harder rungs, admitted by the same gate. A pilot with a stronger model at xhigh reasoning effort, below its “max” setting, solves most of that tier, and so does Flash at its maximum reasoning effort, so difficulty has to be a ladder that keeps climbing. Probes on development instances show where it can climb: most longer campaigns admitted by the same gate hold the stronger model, while rungs that only add hidden structure do not (Section 7.1).

We evaluate scripted references, two locally run models built on open-weight Qwen models and a fast frontier model through its API on the withheld instances (Section 6). The core tier separates the local models from the oracle and approaches saturation for frontier models. On its discovery worlds, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 0.58 of its episodes; most of the others end without a legal action because its turns are cut at the per-call token limit, and of the episodes it finishes it solves 0.93. On the frontier tier, Flash solves 0.27–0.49 of its episodes on each of the five rungs H1–H3, L1 and L2, and 0.11 on the eight-stage campaigns (L3), where only a window of recent records stays visible; the oracle solves 0.91–0.94 on every rung. Qwen3.8-27B reaches 0.04–0.16 there. Most failed episodes of both models end on a committed wrong answer rather than on malformed output; for Flash, whose thinking reaches its per-call limit of 16,384 tokens on 27% of frontier decisions, these endings do not separate reasoning errors from the budget, and episodes that end on a turn re-asked after the limit succeed on 0.18, against 0.69 for the others. Its frontier numbers therefore measure reasoning under that budget, and much of the difficulty is a budget effect: on the o=0o=0 frontier instances, one per family and rung, Flash at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call solves 57 of 84, against 32 under the cap and 79 for the oracle (Section 6). A pilot with GPT-6.1 Sol via the Codex CLI’s “ultra” preset (server-reported reasoning effort xhigh), not the API protocol, on one final instance (o=0o=0) per family and rung or level, succeeds on 0.85 of frontier episodes, +0.46+0.46 [+0.36+0.36, +0.57+0.57] above Flash capped at 16,384 tokens per call but +0.17+0.17 [+0.07+0.07, +0.26+0.26] above Flash at its maximum effort, and stays below the oracle, −0.10-0.10 [−0.18-0.18, −0.01-0.01], a gap that a bootstrap over families resolves only on the long-horizon rungs (Appendix D). The headroom that holds is therefore measured against the oracle, not against Flash’s capped rates: Flash at its maximum effort stays below the oracle over all rungs (−0.26-0.26 [−0.36-0.36, −0.18-0.18]), in the eight-stage campaigns the stronger model solves 8 of 14 (oracle 13; −0.36-0.36 [−0.64-0.64, −0.14-0.14]) and Flash at its maximum effort 7 of 14, and development-instance probes find more headroom in the longer campaigns of Section 7.
